text:
Day 32 of writing ancient sales letters by hand to become a skilled copywriter.

I struggle in feeling guilty for not doing more.

But another day is in the books.

I did a good deal today but actually relaxed for once.

If only for a moment.

My hips are thanking me; I could feel my body's inflammation.

I still did some sprints today, and they felt great.

But I also did some laying down on the bed.

Watched the new Black Clover episode and played some Final Fantasy VII with my girlfriend watching me.

Sometimes it’s not a bad thing to breathe.

I genuinely haven’t been wanting to play games.

There is more resistance towards playing than towards leaving it alone at the moment.

Although I found myself struggling with focus.

So, taking my mind away from all that I want to do allows me to recalibrate.

Every morning I wake up having some new and improved way to tackle the tasks in my day.

Even if it’s something small, it still counts.

Because these things add up.

Especially skills that you build.

The only time that you are ever learning is when you are frustrated.

So, I am grateful for it.

I am also grateful for whatever stresses me out, and whatever causes me confusion.

There is a lesson in every moment that we have. 

I do my best to listen and learn over complaining

Momentum is growing, the only time I ever lose it is when I skip ONE day.

Doing less one day is fine.

Making excuses and skipping the entire day is not.

That is why something like this daily post is so important.

My mind must know what is required of me every day, even if some days it is less effort than others.

It makes my average go up in regard to more.

When you keep it going this effect will always be far greater.

I realized something recently about this momentum.

My body has been expecting everything to go wrong when in reality it has been going right.

Breathing has become harder, my stress caused two panic attacks in the middle of the night, and my body has been tense.

It’s almost bracing for impact.

I HAVE to keep going because the impact MUST be me.

I’m bracing for something that I have assumed to be a constant.

It is not a constant, it is an assumption made by my memories and past failures.

So, I will keep going.

I’m building resiliency and capacity.

Here is the second and final iteration of the man in the Hathaway shirt.

Sales letter:

“The Gun from England” advertisement

This was written by David Ogilvy.

Swiped by Mike Schauer.

It ran in 1951.

The product is Hathaway shirts.

Headline:

“The Gun is a $2,000 Purdey from England”

Key takeaways and learnings:

So instead of an eyepatch here they gear for eliciting attention with a gun.

For no reason other than that actually.

The next thing they do is immediately pivot to the topic of the man's shirt.

“(The Shirt: A Sylex. Sea Island Cotton from Hathaway)”

They label this particular type of cotton as “astounding stuff.”

Using the specificity principle to wow the prospect with this material, they declare the fibers to be three times longer than cotton.

They then say, “It is described in the advertisements as...”, this makes it feels almost as if an outside perspective is remarking these facts and not the brand itself.

“Soft as swansdown, lustrous as satin, absorbent as wool, durable as linen.”

Lots of comparisons here that all appeal to the sense of touch.

Drawing extreme attention to the feel of the fabric. 

Wonderful descriptions here.

Then they go into detail on the whereabouts of this particular type of cotton.

Listing exotic places to make the item sound luxuriously sourced.

The next part is a story of where the ingredients go to eventually be made into a shirt.

“This nonesuch among cottons has been to England and back.”

Continuing the journey, Ogilvy writes on the production next.

“Spun with loving care by Thomas Oliver & sons.”

“Woven on the looms of Ashton Brothers”

Taking you along this handcrafted process to increase the perceived value.

“Two of the finest mills in England.”

Everything they provide detail on is highlighting the quality of either the ingredients or the process of production.

All while reading you a tale.

“Notice the extraordinary sheen.”

That sentence is great, as it draws the prospect back to the picture that originally caught their attention.

Indeed, it is a strikingly shiny and vivid shirt.

“You can almost feel its downy softness.”

Once again remarking on the comfort this fantastic cotton provides.

Having you imagine it in your head.

They go into the branded detail in the last paragraph.

“The shirts are superbly tailored, with all the Hathaway hallmarks - long tails, single-needle stitching, big ocean pearl buttons.”

All of the qualities that make their shirts unique.

That will also make you look unique while wearing them.

Attention to detail is something the previous iteration also focused heavily on.

Then they go into their offer.

Not much to be said on that.

THIS TIME IT’S AVAILABLE IN COLORS AND WHITE!

Can you believe it?

Not just focusing on white or colors.

They give you options instead.

Just goes to show the people whom you think take a side.

Only do so in their best interest.

In conclusion:

I may start working with newer copy material.

Swiped has some available, but I am also open to suggestions.

It may be a good idea to connect my learnings with something more modern that has worked within the last 10-20 years.

So that I can see how the patterns and skills have changed.

Or been adapted to the modern world of copywriting.

As well as marketing.

Now…

…for those of you who are copy lovers, new and old...

Or maybe someone who wants to make more persuasive content…

To get more leads, sales, or even views…

I highly recommend two things!

1. Do the same as I, handwrite old sales letters and work on learning just as much as writing.

AND

2. Join @TheCopyTitan Svet Dimitrov's Skool for copywriting.

They are an extremely pleasant bunch, and I see it growing to become much larger in due time.

I really cannot recommend this guy enough.

If you’d like to see all the recorded masterclasses…

…as well as Svets weekly copy breakdowns.

My affiliate link to his wonderful community is in my bio.

Please do take a peek.

Now.

To end in similar fashion.

Please feel free to point out where I'm wrong…

…where I'm Mistaken…

OR

Perhaps even where I'm right.

Although I do learn the most in knowing what I did wrong.

Thank you for reading this!

"…which color, meimei?" your vision goes in and out, wine red walls slowly coming into focus.

when you come to, caleb is holding up a black lingerie set and a maroon lingerie set. the chill air of the manor nips at your skin, nipples pebbled, goosebumps rising. he wiggles the hanger of the two sets.

when you don't reply, he sighs and racks the black set.

"well, i like this one," he says, coming towards you and clasping the maroon bra over your chilled breasts. he guides you to stand, picking up one foot before the other to slide your panties up your legs. lotion squirts on his hands before he covers every inch of your skin in the neutral scent. "such a pity you wake fatigued."

"what?" you croak, vocal chords unused for who knows how long.

caleb doesn't reply, covering the lingerie up in nice, warm clothes.

he guides you out of your bedroom. the halls all look the same, either black wood or this dark red paint. the air smells old, but there's a weird chill in the air despite the many candles and the several fireplaces lit. whispers just barely reach your ears as you follow him to the banquet hall. there, another fire is lit even in this early morning, the entirety of the long dining table filled with breakfast food only you can eat.

"breakfast," caleb says. at the head of the table is a single glass of what looks like red wine. he sits there, placing you to his right. "eat."

"where am i?" you ask, memories fuzzy. the last thing you can just barely remember is going home. "i thought we were going home."

"you asked me that yesterday, too," he chuckles, sipping the wine that looks all too thick to be just wine. "you may leave when you like, you just have to 𝘸𝘢𝘯𝘵."

…

caleb's hand is heavy on your back, a guide, but your stomach doesn't settle.

"the ballroom," he introduces to a grandiose room, three large chandeliers hanging down the middle of the ceilings. though unused, the floors are pristine, candles lit. the whispers in the wall invite you to dance. caleb's hand leaves your back, offered to you instead. "care to dance, my princess?"

you take his hand, mumbling something about not knowing how to dance.

"trust me," he murmurs, breath absent when he whispers in your ear.

step by step, he dances you through the ballroom with an almost effortless familiarity of someone who's done this thousands of times. there's something undeniably romantic about the weight of his hand on your waist, the low candlelight of the chandeliers, and the music that seems to be playing from the empty corner of the room.

the musical instruments are untouched, the grand piano playing alongside the strings seemingly ghostly. he dances you past large mirrors between the windows. when his back is to one, you notice your reflection standing still. you fumble your steps, tripping. you catch a glimpse of the mirror again when caleb catches you, but your reflections are dancing now.

"t-the mirror—" you begin, startled.

"what about it, lovely?" caleb asks, twirling you before resuming the graceful dance across the ballroom.

your eyes flit from his handsome, pale face then back to the mirrors. the further down the room you dance, the more the mirrors seem to reflect something different. the third mirror shows the steps you and caleb take, but with a ballroom teeming with life behind you.

you whip your head back, only to find an empty room that solely yourself and caleb occupy. the whispers in the wall are louder, like the crowd is present but unseen. when you look back at caleb, he's smiling, dancing with his eyes closed like he's unaware of the noise. the whispers echo the noise of a gossiping crowd.

"…there she is…"

"…she has waken…"

"…quiet, don't frighten the girl…"

caleb dips you just as the music comes to an end, but you can't help but flit your eyes over to the mirrors again. your face pales at the sight of the reflections continuing the dance without you.

"do i not lead well?" caleb asks as he sets you back upright.

you hesitate, "our reflections are still dancing."

caleb doesn't bother to glance at the mirrors, leading you out of the ballroom.

"this room has a habit of remembering things that should have been forgotten."

text:
Limbo

The article brought me back to my journey from Kuwait to Riyadh and reminded me how differently it might have ended. From the safety of home, I can call it an adventure. While living it, I knew only that my family was waiting, the flights had stopped, and the way home was uncertain.

I had gone to Kuwait for work. The year before, I had been in Qatar during the attack there. That crisis passed quickly. Those in authority called it a coordinated exchange—a “tit for tat.” I could not judge their explanation; I knew only that the danger passed and our work continued.

But this time felt different.

Yesterday’s escape offered little comfort against today’s fear. A danger once survived is a memory, not a promise.

With flights canceled and hotels filling, we sheltered in place, watching the news while the company arranged our evacuation. There were many people to bring out. The plan took about five days; the uncertainty stretched to nearly a week.

We watched and waited, hoped and hesitated. The news moved swiftly. We did not.

At home, my family worried. While I waited for a way to leave, they waited for me. Each day of delay belonged to them as much as it belonged to me.

Brian initially insisted that we return to the base and finish our work. As further reports revealed the seriousness of the situation, he changed his mind. He has since returned to the Gulf region to complete the assignment. I was grateful that the work could wait—and that we did not have to.

At last, the company hired a limousine bus to take us across the border into Saudi Arabia.

Among our companions were a husband, a wife, and their two little girls. They had moved to Kuwait that very weekend. The husband had come to work as a mechanic on one of the defense systems. Almost before they could begin, he was being sent back to Texas.

They had uprooted their lives, only to turn around. I felt sorrow for their broken plans, but relief that the children were leaving danger behind. Whatever opportunity had brought them there, those little girls deserved room to grow and play, not fear of what might come their way.

The bus journey lasted eight hours. I worried that we might be stopped at the border, exchanging one uncertainty for another. But the crossing went smoothly, and we continued toward Riyadh.

The road was bumpy; beyond the windows lay desert. Every mile carried us farther from our confinement and nearer to home.

At the hotel, relief came at last. Two more nights, and then we would fly out—if our flights held.

There I saw four or five Japanese families checking in with young children, discussing outings and amusement. Someone mentioned the tallest building in Riyadh. I knew nothing of their private worries, but their apparent ease surprised me. With reports of drones and missiles, sightseeing held little appeal.

They spoke of where to go. I thought of how to leave.

On departure morning, a message told me that my flight had moved to an earlier time. I believe it was a British Airways booking operated by American Airlines, but the American Airlines website still showed the original hour.

We went early rather than risk being late. Fortunately, the earlier time was correct.

At the airport, alarms sounded. There was concern about a possible drone threat, though I could not confirm the cause. No instruction came to evacuate, so we stayed inside, listening for guidance that did not come.

My family felt both nearer and farther away. I was close to departure, but still unable to say I was safely on my way.

Our flight was delayed, and conflicting gate information added to the confusion. Eventually, we found the right gate and boarded.

We reached London, then home.

How few words describe the ending; how much waiting lies beneath them.

Looking back, I cannot pretend our safety was assured. Not in the hotel, not at the border, not beneath the alarms at Riyadh. Only afterward could uncertainty become a story with a fortunate end.

The article reminded me of that distinction. We had come through safely, but that did not mean there had been nothing to fear.

I am grateful that we got out. I am grateful that the two little girls and their parents came with us. Above all, I am grateful that I returned to those whose worry had followed me through every mile.

I came home with a story.

But my family had not been waiting for a story.

They had been waiting for me.

text:
India seeks a partner, not bully

By Prabhu Chawla, 

India spent 25 years believing it had moved from America’s waiting room to its drawing room. Trump’s second term is showing New Delhi the door.

Shakespeare warned in Coriolanus that “friends now fast sworn, whose double bosoms seem to wear one heart” can, “on a dissension of a doit, break out to bitterest enmity”. Two centuries later, in 1848, Lord Palmerston told the UK House of Commons that nations have no eternal allies and no perpetual enemies, only eternal interests. India spent a quarter century under an illusionary conviction that it had graduated from America’s waiting room to its drawing room. Tragically, Donald Trump during his second stint is now showing New Delhi the door it came in through.

The latest surgical strike came last week from the White House itself. Speaking to the press, Vice President J D Vance announced that eight companies had been suspended from the US labour department’s PERM programme, the gateway to employer-sponsored green cards. Singling out Microsoft, he declared, “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”

It’s not a coincidence. It had a hidden message because seven of the eight—Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL and Cognizant—were steered by Indians or people of Indian origin, with CapGemini the lone exception.

Indenture is a word that once shipped more than a million Indians to the cane fields of Fiji, Mauritius and the Caribbean, and flinging it at the engineers who write America’s software is a tight slap with a very long memory. The ministry of external affairs was right to call it deeply offensive.

The irony is almost ostentatious. Every evening, Vance returns home to Usha, the daughter of parents of Indian origin, and to his son named Vivek. So, the Vice President who brands Indian professionals as servants need look no further than his own dinner table to see what Indian mobility has in his own country.

The venomous formulations make more sense if these are read alongside the tardy trade calendar. For months, Washington has hammered at the gates of India’s farm and dairy sectors. India has justifiably refused to open them, because nearly half its population survives on agriculture. When a negotiator cannot win at the table, he sometimes kicks it.

If India recounts the administrative atrocities unleashed on Indians during the past two years, a hostile pattern emerges. Indian deportees were flown home in shackles on a military aircraft. The H-1B visa was slapped with a $100,000 fee. Last week, Trump’s government proposed that universities pay $70,000 for every foreign student entering the optional practical training programme. The target was India, America’s largest source of international students. And Trump has armed himself with legal power to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on buyers of Russian oil. Taken alone, each action can pass for domestic housekeeping; but taken together, they look like a siege around India.

Meanwhile, the long awaited trade deal is dead. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman admitted that negotiations have hit a plateau beyond which further give-and-take becomes very difficult. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, too, has conceded that a deal is not imminent.

The arithmetic Washington hates is simple, since India ran a surplus of about $12.3 billion with the US between April and July. Is this hard bargaining in a bully’s coat? Is India being punished for its strategic autonomy and its Russian crude? Or has the Indian techie become a convenient effigy for MAGA’s domestic bonfire?

Now look at another irony. Ambassador Sergio Gor has enjoyed a red-carpet run of India that few envoys get. He became the first US ambassador to visit Srinagar in six years and the first ever to Ladakh, moving freely through sensitive regions and hosting the chiefs of India’s armed forces at his residence. None of this is improper, and his words on J&K pleased New Delhi. But why do the velvet glove in Delhi and the iron fist in Washington belong to the same body? This is coercive, transactional diplomacy, the kind that treats a civilisational partner as a ledger entry to be balanced every quarter.

Henry Kissinger once quipped that it may be dangerous to be America’s enemy, but to be America’s friend is fatal. India dismissed that as cynicism through the nuclear deal, the Obama years, the stadium hugs of Trump’s first term and Biden’s technology pacts. The banyan of that relationship took decades to drop its aerial roots, and it is being hacked at in a single season.

Yet the probing torch must also turn inward. Did New Delhi mistake personal chemistry for institutional commitment, reading hugs and rallies as treaties? Why did we let our students’ futures and our IT earnings hang so heavily on one capital’s mood? And why are our universities still not good enough to keep our best minds at home?

The warning should be stated plainly. If Washington continues with confrontationist course, it should not get a pliant India—but one that hedges its bets with deepening its compact with Europe, keeps Russian energy flowing, explores a cautious thaw with Beijing and concludes that American promises carry an expiry date. The US would lose the one large Asian democracy that could balance China—all over a trade deficit smaller than a quarter’s profits at some of its tech giants.

The solution lies in firmness without hysteria. India should refuse to sign anything under duress and draw non-negotiable public red lines on agriculture and dairy. It should offer targeted bargains that shrink the surplus on its own terms, buying American energy, aircraft and defence equipment tied to co-production and technology transfer.

It should fast-track its agreements with the European Union, Britain, the Gulf and ASEAN so that no single market can hold its exporters hostage. It should treat the visa squeeze as a 1991 moment for higher education and build universities that reverse the brain drain. And it should work the American system itself through individuals who don’t double cross. They should cultivate Congress, governors, universities and the very companies now bleeding from these policies, with the diaspora as a bridge.

Protocol, too, must run both ways. So the way doors open for America’s envoy in Srinagar and Leh should open equally for India’s ambassador in Washington. Or shut the doors on Gor. A friendship that must be renegotiated every quarter is not a friendship but a lease. India has no need to be anyone’s tenant.

New Delhi should tell Washington—courteously, but without blinking—that it seeks a partner and not a bully, and that the window to choose is narrowing faster than the White House seems to realise.

My current strategic assessment: Trump has offered Moscow a substantial economic carrot, but Russia can only fully realize its benefits by agreeing to a ceasefire or ending the war.

Meanwhile, additional pressure is mounting; Carlyle Group's withdrawal from the $22 billion Lukoil asset acquisition and the October 18th deadline for sanctions under the Lindsey Graham Act. Moscow faces immense and immediate pressure. The cost of continuing this war is rising.

An energy ceasefire is the clearest near-term outcome to watch, especially heading into winter. Russia wants relief and export revenue; Ukraine continues striking its energy infrastructure. A reciprocal ceasefire offers Moscow a way to preserve that economic value without ending the entire war.

If sustained Ukrainian strikes are followed by negotiations over energy infrastructure, a reciprocal ceasefire, and expanded Russian economic access, that sequence strongly supports my coercive diplomacy model.

Critics can always move the goalposts afterward: "It would have happened anyway," "Ukraine forced it independently," or "The diesel deal was irrelevant." That's classic post hoc rationalization.

Conversely, if Russia receives the economic benefits without changing its behavior, or Washington actually implements policies that halt Ukrainian strikes without securing a strategic concession, my model requires reassessment.

Public rhetoric is weak evidence. Statements, threats, and political theater are not implemented policy or measurable strategic outcomes. Actual changes in weapons deliveries, intelligence sharing, sanctions, military operations, and diplomatic agreements carry far greater evidentiary weight.

That's the strength of my temporal analytical framework. It establishes observable conditions and outcomes in advance, allowing the evidence to validate or challenge the model rather than retroactively rewriting events to accommodate political prejudices.

text:
The person is at the desk. Deep work is gone

The most expensive mode on a team is not sick leave. Sick leave at least shows. It costs more when an engineer is in Slack, in Jira, and no longer in the task. The body is on shift. The attention is not. That is presenteeism: presence without presence.

It looks polite. The person delivers. Jokes less. Replies at 23:40. Management reads it as "holding up." Often it is compensation: the toil is closed, there is no recovery, and context switching has eaten the morning before the first ticket. Lead time grows not because the code is hard. It grows because attention is gone while velocity is still being held up by two strong people. At that moment the strong are not the culture. They are a buffer the company mistook for resilience.

Gallup's work on burnout hits the same till: burned-out employees are several times more likely to be looking elsewhere, before they ever give notice. Metrics lag because in the first weeks heroism covers the hole. People analytics stays calm. LinkedIn does not. Philosophically, presence without attention is an empty form of work. We are used to trusting form: the green avatar, the "in the office of meaning" status, a comment in the thread. Form can live a long time after the content has left.

The test is simple. If you switch one person off for two weeks and half the team falls over, that is not resilience. That is a single point of failure that still says "ok" at the daily. "Ok" here is not a diagnosis. It is the politeness of a person to whom nobody has given the language for the red zone.

What the classics of our industry saw decades ago

Paul Graham described it in "Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule": a single meeting can blow a whole afternoon, because it breaks the day into two pieces, each too small to do anything hard in. A manager sees a thirty-minute slot. A maker sees a day cut in half.

Gloria Mark, who has studied interrupted work at UC Irvine for years, found that it takes people about 23 minutes to get back to the original task after an interruption. Count the pings in your team's Slack on an ordinary Tuesday and do the multiplication. Then add the news cycle, which does not respect your calendar at all.

DeMarco and Lister called it flow in Peopleware: a state of deep involvement that takes time to enter and can be destroyed by a single phone call. Their point was blunt. You cannot demand flow and schedule its destruction in the same week.

Cal Newport's argument in Deep Work is that the ability to focus without distraction on a cognitively demanding task is becoming rarer at exactly the moment it is becoming more valuable. In a Ukrainian product company that scarcity has a second, heavier source. Attention is not only fragmented by tools. It is occupied by life.

Gerald Weinberg offered a rule of thumb in Quality Software Management: every additional parallel project costs roughly a fifth of a person's capacity in switching alone, and the losses climb fast. A person who is carrying a war in the background is running one more parallel project that nobody has put on the board.

Kent Beck, in Extreme Programming Explained, treated chronic overtime as a symptom of a serious problem on the project, not as a sign of commitment. A reply at 23:40 is not dedication. It is a line in the incident report you have not opened yet.

Gallup's 2018 burnout study put numbers on the exit: employees who feel burned out very often or always were about 2.6 times as likely to be actively seeking a different job, and 63% more likely to take a sick day. The sick day is the visible part. The job search is the bill.

What changes in practice

1. Look for compensation signals, not absence. Fewer jokes, late-night replies, shorter comments in code review, silent dailies, cameras off. These show up weeks before the sick leave.

2. Count deep-work hours the way you count story points. Protect a daily no-meeting block and look at how fragmented your team's calendars actually are.

3. Take load off before the sick leave, not after. When someone strong is on the edge, remove one commitment from them instead of rewarding them with two more.

4. Run the two-week test. If one person's absence stops the team, fix the bus factor now, while it is still an engineering problem and not a human one.

5. Replace "how are you?" with a concrete question: "What can I take off your plate this week?" The first gets "fine." The second gets a real answer.

The philosophy of presence

A company that measures presence will get presence. It will get green statuses, quick replies and neat avatars, and it will be surprised when the substance behind them thins out. Attention cannot be forced; it can only be protected, the way you protect a fragile process from noisy neighbors. The best managers do not ask how to make people more present. They ask what is standing between this person and the task, and they take it away.

If you recognized your own "holding up" people, like this post.

If you have already told compensation from the norm and removed load before the sick leave, tell me which signal fired first.

X (formerly Twitter) functions as a critical global utility for news, communication, and emergency updates. However, under current ownership, it has mutated into a personal bulletin board. Engineered algorithmic overrides artificially boost Elon Musk's personal content onto millions of feeds regardless of user choice, turning a global public sphere into a megaphone for a single individual. Independent journalists, critics, and dissenting voices face sudden bans or algorithmic throttling, highlighting a stark hypocrisy where one individual enjoys total impunity to launch groundless attacks against private citizens while censoring opposition.

3) Orbital Monopolies:
The concentration of power extends far beyond social media into low Earth orbit. With over 12,000 Starlink satellites currently in orbit and plans expanding up to 40,000, SpaceX holds a near-monopoly on global satellite internet. This infrastructure has granted a private citizen unilateral veto power over sovereign military communication.

4)Geopolitical Sabotage.
Unilateral veto power over sovereign military communication:
During the Ukraine-Russia conflict, the capacity to shut down aerial transmission in specific regions altered tactical operations on the ground. The ability of an unvetted corporate executive to manipulate or threaten geopolitical communications introduces a severe national security vulnerability. Furthermore, the rapid proliferation of orbital satellites poses significant environmental risks, including the accumulation of space debris and the potential for a Kessler syndrome scenario.

4)Erasure of Data Privacy:
The casual disregard for institutional norms observed during the Twitter takeover, including the exposure of confidential internal data and user logs, offers a chilling preview of future data architectures. This track record raises serious concerns about Musk's biomedical and AI ventures, notably Neuralink.

5) Neural Frontier:
As brain-computer interfaces advance, the integration of social media infrastructure with neural tracking threatens the core of cognitive liberty. Entrusting intimate neural data, cognitive patterns, and biological indicators to a corporate apparatus that treats user privacy as a discretionary asset risks creating a system of unprecedented biometric exploitation.

6)Boundaries of Real-World Consequence:
While internal platform immunity shields this behavior on X, external institutions continue to enforce limits. Mass advertiser boycotts, multimillion-dollar defamation settlements, SEC compliance penalties, and robust regulatory actions under frameworks such as the European Union's Digital Services Act prove that global governance can and must establish boundaries against absolute corporate autocracy.

text:
Part 7 

Community, as King understands it, requires more than the absence of open hostility. It requires institutions that recognize equal human worth, economic arrangements that provide genuine opportunity, and political structures through which ordinary people can influence decisions affecting their lives. It requires Americans to confront the injuries of the past without treating those injuries as proof that a shared future is impossible. It demands responsibility from government, employers, communities, and individuals alike.

The book’s significance becomes even more powerful when considered alongside the final months of King’s life. In April 1968, less than a year after its publication, he would be assassinated in Memphis, where he had traveled to support striking sanitation workers. Their struggle concerned wages, working conditions, recognition, and human dignity. His presence among them reflected the same conviction that runs throughout Where Do We Go from Here: the struggle for civil rights could not be completed without confronting economic injustice.

King’s final years reveal that he was not content to become a symbol of past victories. He continued challenging institutions, questioning national priorities, and advocating reforms that many Americans considered controversial. His vision demanded more than polite agreement with the principle of equality. It required changes to the conditions under which people lived. That is why the book remains such an important statement of his political and moral philosophy.

The conclusion is not that Black and white Americans have suffered identically, nor that every conflict between them was manufactured by politicians. King recognizes the reality of racial injustice and the responsibility of individuals and institutions that perpetuate it. But he also insists that economic deprivation, political exclusion, and the denial of human dignity cannot be addressed by treating Americans as permanently hostile populations. He believes the country must develop a broader commitment to justice that includes every person while confronting the specific wrongs imposed upon particular communities.

The significance of Where Do We Go from Here: Chaos or Community? lies in King’s insistence that moral ideals must become material realities. Equality must mean access to opportunity. Freedom must include the ability to live with dignity. Political rights must be accompanied by the capacity to participate meaningfully in society. And national unity must be built upon justice rather than upon demands that people remain silent about their suffering.

He does not offer Americans the comfort of believing that their problems can be solved by changing a slogan, electing a particular politician, or condemning one group of people. He asks them to examine the institutions that shape their lives and the responsibilities they owe one another. His vision is difficult because it requires both structural reform and moral transformation. It asks people to confront injustice without surrendering their belief in human community.

Martin Luther King Jr.‘s final book is ultimately an argument that America cannot become a genuine community while tolerating any racial injustice, widespread poverty, and political arrangements that deny ordinary people meaningful opportunity.

He refuses to sacrifice justice for unity, and he refuses to sacrifice the possibility of unity in the pursuit of justice.

That is the choice he leaves with his readers. America can continue allowing inequality, resentment, and violence to deepen its divisions, or it can undertake the difficult work of building a society in which equal human worth is reflected in law, opportunity, and everyday life.

The 65% (Māori/priority groups) vs. over 90% (general/“white”) figures refer to average academic grade thresholds for entry into the University of Otago medical programme (MB ChB), especially via the Health Sciences First Year (HSFY) pathway.⁠Odt

This is stated in a March 2025 Otago Daily Times opinion piece: “Māori and members of other priority groups’ entry to Otago Medical School require 65% average grades. Others need to achieve over 90%.” It notes that first-round offers for non-priority (“general”) applicants in 2024 required over 96%, with the effective threshold still over 90% after accounting for dropouts/waitlist movements.⁠Odt

Official university data (2026 admissions statistics)
From the University of Otago’s published MB ChB Admissions Statistics (April 2026 report):

Minimum average academic scores for offers (HSFY):Māori pathway: ~65.3–65.7% in recent years (e.g., 65.29 in 2026).
General pathway: ~89–93%+ (e.g., 93.14 in 2026; non-waiting-list minima often higher, such as ~95% in some prior years).

Similar patterns hold for other priority/equity pathways (Indigenous Pacific, socioeconomic equity, refugee, rural), with minima typically near the basic eligibility floor of 65%, while general entry is highly competitive.⁠Otago
Offer rates (HSFY, recent years):
Māori: often ~90%+ of applicants (e.g., 66 offers out of 72 applications in 2026 ≈ 92%).
General: ~30–35% (e.g., 118/379 ≈ 31% in 2026).⁠Otago

All applicants must meet basic requirements (including passing papers at ≥50%, overall average ≥65% in the best seven papers, and UCAT thresholds). Priority/equity applicants (Māori, Indigenous Pacific, rural, socioeconomic equity, refugee) who meet the minimum are prioritised in selection. Remaining places go to the competitive general category. “White” is informal shorthand for the general pathway, which is predominantly European/Pākehā students; it is not an official category.⁠Otago
Policy context
This operates under the university’s Te Kauae Parāoa (formerly Mirror on Society) admissions policy for health professional programmes. It aims to increase representation of under-represented groups in the medical workforce. Māori students have reached ~20% of recent incoming medical cohorts (closer to their population share among young adults), up significantly over prior decades, though Māori remain under-represented among practicing doctors (around 4–5%). Studies note gains in ethnic diversity but limited progress on socio-economic diversity.⁠Nzherald

The system has long been debated in New Zealand over equity goals versus academic competitiveness and fairness for high-achieving general-category applicants. Official statistics and the ODT piece are the primary sources matching the query’s figures.

True. Any competition involving real value carries risk, and players should understand that before entering a game.

But Web3 skill-based gaming offers a different model.

You're not playing against a house designed to profit from your losses. You're not competing against an AI pretending to be an opponent. You're challenging another real player, with the outcome determined by the competition.

With Chess Dawgs, players connect their own wallets, and rewards are handled through smart contracts rather than a centralized operator holding their funds.

No house edge. No custodial middleman. A real opponent. A real challenge. Real value at stake.

The value doesn't come from thin air. Players compete over value they put into the game, with transparent rules governing the outcome.

That's the distinction: instead of simply wagering against a casino, you're putting your skill to the test against another person.

Web3 doesn't eliminate risk. It changes the structure of the game — giving players more transparency, control, and ownership over how they compete.

text:
I think $SPCX ’s latest move changes the $ASTS  framework, but not in the simple “SpaceX kills ASTS” way.  My view is still that direct-to-device satellite connectivity is probably the future. I don’t think the real question is whether normal phones will eventually connect directly to satellites. That feels almost inevitable.  The real question is: who captures the economics?  Is it AST SpaceMobile with a purpose-built satellite-to-phone architecture? Is it SpaceX with Starlink, launch cadence, manufacturing scale, and now more spectrum? Or do traditional carriers like AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile still control the customer relationship and turn satellite coverage into an add-on inside existing mobile plans?  That is the actual investment debate.  D2D is not just about emergency texting. The bigger idea is that the world is moving toward always-on connectivity. More phones, cars, wearables, sensors, ships, aircraft, drones, industrial equipment, and eventually AI hardware all want to stay connected.  Wi-Fi and towers cover dense areas well, but there is still a missing layer: rural roads, oceans, mountains, disaster zones, aviation, maritime, and remote industrial sites. If a company can provide that missing layer, it can capture monopoly-like value — not necessarily a legal monopoly, but a scarcity premium because when there is no signal, customers do not have many substitutes.  That is why D2D matters. It could become the last missing coverage layer of the internet.  The technical problem is hard though. A normal phone has a tiny antenna and limited power. It was designed to talk to a tower a few kilometers away, not a satellite hundreds of kilometers above Earth moving at high speed.  

So the key question is not just “can the satellite see the phone?” The real question is whether the satellite can hear the phone clearly enough, with enough signal quality, capacity, handoff reliability, and economics to support real commercial service.  This is where ASTS has had the cleanest technical argument.  Lower-frequency spectrum like 700/800/850 MHz generally has longer wavelengths, better coverage, and better penetration. That matters a lot when the phone uplink is weak. Higher-frequency spectrum can offer more bandwidth, but only if the signal quality is good enough to use it.  More MHz does not automatically mean better service. Bandwidth is the size of the pipe. SNR determines whether the pipe is usable.  ASTS’s pitch is basically: build a huge phased-array satellite that acts like a cell tower in space, use MNO spectrum, and connect directly to normal phones. That architecture is purpose-built around solving the weak-phone-uplink problem.  That is why ASTS bulls care so much about link budget, aperture, beamforming, and low-band partner spectrum.  ASTS has shown important technical proof points: voice, video, data, and high peak speeds to unmodified phones. That matters because it suggests the system can do more than emergency messaging.  But a demo is not the same as scaled commercial proof. ASTS still has to prove repeated Block 2 production, launch cadence, deployment, handoffs, loaded-beam capacity, concurrent users, country approvals, MNO economics, and revenue conversion.  So I would frame ASTS as having strong technical evidence, but not yet full commercial proof.  Now SpaceX changes the debate.  Historically, the simple framing was: ASTS has the better direct-to-phone architecture, while SpaceX has the better launch and manufacturing machine.  That is still mostly true, but SpaceX’s low-band move makes the ASTS story less clean.  

SpaceX moving into 800 MHz low-band spectrum matters because this is not just “more spectrum.” It is better coverage spectrum. It directly attacks one of the cleanest ASTS bull arguments, which was that ASTS had low-band phone-link physics while SpaceX was stuck with less favorable spectrum.  That argument is now weaker. Not gone, but weaker.  SpaceX also has the operational machine: launch, satellite manufacturing, software iteration, constellation operations, and the ability to compress learning cycles faster than almost anyone else.  This is why the ASTS valuation model has to change.  Before, ASTS could be framed as a potential monopoly-like winner in satellite-to-phone broadband. Purpose-built architecture, MNO partnerships, low-band access, and Starlink lacking the same phone-link quality.  That was a very clean story.  But SpaceX is now starting to impact the upstream assumptions in the ASTS valuation model.  By upstream, I mean the assumptions before you even get to revenue and margins:  How scarce is ASTS’s technology?  How strong is its spectrum advantage?  How much pricing power can it have with carriers?  How long can it stay ahead before SpaceX becomes good enough?  Those assumptions feed the terminal value, the multiple, the probability weighting, and the strategic premium investors are willing to pay.  So yes, SpaceX affects the valuation model.  But I don’t think that is necessarily only bad for ASTS.  In some ways, SpaceX entering more aggressively also highlights the strategic value of the entire D2D layer. If SpaceX is willing to buy spectrum, build mobile-optimized satellites, and push Starlink deeper into direct-to-phone, that tells you this is not some small emergency-texting niche.  It validates that D2D is becoming a strategic connectivity layer.  

And if the layer is strategic, then ASTS’s assets may also become more strategically valuable: its architecture, carrier relationships, low-band route, regulatory work, technical learning, and position as one of the few credible broadband D2D paths.  So the framework becomes more nuanced.  ASTS should probably be valued less like a clean monopoly winner and more like a probability-weighted race. But it could still deserve a strategic scarcity premium if investors believe ASTS owns one of the few credible ways to deliver true broadband D2D.  SpaceX reduces the pure monopoly multiple, but may increase the perceived strategic importance of the whole D2D stack.  That is the tension.  ASTS may still be one to two satellite architecture cycles ahead on true high-throughput direct-to-phone link-budget design. But SpaceX is multiple operational cycles ahead on launch, manufacturing, production, software iteration, and constellation operations.  Those are different types of lead.  ASTS may be ahead on the hard phone-link physics. SpaceX may be ahead on the machine that turns good-enough technology into global scale.  This also matters for AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile.  In the ASTS model, D2D is very carrier-friendly. AT&T or Verizon can partner with ASTS, keep the customer relationship, and offer satellite coverage as a premium add-on or coverage extension.  SpaceX is more complicated. If Starlink Mobile becomes a hybrid terrestrial-plus-satellite network layer, then it is not just emergency backup. It could become a new mobile infrastructure layer. That could be complementary in some markets and competitive in others.  For T-Mobile, SpaceX is a partner. For AT&T and Verizon, SpaceX may be both a threat and a strategic question.  Do they partner? Compete? Use ASTS to neutralize SpaceX? Build their own satellite strategy?  

That is why this matters beyond ASTS. It suggests satellite connectivity is moving from emergency coverage to a structural layer in wireless competition.  To be clear, this does not mean SpaceX has already won.  SpaceX still has to prove low-band approval/integration, mobile-optimized satellite deployment, high-speed direct-to-phone performance at scale, indoor performance, loaded-beam capacity, handoffs, interference management, and economics.  Authorization is not deployed capacity. Roadmap is not commercial proof. A speed claim is not the same as real service under load.  So I would not say SpaceX has killed ASTS.  I would say SpaceX has made the ASTS monopoly narrative harder to defend.  ASTS also has a lot to prove. The technical demos are impressive, but the market needs proof of scale: Block 2 production, launches, deployment, concurrent users, handoffs, revenue conversion, and dilution control.  The key variable is time.  If ASTS commercializes quickly, it can prove real economics before SpaceX’s next-gen mobile network is ready. If ASTS slips, SpaceX gets more time to turn its scale machine toward the same market.  That is the risk.  So my conclusion is not “buy ASTS” or “sell ASTS.” My conclusion is that the valuation model should change.  D2D still matters. I think it matters a lot.  But ASTS should not be valued as a guaranteed monopoly D2D winner. It should be valued as a high-quality architecture leader racing against SpaceX’s good-enough scale machine.  The recent selloff may have gone a bit too far if the market is simply pricing “SpaceX kills ASTS.” I don’t think that is the right framing.  The better framing is:  Lower clean-monopoly multiple, but higher validation that the category matters.  More competitive risk, but also more evidence that D2D is strategically valuable.  Less certainty around ASTS’s terminal share, but potentially more strategic value if ASTS remains one of the few credible broadband D2D assets.  

Could be wrong, but that is why I think the ASTS setup is more nuanced than the market reaction. The debate is no longer whether D2D matters. The debate is who captures the economics, how fast they scale, and whether ASTS’s better specialized architecture can beat SpaceX’s execution machine.

text:
Walk into a Japan surplus shop in the Philippines and you’ll find almost anything: wooden cabinets, ceramic plates, bicycles, rice cookers, stuffed toys, and occasionally an expensive-looking piece of furniture selling for a surprisingly low price.

For many Filipinos, visiting these stores has become a treasure hunt. You never know what you’ll find, and that is precisely part of their appeal.

But have you ever wondered why there are so many Japan surplus shops in the Philippines? And why are they called “surplus” when most of their merchandise is actually secondhand?

The answer involves Japan’s consumer culture, disposal regulations, and a Filipino shopping tradition that dates back to World War II.

WHY JAPAN HAS SO MANY USED GOODS

Japan has a well-established market for secondhand goods, supported by household cleanouts, estate sales, office renovations, and consumers replacing old possessions.

Its strict waste segregation and recycling regulations also encourage organized collection and disposal of unwanted household items.

Under Japan’s Home Appliance Recycling Law, consumers generally pay recycling fees when disposing of certain appliances, including televisions, refrigerators, washing machines, and air conditioners.

Rather than discard usable belongings, households can sell or surrender them to secondhand dealers and collection companies.

Some of these goods eventually enter international resale markets, including the Philippines.

Exporters consolidate furniture, kitchenware, electronics, decorations, and other household items into shipping containers purchased by Filipino importers.

WHY FILIPINOS CALL THEM SURPLUS

Interestingly, most products sold in Japan surplus stores are not technically surplus.

In its traditional commercial meaning, surplus refers to excess inventory, unused merchandise, or goods left over after demand has been met.

The term became familiar to Filipinos following World War II, when American military equipment, vehicles, and supplies entered the local resale market.

The country’s iconic jeepney even evolved from surplus American military jeeps.

Over time, the word became associated with affordable imported merchandise.

When secondhand Japanese household goods became increasingly popular in the Philippines during the late 20th century, the term “Japan surplus” became a convenient label for the business.

It also sounded more appealing than simply calling the merchandise used or secondhand.

Today, Japan surplus stores may carry genuine unused excess inventory, but much of their merchandise consists of previously owned belongings.

WHY FILIPINOS LOVE JAPAN SURPLUS

One major attraction is the reputation of Japanese products for durability and craftsmanship.

A solid-wood cabinet, ceramic dinnerware set, or Japanese-made bicycle can appeal to buyers who want quality without paying full retail prices.

The stores also offer unusual merchandise rarely found in conventional Philippine retailers.

Vintage clocks, traditional Japanese ceramics, decorative figurines, and collectible items can sometimes be discovered among ordinary household goods.

Unlike department stores with predictable inventories, surplus shops receive mixed shipments, making every visit different.

However, shoppers should remember that imported secondhand merchandise does not automatically guarantee quality.

Electrical appliances require particular caution because Japan commonly uses 100-volt electricity, compared with the Philippines’ standard 230 volts. Some appliances require an appropriate transformer.

A BUSINESS BUILT ON SECOND CHANCES

Japan surplus shops have become a familiar sight along Philippine highways, neighborhood commercial strips, and provincial shopping districts.

Their popularity reflects a practical consumer habit: Filipinos are often willing to buy previously owned merchandise when the price and quality make sense.

The trade also gives usable household items another life instead of sending them directly to disposal facilities.

Ultimately, the success of Japan surplus shops reveals something interesting about the way Filipinos shop.

What one Japanese household no longer needs may become another Filipino family’s prized possession.

And sometimes, the best bargain isn’t something brand-new. It’s something that has already lived another life.

text:
Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing them https://t.co/6Xo2k2evCN 

Las GPU de Nvidia están en todas partes. Estas son las formas en que las empresas acceden a ellas:
Publicado el sábado 10 de octubre de 2026.7:00 AM EDT

Jordan Novet
@in/jordannovet/

Los laboratorios de IA están gastando decenas de miles de millones de dólares al año en chips Nvidia que ejecutan sus modelos.
La demanda ha llevado al florecimiento de una industria que los hiperescaladores alguna vez tuvieron para sí mismos, incluyendo lucrativos acuerdos únicos y estrategias de luz de activos.
Más de 300 neoclouds ahora alquilan GPU a empresas, según una revisión del investigador SemiAnalysis, un 55% más en menos de 11 meses.

Marc Benioff, director ejecutivo de Salesforce Inc., a la izquierda, y Jensen Huang, director ejecutivo de Nvidia Corp., durante la conferencia Dreamforce de 2026 en San Francisco, California, Estados Unidos, el martes 15 de septiembre de 2026.
David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images
Nvidia
Las GPU son los procesadores más buscados en IA, y tienen tal demanda que las acciones del fabricante de chips subieron a otro récord esta semana, elevando su capitalización de mercado cerca de los 6 billones de dólares.

Los clientes ahora pueden buscar acceso a los chips en las nubes gigantes de Amazon, Microsoft y Google, así como en las llamadas neoclouds como CoreWeave. También pueden ir a varios mercados en línea o incluso comprar el costoso hardware directamente.

Para Nvidia, todo se suma a un crecimiento implacable, ya que la administración prevé US$108.000 millones en ingresos para el trimestre de octubre, lo que marcaría un salto interanual del 89%.

Pero la paradoja de la elección puede ser un dolor de cabeza para las empresas que necesitan poder de computación ayer.

Si bien los proveedores de infraestructura en la nube se han posicionado en la cima de la lista de clientes de Nvidia durante varios años, el negocio se está diversificando. Cinco clientes representaron al menos el 10 % de las cuentas por cobrar de Nvidia en el trimestre de julio, frente a las tres de enero, según una presentación.

La firma de investigación de la industria SemiAnalysis contó con 323 proveedores de GPU de Nvidia en septiembre, frente a 209 menos de 11 meses antes.

Van a ver una nueva cosecha de neonubes realmente emocionantes con cientos de miles de millones de dólares acumulados juntos, dijo el CEO de Nvidia, Jensen Huang, en una conferencia de tecnología de Goldman Sachs en San Francisco el mes pasado.

Aquí hay un resumen de las diversas opciones para acceder a las GPU, y por qué cada una podría tener sentido:

Hiperescaladores
Muchas grandes empresas gastan decenas de millones de dólares al año en una mezcla heterogénea de servicios en la nube de Amazon, Google y Microsoft. Desde el lanzamiento de ChatGPT en 2022, las empresas han recurrido cada vez más a los hiperescaladores de las GPU para que puedan ejecutar cargas de trabajo de IA generativas.

Los principales proveedores de servicios en la nube tienen una ventaja de reputación. Si una empresa de software confía en Amazon y Microsoft para obtener GPU y otras capacidades, no tendrá que entrar en pánico por los posibles clientes que cuestionan a sus proveedores.

Señalización de Microsoft Azure en el piso de la exposición durante la conferencia Nvidia GTC en San José, California, el 18 de marzo de 2026.
David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images
Cuando hablas con empresas, es mejor que tu subprocesador sea Azure, dijo Bindu Reddy, CEO de la empresa asistente de IA Abacus, refiriéndose a la infraestructura en la nube de Microsoft.

En el último año, los principales laboratorios de IA Anthropic y OpenAI se han comprometido a gastar más de US$500.000 millones entre Amazon y Microsoft, que controlaron el 59% del mercado de infraestructura en la nube en 2025, según el investigador de la industria Gartner.

Los hiperescaladores están en una buena posición para mostrar confianza en las empresas debido a sus más de 10 años de capacidades completas, dijo el analista de Gartner Hardeep Singh. Pero los hiperescaladores no siempre tienen tantas GPU como las empresas requieren, dijo.

Andy Jassy, CEO de Amazon, dijo a los analistas en julio que el minorista y pionero de la nube no podrá satisfacer toda la demanda que prevé este año.

Creo que esta dinámica también será cierta en 2027, dijo.

Las neonubes insignias
Si los hiperescaladores fueran adecuados, las neonubes no estarían proliferando.

Modal, una startup que opera sandboxes virtuales donde los agentes de IA trabajan independientemente de los principales entornos de TI, pasó de ejecutarse en los hiperescaladores a inscribirse en las principales neoclouds, y ahora utiliza 25 de ellas, dijo el CEO Erik Bernhardsson.

Se pueden obtener unos cientos de GPU o tal vez mil, pero a nuestra escala, necesitábamos muchas más GPU, dijo.

Los propios hiperescaladores también están persiguiendo las neonubes. Google y Microsoft han comenzado a aprovechar CoreWeave, incluso cuando todos compiten entre sí.

Algunos de los hiperescaladores se han acercado a nosotros para cuidar de los clientes que les preocupan porque no tienen la capacidad de atender a esos clientes cuando lo necesitan, dijo Marc Boroditsky, director de ingresos de Nebius, una neocloud con sede en los Países Bajos con operaciones en Estados Unidos.

Video generation startup Reactor uses GPUs through Nebius and hyperscalers, said CEO Alberto Taiuti. The location of data centers matters, he said, because Reactor wants user-created videos to show up right away. Nebius delivers the specific GPUs Reactor needs, solid customer service and sufficient hardware and software, at a good price, Taiuti said.

Michael Intrator, co-founder and CEO of CoreWeave, speaks during an interview with CNBC on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Feb. 27, 2026.
Brendan McDermid | Reuters
The most visible neoclouds can require some upfront payment, and chips might not come online for months, because providers raise funding based on contracts and set up the data center equipment, Bernhardsson said.

It would be difficult for CoreWeave to turn over 10,000 GPUs to a new customer with one day’s notice, said Chen Goldberg, an executive vice president. CoreWeave’s near-term capacity remains essentially sold out, CEO Mike Intrator said on the company’s August earnings call.

Baby neoclouds
If companies want GPUs immediately, they might have to go beyond the name brands. Some neoclouds aren’t household names because they target specific countries, which can be viable in certain cases.

“Capacity right now is tight, and your relationships with your suppliers is actually one of the most closely guarded secrets for companies like ours,” said Zhen Lu, CEO of Runpod.

Specialist neoclouds can offer more flexibility than the larger GPU clouds, which often require upfront payments and long-term commitments. Some sell so-called bare-metal GPUs, which give customers more control but also require them to manage more of the technical work themselves.

Companies using these smaller neoclouds share the same concerns: When can they get the GPUs, and at what price? Sunny Smith, co-founder and technology chief at Massed Compute, said customers are often willing to commit to capacity when they expect prices to rise.

Bring your own
Oracle
, one of the world’s largest cloud providers, is letting clients bring in their own GPUs. The software maker has more debt than Amazon or Microsoft, and its credit rating is lower so it has less flexibility to go on a GPU spending spree. But it’s happy to operate the technology.

“As we’re generally able to preserve and improve margins in the case of things like bring-your-own-hardware, the ROIC for those types of structures will be even higher,” Oracle CFO Hilary Maxson told analysts on a June earnings call, using the acronym for return on invested capital.

Oracle hasn’t disclosed the names of companies that choose this path. John DiFucci, a Guggenheim Securities analyst who recommends buying Oracle shares, said it would make sense for Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia, the top two producers of GPUs, to bring their own to Oracle.

Super Micro Computer CEO Charles Liang speaks at the Computex conference in Taipei, Taiwan, on June 5, 2024.
Annabelle Chih | Bloomberg | Getty Images
Instead of buying thousands of GPUs, early-stage startups with limited capital can borrow them for hours at a time for less through clouds. And for companies with heavy-duty computing needs, Oracle’s new route might be more attractive than building whole data centers. OpenAI committed to spending over $300 billion with Oracle over five years, but it hasn’t mentioned anything about bringing in GPUs.

OpenAI declined to comment.

The method might make sense for companies that have the capital to purchase AI chips but don’t have enough power, data center space or skilled labor. Like its hyperscaler peers, Oracle works hard to secure all three in healthy quantities.

Tactical deals
Another emerging option is to cut large deals with firms that have truckloads of GPUs for rent.

SpaceX arranged to turn over excess capacity in separate deals with hyperscaler Google and open-source startup Reflection.

SpaceX builds a data center in Southaven, Mississippi, on Aug. 2, 2026.
Brandon Dill | Afp | Getty Images
In April, SpaceX agreed to provide Cursor with GPUs and then bought the AI coding startup outright for $60 billion. And in May, SpaceX landed a deal to rent GPUs to Anthropic for $1.25 billion each month through mid-2029. That’s more than what most startups can afford.

For SpaceX, though, the numbers work out nicely.

“The current economics have translated into a less than one-year payback on our new capital deployments for compute,” Bret Johnsen, the company’s finance chief, told analysts in August.

It’s not only SpaceX. In July CNBC reported that Meta
 was working to form a cloud unit that could sell AI computing power.

Going old school
Meanwhile, companies continue to install GPU-filled servers in on-premises data centers the old-school way as CEOs work to balance capability with cost control.

Revenue nearly doubled in the enterprise and small and medium business parts of hardware maker Lenovo’s
 Infrastructure Solutions Group during the June quarter. “We’re seeing more and more enterprises now starting to say, ‘How do I bring AI into my four walls?’” said Vlad Rozanovich, a senior vice president.

People walk through the hallways at Equinix Data Center in Ashburn, Virginia, on May 9, 2024.
Amanda Andrade-Rhoades | The Washington Post | Getty Images
The hourly spot price for an Nvidia B200 GPU has more than doubled since March, according to data from Ornn, a startup that maintains indexes.

Collaboration software maker Dropbox
 relies on GPUs in its data centers, CEO Ashraf Alkarmi said.

“If we want to do a lot more, I think our supply chain connections will still be beneficial and a structural advantage,” he said.

Everpure
, which sells data center storage hardware and software, has acquired its own GPUs, to run open-weight AI models for the company’s software engineers, said CEO Charlie Giancarlo.

“In a very dynamic pricing environment, it’s always good to have multiple sources that you can go to,” he said.

Parampreet Singh who coordinated drug deals into Canada sentenced in California https://t.co/cIu7KHvg6y via @Indo-Canadian Voice 
SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Parampreet Singh, 60, of Davis, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge John A. Mendez to 10 years in prison and ordered to forfeit $2 million for conspiring to distribute and possess with intent to distribute cocaine, heroin, opium, and ketamine, U.S. Attorney Eric Grant of the Eastern District of California announced this week.

According to court documents, Parampreet Singh, was the leader and organizer of a conspiracy to coordinate drug deals involving cocaine, heroin, opium, and ketamine in Canada. He and co-defendants Ranvir Singh, 43, of Sacramento, Amandeep Multani, 38, of Roseville, and others arranged these transactions from California using encrypted cellphone apps.

Between October 2020 and April 2021, they coordinated sales to undercover officers totaling approximately 10 kilograms of cocaine, 1.5 kilograms of opium, 2 kilograms of ketamine, and multiple samples of heroin, generating $637,600 in Canadian currency and $75,190 in U.S. currency, in deals in Canada and Sacramento.

In addition, between September 2020 and April 2021, Parampreet Singh and his co-defendants repeatedly offered to sell up to 100 kilograms of cocaine, up to 25 kilograms of heroin, up to 100 kilograms of opium, and up to 200 kilograms of ketamine.

The Drug Enforcement Administration conducted the investigation with assistance from Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the York Regional Police in Canada, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and the Placer County Special Investigations Unit. Assistant U.S. Attorney David W. Spencer prosecuted the case.

Parampreet Singh pleaded guilty on September 9, 2025. Multani pleaded guilty on December 13, 2022, and agreed to cooperate fully with the United States. He was sentenced to time served on December 10, 2025, after spending more than four years and eight months in custody.

On October 15, 2025, a jury found Ranvir Singh guilty of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and ketamine and one count of distribution of cocaine. He is scheduled to be sentenced on December 1, 2026. Ranvir Singh faces a maximum statutory penalty of life in prison and a $10 million fine. The actual sentence, however, will be determined at the discretion of the court after consideration of any applicable statutory factors and the Federal Sentencing Guidelines, which take into account a number of variables.

No. Teams can refer doctors but players actually get to choose. As a pacers fan, I remember it being reported that Victor opted for a Miami bases surgeon because Miami is his offseason home. He also opted to rehab in Miami instead of with the Pacers.

I think his choice to be apart from the organization throughout all this was because he wasn't getting what he wanted in terms of a contract extension. Pre-injury, talks were at 4 years 80 million. His previous deal was 4 years 86. So the pacers were seeking a hometown discount. Again, this was pre-injury. 
 
He gets injured, takes off to Miami and talks break down while he rehabs. The next year, as he enters camp, talks resume. The pacers drop a year off the offer and offer 3 for 86. Vic declined seeking something closer to the Max extension which at the time was 4 for 116. 

He has stated in the past (if you can find the interview) that negotiations were different after his return because, as he put it, "The pacers knew my knee wasnt right." 

So its interesting that the Pacers suspected something wasnt right with a surgery performed by Olidipos choice and still offered him 3 at 86. Of course, he declined, sent to Houston and then to Miami where his career fizzled out because of his knee. 

I do wish him well. I wouldn't be upset if he could make it back to indy on a fresh start, if his knee is right.

The Lead
To Student Protestors: 'Our Future Is Your Future'

by Marcia Merry Baker (EIRNS) — Oct. 10, 2026

This past week the Solidarité et Progrès Party in France, part of the international LaRouche movement, released a statement for circulation among the masses of students and others now protesting  on the streets, headlined, “Our Future Is Your Future", posing the  necessity “to fully demand a future for the country.”

This coming  week will see more protests in many international locations, with a  focus in France on Oct. 13 for a nationwide action, and in Argentina for  an Oct. 15 action, instigated by students, and a pending march on Rome  by a farmer-instigated mobilization, which today had a demonstration in  Calabria, in southern Italy.

These actions are all concrete  expressions of rejecting the current conditions of economic breakdown,  and the killing and genocide associated with continuing the paradigm of  geopolitics and might-makes-right.

In Argentina on Oct. 7, some  100 students from four universities staged a non-violent sit-in in  Buenos Aires at the historic palace housing the office of the Minister  of Education, to protest the withholding of funding to the national  university system, perpetrated since October 2025 deliberately and  unlawfully by the Javier Milei government. It’s time to “create a Paris  in Buenos Aires,” was one of the students’ messages, emulating the fight  in France to restore a quality education system. Public universities in  Argentina are tuition-free, and are the backbone of the country’s  higher education system, bolstering science and culture. “France is our  model,” was another sign. The government deployed force, arresting and  evicting the demonstrators, after which students and collaborators have  now set the date of Oct. 15 for a march on the congress. This has been  done four times before, but this time, there is international attention  and support. Scientists, trade unionists, and others will join with  students, teachers, and staff.

In Italy today, a few hundred  farmers, truckers, community business people, fishermen, and others  gathered in the central plaza of the historic town of Cosenza,  protesting both the impossible conditions of high diesel prices,  globalist food imports into Italy, and also the pathetic government  response to the crisis. The farmers and others are offered 15 million  euros to slightly cushion costs of production. Today’s action comes  amidst others throughout the region over nearly two weeks. Organizers  announced their intention now to stage a march on Rome in the near  future.

The common denominator in all these instances, and other  examples that could be cited, is that the economic system itself is  failing, while armament and war are promoted, as in the extreme  situations in West Asia, with the ongoing U.S.-Israeli warfare, and the  Western backing of Ukraine as a proxy against Russia. In the United  States, though no demonstrations have broken out, fierce pressure has  come down on the White House from the impossible diesel and other costs  of production, from truckers, farmers, and those involved in production  and essential services.

Under the logic of appearing to relieve  the cost pressures for Americans before the election, as well as “doing  something about wars,” President Trump yesterday had a  one-and-a-half-hour phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin,  after which Trump announced that Russia agreed to supply the United  States and global markets with some diesel fuel. The amounts happen to  be not significant, but the follow on to the call has had impressive  results.

Today President Trump vociferously announced that  Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky should leave office and make way  for someone who will settle the war. Trump scored Zelensky for bombing  Russian fuel infrastructure in recent months. This came after Zelensky  last night condemned Trump for making a deal with Putin. In addition,  there came the report overnight that Ukraine drone attacks inside Russia  hit the fuel-loading terminal at Novoshakhtinsk refinery in  Rostov-on-Don.

At the same time, yesterday’s Ukraine talks in  Miami were concluded after only one day, not the originally announced  two, ending the discussions among delegations from the United States,  Ukraine, the European Big Three (UK, France, Germany), the EU, and NATO.  No joint announcement was issued, except for U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff  saying talks were “constructive.”

Don’t look for strategic grand  design, or even coherency to all this, maybe with the exception of  President Trump’s signature “make a deal” approach.

Look instead for the opportunity and necessity to inject principles for policies based on promoting economic development and peace, as the  only way to proceed out of war and chaos, to security for all. This is  the answer to the demands of mass actions, and to those gathering and  pressuring for peace.

It is of note that Putin and Trump spoke of  economic projects in their call yesterday. Putin briefed Trump on both  the Ukraine and Iran situations, and also reported to Trump on his own  personal meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in  Turkmenistan this week, at the meeting of the Commonwealth of  Independent States, where Iran was a guest nation. Pezeshkian addressed  the CIS, pointing out the optimum role of Iran to serve both North-South  and East-West economic corridor development, linking together the  continents of Eurasia and Africa.

The International Peace  Coalition is playing an incomparable role as a platform to put forward  the economic fundamentals to peace. text:
😂 MUSK DISCOVERED COMPETITION YESTERDAY AND ECONOMICS TODAY!
“Ambani’s profits will fall, but he won’t go out of business.” Thank you, Captain Obvious! Now apply the same logic to Starlink: competition is welcome, but affordability is not something you can establish with an X post.

Let’s get a few facts straight:
🚀 1. Satellite internet is NOT the same product as cheap mobile data. Jio’s mobile and fibre networks serve a different market from satellite broadband, which is particularly useful in remote areas where terrestrial connectivity is difficult. Comparing them as if every Indian consumer has identical needs is marketing, not economics.
💰 2. “If it’s expensive, nobody will buy it” — what a revolutionary business strategy! Indian consumers already have affordable internet options. Starlink must demonstrate that its price, equipment costs and performance justify the premium. Customers don’t owe Elon Musk their wallets just because he launched rockets into space.
📉 3. Cheap internet in India didn’t fall from the sky. Jio’s aggressive pricing helped transform the mobile-data market. You can debate market concentration, but dismissing affordability as merely Ambani’s “amazing low prices” conveniently ignores the value Indian consumers already receive.
🤡 4. Calling critics “internet shills” is not a substitute for evidence. Someone can support competition while questioning Starlink’s pricing, spectrum policy, security requirements or commercial viability. That is not hypocrisy; it is called having more than one brain cell.
⚖️ 5. And the monopoly allegation needs evidence, not billionaire-level sarcasm. India’s government has stated that Starlink, Jio Satellite Communications and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb are at broadly similar stages of regulatory clearance. Starlink’s entry involves spectrum allocation and security requirements, not simply Musk demanding a market and expecting the doors to open.
🎯 The real test is simple: Can Starlink offer Indian consumers a compelling service at a competitive price, comply with Indian regulations and expand connectivity where existing networks struggle?

If yes, let it compete. If not, no amount of billionaire tantrums on X will change the economics.
India is not a charity project for Ambani, and it is not a guaranteed customer base for Musk. Neither billionaire deserves special treatment. Let the services compete, let the regulators do their jobs, and let Indian consumers decide.
🇮🇳 We need affordable internet, genuine competition and a level playing field—not a billionaire ego battle marketed as a revolution for the common man.
