text:
The Unspoken Wound

Morning sunlight should be the opening notes of hope. But when I was ten, an ordinary walk to school was permanently rewritten by a scream that tore through the sky. The sound hit my ears like a blunt object. Then an elderly woman with graying hair, her face wild with the terror of someone about to die, came running toward me. Behind her was an old man gripping a weapon, like a shadow coming to collect a life. Time froze. There was no time to think, not even time to be afraid. The cold flash of a knife cut through the morning mist and went into her neck. She fell right at my feet, like a sack of grain suddenly dropped. Her wide-open eyes locked onto me, empty. Warm, dark red blood, thick and metallic-sweet with a life draining away, spread silently and greedily licked at the tips of my shoes. I stepped back without thinking—one step, two—my mind blank except for those eyes and that spreading, glaring red.

A crowd gathered without my noticing, their murmuring buzzing as if through thick glass. I—a ten-year-old child—somehow “calmly” walked around the still-warm body as if it were a puddle in my way, and went straight through the school gate. No crying. No shaking. As if the violence I had just witnessed were a silent film that had already ended. What was taught in class that day? I don’t remember. I only remember that when school let out, the gate was back to its usual noise, and the ground was so clean it seemed nothing had ever happened. So my mind carefully folded it, flattened it, and shoved it into the darkest corner of memory, labeled “Nothing happened.”

But the body remembered. The soul remembered.

As an adult, I discovered I had an almost pathological fear of killing anything. If I accidentally stepped on a bug, my fingertips would go numb. Roadkill on the highway would make my whole body go numb as if I’d been shocked. Even just watching blood—bright red—flow from a needle during a blood draw would send a strange chill up my spine. The fear was irrational, illogical, and yet it controlled my senses so completely. I used to blame it on being “too sensitive” or “too soft,” trying to reason it away or suppress it. Then recently, the phrase “psychological trauma” turned like a rusty key in a door that had been sealed for years. Behind it was that blood-soaked morning, those eyes that died without closing, that thick dark red that seemed ready to swallow me whole.

So that was it. A wound deep in my soul, never healed, was inflamed and growling.

That ten-year-old girl’s “calm” wasn’t bravery. It was an emergency freeze response—a survival mechanism a young mind activates when faced with extreme terror. It’s called dissociation. The enormous fear, helplessness, and shock couldn’t be understood or digested at the time, so they were stripped of emotion, packed away, and sealed off. They didn’t disappear. Like cursed amber, they hardened deep in time and became the “out of place” physical reactions and dreams I had as an adult. (In my twenties, the old woman’s eyes still broke into my nightmares now and then.) The cruelest thing about psychological trauma is how hidden it is. It isn’t as visible as a broken bone. It disguises itself: as unexplained anxiety, strange physical symptoms, excessive avoidance of certain things, sudden emotional meltdowns, or—like in my case—an intense, irrational physical disgust toward certain scenes. People live with these “symptoms” all the time, with no idea where they come from, assuming they’re just “flawed,” “bad at handling stress,” or “just tired and in a bad mood lately.”

Wake up. A bad mood is a cloud passing through the sky; it will drift away. Psychological trauma is a fault line deep in the earth. It is silent, but it keeps shaping the landscape above and changing the direction of the river of your life. It will not heal on its own just because time passes. Memories and feelings that are forcibly suppressed will look for an exit in more twisted, more destructive ways. Ignoring trauma is the same as letting it ferment and rot in the dark, which can eventually lead to a deeper swamp: chronic depression, anxiety disorders, even a warping of the personality.

So how do we face a wound buried this deep—before it finally swallows the light?

First, see it and admit it. Like me, bravely trace the irrational fear and reactions back to their source. Recognize it. Name it: “This is a trauma response. It is not who I am. It is not weakness.” Admitting it exists is the first step toward healing—and the one that takes the most courage.

Second, understand and accept. Understand that the child who went “numb” and “calm” at the scene wasn’t cold or heartless. It was the instinctive reaction of someone small and helpless. Accept every feeling that came from it—fear, anger, grief, helplessness, even the shame of thinking you “weren’t brave enough” back then. Tell yourself: “This was not my fault. In that situation, I did everything I could.”

Third, seek safety and connection. Building a sense of safety in the present is essential. Identify the scenes that tend to trigger traumatic memories—bloody images, sudden screams—and prepare “anchors” for yourself in advance: deep breathing, focusing on the feeling of your feet on the ground, holding a small object that comforts you, telling yourself, “I am safe right now.” Carefully but firmly look for people you can trust to talk to—friends, family, or a professional support group—so the suppressed pain can be released inside a safe container. You don’t have to carry this heavy secret alone.

Finally, learn to make peace with your body. Traumatic memories don’t live only in the brain; they are imprinted in the body. Learn mindful breathing, body scans, and gentle movement—yoga, walking—to help your body relax out of its long-term “alert” state and rebuild the mind-body connection. When fear comes, try to soothe yourself gently, the way you would comfort a frightened child.

But I have to be honest: for trauma buried for years and affecting so much of your life—especially something like witnessing extreme violence as a child—professional psychological help, such as trauma-focused therapy or EMDR, is an irreplaceable bridge. It offers a safe harbor, professional guidance, and effective tools to help us safely approach, process, and integrate those frozen painful memories, finally completing the “digestion” that never happened back then. Seeking professional help is not weakness. It is the deepest form of responsibility and care you can give yourself.

That blood-colored morning splashed an indelible shadow across the canvas of my life. It made me carry a nameless fear in ignorance, and it took years before I realized the wound was there. But now, as I look at that wound, I no longer feel only fear. I see it. I admit it. And in doing so, I have taken back part of the territory it once occupied. It reminds me how fragile life is, and it also reveals how stubbornly life seeks to heal after being broken.

If there is unexplained pain, fear, or avoidance hidden in your heart, don’t just dismiss it as “a bad mood” or “just my personality.” It may be the unheard crying deep inside you, or a sealed-off trauma knocking at the door. Seeing it is the moment light begins to enter the darkness. Admitting it is the beginning of putting down the weight. Seeking understanding and help is a brave declaration that you are walking toward real freedom. Trauma may have shaped part of us, but it has no right to define all of us. The wounds that were never spoken will, through being seen and healed, turn from chains that imprison us into a source of strength—a deeper understanding of life’s hidden places, and a tougher, more resilient way forward. Don’t let your past, in silence, murder your present and your future. Face it bravely. Heal it gently. You deserve a life that is whole and peaceful, no longer shadowed by invisible darkness.

Land.

Minerals.

Sovereignty.

People.
Planet.
Peace.
Progress.

Stand for a better tomorrow.
Or continue performing resistance inside a system that has already priced your performance.
We are Anonymous.

     And here is a portion of Chapter 20. As you will see, conspiracy is how the enemy wages war:

CHAPTER 20

CONSPIRACY IN SCRIPTURE

THE DARK ART OF CONSPIRACY

A conspiracy takes place when two or more people plot to commit an illegal act and, according to the Bible, conspiracy is the modus operandi of the evil one. Since many of the Bible’s conspiracies involve plotting to murder someone, the conspirators often operate in the shadows to avoid being caught. They also work under the cover of darkness because the children of the evil one hate the light:

For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed (Jn 3:20, italics added).

Paul warned the Corinthian church: “For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Cor 11:13-14, italics added).
      Darkness, disguises, deception, death… we find all these elements in the enemy’s conspiratorial war against the saints. We will now examine some of the conspiracies found in the Old Testament.

OLD TESTAMENT CONSPIRACIES

THE CONSPIRACY AGAINST JOSEPH

Joseph’s brothers entered a conspiracy against him. We read: “So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan. They saw him from afar, and before he came near to them they conspired against him to kill him” (Gen 37:17-18, italics added).
      Unlike many of the conspirators we will study, Joseph’s brothers were not children of the evil one. They would become the heads of eleven of Israel’s twelve tribes. But when they conspired to murder their brother, they were influenced by Satan. We see Satan’sinfluence in the life of King David. David was a man after God’s heart, and yet we read of him, “Then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel” (1 Ch 21:1).
       Every child of God can be influenced by Satan, but this is not the same thing as belonging to him. To protect ourselves from this evil influence, Jesus taught us to pray: “And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.” 
     [Footnote: The New International Version (Mt 6:13). (2011). Zondervan. As The ESV Study Bible notes, “The phrase translated ‘evil’ (Gk tou ponērou) can mean either ‘evil’ or ‘the evil one,’ namely, Satan.” p. 1832. The ESV translates tou ponērou in Mt 6:13 as “deliver us from evil.” But this same word appears in Jn 17:15, quoted next, and the ESV translates it as “keep them from the evil one.” The X platform does not allow footnotes.]  
     Jesus also prayed the following prayer for our protection: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one” (Jn 17:15).
      Instead of killing Joseph, as they originally had planned, his brothers sold him into slavery. Then, by the providence of God, this treacherous act was turned into a good outcome for Joseph and many others. Joseph said to his brothers, “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today” (Gen 50:20).
     God’s sovereign will cannot be thwarted by the conspiracies of evildoers. His plan advances irresistibly toward its fulfillment.

THE CONSPIRACY AGAINST KING DAVID

Absalom masterminded a conspiracy against his father, King David. We read, “And while Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor, from his city Giloh. And the conspiracy grew strong, and the people with Absalom kept increasing” (2 Sam 15:12, italics added).
A king often suffers from palace intrigues and David’s Psalms frequently refer to conspiracies against him:

For I hear the whispering of many—
terror on every side!—
as they scheme together against me,
as they plot to take my life (Ps 31:13).

People plotting to commit murder are conspirators. After writing the sobering words, “as they plot to take my life,” David revealed how he took courage while his life was being threatened. He affirmed his belief in a sovereign God:

But I trust in you, O Lord;
I say, “You are my God.”
My times are in your hand;
rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from my persecutors! (Ps 31:14-15).

I used part of the above quote in the dedication of this book. During these times of testing, we need to believe that our good times, our bad times, all our times are in the hands of a God who “has made everything beautiful in its time” (Ec 3:11). Random chance cannot make “everything beautiful in its time.” Only a sovereign God can. And because our times are in God’s hands, and He loves us, we can stand with courage and testify that Jesus is Lord. For we are subject to His sovereign will and not the vagaries of chance.
      The enemy’s weapon of choice against the people of God is conspiracy. Many Psalms support this assertion. They abound with conspiracies. For example:

Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked,
from the throng of evildoers…
who aim bitter words like arrows,
shooting from ambush at the blameless,
shooting at him suddenly and without fear.
They hold fast to their evil purpose;
they talk of laying snares secretly,
thinking, “Who can see them?” (Ps 64:2-5, italics added).

They plan in secret, and launch their attacks from hidden places, ambushing “the blameless.” This calls to mind the words from Voltaire’s letter, “for the monster must fall pierced by a hundred invisible hands; yes, let it fall beneath a thousand repeated blows.” Clearly, Voltaire hated the light.

EZEKIEL AND THE CONSPIRACY OF PROPHETS

Through the prophet Ezekiel, the Lord speaks of a conspiracy against His people led by religious leaders, including prophets and priests:

And the word of the Lord came to me: “Son of man, say to her, You are a land that is not cleansed or rained upon in the day of indignation. The conspiracy of her prophets in her midst is like a roaring lion tearing the prey; they have devoured human lives; they have taken treasure and precious things; they have made many widows in her midst. Her priests have done violence to my law and have profaned my holy things” (Ez 22:23-26, italics added).

The above verse reminds me of Peter’s description of the devil, “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet 5:8, italics added). Not only does Satan look for prey to devour, so does the conspiracy of false prophets, who are also likened to “a roaring lion.” And like Satan, this conspiracy despises God’s law, loves to treat His holy things with blasphemous contempt, and serves the god of this world, money, by stealing the treasure of others. It is also murderous: “they have devoured human lives,” turning married women into widows.

ZECHARIAH IS SLAIN BY A CONSPIRACY

Jesus mentions the slaying of Zechariah who was “murdered between the sanctuary and the altar” (Mt 23:35), and his murder was the result of a conspiracy:

Then the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you break the commandments of the Lord, so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the Lord, he has forsaken you.’ ” But they conspired against him, and by command of the king they stoned him with stones in the court of the house of the Lord (2 Ch 24:20-21, italics added).

A few verses later another conspiracy was launched to kill the king, and it succeeded. Then, when the dead king’s son acceded to the throne, he murdered the conspirators who killed his father. Such is the sad spiral of violence that can come from conspiratorial activity. Like the serpent ouroboros, it is self-devouring.

NEHEMIAH AGAINST THE CONSPIRATORS

Almost a century after the Jews were liberated from Babylon by King Cyrus of Persia, we arrive at Nehemiah’s story. He was a Jew of high rank, living in the kingdom of Persia. After he received word from Jewish countrymen about Jerusalem still being in a state of ruin, Nehemiah began to feel a heavy burden for his people. After praying to God, he received the blessing of Artaxerxes, the King of Persia, to return to Jerusalem and lead the Jews in the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s walls. But the enemies of God’s people conspired against him:

But when Sanballat and Tobiah and the Arabs and the Ammonites and the Ashdodites heard that the repairing of the walls of Jerusalem was going forward and that the breaches were beginning to be closed, they were very angry. And they all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to cause confusion in it. …And our enemies said, “They will not know or see till we come among them and kill them and stop the work” (Neh 4:7-8, 11, italics added).

To paraphrase Voltaire, “for the Jews must fall pierced by a hundred invisible hands.” Or in the words of the conspirators, “They will not know or see till we come among them and kill them.” Plotting to ambush the unsuspecting, and commit murder, is the definition of a conspiracy.
     In Nehemiah, chapter six, there are two more conspiracies. I will cover the second one:

Now when I [Nehemiah—my note] went into the house of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his home, he said, “Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple. Let us close the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you. They are coming to kill you by night.” … And I understood and saw that God had not sent him, but he had pronounced the prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. For this purpose he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin, and so they could give me a bad name in order to taunt me (Neh 6:10, 12-13).

This conspiracy involved an enemy disguising himself as a friend to deceive Nehemiah into acting in a cowardly, disreputable way. And “Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.”

THE CONSPIRACY AGAINST THE JEWISH PEOPLE

One of the best-known conspiracies in Scripture was the plot of Haman to kill all the Jews in Persia. When Mordecai discovered this conspiracy, he went to Esther, whom he had raised from childhood. She was a beautiful Jewess chosen by the king to be his queen. Mordecai presented evidence of this plot to Esther and asked her to use her influence on the king to prevent it.
      Mordecai was the focus of Haman’s fiercest hatred. Haman built a scaffold some fifty cubits high—about 75 feet high—near his home for the express purpose of hanging Mordecai. But before this could take place Esther prepared two feasts. She invited the king and Haman to these feasts and no one else. After the second feast the king again offered to grant Esther any wish she might have, even up to half of his kingdom. Esther then turned the tables on Haman. She said:

“If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request. For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated. If we had been sold merely as slaves, men and women, I would have been silent, for our affliction is not to be compared with the loss to the king.”
      Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, “Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?”
      And Esther said, “A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman!”
     Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen (Es 7:3-6).

Haman was the highest-ranking official reporting to the king. So, the conspiracy to kill God’s chosen, taking place at the highest levels of government, was revealed and Haman was hanged from his own gallows. This is a parable of our times. The governments of many nations have been penetrated by evil men and women who intend to harm the children of God.

DANIEL: CONSPIRACY LEADS TO THE LION’S DEN

The prophet Daniel was the victim of a conspiracy. He was the most-favored high official in the land, and his standing before the king excited envy. So, the other high officials and satraps entered a conspiracy against Daniel.
     Daniel’s enemies got the king to issue a mandate requiring everyone to pray to the king for one month. If you prayed to anyone else, then you would be tossed into the lion’s den. The conspirators knew that Daniel would only pray to the God of Israel. Then, when they caught him doing so, they achieved the goal of their conspiracy. They reported Daniel’s violation of the king’s edict to the king and Daniel was tossed into the lion’s den. This conspiracy is a prefiguration of the beast’s plan to murder the saints. You will either worship the king—i.e., the beast—or be killed.
      After Daniel emerged from the lion’s den without a scratch the conspirators were tossed into the lion’s den, and their bones were broken by the jaws of hungry lions. It is a variation of what happened to Haman. Haman prepared the noose for Mordecai’s neck only to be hung with it. In the words of Shakespeare, he was “hoist with his own petard,” or blown into the air by his own bomb.

NEW TESTAMENT CONSPIRACIES

JESUS AND THE RELIGIOUS AUTHORITIES

We see a conspiracy forming against Jesus very early in His ministry. After Jesus healed a man’s withered hand on the Sabbath, we read:

The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him (Mk 3:6).

Note who is entering this conspiracy to kill Jesus. The legalistic and self-righteous Pharisees, and the Herodians, or the supporters of the Herodian dynasty, who were worldly and not religious. These two groups could not have been more different. Yet evil men will overlook their differences when it comes to destroying God’s people or, in this instance, the Son of God.

As Nehemiah experienced, Jesus was faced with conspirators who disguised their true intentions:

The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour … but they feared the people. So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said … (Lk 20:19-20, italics added).

As Jesus’ ministry on earth approached its end, the conspiracy to kill Him gained momentum:

Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas, and plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him (Mt 26:3-4, italics added).

The conspirators had to contend with the popularity of Jesus. So, they planned to conduct their operation at night, using the “stealth” provided by the cover of darkness.
     An active member of this conspiracy was one of the twelve, the “apostle” Judas Iscariot. He was a servant of Satan, and his relationship with Satan seems to have gone from being influenced by him to being possessed by him:

Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve. He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd (Lk 22:3-6, italics added).

After Judas served his purpose by betraying Jesus, Satan abandoned him and he committed suicide. Every servant of Satan can look forward to a similar fate. They live their lives staring into the abyss, and they will eventually be swallowed by it, entering the fellowship of hell.

CONSPIRACIES TARGET THE APOSTLE PAUL

Finally, there were several conspiracies to kill the Apostle Paul (called “Saul” in the verse below; his name was changed to “Paul” after his conversion). One of them began shortly after his salvation:

When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him, but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket (Ac 9:23-25, italics added).

Another plot to kill Paul appears toward the end of the Book of Acts:

When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. There were more than forty who made this conspiracy (Ac 23:12-13, italics added).

As you can see, according to Scripture, conspiracy is the favored war strategy of the children of the wicked one. Which prompts the question: “If throughout the Bible the children of the evil one launch conspiracies against the children of God, then why would we expect it to be different today?”
     Therefore, as the war between the fourth kingdom and the Kingdom of God continues, the Bible suggests we can anticipate conspiracies will be a primary strategy of the children of the devil.

THE FINAL CONSPIRACY

Two of the primary goals of Satan’s many conspiratorial activities are: first, establishing One World Government under the rule of his proxy, the beast; and second, eliminating the children of God. This conspiracy operates in secret. It will not be revealed until the beast steps out of the shadows and into the light:

For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction, who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God (2 Thes 2:3-4, italics added).

The beast’s identity is hidden. He will be revealed after a rebellion occurs that results in his rule. Until then, he is patiently waiting in the wings until this conspiracy is launched. Based on the strong suggestions of the blueprint of time, the beast is almost certainly alive right now and will likely be revealed toward the end of this decade, c. 2030. The suggestions of time that support this assertion will be examined in the chapter “The Beast: 666.”

DECEPTION CLOAKED IN DECEPTION

To show just how crafty Satan and his children are, they created another layer of camouflage to make their already-hidden, illegal, conspiratorial activity even more difficult to detect. The conspirators use the dismissive label “conspiracy theorist,” or “conspiracy theory,” to both destroy the credibility of those who would expose their conspiracies, and to hide the actual conspiracy taking place. It is a diabolically clever strategy.

Today we are seeing an assortment of actual conspiracies being hidden behind the smoke screen of “that’s a conspiracy theory.” Take the Wuhan-China Lab Leak “conspiracy theory.” Whoever suggested the possibility that Covid-19 might have originated from a lab leak in Wuhan China was immediately branded a conspiracy theorist, and/or a racist.
Even once-prestigious medical journals, now given to publishing political screeds, weighed in. The UK’s leading medical journal, the Lancet, stated in an op-ed, “We stand together to strongly condemn conspiracy theories suggesting that Covid-19 does not have a natural origin.”
If you simply mentioned the possibility of a lab leak you were ridiculed by the media. Senator Tom Cotton noted how a lab leak in Wuhan was possible, and the Washington Post chastised him for repeating a debunked coronavirus conspiracy theory.
But what if this “conspiracy theory” was and is true? This appears to be the case according to a Department of Energy report and the FBI. And there is this small matter: people working in the Wuhan Institute of Virology (WIV) were the first to die from Covid-19.
Recently, FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary, said in a November 2025 Pod Force One podcast, that Dr. Anthony Fauci was not merely wrong about the origins of the virus, he actively led other scientists in the coverup of its WIV origin. We read the following from the Public Health Policy Journal:
After IPAK broke the Internet with the news on January 30 that sequence evidence existed of direct laboratory manipulation, a top virologist told Fauci the virus appeared lab-derived the next day.

Four days later, those same voices flipped. Per script. They co-authored a paper claiming the virus could not have been engineered. The reason? Fauci and NIH Director Francis Collins asked them to. And in the months that followed, those authors received millions in NIH funding.
…The media fell in line. Social platforms weaponized terms of service to suppress dissent. Lab-origin theorists were deplatformed while WHO, NIH, and CDC recited a chorus of natural spillover with no proof. [https://t.co/16Wewppv7r]
Yet Senator Tom Cotton was “guilty” of spreading a debunked conspiracy theory.

We have been conditioned to believe that a “theory” about a “conspiracy” makes it automatically wrong, and any person proposing such nonsense is a fool. That is what the forces of darkness would have us believe, because their method of waging war, until they achieve total power, is through conspiracies.

The World of Flying Saucers (1963) 👽📕

By 1963, the UFO debate had become a battle between believers and sceptics.

Donald H. Menzel, a Harvard astronomer, teamed up with writer Lyle G. Boyd to publish The World of Flying Saucers.

Their argument? You don't need aliens to explain every strange thing in the sky.

Menzel examined famous UFO cases and offered possible explanations involving mirages, weather phenomena, balloons, aircraft and optical illusions.

They revisited classic incidents, including Kenneth Arnold's 1947 sighting and the mysterious objects reported over Washington, D.C., in 1952.

But Menzel wasn't simply saying witnesses were making things up. He argued that perfectly sincere people could see something unusual and still misidentify what it was.

And here's the interesting twist.

Menzel was a respected astronomer, not an outsider dismissing the subject from a distance. His scientific credentials made the book an important counterweight to claims that UFOs had to be extraterrestrial spacecraft.

Of course, critics argued that some of his explanations were too speculative themselves.

The book highlighted a problem that still defines UFO investigations today: An unexplained sighting isn't automatically evidence of aliens, but an explanation needs evidence too.

By the 1960s, the real fight wasn't just over whether UFOs existed.

It was over how you could tell a genuine mystery from a mistaken observation.

Iraq and US discuss post-coalition ties and dinar exchange rate in Istanbul
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein met with US Special Envoy Tom Barrack in Istanbul on Saturday to discuss the future of Iraq-US ties after the departure of American soldiers, as well as regional security problems and the Iraqi dinar exchange rate.

The meeting comes less than two weeks after the US-led coalition officially terminated its military operation in Iraq on September 30, thereby ending the country’s security connection with Washington.

According to Iraq’s Foreign Ministry, the conversations centered on increasing bilateral cooperation as part of Baghdad and Washington’s new partnership, as well as the effect of continuing regional crises on Iraq’s security and stability.

The two officials also discussed Iraq’s financial and economic condition, especially changes in the Iraqi dinar exchange rate; however, the ministry did not offer specifics on any suggested steps or agreements.

The inclusion of the dinar in the negotiations emphasizes Iraq’s economic link with Washington, especially given the country’s dependence on the US dollar for international commerce and the significance of its banking relationships with the US.

The group also discussed larger regional trends and the need of sustained diplomatic cooperation as Iraq strives to improve its security and economic ties after the coalition exit.

Barrack, who also serves as the US ambassador to Turkey, greeted Hussein in a post on X, praising the connection between Iraq, the US, and Turkey as durable and emphasizing the significance of regional collaboration in solving common difficulties.

The American ambassador also emphasized Istanbul’s historical position as a diplomatic meeting place between East and West, emphasizing the need for holding the meetings at Tersane on the Golden Horn.

Both parties agreed to keep frequent contact and conversations on matters of mutual interest.

The summit underscores the transition in Iraq-US ties from a coalition-led military mission to wider bilateral collaboration, with economic stability, regional security, and diplomacy emerging as key areas of interaction. https://t.co/WOvmQkJCmC

Market Report 🌞 Sunday, October 11, 2026

A Trillion-Dollar Resource Transfer Enabled by Systemic Leverage

The standard narrative of the 2014 Crimean crisis centers on sudden military aggression and a democratic uprising. A timeline-driven reading of the geopolitical and economic sequence reveals a more coherent mechanism: the bloodless transfer of a major energy asset, made possible by the prior collapse of the Ukrainian state and the West’s strategic paralysis in the face of its own systemic corruption.

The speed of the Crimean annexation indicates it was not a reactive scramble but the execution of an established plan against an already hollowed-out target. Years of systemic corruption under Viktor Yanukovych had thoroughly degraded Ukraine’s military and chain of command. When Yanukovych was ousted on February 22, 2014, the state effectively collapsed. The defense minister, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and the interior minister all fled. Mass defections followed in Crimea itself. These conditions were amplified by the pre-existing presence of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet at Sevastopol and a large ethnic Russian population that provided both operational cover and political cover for a bloodless outcome.

Ukraine under Yanukovych functioned as one of the most thoroughly captured states in Europe. It was not merely corrupt; it was a highly efficient extraction machine. The post-revolution government accused Yanukovych and his predecessors of stealing up to $100 billion from the state—a high-end estimate from Ukraine’s acting prosecutor general that reflected the scale of the problem even if actual recovered sums proved far smaller. This kleptocracy was entirely dependent on Western participation. It operated as a lucrative cash cow for domestic oligarchs and their Western financial facilitators, relying on shell companies, offshore accounts in Cyprus and the British Virgin Islands, and high-end lawyers and accountants in financial hubs like London who legally shielded the oligarchs’ wealth.

When Yanukovych fled to Russia, he carried intimate knowledge of that system. The analytical claim advanced here is that this knowledge constituted usable leverage: the credible threat that Western financial institutions and political figures had actively facilitated the laundering of this staggering oligarchic wealth. Whether or not explicit blackmail occurred, the West’s subsequent restraint is consistent with a calculation that open confrontation risked exposing profitable corruption networks on both sides of the Atlantic. The Obama administration and the EU condemned the annexation and imposed sanctions, yet offered no military resistance. Ukraine’s interim government was left to manage the loss alone.

The annexation was, among other things, a large-scale seizure of Ukraine’s energy future. The Crimean peninsula and its territorial waters hold substantial offshore hydrocarbon potential. Ukrainian officials estimated roughly 2 trillion cubic meters of natural gas across the broader Black Sea shelf resources associated with the peninsula. Western energy firms had already signed or advanced production-sharing agreements and leases for blocks such as Skifska. Existing leases plus the abundance of untapped future leases—many of which had not yet been developed with platforms—brought the total potential into the trillions when valued at then-prevailing energy prices. By annexing Crimea on March 18, 2014, Russia secured the Sevastopol naval base and simultaneously seized control of Ukraine’s primary offshore energy assets, removing a potential future competitor that could have reduced European dependence on Russian gas.

Despite the loss of Crimea, a the most vital, strategic, and economic asset in the European continent, the United States and European Union instructed Ukraine’s interim government not to escalate militarily. That defies logic. Three interlocking constraints explain the restraint.

First, energy dependence. The EU remained functionally hostage to Russian pipeline gas. European leaders were unwilling to risk an immediate supply crisis over future Crimean leases when Russia could shut off existing flows.

Second, exposure. Ukraine’s military was compromised, and any sustained firefight risked broader Russian intervention and the public unspooling of corruption networks that had long connected Ukrainian and Russian oligarchs to Western banking systems.

Third, massive corruption. Yanukovych was expelled inside Russia for one week before Putin just walked in and took control of Crimea without a shot being fired. One week was plenty of time for Yanukovych to provide details of the level of Western participation in the past decade worth of money laundering out of the country.

Later efforts by Western governments to freeze some of these looted assets—such as a highly publicized $23 million London account linked to Yanukovych-era ecology minister Mykola Zlochevsky—predictably collapsed in court, exposing the West’s inability to actually dismantle the financial networks they had helped build. In this reading, the West prioritized containment of its own liability over the defense of Ukrainian sovereignty.

The capitulation in Crimea forced a post-hoc strategic adjustment. After Ukrainian forces withdrew in late March 2014, Western media coverage of the peninsula rapidly receded as attention shifted to the Donbas. Concurrently, NATO and associated institutions formalized a doctrinal shift. At the 2014 Wales Summit and in subsequent statements through 2015, the Alliance made explicit that a sufficiently severe cyberattack could trigger an Article 5 collective defense response. While this doctrine could not be applied retroactively to non-member Ukraine, it signaled the search for new forms of leverage once kinetic options had been ruled out.

That doctrinal opening coincided with the 2016 U.S. election. Under this thesis, the public narrative of Russian cyber interference served as a manufactured geopolitical pretext after a kinetic response to Crimea had been declined.

Crowdstrike, the private cybersecurity firm retained by the DNC, attributed the intrusion on the basis of disk images rather than live memory dumps, full network packet captures, or contemporaneous firewall activity. These standard forensic limitations leave room for uncertainty about the precise chain of custody and metadata integrity.

An April 2016 email among academic researchers specializing in DNS security explicitly referenced a source for DNS traces that would cost “7 figures,” raising the possibility that expensive collection was obtained and then introduced into the environment. Under the analytical claim advanced here, a subsequent firewall change—performed by the DNC’s contracted IT vendor—could have been used to mask the insertion of doctored metadata, including a large volume of email headers, because firewall changes routinely permit the deletion or alteration of logs at the moment of the change.

The same IT director later delivered logs to the FBI and provided congressional testimony that tracked lockstep with the narrative first published in the December 2016 New York Times account of the purported events. The contracted vendor himself had deep prior ties to the Obama campaigns’ technology operations. Furthermore, the Steele dossier, commissioned as opposition research for the Clinton campaign and built on unverified sub-sources, supplied the core allegations that animated the Crossfire Hurricane investigation. Taken together, these elements supplied the sustained political momentum for sanctions and isolation of Russia that Western capitals had been unwilling to enforce through military means in 2014.

The same priorities—energy pragmatism and the management of political liability—now shape policy under the Trump administration. In early October 2026, following a direct call between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the U.S. Treasury issued a general license suspending sanctions on Russian diesel transactions until April 2027. The arrangement contemplates immediate and staged deliveries totaling millions of tonnes to global markets.

Simultaneously, U.S. negotiators have reportedly warned Ukraine that the U.S. could halt intelligence sharing if Kyiv continues striking Russian oil refineries. Washington continues to seek a deal that could persuade Putin to end the war, with Trump publicly stating they want to work on a proposal to stop the conflict. The trajectory converts the 2014 non-response into a longer-term return toward market integration: the economic levers that allowed the seizure of a major energy asset without a fight remain the dominant constraint on Western policy.

The throughline is consistent. Energy dependence and the protection of entrenched financial and political interests have repeatedly outweighed military alliances and democratic rhetoric. Years of isolation, sanctions, and conflict have been sustained in significant part to avoid a fuller accounting of how Ukraine and related networks functioned as extraction points for oligarchic wealth.

Reintegrating Russia into global energy and financial markets while seeking to end the war is, under this framework, less a reversal than the recognition of constraints that were never actually transcended.

A LOT HAS HAPPENED IN THE WORLD THIS WEEKEND:

Sunday is bringing two developments that could influence Monday’s opening, and neither has much to do with Friday’s stock market performance.

First, geopolitical tensions are escalating again.

A missile attack on Riyadh’s international airport killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300 on Saturday. Saudi authorities blame the Iran-backed Houthis, while Washington is reportedly considering military support for Saudi retaliation.

Saudi stocks fell around 1% on Sunday.

For investors, the immediate concern is whether the conflict spreads further into energy infrastructure and shipping routes.

With Brent already above $100, another supply disruption would complicate the inflation outlook just days before Wednesday’s US CPI report.

The second development is coming from AI financing.

According to Morgan Stanley data reported this weekend, global AI-related debt issuance fell to $23B in September, down from a peak of $113B in June.

That slowdown deserves some context. Much of this year’s borrowing was frontloaded, so lower issuance does not automatically mean investors are abandoning AI infrastructure.

But financing conditions are becoming increasingly important.

Companies with strong balance sheets can fund expansion internally. Smaller infrastructure developers relying on external capital are more exposed to higher borrowing costs and tighter credit conditions.

We will be watching whether this starts affecting project timelines rather than just financing activity.

LOOKING AHEAD:

Monday: US equities trade normally, but Treasury markets are closed for Columbus Day.

Wednesday: September CPI. Another upside surprise could put renewed pressure on growth valuations.

Thursday: $TSM reports Q3 earnings. Management’s commentary on advanced-node demand, capacity and capital spending will offer another important indication of where AI infrastructure investment is heading.

Our focus this week is on the interaction between three variables: energy prices, inflation and the availability of capital.

AI demand can remain strong while financing conditions become more restrictive.

The question is which companies can continue growing without depending on increasingly expensive external funding.

🇺🇦🇺🇸🇷🇺 RUSSIAN DIESEL: WHY KYIV REFUSES TO SPARE THE REFINERIES

Trump wants to bring fuel prices down. Ukraine wants to weaken Russia’s war economy. Those two goals are now directly at odds.

On October 9, Trump announced a deal with Putin: more than 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel would immediately be made available to U.S. and global markets, followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November. Washington is granting a sanctions waiver. One key distinction: these are announced commitments, not completed deliveries.

The following night, an attack attributed to Ukraine sparked a fire at the Yug Rusi oil terminal in Rostov-on-Don. The timing is striking, but it does not prove the operation was ordered in response to the deal.

The Financial Times also reported this statement from an anonymous senior Ukrainian official: “We will burn Russian refineries.” This was not a public statement by Zelensky.

For Kyiv, these facilities offer two sources of leverage: they produce fuel needed for Russian military logistics and supply exports that generate revenue for Moscow. Sparing them to accommodate the U.S. deal would mean giving up a pressure point while Russia continues to attack Ukraine.

But this strategy could also come at a cost to Ukraine’s supporters. Less diesel available on the global market can drive up costs for transportation, agriculture, and some industrial operations, in Europe and the United States alike. The size of that impact, however, depends on how much capacity is actually knocked out, how long repairs take, and whether alternative supplies are available.

It would therefore be an overstatement to blame Kyiv for the entire fuel crisis. The war against Iran and disruptions to supplies from the Gulf are also weighing heavily on the market.

Crucially, on October 11, Zelensky clarified his position: Ukraine is prepared to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow stops attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, with reciprocal commitments and guarantees.

The disagreement is therefore over the terms for halting the strikes. Trump wants quick economic relief ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Kyiv insists that this relief must not allow Moscow to sell more fuel while continuing to destroy Ukraine’s energy system.

The risk is real: a strategy aimed at Russia can also put pressure on allied economies. But that does not mean Ukraine is trying to hurt its friends. It shows how an energy war can pit the priorities of partners against one another, even when they are involved in the same conflict.

text:
An Open Letter to Elon Musk

Dear Mr Musk,

Before addressing Mukesh Ambani as “Prime Minister”, explain why his own satellite venture is still awaiting the clearance you suggest he has prevented Starlink from receiving. An accusation that India’s government serves a businessman requires evidence. Sarcasm, however widely circulated, does not provide it.

Starlink already holds an Indian telecom licence. On October 8, the Ministry of Communications stated that Starlink, Jio Satellite Communications and Bharti-backed OneWeb remained at broadly the same regulatory stage, undergoing security assessment. You are entitled to question the duration of that process. A shared delay does not establish discrimination against your company.

India should provide a transparent, consistent and timely approval process. Its consumers deserve competition, and its domestic operators deserve no exemption from scrutiny. The same principle applies to you. Your wealth, technological achievements and political connections cannot confer privileges that you would condemn an Indian competitor for enjoying.

When did concern for poorer Indians become an entitlement to speak on their behalf? If affordability is your argument, present the service, the final price, the equipment costs and the conditions. Indian consumers can assess that proposition themselves. Their interests should not become a convenient justification for treating your commercial expansion as an obligation imposed on their government.

Improving those citizens’ lives is a responsibility shared by India’s elected government and Indian society. Foreign businesses can contribute substantially. That contribution earns revenue and, where deserved, respect. It does not give a company authority to decide which national safeguards are acceptable or to portray every unresolved requirement as an injustice against its prospective customers.

India has historical reasons to examine such claims carefully. The East India Company entered as a trading enterprise and accumulated political power. That history does not make every foreign investor a colonial project. It does explain why promises of progress will never be sufficient grounds for this country to stop asking who controls essential infrastructure, whose decisions govern it and where accountability lies.

Your own company’s record makes those questions concrete. A Reuters investigation reported that you ordered Starlink coverage cut in parts of Ukraine during its September 2022 counteroffensive, disrupting military communications. Reuters could not establish your precise motivation or the duration of the outage. Its findings nevertheless illustrate the vulnerability created when a country’s essential connectivity depends on decisions concentrated within one private company.

In Iran, you announced that Starlink’s beams were active despite the service lacking a local licence. Connectivity during a blackout can help civilians contact family, obtain information and document abuses. Those benefits deserve recognition. They also demonstrate the considerable influence exercised by whoever decides where service becomes available and under what conditions.

Power of that magnitude requires enforceable accountability. A government considering dependence on your infrastructure has to examine what happens when its requirements conflict with your judgement, your company’s interests or demands from another government. Personal assurances cannot resolve questions that must remain answerable through a crisis.

Myanmar provides another reason for scrutiny. Published reporting has documented Starlink terminals operating there without an official licence. What authorisation, if any, does SpaceX hold, and what controls determine which terminals can operate where commercial service is not approved? Indian regulators are entitled to establish how those controls would function along a sensitive international border.

The users of those connections include civilians and humanitarian organisations, as well as documented criminal networks. American lawmakers have themselves questioned Starlink’s alleged use by Southeast Asian scam operations. SpaceX subsequently reported disabling more than 2,500 terminals around suspected scam centres in Myanmar. That makes the effectiveness of your safeguards a practical question deserving a detailed answer.

None of this establishes a hidden operation against India. It establishes why security assessment cannot reasonably be dismissed as the work of an oligarch. Explain how unauthorised use is detected, how abuse is investigated, how geographic restrictions are enforced and how lawful Indian requirements will be met. These are ordinary responsibilities for a company seeking an extraordinary role in national communications.

The United States raised its Section 301 tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 100% in 2024, placing a formidable barrier before manufacturers such as BYD and protecting domestic producers, including Tesla. You publicly opposed those tariffs, which deserves acknowledgement. India’s security clearance process is a different measure, but the underlying expectation should be consistent: access to a foreign market comes with conditions. Your objection to those conditions does not establish that the country imposing them has been captured by a competitor.

You will find local admirers willing to repeat your accusations. Their agreement does not substantiate them, nor does it authorise them to speak for the country. Indians can demand better governance at home while rejecting the assumption that a foreign billionaire’s frustration is an authoritative judgement on their institutions.

The wider inconsistency is also difficult to overlook. Washington reserves substantial discretion to restrict market access and adjust sanctions in response to its domestic priorities. Its October 9 authorisation of Russian-diesel transactions illustrates that flexibility. India’s energy needs, economic interests and security responsibilities deserve equally serious consideration.

Those American decisions are not yours to answer for. Your portrayal of India is. Calling the alleged obstruction of your business a “crime against the people of India” assumes that your preferred commercial outcome represents their interests more faithfully than a process you have yet to demonstrate is discriminatory. That is an extraordinary claim for a company seeking permission to operate.

India is a democracy with a civilisational history that long predates your businesses. Its people are capable of judging foreign technology, questioning their government and deciding which trade-offs they will accept. Criticism is part of that process. Belittling the country does not strengthen your case.

Your achievements have given you unusual influence over communications, commerce and public debate. That influence should deepen your sense of responsibility. Do not allow the power you have accumulated to persuade you that scrutiny is an insult or that disagreement must be evidence of corruption.

Offer India a competitive service. Demonstrate compliance. Publish evidence of obstruction if you have it. Your technology may earn Indian customers and a substantial place in their economy. Neither your ambition nor your impatience gives you authority over their country.

text:
Match Analysis: Arsenal vs Leeds | #AFC

Consistent patterns I noticed.

1. High Regains, Verticality and Attacking Transitions

One thing I enjoyed was our willingness to progress vertically and attack immediately after regaining possession. Compared to Brighton, we clearly adapted our approach, increasing tempo and looking to bypass Leeds' aggressive press, whether through quick combinations, direct balls over the top or immediate line-breaking progression.

Our high regains were particularly encouraging, allowing us to attack retreating defensive lines before Leeds could reorganise. It was a clear weakness in Leeds' system as I alluded to in my pre-match analysis. Madueke was a clear outlet alongside Havertz and Gyokeres, with his pace proving particularly effective in exploiting space in behind and delivering dangerous, varied balls into the box. However, there were recurring issues with decision-making and the execution of the first pass following regains, particularly surrounding Odegaard, Rice and MLS. At times, we dwelled in possession rather than immediately progressing, allowing Leeds to recover, challenge and reset (Especially in the first half).

Raya's direct distribution was also effective, particularly when finding Havertz to initiate transitions and using second ball chasers or runners in behind.

Nevertheless, I really enjoyed the tactical adaptation and our intent to attack quickly rather than settle into slower circulation.

2. The Impact of Noni Madueke and Holding Width

We saw a clear difference in our attacking structure, particularly in final-third progression and box entries. Madueke was excellent, recording 9 box entries (@kashONdaCounter), 4 key passes, 2/2 successful dribbles and an incredible 11 of his 27 carries were progressive, with 168.1m in total progression.
What I particularly enjoyed was how consistently he was allowed to repeat his actions. I feel that repetition will be crucial in helping him develop consistency in a relatively unfamiliar position.

His width was a constant feature, allowing him to repeatedly isolate Bogle before driving inside or delivering dangerous crosses. His relationship with Calafiori was especially encouraging, with the Italian's underlapping movements exploiting the LHS created by Noni's positioning. I particularly enjoyed seeing Noni hold maximum width before accelerating at a retreating Bogle.

He also offered a clear (and our primary) outlet in transition, consistently looking to run in behind and exploit Leeds' high defensive line. There appeared to be a trade-off in his defensive responsibilities to maximise this threat (didn't track for Leeds' goal), although his recovery runs were encouraging at times. His body manipulation when dribbling was another positive, allowing him to create separation and attack defenders more effectively.

There are still limitations with his weaker foot (despite his fantastic cross), but for his first game on the left wing in a year, I came away very impressed.

3. Dealing with Wide Threats

Dealing with wide threats was an area I thought we struggled with today. Leeds repeatedly created dangerous situations through wide areas, with Bogle especially threatening both with his deliveries and attacking alongside DCL. I'd rather give credit to Leeds than overly criticise Konsa and Gabriel, although I do feel they could have done better in certain situations, specifically the goal where Konsa jumps out.

There was a clear attacking emphasis down our left, with Noni acting as the primary outlet in transition. This occasionally came at the expense of our defensive coverage, with Noni's failure to track his man particularly evident for the goal with Justin bombing forward from wide CB.

Leeds' back post runs were also dangerous, as we struggled to track runners and defend deliveries into the box. On a few occasions, they managed to find a free man at the back post, exposing weaknesses in our defensive organisation.

4. The Clear Impact of Bruno Guimaraes and Viktor Gyokeres

Bruno's introduction brought a level of directness through central areas that we'd been missing, especially before the second goal. His willingness to carry forward, break lines and occupy advanced spaces offered considerably more verticality than MLS and I believe the substitution was fantastically timed. For me, these are exactly the in possession qualities we signed him for, alongside his brilliantly taken goal with a fantastic ability to set himself for the strike.

Gyokeres was encouraging too IMO. His first touch and hold up play looked much improved, while his physical presence and consistent channel runs helped stretch Leeds' back line and open space for wide players to receive under minimal pressure. His decision-making when Trafford came out was frustrating, as it was a genuine goalscoring opportunity.

Other Notes:

Hincapie was excellent with his overlapping movements, showing a nuance with Noni drifting centrally. Timber was solid throughout, occasionally showing good attacking intent as well. Merino was brilliant in the final chance with his flick on to Gyokeres before Saka missed the chance.
Other Patterns:

Cutbacks from high regains against retreating defences kept creating the best chances, with Odegaard as the spare man/late runner again. Same theme as previous games.

This game was built for direct play, not the calm, patient circulation we're used to and we adapted well. Once Bruno and Gyokeres came on, Leeds' back line dropped a few yards deeper and the channel runs continued.

Leeds' press was aggressive throughout, with strong challenges from Tanaka, Ampadu and Stach. I thought Tanaka was fantastic in the first 60 minutes. Felt like he was absolutely everywhere.

Quick re-watch this morning. A few thoughts:

Madueke at LW gives us good balance. He needs more minutes there, and I think his instructions should be simple. Get on the outside and hit the ball hard across the six-yard box.

He has the physical attributes to do this repeatedly. If the other attackers know what's coming, they can attack the six-yard box looking for tap-ins. Sometimes simplicity is the best way to maximise a player's strengths, particularly when decision-making isn't their strongest attribute.

Havertz offered very little, while Gyökeres looked much more threatening off the bench. He still loses too many duels for someone of his size, but that performance gave me hope he can become a real weapon against tiring defences and decide games from the bench.

Lewis-Skelly and Rice should be our starting midfield. We lose some verticality compared with Bruno G, but we gain control. The Premier League is fiercely competitive. You can't win a game in the first half, but you can certainly lose it.

I'd keep starting those two, establish control, then introduce Bruno when the game opens up and there's more space for his progressive passing and creativity to make a difference.

Defensively, we were fine. Raya was excellent.

Saka just needs to find his shooting boots. He's consistently getting into excellent positions and generating good chances. The goals will come if he keeps doing that.

Overall, a good win, if slightly unconvincing.

Three points and onto the next.

On the seventh day of Navratri, on the day of Moolakshatra, the throne in the palace is decorated with swords, shields, horns, daggers, palanquins used by previous kings, and the sword of the crown is placed on the throne and worshipped for three days. 

On Dashami, a new rice meal is served. In the afternoonand evening, a mass meal is served to the Jain devotees,Gurikars and the people of the village. Later, at night, the kings, as a symbol of victory, wear the 'Pattada Ring' and ride on a palanquin. The Gurikars, along with the people, march in a procession to Pavanjigoli, where the coconuts placed on a triangular wooden barrier are broken by the Billava Gurikars. 

After completing this gathering, the kings enter the temple only that day and participate in the Ranga Puja. Then, the ring of the throne should be placed before Goddess Padmavati which are the household deity. After the puja, the Daivas is immersed in the Okuli water and the holy water is offered. Thus are the  Navratri program in our tulunaadu.

text:
THE PASTOR WHO KILLED HIS WIFE AFTER SHE FILED FOR DIVORCE (Reader Discretion is Advised)

It sounds like something written for a Hollywood crime thriller.

A young woman falls in love with a pastor who claims to have been chosen by God. She marries him, builds a life with him, and stands beside him as he leads a church.

But behind the pulpit was a very different man.

This is the tragic story of Barbara Tommey.

In 2015, 22-year-old Barbara had just graduated from university when she met Sylvester Ofori, a 38-year-old Ghanaian pastor living in the United States.

Barbara’s family reportedly had concerns about the relationship. But then something happened that appeared to remove every doubt.

Sylvester’s own brother, who was also a pastor, allegedly told Barbara that God had revealed that she was destined to marry a pastor named Sylvester.

What may have looked like a divine sign at the time would later become deeply disturbing in hindsight.

Barbara eventually married Sylvester, and the couple settled in Orlando, Florida, where Sylvester became the leader of a church called The Floodgates of Heaven.

To those around him, he presented himself as a man of God.

But inside their home, Barbara was allegedly experiencing something completely different.

According to reports, she endured years of physical, emotional, and verbal abuse.

Police had reportedly been called to intervene as early as 2016, but the relationship continued.

Eventually, Barbara decided she had endured enough.

She left the marriage and moved in with her brother while beginning divorce proceedings.

But leaving was not the end of the nightmare.

Barbara still had belongings and important documents inside the home she had shared with Sylvester. Knowing how volatile the situation could become, she returned with her brother to collect them.

What happened during that visit was captured on video.

Sylvester became violent toward Barbara and issued a chilling threat in front of her brother. During the confrontation, he reportedly said that if he did not kill her, then he was sick.

It was a terrifying statement.

But Barbara may not have known just how seriously she needed to take it.

Three weeks later, on September 8, 2020, Barbara went to work in Orlando.

She never made it home.

Sylvester reportedly followed her to the workplace parking lot.

Then, in broad daylight, he confronted her.

What happened next was horrifying.

Sylvester shot Barbara multiple times as she struggled for her life in the parking lot. He continued firing even after she fell to the ground.

Then, instead of escaping, he remained at the scene.

Police arrived and arrested him.

The woman who had once believed she was entering a marriage guided by divine destiny was now dead.

And the man who had presented himself as a spiritual leader was facing a murder case.

Investigators had powerful evidence, including surveillance footage and other material connecting Sylvester to the killing.

Prosecutors eventually offered him a plea deal that would have resulted in a 50-year prison sentence.

But Sylvester rejected the deal.

He chose to take the case to trial, apparently believing he could do better in court.

The story of Barbara Tommey is more than a tragic murder case.

It is a reminder that abuse does not always begin with something obvious.

Sometimes it begins with control disguised as love.

Sometimes manipulation is presented as destiny.

And sometimes the person everyone sees as a respected leader can be hiding a completely different reality behind closed doors.

Barbara tried to leave.

But the man she was trying to escape allegedly refused to let her go.

And on September 8, 2020, that decision ended in tragedy.

'On September 8, 2026, Meta launched Muse, a personal agent with its own secure virtual computer. It does not merely answer questions. In Meta's own words, it "actually does the work": emails, travel plans, forms, customer service, tasks across applications. Within weeks it was available in the United States, Canada and Mexico. Europe was not on the list, and Meta offered no date for release there.

This failure is not a one-off. Meta AI launched in the United States in 2023. Europeans did not receive even a stripped-down chatbot until March 2025. Meta said the delay had lasted longer than it wanted because it had to navigate Europe's "complex regulatory system." The European version arrived without image... generation, without multimodal features, and without training on European public content — the Irish Data Protection Commission having frozen that plan in 2024. Parity was postponed to a future that still has not arrived. Meta's own public-policy director put the result plainly: products "get delayed or get watered down and European citizens and consumers suffer." (...)
For years, EU policymakers congratulated themselves on becoming a "regulatory superpower." They succeeded. The question is whether this ambition is sane for a continent with weak productivity, poor technological scaling, shallow capital markets and a widening income gap with the United States.
A continent that measures success by the rules it writes for other people's inventions should not be surprised when the inventions keep being launched somewhere else.

Europe is not being regulated into prosperity. It is being regulated out of the future — by a Franco-German reflex that was national, is now EU law, and that kills at both levels.

Europe is missing the AI train. By withholding the tools of artificial intelligence from its firms and its citizens, it is cementing the decline of the continent.'

text:
Gospel
Matthew 22:1-14
Jesus again in reply spoke to the chief priests and elders of the people 
in parables, saying, 
"The kingdom of heaven may be likened to a king
who gave a wedding feast for his son. 
He dispatched his servants
to summon the invited guests to the feast,
but they refused to come.
A second time he sent other servants, saying,
'Tell those invited: "Behold, I have prepared my banquet,
my calves and fattened cattle are killed,
and everything is ready; come to the feast."'
Some ignored the invitation and went away,
one to his farm, another to his business. 
The rest laid hold of his servants,
mistreated them, and killed them. 
The king was enraged and sent his troops,
destroyed those murderers, and burned their city. 
Then he said to his servants, 'The feast is ready,
but those who were invited were not worthy to come. 
Go out, therefore, into the main roads
and invite to the feast whomever you find.'
The servants went out into the streets
and gathered all they found, bad and good alike,
and the hall was filled with guests. 
But when the king came in to meet the guests,
he saw a man there not dressed in a wedding garment. 
The king said to him, 'My friend, how is it
that you came in here without a wedding garment?'
But he was reduced to silence.
Then the king said to his attendants, 'Bind his hands and feet,
and cast him into the darkness outside,
where there will be wailing and grinding of teeth.'
Many are invited, but few are chosen."
Background: Matthew, a Jewish Christian writing after the destruction of the Temple in AD 70, encourages believers who had been expelled from the synagogues. He presents Jesus as the new Moses who leads His people out of slavery to sin. In this parable the king is God the Father, the wedding feast is the Kingdom of Heaven, and the son is Christ. The first guests (Israel) reject the invitation to repent and enter the feast; the man without a wedding garment represents those who refuse ongoing conversion.
Lesson: The same invitation is offered to us today. Accepting it means repenting, living a faithful and moral life, and remaining clothed in the grace that comes from conversion—only then are we ready for the heavenly banquet. Those who decline or persist in sin face the consequences. As Jesus warns, “Many are invited, but few are chosen.” The Catechism reminds us that Jesus’ call to the Kingdom begins with repentance: “Repent, and believe in the gospel” (CCC 1427).
Parable of the Wedding Feast, A.N. Mironov

𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗪𝗘 𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗣𝗢𝗡𝗗 𝗔𝗙𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗥𝗘𝗖𝗘𝗜𝗩𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗛𝗢𝗟𝗬 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗠𝗨𝗡𝗜𝗢𝗡?

The moment after Holy Communion is unlike any other in the Christian life. The same Jesus who was conceived in Mary’s womb, who died on the Cross, and who rose from the dead is now truly present within us — Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity. For a brief time, the Creator of the universe dwells in the temple of our body.

What we do in those minutes matters more than we often realize.

𝗔 𝗧𝗜𝗠𝗘 𝗢𝗙 𝗦𝗔𝗖𝗥𝗘𝗗 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗠𝗔𝗖𝗬

The Church has always understood the period after Communion as a privileged time of thanksgiving and interior conversation with Christ. This is not the moment for immediate conversation with those around us, for checking a phone, or for rushing toward the door. It is the moment when the soul is invited to remain still and allow the Lord to speak.

St. Teresa of Ávila once remarked that if we truly understood what happens in Communion, we would not be so quick to leave the church afterward. The saints treated these minutes with great care because they knew Who had just entered their hearts.

𝗣𝗥𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗪𝗔𝗬𝗦 𝗧𝗢 𝗣𝗥𝗔𝗬 𝗔𝗙𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗠𝗨𝗡𝗜𝗢𝗡

There is no single required formula, yet certain practices have nourished Catholics for centuries.

Begin with simple gratitude. Speak to Jesus from the heart: thank Him for coming, for His mercy, for the gift of Himself.  
Make acts of love, faith, and adoration. Tell Him you believe He is truly present.  
Offer yourself to Him in return. Ask Him to transform your thoughts, your will, and your daily life.  
Pray for the intentions that weigh on your heart, knowing you now carry them into the presence of Christ Himself.  
If words fail, remain in silent awareness of His presence. Silence itself can be the deepest prayer.

Traditional prayers such as the Anima Christi or the prayer of St. Thomas Aquinas after Communion can also guide the soul when personal words feel difficult.

𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗦 𝗧𝗜𝗠𝗘 𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗕𝗘 𝗥𝗨𝗦𝗛𝗘𝗗

As long as the sacred species remain within us, the Real Presence continues. This usually lasts about ten to fifteen minutes. Those minutes are a true extension of the Mass — a personal audience with the Lord. To treat them lightly is to miss one of the most intimate gifts the liturgy offers.

Leaving immediately after Communion without serious reason, or filling the time with distraction, gradually weakens our sense of what has just occurred. Guarding this quiet space strengthens faith and deepens love.

𝗔 𝗛𝗔𝗕𝗜𝗧 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗠𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗢𝗨𝗟

The way we respond after Communion slowly shapes the way we live. When we learn to remain with Jesus in those sacred minutes, we become more capable of remaining with Him throughout the rest of the day. The thanksgiving that begins at the altar continues in the ordinary duties of life.

Christ has given Himself completely. The least we can offer in return is a few undivided moments of attention and love.

How do you usually spend the time after receiving Holy Communion? Has any particular practice helped you remain more recollected?

Ignatius Catholicum ✍️✝️
