text:
Alex Manly printed one editorial, and his enemies reprinted it across North Carolina. He was 32, editor of the Daily Record in Wilmington, and he had answered a white woman's call for mass lynching with the plain truth about who preyed on whom. Armed men were told to hold off until after the November election. When five hundred of them finally marched on his newspaper, who ever paid for what they burned?

What they burned was a paper Manly had run with his brother Frank since 1895. By that November it sat in Love and Charity Hall on Seventh Street, a building owned by Black people in town.

It had landed there after a white paper told landlords not to rent the Record a home. The Record printed its answer under the words "Our removal."

"We have found it and will hereafter use a negro home for a negro paper," it said.

They had tried to put the paper out on the street, and the Record told them it thought their idea a good one. That is how you answer an eviction.

Back on August 18, 1898, the Record had printed the editorial that Democratic speakers would quote all fall. It answered Rebecca Felton, a white speaker in Georgia who had called for widespread lynching to protect white women.

The editorial opened with an offer, not a threat. Condemn rape because it is a crime, it told white editors, and stop blaming every Black man for the few who may be guilty.

Do that, it said, and your strongest allies will be educated Black people themselves. Together, it said, the two races could root the evil out of both.

Then it turned the mirror around.

"Teach your men purity," it told Felton. Near the end came this: "Don't ever think that your women will remain pure while you are debauching ours."

That line was about Black women, and what had been done to them since slavery. The journalist David Zucchino won a Pulitzer Prize for his history of Wilmington in 1898. White men had preyed on Black women for generations, he has said, and nobody talked about it.

A Black paper in a Southern city had just talked about it, in print, in an election year.

The editorial went down as Manly's, though some historians think his associate editor may have written it. It was Manly the mob would come looking for.

Plenty of Black Wilmington was angry with him too. Many feared he had put every Black family in the city in danger, and Black Republicans urged him to take it back.

They were right to be afraid.

The plan had come before the editorial ever ran. In the spring of 1898, Zucchino has said, two men met to work out how to take Wilmington back.

One published the state's largest newspaper, and the other ran the Democratic Party. The campaign they built had block captains, and guns brought in from as far away as Richmond and Baltimore.

By Zucchino's account, Manly's editorial started none of it. It gave the campaign a face.

The Red Shirts, the campaign's private militia, wanted Manly dead the day the editorial ran. The order to hold off came from the campaign's own leaders, Zucchino has said, because a killing after the vote would count for more.

So Manly kept putting out a paper that fall, with a date already chosen for him by somebody else.

On November 8, the Democrats took the legislature, with Black voters scared off and ballot boxes stuffed. The next day, white leaders in Wilmington read out a document they called the White Declaration of Independence.

It demanded that the Record stop publishing and that its editor be "banished from this community." Manly had twenty-four hours.

The same resolution called his editorial so vile that in most places it would have ended in the lynching of its editor. Then it said, with a straight face, "We deprecate lynching."

That afternoon the white leaders summoned a group of Black leaders and gave them until 7:30 the next morning to answer. The letter those men wrote disowned Manly to keep the peace.

They were "in no ways responsible," they wrote, and they did not "in any way endorse the obnoxious article." The youngest of them, a lawyer, was sent to carry it to Alfred Waddell, a former Confederate colonel who led the white side.

The lawyer found Red Shirts posted outside Waddell's house, so he put the letter in the mail. Waddell had been told it was coming, Zucchino has said, and he made a show of waiting for it.

At eight the next morning, a crowd gathered at the armory, and Waddell led it across town to Love and Charity Hall. By the time it arrived, it had grown to perhaps 2,000 men.

They broke in, a fire started, and the top floor burned out. Then they posed for a photograph in front of what was left.

The violence spread from there into the Black neighborhoods. A state commission concluded in 2006 that as many as 60 Black residents were killed. Other estimates run from about a dozen to several hundred.

The hospital, the churches and the coroner kept records too thin to settle it.

By four that afternoon, Waddell had been installed as mayor. He was running the city on the same day he marched on its Black newspaper.

Manly was already gone.

Accounts differ on when he left, whether days before the election or early that morning. His son Milo, born five years later, told the story in 1984 the way his father had told it to him. "It was a planned deal," Milo said.

The mob had thrown a ring around the town, and nobody got through it without a password. A German grocer who knew Manly gave it to him, and told him that if anyone found out, they would kill the grocer too.

Manly drove up to the line in his buggy, with a friend from the paper along. The men on the line stopped him and asked where he was going.

He named a town up the road and said he was "going up there to buy some horses." There was an auction up there, he told them, or something like that, as Milo put it.

He gave the password, and the men waved him through. Using the slur of the era, they told him that if he saw Manly up the road, he should kill him on sight.

"And they gave him two rifles," Milo said. "That's right. Off away he went."

The men hunting Manly had just armed him and sent him on his way. His face had helped get him through.

Family tradition says Charles Manly, a white governor of North Carolina, was his grandfather or possibly his father, and Manly could pass for white. Zucchino has argued that Manly could have lived as a white man and chose to live as a Black one. He had spent that choice on a Black newspaper in a Southern city.

He made it to Washington and stayed with the only Black man still in Congress. His fiancée, Caroline Sadgwar, who grew up in Wilmington, had been in London singing with the Fisk Jubilee Singers during the massacre. They married in 1900 and settled in Philadelphia.

Manly made his living there as a painter, and later ran a painting and decorating business.

In 1906 he helped found the Armstrong Association, which worked to open skilled jobs to Black tradesmen coming up from the South. The name, Milo said, honored the founder of Hampton Institute, the Virginia school where Manly had learned the printing trade.

The Association became a forerunner of the National Urban League. It also sent Manly through the South to recruit workers, and his face opened doors there too.

"Nobody would expect anything," Milo said. "He was accepted anywhere he went."

The crash of 1929 took the painting business.

Manly died in Philadelphia on October 5, 1944, at 78. He had driven out of Wilmington with two of their rifles. I could not find a record that anyone ever paid him for the press they burned.

For nearly a century, the official story called that day a riot and the men who planned it heroes. What Manly is owed costs nothing: his own words, read to the end, with his name on them.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXcAK
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

text:
🌏 ASEAN isn't one nuclear market.

It's six countries at different stages, on different timelines.

That's exactly what makes it the best case study for anyone planning an SMR programme.

Five lessons:

1. Regulatory readiness is a precondition, not a formality

The 🇵🇭 Philippines moved fastest — because it built its regulatory foundations first.

123 Agreement. PhilAtom working with the US NRC. DOE, State, and USTDA all engaged.

Without that framework, the $2.7M Meralco feasibility study couldn't have happened.

🇮🇩 Indonesia proves it from the other direction: ThorCon's BAPETEN approval took years of preparation.

Licensing isn't a downstream task. It's the binding constraint.

2. Technology and financing are one decision

Meralco's MoU with 🇰🇷 KHNP and KEXIM, March 2026.

They presented as a combined offer: technology plus state-backed financing, through one relationship.

Barakah gave that offer credibility pure tech comparisons can't match.

Same principle everywhere — 🇺🇸 FIRST programme and EXIM, 🇨🇳 state-directed financing, 🇷🇺 Rosatom's vertically integrated model.

The financial structure is part of the product.

3. Grid architecture decides viability before economics do

🇻🇳 Vietnam: 4,000–6,400 MW between 2030 and 2035
🇮🇩 Indonesia: 500 MW across two 250 MW units — aimed at Sumatra and Kalimantan industry
🇹🇭 Thailand: two 300 MW units
🇲🇾 Malaysia: 1.2 GW, post-2035
None of these numbers are arbitrary. They reflect grid absorptive capacity.
No amount of political commitment overrides that constraint.

4. Supply chain gaps are programme risks

No ASEAN country has HALEU fuel production. None has a finalised waste strategy. None has full nuclear-grade component manufacturing.

Governments that address these early through international partnerships build more bankable projects.

Countries that leave it to vendors lose negotiating power on everything downstream.

5. Early engagement shapes outcomes. Late engagement accepts them.

🇻🇳 Vietnam is the window still open. Vendor field open. EVN and PetroVietnam designated. PDP 8 approved April 2025.

🇵🇭 The Philippines window has largely closed — US and Korean positions are established.

🇲🇾 Malaysia and 🇹🇭 Thailand are at feasibility stage. That's where regulatory capacity building, workforce training, and site characterisation carry real value.

Those contributions don't need a procurement contract to exist.

Six markets. One conclusion:

Whoever engages before the framework is set, shapes it.

Whoever arrives after, negotiates against a structure they had no hand in building.

text:
-The Limitations of Jyotish and the Supreme Grace of Maa Kamakhya-

Jyotish, at its very essence, is the reading of one’s karmic account—the deeds of past lives whose Karmaphala (the fruits of karma) one is destined to experience in the present life. It may offer a glimpse into the road that lies ahead, but foreseeing one’s destiny is not the same as possessing the power to change it. To understand one’s karma is one thing; to transform the course of one’s destiny is quite another.
This brings us to a question of profound spiritual significance: if Jyotish reveals the karmic consequences awaiting an individual, how can one achieve the desired results when one’s karmic circumstances are unfavourable?
Within the spiritual framework of Parashakti, a deeper phenomenon is believed to operate. Certain departed ancestors of Jyotish practitioners, as well as deceased Gurus who have attained a state of union with Parashakti, may intervene in the distribution of an individual’s Karmaphala. Without erasing or changing the original karma, they may bring forward the positive karmic fruits that the individual would otherwise have experienced in the future, attempting to deliver the desired results in the present under the guise of Kripa (divine grace).
Yet, therein lies the hidden peril: what appears to be a blessing today may come at the expense of one’s positive Karmaphala in the future.
When the positive karmic fruits accumulated for future experiences are exhausted prematurely, the individual may become increasingly vulnerable to adverse circumstances. When these intervening entities realise that no further positive Karmaphala remains to be brought forward, they may abandon the individual, leaving them to face their difficulties alone and endure the resulting suffering.
After all, one cannot keep borrowing from tomorrow without eventually paying the price.
There is another important aspect to consider: Tantra Badha. When an individual faces such an obstruction, the entities or forces upon which these jyotish practitioners depend may be unable to deal with its intensity. In such cases, they may retreat, leaving the individual to face the problem alone. Not every source of power is strong enough to overcome every obstacle.
Therefore, one must understand the true scope and limitations of Jyotish. It may help us understand our karmic tendencies and gain insight into the probable course of our present lives. However, the ability to read one’s Karmaphala should never be mistaken for the supreme authority to transform one’s destiny.
Reading karma is not the same as becoming free from karma.
For those who seek genuine spiritual upliftment, freedom from obstacles, and ultimately Moksha, the path lies in sincere surrender to Maa Kamakhya at Shri Siddharaj Sarkar Dham. Through Her supreme Kripa, a devotee seeks not merely temporary relief or a change in worldly circumstances, but a deeper transformation of life—one that leads towards greater harmony, freedom from obstacles, spiritual evolution, and ultimately, liberation.
Worldly remedies may offer temporary relief, but the grace of the Supreme Shakti is the refuge towards which a true seeker aspires.
Do not merely seek to know what destiny has written. Seek the grace of Maa Kamakhya to transcend the limitations of destiny itself.
Jai Maa Kamakhya Tripurasundari.

text:
Pentagon raises official US death toll in Iran war
Two noncombat deaths have been added after Secretary of War Pete Hegseth dismissed reports that the tally was incomplete
Published 11 Oct, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/32Ws14PkuA
The Pentagon has revised its previously underreported tally of US military deaths linked to the war with Iran, raising the official count to 21.
The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) initially listed 18 US military deaths from hostile and non-hostile causes since the conflict began on February 28. The Washington Post reported last month, citing six US officials, that the database understated the number of deaths. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called the findings “a complete lie.”
On Friday, the database was updated to include Army National Guard Maj. Sorffly Davius, 46, who died in Kuwait on March 6, and an unidentified Navy member who died by suicide in September.
It also recorded the death of Sgt. Devin A. Seibel, 26, who died in a training accident in Iraq in May. The military, however, did not link the incident to the war with Iran and classified it under Operation Inherent Resolve, the decade-long campaign against Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS). His inclusion brings the broader number of US military fatalities in the Middle East since February 28 to 22, in line with the figure previously reported by the newspaper.
The updated records also show 865 wounded service members.
Democratic Representatives Adam Smith and Chrissy Houlahan criticized the incorrect count, calling it “an embarrassment” for the military.
“There is no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude,” they said in a joint statement.
Approached by the Washington Post, the Pentagon did not address the changes but said it “continues to maintain a steadfast commitment to the transparent, accurate accounting of all service member casualties.”
Last month, the US Navy acknowledged that eight sailors assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a ten-month deployment that included the Iran war. The disclosure followed reports of burnout, declining morale, and shortages of food and basic supplies.
Despite US President Donald Trump’s insistence that the campaign has been a success, a Reuters/Ipsos poll in September found that 62% of Americans disapprove of military strikes against Iran.
The conflict has also deepened political divisions ahead of November’s midterm election, with the financial cost and economic fallout drawing scrutiny. US Central Command estimated the bill at $43.6 billion through September 3, according to figures provided to lawmakers and seen by AP.
Trump previously said the war would end immediately after the election, subsequently telling Axios that he faces a “big decision” over whether to resume major attacks to bring it to a close.
In a phone call on Friday, Trump discussed Iran with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who stressed that a diplomatic settlement remains possible and reiterated Moscow’s offer to accept Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium to help resolve the dispute over its nuclear program. Trump welcomed Russia’s diplomatic involvement, according to presidential aide Yury Ushakov.

Elon Musk's Starlink India pitch raises a question about business ethics that has nothing to do with whether Starlink is good.

Competition is definitely good for a fair market . Rural connectivity matters. Disaster response matters. I agree with all of it.

But look at the method he is using. 
A businessman wanting regulatory approval publicly addressed a head of government, in a post seen 110M times, on a platform he personally owns. Then he called his critics an 'army of shills,' with no evidence offered.

Ask yourself:

1Would any other founder get 110M impressions for a lobbying pitch? Or is that reach a private advantage nobody else can buy?
2Is it ethical to use a public square you control as a pressure tool in your own commercial negotiation?
3If a newspaper owner ran front-page campaigns for his own business, we'd call it a conflict of interest. Why is it 'free speech' when it's a timeline?
4Calling opponents paid shills is a convenient way to avoid answering their arguments.

Business ethics isn't just about what you want. It's about whether you use power that others don't have, and whether you're willing to argue on a level field.

Starlink may well deserve to compete in India. But that case should be won on merit, not megaphone.

Where do we draw the line? 👇

89% of healthcare companies beat earnings. Nobody noticed.

While the market obsessed over artificial intelligence valuations, the healthcare sector quietly stacked four straight quarters of earnings beats — 89% of S&P 500 healthcare companies exceeded expectations. The headline performance hid it: biotechnology gained 33% in 2025 while healthcare providers fell 7%, and through May the Morningstar U.S. Healthcare Index was still down 4.4% for the year against a 7.6% gain for the broader market.

That divergence is now closing. Healthcare was among the market's strongest sectors this week, and the sector has turned positive year-to-date. The Health Care Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLV) closed Friday at $170.81 — up about 2.8% in one week and 2.5% in one month — holding above both its 50-day ($168.77) and 200-day ($156.98) moving averages.

Here is the part value investors should not skip: healthcare trades at roughly a 16% discount to the S&P 500, despite historically commanding a premium. You are being offered an innovation cycle — AI-assisted drug discovery, robotic surgery, machine-learning diagnostics — at a value multiple. Eli Lilly trades at 24.8 times forward earnings. Pfizer yields 6.2% at 9.5 times forward earnings. Johnson & Johnson pays 2.1% with a 60% payout ratio.

And the demand curve does not depend on the next product cycle: Americans aged 65 and older are projected to reach about 20% of the population by 2030, with chronic care, pharmaceuticals, and diagnostics spending rising with age. Meanwhile, patent expirations are pushing cash-rich pharmaceutical giants into acquisitions — another growth lever.

One caution: healthcare had the second-highest single-stock return dispersion of any Russell 1000 sector last year, behind only technology. Picking wrong hurts. Cardinal Health returned 77% over the past year while Pfizer returned nearly nothing. If you do not want to pick, diversified sector funds spread that risk.

My read: the AI trade's wobble this week is pushing money to hunt for growth that is actually cheap. Healthcare is the rare sector offering both innovation and a discount. Watch whether XLV holds its 50-day line near $169 — above it, this rotation has legs.

Not financial advice. Do your own research.

text:
As a freshman at Illinois, Brandin Podziemski averaged 1 point a game. He just signed for $110 million guaranteed.

You can see why people hate this deal. He's 23, he's never averaged 14 a game, and the Warriors handed him starter money anyway.

But sit with the alternative for a second. Without this deal, Podziemski hits restricted free agency in 2027. Some team with cap space writes him an offer sheet, and Golden State either matches a number they never negotiated or watches a homegrown starter walk for nothing. They just lived through the preview of that movie, because Kuminga's standoff froze their whole offseason and left the roster unfinished until the first day of training camp.

So they paid now.

His camp wanted $22 to 24 million a year back in August. The deal landed at $22 flat, the bottom of his own ask.

And honestly, the market had already decided this number. Christian Braun got $125M. Ayo Dosunmu got $112M. Dyson Daniels got $100M. None of those guys average 20 either. $110M is just what a 23-year-old starter costs now, and that price only moves up.

Then there's the part casual fans never price in. The NBA's new $76 billion TV deal lets the salary cap grow 10% a year. Podziemski's $22M starts out around 12% of the cap. By the final year it's closer to 9%. A flat contract in a rising-cap league gets cheaper every single season while he does nothing but stay the same player.

The trade kicker is the tell that the front office already knows this. $22M is clean matching salary in any deal, so if he levels up it's a bargain, and if he stays flat it's still one of the most movable contracts in the league.

Every team ends up paying market price for its young starters eventually. You either pick the number yourself or let the other 29 teams pick it for you. Golden State picked.

 — Laurie Klein (1976)

By the age of 24, Laurie had married Bill Klein, and the couple welcomed their first child, a little girl. Bill was studying forest technology at Central Oregon Community College, a demanding course of study that kept him occupied much of the time.

Living in a mobile home along a highway in rural Oregon, a young Laurie Klein felt isolated. She had a toddler, no car or driver’s license, no extra money for long-distance calls, and no local church home.

Waking up early one morning before her child woke, she sat with her Bible and guitar, feeling completely empty and unable to muster up anything to offer God.

So she prayed.

“Lord,” she said, “if You want to hear me sing, would You give me something that You would like to hear?” Then she began to strum the guitar, the words and melody flowed out effortlessly. The first two lines came instantly, followed just as easily by the final two lines

Simple as it was, it became a turning point. In the middle of a dark and lonely season, God had given Laurie a song of light. That gift did not merely fill a moment of silence; it changed the direction of her life. It reminded her that when the Lord brings light into a dark valley, everything can begin to change.

Years later, in the fall of 2000, Laurie and Bill were attending a Discipleship Training School. Late one night in the dormitory, Laurie heard a baby crying somewhere down the hall. Quietly, she slipped from her room and stood outside the door, intending only to pray that the child would settle and sleep.
Inside, the mother tried singing to soothe the baby, but the crying continued. Then she began to sing a familiar worship song: “I love You, Lord…”

As the mother sang, the baby gradually grew quiet and fell asleep.
The mother never knew that the woman who had written the song was standing just outside the door, praying in the hallway.

text:
Nithya Raman can’t keep story straight on LAPD chief she vowed to fire | Jamie Paige, New York Post

Los Angeles mayoral hopeful Nithya Raman is sending mixed messages about her pick to the lead the LAPD after committing to oust the city’s current top cop if elected.

During an interview with ABC 7, the socialist city councilmember insisted that booting Chief Jim McDonnell was not on her list of priorities if she beats incumbent Mayor Karen Bass.

“You know, replacing the chief of police is not on my 100-day agenda. Restoring trust with our law enforcement and the public is on my 100-day agenda,” Raman said, adding that McDonnell has not “met the moment.”

When pressed about a warning from Bass that firing McDonnell 18 months before the 2028 Olympics could be disastrous, Raman appeared to pump the brakes.

“That’s all stuff that I think about now and things that certainly I will be weighing and considering as we move forward,” she told the outlet.

“I believe his term goes through 2030, if I’m not mistaken, and at that point I think I would be looking to appoint a new chief.”

When the California Post sought clarification on Saturday — after the radical candidate had repeatedly insisted on sending McDonnell packing if elected — Raman offered a different timetable.

“Chief McDonnell is Mayor Bass’s police chief. I have made it clear that I would seek a chief who can keep Angelenos safe and restore trust with our immigrant communities,” she told The Post, promising to work with the Police Commission and LAPD command staff on a “careful, orderly transition.”

“Chief McDonnell’s term ends in 2030 and I would expect to replace him prior to that,” she said.

The shifting timeline caps a turbulent week for Raman, whose since-deleted “fascist liars” video featured McDonnell with a giant red X across his face, sparking outrage from Bass, McDonnell and the police union just weeks before the Nov. 3 election.

She appeared in controversial clip with lefty influencer Ed Choi, who interviewed Raman for a 90-second Instagram video filmed Sunday at Los Angeles Trade-Technical College.

Choi accused LA of becoming “extremely fascist” and asked Raman how she would “de-fascist-ize” the city.

The pair stated “Only you can stop fascist liars” in a video featuring images of Bass and McDonnell, whose face was crossed out in red.

Bass blasted Raman as “incredibly irresponsible” and “not ready for prime time,” while the Los Angeles Police Protective League warned the imagery could endanger the chief.

Raman’s campaign blamed Choi’s editing, insisting her remarks targeted ICE and the Trump administration, not McDonnell or LAPD officers.

But Choi has since claimed on Instagram that Raman told him defunding the police was on the table and McDonnell would be out.

The claim adds another wrinkle to Raman’s changing positions on policing.

In 2020, she embraced “defund the police” and proposed transforming the LAPD into a much smaller force.

In February, she said the department should maintain its roughly 8,700 officers, despite voting against hiring 170 additional cops weeks earlier.

And in September, Raman acknowledged her thinking on defunding had changed.

Raman voted to confirm McDonnell as police chief in November 2024, when the City Council approved his appointment 11-2.

Thinking about buying a property? One of the biggest decisions you'll make is choosing between a CONDOMINIUMand a SINGLE-FAMILY HOME!
Both can be great investments in your lifestyle, but the differences go WAY beyond the purchase price! 👀

🔑 HERE ARE 7 IMPORTANT THINGS TO CONSIDER:

🏦 1. HOA FEES & RULES
🏙️ CONDO: Most condominiums have HOA fees that help cover common-area maintenance, shared amenities, and other association expenses.
🏡 HOUSE: Some single-family homes also have HOAs, while others have none.

🔧 2. MAINTENANCE RESPONSIBILITIES
🏙️ CONDO: The association often handles certain common areas and exterior maintenance.
🏡 HOUSE: Owners are generally responsible for maintaining their property, including the roof, yard, and exterior.

🏊 3. AMENITIES
🏙️ CONDO: May include swimming pools, fitness centers, security, and shared recreational areas.
🏡 HOUSE: May offer private pools, gardens, garages, and outdoor entertaining spaces.

🔒 4. PRIVACY
🏙️ CONDO: Shared walls, hallways, or common areas may mean less privacy.
🏡 HOUSE: Detached homes often provide more separation and personal space.

🛡️ 5. INSURANCE
🏙️ CONDO: Owners generally need their own condominium insurance, while the HOA may carry a master policy covering certain shared structures.
🏡 HOUSE: Owners generally need homeowners insurance covering the home and applicable personal property and liability risks.

📋 6. RULES & FLEXIBILITY
🏙️ CONDO: HOA rules may limit renovations, rentals, pets, or exterior changes.
🏡 HOUSE: Often offers more flexibility, although local regulations and any applicable HOA restrictions still matter.

🏙️ CONDO: Could be ideal for someone seeking convenience, shared amenities, and less direct exterior upkeep.
🏡 HOUSE: Could be ideal for someone wanting more privacy, outdoor space, and control over their property.

text:
FBI Operation Summer Heat Nets Nearly 9,000 Arrests And Locates 1,410 Child Victims | Donald, WLT Report

The FBI’s summer crackdown on violent crime produced a number that deserves attention: 8,927 arrests in less than four months.

Operation Summer Heat 2.0 also recovered 5,013 illegal weapons, seized enormous quantities of fentanyl and cocaine, and identified or located 1,410 child victims, according to results released Friday.

These are operational results, not talking points. Federal agents and local police went after violent offenders, took guns away from criminals and worked to get endangered children out of danger.

The FBI’s official results show the nationwide operation ran from June 1 through September 20 and involved every FBI field office working with federal, state and local partners.

The numbers are big because the mission was broad. Agents targeted violent fugitives, gangs, gun offenders, drug traffickers and people accused of crimes against children rather than building the operation around a single city or a single category of offense.

Across the country, authorities seized 687 kilograms of fentanyl and 27,512 kilograms of cocaine. They also recovered more than 5,000 illegal weapons and located or identified 1,410 child victims.

Those figures are not interchangeable. Each defendant remains entitled to due process and the government must prove its case in court.

An arrest backed by probable cause, however, removes an accused violent offender from the street long enough for the justice system to do its work.

The child-recovery number may be the most important of all. Behind each of those 1,410 cases is a child who was missing, exploited or otherwise in danger—and a family or investigator who needed an answer.

The FBI’s Boston division offered a closer look at what the national totals mean on the ground. Its agents and partners made 176 arrests, seized nearly 50 kilograms of drugs, recovered 69 illegal weapons and located or identified 44 children.

That one field office worked cases ranging from gang violence and firearms offenses to child exploitation. Multiply that kind of work across the bureau’s nationwide footprint and the scale of the operation begins to make sense.

The operation also exposes a truth Washington too often tries to bury under slogans: violent crime is fought case by case, warrant by warrant and neighborhood by neighborhood.

National leadership matters because it sets priorities and moves resources. Yet the arrest itself is usually made by agents, deputies and officers who know the local gangs, the repeat offenders and the addresses where trouble keeps returning.

That is why cooperation between the FBI and local departments matters so much. Federal investigators can bring intelligence, interstate reach and specialized resources.

Local officers bring relationships, street-level knowledge and the ability to spot patterns before they become national headlines.

The Trump administration has made that partnership central to its law-and-order agenda. The message is straightforward: stop treating violent offenders as an abstract social problem and start treating them as people who must be found, arrested and prosecuted.

Critics will inevitably argue about the politics surrounding the operation. Fair enough.

Public power deserves scrutiny, and impressive press-release totals should never replace courtroom evidence.

But scrutiny cuts both ways. Anyone who dismisses nearly 9,000 arrests as mere political theater should also explain why thousands of illegal weapons and massive drug loads were in criminal hands in the first place.

They should explain why more than 1,400 endangered children had to be found.

And they should explain what alternative they would offer to the communities where armed gangs and repeat violent offenders have made ordinary life more dangerous.

The comparison with the first Operation Summer Heat is striking. FBI Louisville reported that the new effort recovered 120 percent more illegal weapons, seized 63 percent more fentanyl and identified or located 34 percent more children than the 2025 operation.

Those gains suggest the bureau did more than repeat an old playbook. It expanded the work, tightened coordination and produced more measurable results in several of the categories that matter most.

The fentanyl figure deserves special emphasis. A tiny amount of the synthetic opioid can kill, and traffickers distribute it through networks that cross state and national boundaries.

Seizing hundreds of kilograms means disrupting supply before it can be broken into countless potentially lethal doses.

The weapons tally tells a similar story. More than 5,000 illegal guns were tied to suspects and criminal activity rather than sitting in a warehouse as a statistic.

In a violent neighborhood, one gun can fuel a series of robberies, shootings or retaliatory attacks.

There will be prosecutions to follow, evidence to test and defendants who challenge the government’s case. That is how the system is supposed to work.

But there should be no confusion about the operational result. For 112 days, law enforcement agencies across the country concentrated manpower on violent crime—and they came back with arrests, guns, drugs and rescued children rather than excuses.

That is what federal law enforcement should look like when it is focused on public safety instead of political games.

The final test is whether the momentum continues after the summer operation ends. Violent organizations adapt, trafficking routes move and fugitives do not surrender because Washington held a press conference.

The administration now has a blueprint that produced results. Keep the partnerships intact and the pressure on repeat offenders.

Then keep measuring outcomes the public can understand.

Nearly 9,000 arrests will not end violent crime across America. The result still matters—and 1,410 children being found is worth celebrating.

text:
500,000 tons. That is the amount Moscow authorized on Saturday. Trump had promised up to 4.8 million.

The Russian government partially lifted the ban on diesel exports on October 10, implementing the agreement between Putin and Trump. The text on https://t.co/XNfWT57TDl specifies no expiration date and names no specific destination, referring instead to the global market. Novak added that production covers both domestic demand and the agreed-upon volumes.

On October 9, OFAC issued General License 135. It authorizes the sale, delivery, unloading, and import of Russian diesel, including into the US, until April 7, 2027. It does not affect the accounts of the Central Bank, the National Wealth Fund, or the Ministry of Finance.

The 2022 law banning Russian energy imports remains in effect. The license is a temporary exemption, not a repeal. EU and UK bans, as well as the price cap, remain in place.

Trump’s figures, posted on Truth Social following a 90-minute call, were: over 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 in November, one million thereafter, and then another 3 million, depending on the status of refineries. The WSJ tallies this at 4.8 million tons, or approximately 36 million barrels.

The 500,000 tons authorized on Saturday amount to roughly 3.7 million barrels. Prior to the July 8 ban, Russia was the second-largest seaborne exporter of diesel, trailing only the US, with shipments exceeding 800,000 barrels per day. 500,000 tons represents roughly one week at that previous pace, not a whole winter.

The refineries are not fully operational. According to the IEA, a Russian refinery was hit on average every three days during the first eight months of 2026. Crude processing fell by 30% in June compared to the previous year.

In August, net exports of diesel and gasoil from the Gulf and Russia were 1.6 million barrels per day lower than in February. Shanaka notes that over 370,000 tons were exported in August anyway, thanks to regional exemptions. A license grants permission to sell; it does not repair a damaged unit.

For Washington, the focus is on the gas pump, not Kyiv. US diesel prices hit $6.53 per gallon on September 23. The midterm elections are on November 3. Trump has stated he would not strike Iran before the election.

Zelensky called the deal a gift. CNN, citing a US official, reported that Washington had unsuccessfully asked for a halt to refinery strikes. On Saturday, Trump suggested that Ukraine should change its leader.

Times of Defence reports that the US threatened, during a meeting in Miami, to curtail intelligence sharing if strikes on energy infrastructure continued. Kyiv proposed a mutual halt. No Russian halt to strikes on the Ukrainian grid has been announced; the OFAC license does not require one.

Prices reacted at the product level rather than the crude level. The ULSD crack spread on NYMEX fell by $6.45 per barrel on Friday, settling at  104$-$105 mark, showing a slight gain, as geopolitical risks in the Strait of Hormuz overshadowed the news.

For Moscow, the license offers three things: a six-month window into the US market while the EU remains closed off; leverage to pressure Zelenskyy into halting the campaign against refineries; and revenue, provided the barrels actually ship.

AJ Inapi cites CREA data regarding the hundreds of billions the EU has spent on Russian energy since 2022; however, the argument of hypocrisy relies on outdated figures and fails to account for current outflow levels. Gandalv reduces the entire issue to a connection with Iran, yet the OFAC text authorizes a diesel sale, not funding for the IRGC.

What matters as of October 11 isn't the announcement itself, but the actual volume of diesel exported, whether queues in Russia shorten, and whether Ukraine halts its strikes without a Russian cessation of hostilities. The 500,000-ton figure represents an authorization; winter demands supplies.

🇺🇸 We the People: The Flame of Liberty and Independence Still Burns

1776–2026: 250 Years of American Independence

In his February 24, 2026, State of the Union address, President Donald J. Trump reflected on America's founding and the enduring spirit of liberty.

His words invite us to consider what independence means—not only as a historical achievement, but as a responsibility entrusted to each generation.

As we continue commemorating America's 250th anniversary throughout 2026, four enduring themes guide our reflections:

1. Our Constitution — The inheritance entrusted to us.

2. Our Responsibility — Our duty to preserve and uphold it.

3. Our Future — The generations who will inherit it.

4. Our Hope — Our aspiration for a nation guided by justice, human dignity, and the common good.

For Catholic fathers and families, this anniversary offers an opportunity to teach our children that freedom carries moral responsibilities.

The SMR business has a problem nobody wants to say out loud.

Everyone's selling the same three promises:

But almost nobody can actually deliver them.
Here's why:

1. The design isn't the product.

Four American SMR companies went to the same Korean factories to build their plants.

🇺🇸 Westinghouse → 🇰🇷 Hyundai E&C
🇺🇸 Holtec → 🇰🇷 Hyundai E&C

🇺🇸 X-energy → 🇰🇷 DL E&C

The 🇺🇸 US lost most of its heavy forging capacity decades ago.

A design without a manufacturing partner is just a license.

2. Financing is part of the product.
🇰🇷 KHNP + KEXIM bid as one combined offer — technology and state-backed capital.
🇷🇺 Rosatom offers Build-Own-Operate: they finance, build, operate, fuel, and take back the spent fuel.
🇨🇳 China brings state capital at scale.

🇺🇸 US vendors need EXIM, DFC, and Korean partners just to compete.

3. The customers aren't utilities anymore.

🇮🇩 Indonesia — 500 MW aimed at mining regions in Sumatra and Kalimantan
🇬🇭 Ghana — off-grid industrial demand
🇿🇦 South Africa — data centres needing firm low-carbon baseload
🇮🇳 India — retiring coal captive plants becoming brownfield SMR sites

Industrial offtake, not national tariffs, is what makes these projects financeable.

4. Capacity is finite and being claimed right now.

Forging bays. Welding crews. Module lines. Shipyard slots.

They can't be duplicated on demand.

So the constraint on Western SMR deployment isn't engineering. It's who secured manufacturing capacity first.

5. The reference plant is the real prize.

🇨🇳 CNNC's ACP100 hits commercial operation H1 2026 — the world's first land-based commercial SMR.
Whoever commissions the first SMR in a region holds a credential no feasibility study can replicate.
The global SMR market is projected at $300 billion by 2040.

The winners won't be the best designs.

They'll be the ones who assembled the whole package — tech, manufacturing, financing, and industrial customers — before everyone else.

text:
The lead source said "drive-by." I have my doubts.

Ask a new resident "How did you hear about us?" and you often get the first choice on the list.

I once changed that first choice from https://t.co/wiYQ42B8xy to For Rent. The leading source changed with it.

I get it. They came for an apartment, and the form is in the way. But that answer feeds the report we use to decide where the marketing money goes.

I thought about that last week at The Harbor, our student housing community near ETSU in Johnson City, Tennessee. The Harbor has a yacht club. There is no yacht.

The Yacht Club is what the management team named the local business program. Fifteen members: restaurants, a barbershop, a bank, a tanning salon, a soap shop, Red Bull. Show a Harbor ID, get the deal.

This tray was on a kitchen island. It held a free Sun Tan City pass marked $105 value, a free Buff City Soap mini, five dollars from City Barbeque and ten percent off at Texas Roadhouse. Plus a can of Red Bull, because college.

It looks great. The name is clever and the team earned the credit.

Will it lease an apartment? Probably not by itself. NMHC and Grace Hill asked 172,000 apartment renters in 2024 why they move, and lower rent came first at 49%. A free tanning pass was not the top answer.

The offer is the drive up, the front door, the tour, the unit and the price. The tray is the mint on the pillow.

The value is in the half of the program that isn't on the tray. Those fifteen businesses see students we haven't met, including ones who live somewhere else. With our name on their counter, each one can send us a lease.

Would we know if they did?
A dropdown won't tell us. A QR code for each partner will. So will an offer tied to the partner's name, because the source gets recorded when the prospect claims it. Neither one asks a 20-year-old to remember where they saw us.

Skip that and the program may still be working. You just can't tell which partners send leases and which ones just hold our flyers.

This is the most frustrating part of the business for me. The spend is known to the dollar. What it bought is often a guess.

A lease gets signed and the lead source reads "drive-by." Maybe it was the drive-by. Maybe it was the coaster at the barbecue place three weeks earlier.

Or maybe "drive-by" was the first choice on the list.

Sanjay, its not  “free internet” literally.

 In a disaster, communication is often one of the first services to fail and one of the hardest to restore. Starlink has been used to support emergency response in several parts of the world, including areas affected by natural disasters and disease outbreaks.

His sense of humor can be dark, and people sometimes take his comments literally. That doesn’t necessarily mean he’s against Indians in general; 
Otherwise, he wouldn’t do business in India or hire Indians to work for his company. We also can’t deny that monopolies have existed in the system long before Starlink came into the picture.

Here are the list :

Starlink's Global Reach
1. Philippines Earthquake — Magnitude 7.8, Mindanao (June 10, 2026)
Following a powerful 7.8-magnitude earthquake in Mindanao, Starlink activated free emergency connectivity for approximately 700,000 Globe and TM subscribers across South Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, and Sarangani provinces. This marks Globe's first deployment of Starlink's direct-to-device (D2D) satellite technology in a disaster response scenario, enabling WhatsApp messaging and SMS without any ground infrastructure. The free service runs for up to 30 days while terrestrial networks are rebuilt. PLDT and Smart Communications are running parallel Starlink deployments for recovery operations across the affected region.

2. DRC Ebola Outbreak — Ituri Province (June 6, 2026)
Starlink delivered 150 satellite connectivity kits to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to support the active Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The kits are engineered for rapid field deployment and enable real-time surveillance data transmission, coordination between health facilities, and logistics communication for frontline workers. In outbreak response, the speed at which data moves between field teams and central health authorities can directly affect containment outcomes and that's exactly the gap Starlink is filling here.

3. Medic Corps — U.S. Hurricanes, Floods, and Wildfires (2024–2025)
The nonprofit Medic Corps has become one of Starlink's most consistent disaster-relief partners. Key deployments include Hurricane Helene in Western North Carolina (September 2024), where Starlink was deployed to all area fire departments; Southern California wildfires (January 2025), where it powered command centers and fire rigs; the Guadalupe River flooding in Central Texas (July 4, 2025), where SpaceX partnered with T-Mobile to enable Direct to Cell SMS in affected counties; and Hurricane Melissa in Jamaica (October 2025), a Category 5 storm where Starlink and solar battery systems restored emergency medical communications. In several of these events, SpaceX offered free Starlink service to affected customers for up to one month.

4. South Korea Emergency Grid — KEPCO Pilot (June 2026)
Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) has completed a pilot of Starlink equipment at its headquarters locations in Naju, South Seoul, and Gyeonggi, establishing emergency communication networks for disaster preparedness. The utility plans to expand next month, deploying five vehicle-mounted and two portable

 Starlink units at construction sites in mountainous areas of Gangwon and North Gyeongsang — regions where cellular coverage is unreliable and emergency communication gaps pose real operational risks. This is a notable shift: Starlink moving from reactive disaster response into proactive infrastructure 

5. Starlink Mobile and Government Emergency Alerts
Underpinning all of these deployments is a rapidly maturing technology stack. Starlink Mobile, announced at MWC26 in March 2026, uses second-generation V2 satellites to deliver speeds up to 150 Mb/s — 20 times the link performance of the original constellation.

text:
Comandos de la Frontera are recruiting Peruvian children on the Putumayo River, and no Peruvian agency can say how many.

A 7 October investigation by Pamela Huerta for Amazon Underworld documents Comandos de la Frontera (CdF) recruitment in Peru's Putumayo province, Loreto, along the river border with Colombia. The offer is concrete: about COP 2 million a month (roughly USD 600), rest days, uniforms, equipment, weapons. Some minors cross into Colombia and are not heard from again. Others come home to show off earnings and become part of the recruiting chain.

The context explains the pull. The province has 8,423 residents (INEI). Primary-school dropout is 7.3%, more than four times Peru's 1.73% national rate; secondary dropout is 6.7%. DEVIDA ranked the province third nationally for coca in 2025, with 1,211 hectares, and illegal gold dredging runs along the river. Iquitos is roughly 1,200 km away by river.

According to testimony in the investigation, recruits train for three to six months, then guard coca, work cocaine labs, protect commanders, collect "cupos" (extortion payments), and gather intelligence. Peru's unified command for the area, CUPUMA (police plus Army, Navy and Air Force, created by supreme decree on 6 December 2025), says it found a CdF training site at San Belín de Yaricaya on 22 June with room for 80 to 100 people.

The data gap is the story. The investigation asked Peru's Defensoría, the Women's Ministry and the PCM whether any registry of recruited minors exists; none answered by publication. Families do not report out of fear. On the Colombian side, Putumayo's Defensoría logged 257 recruitment cases in 2025 and calls the figure heavily underreported.

Implication: CdF treats the river as a shared rear area, not a border. Peru's 2025 penal reform (Law 32336) sets 12 to 25 years for adults who draw minors into organized crime, but a statute without a case file does not stop a recruiter.

Practitioner question: what is the minimum cross-border reporting mechanism (Peruvian and Colombian Defensorías, schools, parishes, CUPUMA) that turns anecdote into an indicator before the next cohort crosses the river?

Primary: Amazon Underworld / Pamela Huerta (7 Oct 2026); La República (7 Oct 2026); Human Rights Watch reporting on child recruitment in Colombia.

India’s Air Force chief has questioned American plans to sell the country F-35 stealth fighters, pointing out that US personnel reportedly won’t even allow Indian officers near the aircraft.

Air Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh made the remark during Exercise Tarang Shakti 2026 in Jodhpur, where six US Air Force F-35As participated alongside Indian aircraft.

“Your people don’t even let us go near the aircraft, and you are talking about selling it to us,” Singh reportedly told US Pacific Air Forces commander General Kevin Schneider.

The comment highlights an awkward contradiction in Washington’s efforts to promote the fighter.

President Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would pave the way for India to acquire the F-35, with Vice President JD Vance subsequently discussing the possibility. Yet Singh says India has still received no formal offer.

The restrictions themselves aren’t particularly surprising. The F-35 contains highly classified stealth technology, and American personnel operate under strict security requirements.

India is also developing its own fifth-generation fighter, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft, while Russia’s Su-57 remains another potential option.

Singh confirmed that India’s government has not yet authorised an evaluation of the Russian aircraft.

For now, Washington is publicly discussing selling India its most advanced fighter jet, while India’s Air Force chief says his officers can’t even get close enough to inspect one.

text:
AI may change the price of your Big Mac and groceries — what this means for shoppers | Sawdah Bhaimiya, CNBC

Fast-food giants and supermarkets are rolling out a range of AI tools that could affect the prices shoppers pay, but experts warn the spread of data-driven tools could make personalized pricing easier to deploy.

Just this week, a federal antitrust lawsuit filed against McDonald's alleged the fast food giant uses an AI-powered "pricing engine" to set menu prices across U.S. locations and overcharge customers for Big Macs and fries.

McDonald's has denied that it's using AI to determine what individual customers are willing to pay and said it provides its franchisees with "tools, resources, research and recommendations to help them make informed decisions."

Even so, food businesses globally are increasingly digitizing operations with AI. Earlier this year, American grocery chain Kroger said it's using an AI platform called FlashFood to mark down perishables nearing the end of their shelf life and marketing them to shoppers via an app.

Meanwhile, electronic shelf labels (ESLs), which display the price of items in store on digital screens, are becoming increasingly popular at supermarkets like Kroger, Amazon Fresh, Walmart, and Whole Foods.

The technology is also gaining traction among U.K. supermarkets such as Tesco, Morrisons, and Asda. More recently, global financial platform Revolut trialed facial recognition checkout in select coffee shops, allowing customers to pay with just a glance.

CNBC reached out to Amazon Fresh, Whole Foods, Tesco, Morrisons, Asda and Revolut for comment on the use of AI but didn't immediately hear back.

As AI use becomes normalized among retailers, experts warn that this could lead to more dynamic pricing, which refers to frequent, rapid real-time changes in prices that could dramatically affect shoppers' experiences.

"Dynamic pricing means changing prices in response to changing market conditions, such as demand, timing, capacity or competitors' prices," Miroslava Marinova, a senior lecturer of commercial law at the University of East London, told CNBC. "It is not new. Airlines, hotels, and ride-hailing services have used it for years."

Bank of England economists Clare Lombardelli and Rupal Patel said in April that more sophisticated technology is leading to prices changing more frequently and also becoming more individualized, which could see more firms charging "as close to the maximum price a consumer is willing to pay for a good or service," which they defined as "perfect price discrimination."

These conditions could make it harder for statisticians to "measure and interpret" month-to-month inflation data, as the consumer price index is based on a representative sample of prices for shoppers.

"That works well when prices mostly move slowly and uniformly. But when prices shift continually – and differently for each shopper – the idea of a 'representative' price becomes strained," the BOE economists added.

AI collects more consumer data

While dynamic pricing has been in play for a long time, the BOE economists and Marinova noted that AI tools such as ESLs and facial recognition checkout are changing the amount of information that companies can collect on consumers, from transaction histories to browsing behavior, location, and purchasing patterns.

On Wednesday, U.K. supermarket chain Sainsbury's released "SmartLists," an AI feature that helps customers create shopping lists and find products just by uploading pictures of what they need or by typing out meal ideas.

"This is also why the traditional distinction between dynamic and personalised pricing is becoming less clear in practice," Marinova explained. "Dynamic pricing responds primarily to market conditions, whereas personalised pricing uses information about the consumer to estimate willingness to pay."

As companies use both pricing systems, it raises questions around whether customer information is being used to determine the prices consumers see.

"As retailers combine market-level information with increasingly detailed consumer data, the boundary between dynamic and personalised pricing becomes thinner," Marinova added.

Walmart and Kroger have publicly insisted in recent years that they do not use dynamic or surge pricing to set individualized prices for customers, but have instead used tools to streamline operations.

Several U.S. states are moving to curb data-driven pricing. New York requires most businesses using customers’ personal data to set prices to disclose it clearly. Maryland has restricted food retailers and delivery services from using personalised, data-driven pricing to charge higher prices for certain food, while New Jersey and Connecticut have enacted measures targeting “surveillance pricing.”

Consumer choice compromised

Dynamic and personalized pricing are not automatically bad for shoppers, Marinova said, explaining that it can discount items for some consumers, making some products and services more accessible.

However, the risk of individualized pricing is that consumers are no longer aware of whether the price they're getting reflects general market conditions or if it's been influenced by information about their own behavior.

"That makes it much harder to compare prices and to know whether another consumer is being offered a different price for the same product," she said. "If consumers cannot understand why they received a particular price, cannot compare it with prices offered to others, and cannot effectively switch to another supplier, the normal disciplining effect of consumer choice becomes weaker."

The BOE economists added that an additional challenge is that personalized pricing "splinters the consumer experience," which means households will face increasingly different inflation rates.

"And when prices differ for the same thing, inflation becomes even more personalised – and aggregate measures may no longer reflect households' experience," they said.

The @135SportsData Dynasty Players to Watch tomorrow morning. The London Game. Eagles vs. Jaguars from Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Philadelphia: Darius Cooper undrafted in the 2025 class, former Tarleton State WR listed at 5 foot 11, 210 pounds. Cooper finished his final college season with 76 catches for 1,450 yards and 14 TDs, then became the only undrafted rookie to make Philadelphia’s initial 53 man roster last year. He caught only 9 passes for 92 yards as a rookie, but Year 2 has already become considerably more interesting. Through four games Cooper has 5 catches for 59 yards and 3 TDs, including two scores against the Rams last week. DeVonta Smith and Marquise Brown are both out for the London Game, creating the clearest opportunity Cooper has had yet for meaningful offensive volume. Want to see whether the touchdowns can start being supported by actual target volume, if Jalen Hurts trusts Cooper when Philly needs someone outside its normal receiving hierarchy and if an undrafted receiver who keeps converting limited opps can force way into dynasty role. 

Philadelphia: Will Shipley 127th overall pick in RD 4 of the 2024 Draft, former Clemson RB listed at 5 foot 11, 206 pounds. Shipley produced 1,182 rushing yards and 15 TDs during his best college season and entered the league with a versatile profile as a runner, receiver and returner. His first two NFL seasons offered very little offensive volume, and through four games this year he has only 15 carries for 51 yards plus 4 catches for 24 yards. Tomorrow changes the equation. Saquon Barkley is out with a hamstring injury and Tank Bigsby has been placed on injured reserve, leaving Shipley expected to operate as Philadelphia’s primary back in London. Want to see what the former fourth round pick looks like with legit starting volume, whether receiving ability becomes part of the game plan and if one of the biggest opportunity games of his career can turn Shipley from dynasty handcuff into standalone value. 

135Sports⁠.com

Jacksonville: Josh Cameron 191st overall pick in RD 6 of the 2026 Draft, former Baylor WR listed at 6 foot 1, 224 pounds. Cameron finished five seasons at Baylor with 170 catches for 2,236 yards and 19 TDs, including 69 catches for 872 yards and 9 scores in his final season. The rookie has only 5 receptions through four NFL games, but those catches have produced 74 yards and 2 TDs, with every reception moving the chains. He also brings return value after averaging more than 20 yards per punt return during his breakout 2024 college season. Want to see whether Jacksonville begins expanding Cameron beyond a low volume situational role, whether his early touchdown production earns more trust from Trevor Lawrence and whether the rookie sixth round pick can start building enough weekly involvement to become more than a deep dynasty stash. 

Jacksonville: Parker Washington 185th overall pick in RD 6 of the 2023 Draft, former Penn State WR listed at 5 foot 10, 204 pounds. Washington entered the league with 146 college catches for 1,920 yards and 12 TDs and has steadily outperformed his draft position ever since. After 132 receiving yards as a rookie and 390 in Year 2, he broke out for 58 catches, 847 yards and 5 TDs last season. Through four games this year he leads Jacksonville with 16 catches for 228 yards and 2 TDs, including 83 yards and a score in Week 1 and 98 yards the following week in Denver. The interesting comparison is that Jacksonville now has two sixth round receivers worth watching for completely different reasons: Cameron is the developmental rookie trying to earn volume, while Washington has already turned sixth round capital into a legitimate starting NFL role. Want to see whether Washington rebounds after being held to one catch last week, whether he remains one of Lawrence’s most trusted targets and whether continued production finally forces dynasty managers to value the player he has become rather than the sixth round pick he once was.

text:
Yes, Cancel the Long End and Start YCC. 

Let’s give some context and be explicit.

Cancel the long-end auctions and bring on targeted yield-curve control. Buy time, focus the strategy, rebuild America.

Reagan’s rule was “Trust, but verify.” 

But, the  bond vigilantes have skipped the first half. They don’t trust the Fed, Bessent, Trump or Washington. In a period of historic change, they demand concrete evidence. A rational response, buy time by cancelling auction on the long end and bring back YCC. 

This is about credibility, not simply inflation. The confrontation echoes the Hillarycare era, when bond vigilantes challenged Clinton’s ambitions and ten-year Treasury yields climbed above 8%.

Court action disrupted tariff collections and forced refunds, damaging revenue that could help narrow the deficit. Replacement duties should recover part of the loss. 

The vigilantes don’t care about the explanation. They want receipts.
Cancel the auctions until they are in hand!

Supply-side economics takes time. Full expensing rewards qualifying investment before its productivity dividend arrives. AI offers a generational opportunity. 

The GENIUS Act could strengthen dollar-based finance and Treasury demand. Foundations are forming; results must follow.

Warsh’s Fed needs a makeover. Trimmed-mean PCE near 2.2% is concrete evidence against a broad inflationary cascade, and below the 2.7% reading available when Powell cut rates by 50 basis points in September 2024. 

Recall October 2018: weeks before the midterms, amid the escalating China trade conflict, Powell declared rates “a long way from neutral” and entertained going beyond it. 

By late November, they were “just below” neutral; the following year brought three cuts. Warsh’s Fed is doing the same political maneuver. 

That is a record of miscalculation and inconsistent communication. Warsh must stop repeating it. Let the data discipline the theory, rather than treating economic strength as an automatic invitation to tighten.

Bessent should temporarily suspend new 20- and 30-year auctions, accepting greater refinancing risk. Warsh and Bessent need to revisit the possibility of yield-curve control, aligning Treasury’s financing strategy with an independently determined Fed framework. 

Targeted yield caps should address market dysfunction, not subsidize deficits regardless of inflation. Buying time must not become an excuse to abandon fiscal discipline.

America First requires priorities. No more wars. End the Iran conflict. Rebuild America’s productive economy. Give the Bond Vigilantes the receipts. 

America grew out of debt after World War II. Gross federal debt fell from roughly 122% of GDP to 32.5% in 1981. Nominal growth and fiscal restraint worked together
.
The vigilantes trade by the minute; productive investment takes years.
Make 2027 the proof: recovering revenue, expanding capacity, peace and borrowing growing slower than output.

Buy time, not excuses. Outgrow the debt. Rebuild America.

The two-week festival sees people offer food, drinks, cakes and money to monks in memory of deceased relatives with this year’s ceremonies also honouring soldiers killed in border clashes with Thailand.

The annual festival carries deep significance in Cambodia, commemorating more than a million people who died during the Khmer Rouge regime.

text:
As we wrap up #HispanicHeritageMonth, we want to share the especially inspiring story of El Salvador native Veronica, an incredibly hardworking woman whose daughter's heart surgery inspired her to work at Wolfson Children's Hospital.

Veronica gave birth to her daughter Sophia prematurely at Baptist Medical Center South in 2021, and three years later, Sophia underwent surgery to repair a hole in her heart. Veronica was so impressed by the care she received at Wolfson Children's, and by the surgery performed by Nemours interventional cardiologist Dr. Robert English, that she knew she wanted to work there.

With no previous clinical experience, she applied for a role in Environmental Services and was offered a full-time position as the only dedicated EVS technician on Weaver 4, the Wolfson Children's Hematology/Oncology unit, where she was responsible for the daily cleaning of 24 patient rooms – including the deep, methodical cleaning and disinfection of several bone marrow transplant rooms.

“When I cleaned, I always gave my best because I know everyone here needs our support,” added Veronica, who received the LOTUS Award for providing extraordinary, compassionate care and service to patients, families and team members.

A year later, Veronica decided to become a Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA) to spend more time with patients. And last fall, she completed a Florida Board of Nursing-approved nursing assistant training program and was hired to work as a Health Unit Coordinator (HUC) on Weaver 4.

As the night shift HUC, Veronica, who is bilingual, is responsible for answering phone calls and call lights, maintaining patient charts, and greeting and assisting visitors. She also fills in for other CNAs on the unit. And even though she has changed scrub colors from green to burgundy, Veronica still approaches each shift with the same shade of dedication and commitment. 

“Now as a CNA, I get to spend more time with patients, help with their discharge and be there when they ring the bell after their treatments are finished,” she said. “It’s so uplifting to see the smiles on their faces. It fills my heart with joy every day.”

#BaptistProud

An historical comparison of six countries ranked the US first for violence and aggression over the past 200 years, based on the wars, military interventions, overthrows, and mass bloodshed examined. This poster presents only a summary of that record. A fuller account of the events included in our comparison could fill two living room walls.

We are talking about violence and aggression. The discussion should not be redirected to what the US has contributed to the world. Scientific discoveries, cultural achievements, and humanitarian efforts do not erase the people killed or the countries devastated. Those accomplishments cannot serve as a permanent excuse for bloodshed.

Iran calls the US the “Great Satan,” and, in my eyes, the US has repeatedly stepped into those shoes. Its claims of moral leadership ring hollow against the destruction carried out in its name.

Consider the statement from Rep  Don Bacon of Nebraska supplied here, explicitly endorsing LT GEN  Keith Kellogg’s position: “I agree with LT GEN Kellogg. Ukraine should destroy Russia’s diesel production infrastructure. Totally destroy it.” Bacon then argues that the president should criticize Russia’s bombing of Ukrainian cities rather than Ukraine’s actions, describing Ukraine as the victim defending itself.

Those words show Bacon’s support for destroying Russia’s diesel production infrastructure and his stated agreement with Kellogg. In my view, advocating that destruction is reckless and dangerous. Diesel powers tractors that help produce food and trucks that transport it—just two examples of its essential role. Widespread destruction of that infrastructure could disrupt supplies, increase fuel and transportation costs, and make food more expensive, harming ordinary people far beyond Russia, and could lead to bloodshed of mass protestors protesting lack of food, fuel etc.  Bacon and Kellogg are acting irresponsibly by opposing the president’s decision to obtain diesel fuel from Russia while advocating the destruction of Russian diesel production infrastructure. If the policies they promote contribute to shortages, hardship, or deaths, they should be held accountable for their role.

Instead, they continue backing Zelenskyy, whom I regard as reckless and dangerous. This is the same Ukraine where I believe the CIA helped facilitate the overthrow of a democratically elected government—an allegation I consider central to understanding the events that led to the conflict we are witnessing today..

Bacon frames his support as defending Ukraine, but that does not remove the need to consider the consequences for civilians. He and Kellogg should have to answer for the foreseeable harm of the policies they advocate. Severe shortages and rising food prices could deepen hardship and fuel unrest. Leadership requires responsibility for human life, including lives affected far beyond the battlefield.

Bacon’s endorsement of Kellogg’s position shows, in my view, that even in 2026, the mindset of control through aggression, violence, and destruction persists among influential American figures. Their remarks reinforce the pattern examined in our six-country historical comparison, which ranked the US first for the actions discussed. Rather than demonstrating a change in direction, they offer another example of leaders advocating destructive policies while disregarding the potential consequences for people around the world.

The US continues to elect and appoint people whose decisions endanger both the country and the world.

Congressional leaders voted out for pursuing policies of destruction and war should never be allowed to hold public office again. That same standard should apply to every government official—at the local, state, or national level.

Great leadership requires responsibility, restraint, and accountability. US leaders speak of “peace through strength,” yet repeatedly pursue policies that deepen conflict & risk wider war.

氷見の家で、ふとした日におばあさんが仏間に和菓子を供えたり、ごはんを少しだけよそって「これは神さまのぶん」と言ったりする。理由は語られなくて、でも子どもは「それ何のまね？」って首をかしげてる。

昔は大きな行事があった名残りなんだろうけど、今は毎日の“ついで”みたいに溶けこんでる。

誰かが「こうしなさい」って教えるわけじゃない。だけど、その無言の繰り返しが、家の空気になるんだね。

家ごとのやり方や、口に出さない理由──それが、ささやかな伝承の形なのかもしれない。

In the house in Himi, on some ordinary days, grandmother offers a sweet to the family altar or scoops a small portion of rice, quietly saying, "This is for the gods." No reason is spoken aloud, but the children wonder, "Why do you do that?"

Maybe it’s a remnant of bigger festivals in the past, but now it just melts into the rhythm of everyday life—almost as an afterthought.

Nobody says, “You must do it this way.” Instead, these silent repetitions become the atmosphere of the home itself.

Each family’s method, and the unspoken reasons behind it—perhaps that’s the shape tradition takes, soft and gentle, in daily living.

#年中行事 #五節句 #昔の暮らし
