text:
Nine Harlem mothers built their children a school in a church basement in 1958, then shut it down on purpose. They had volunteers teaching English, math, French, and art appreciation, and it was working, and that was the problem.

As long as those children were learning something, the Board of Education had no reason to prosecute anybody, and without a prosecution no judge would ever be made to look inside the real schools. So they took the classes away from their own kids and sat down to wait for the city.

Thirty-one days after four girls were killed in the basement of a church in Birmingham, a man walked into a room full of New York City schoolteachers and told them they were living through a very dangerous time. He did not have to explain which dangerous time he meant.

It was October 16, 1963, and everybody sitting in front of him had read the same newspapers he had. Addie Mae Collins was fourteen, Carole Robertson was fourteen, Cynthia Wesley was fourteen, and Denise McNair was eleven.

James Baldwin told that room the country was not being menaced by Khrushchev. It was being menaced from the inside, by itself, and the teachers in those chairs were part of the machinery doing it.

Then he did something you would not expect from the most famous Black writer in America.

He apologized for being there.

He told them he was not a teacher himself, that he was fairly easily intimidated, and asked them to bear with him. The man who had been on the cover of Time magazine five months earlier, whose book had come out in January and moved through the country like weather, stood in front of a room of public school employees and admitted he was nervous.

Then he stopped being nervous.

He walked them through what education actually is, from the beginning, like he was explaining it to children. A child gets born, somebody takes on the duty of civilizing that child, and the civilizing happens inside a society that has its own reasons for wanting the job done a particular way.

His example was not Alabama. His example was Germany.

Children raised and schooled to the purposes of the Third Reich, he said, came out barbarians. He was standing in New York City telling American teachers, to their faces, that a school system can manufacture cruelty and hand out diplomas for it.

Then came the sentence.

The paradox of education is precisely this, he told them, and then he finished the thought. The moment a person begins to wake up is the same moment that person begins to examine the society that is doing the teaching.

That is the line you have seen a thousand times, on mugs and T-shirts and classroom walls, on a black square with white letters going around your feed on a Tuesday afternoon. He was not offering it as inspiration.

He was handing out an assignment, and he knew what it would cost the people he handed it to. Because the next thing out of his mouth was about Birmingham.

He told them there must have been a day in this country when children being bombed in Sunday school would have caused a public uproar and put a governor's career in real danger. It happened, he said, and there was no uproar.

Here is the part that falls off the poster.

Baldwin was not in that room to talk about Alabama. He was talking about the school system those teachers worked for.

To make it plain he built them a scene, and it is worth walking through slowly, because it is the whole speech in miniature. Picture a Black boy, seven years old, and a father who decides to take him downtown for the afternoon.

They get on a bus at 131st Street and Seventh Avenue and ride down through the park. They come out the other side into a city that is a few miles and one entire world away from the place they got on.

The Park Avenue the boy lives near is dark and dirty, and nobody is opening a Tiffany's on it. The Park Avenue at the far end of the ride has doormen, and the garbage gets collected, and people walk around like they own the ground under their feet, because they do.

Nobody has to explain any of this to the child.

He works it out himself, and Baldwin told them it gets into a child's head much earlier than adults are comfortable admitting.

A few years on the same boy is a grocery boy or a messenger, and he tries a front entrance, and a man tells him to go around to the back door. Later still, if he happens to know somebody in that building, the same man wants to know where his package is.

Baldwin knew that bus route because he had ridden it. He told the room he had come up a street boy himself, so none of this was theory to him.

Then he turned it around on them and told them what he would do with a Black child if the child were his to teach. He said he would tell that child straight out that the streets and the buildings and the dangers pressing in on him were criminal, and that none of it was an accident.

He said he would make him understand that the real history of this country is bigger and uglier and more beautiful than anything he had ever been handed in a classroom, that the world is bigger still, and that all of it belongs to him.

Near the end he said the poster sentence over again, in harder words.

At the exact moment you develop a conscience, he told them, you are going to find yourself at war with your own country. And if you think of yourself as an educated person, changing that country is your job.

Now here is why that man had the standing to say it in that room.

He was not describing a school system from the outside. He was describing the one that made him, and he could name the people in it.

At P.S. 24 in Harlem the principal was Gertrude Ayer, the first Black woman to run a public school in New York City, and she looked at a small odd boy with enormous eyes and decided he was worth extra trouble. She put him with a young white teacher from the Midwest named Orilla Miller, who he called Bill.

Miller took him to his first play, argued books with him, and quietly funneled help to a family that had close to nothing.

Then he went on to Frederick Douglass Junior High School, at 120 West 140th Street.

Inside that building a Harvard-trained math teacher named Herman Porter walked him into the 42nd Street library for the first time in his life. And inside that building Countee Cullen, the Harlem Renaissance poet, taught him French and put him to work on the school paper.

Cullen is the one who told him to apply to DeWitt Clinton, which is where he met Richard Avedon and started editing magazines. Four people, all of them New York City public school employees, built James Baldwin out of a poor kid from 131st Street.

So when he told that room in 1963 that a teacher's real job is to put a weapon in a child's hand, he was not speculating. Now hold on to that address, because this is where the story you have never been told begins.

Frederick Douglass Junior High School had a number.

It was Junior High School 139.

In December 1957 a teacher in that building named Harcourt Tynes gave his ninth grade class an assignment. Go up to the Schomburg, he told them, and write a book of biographies of Black people.

His students wrote it and illustrated it by hand, with help from the school librarian and the art teacher, and bound it into a volume that sits in the New York Public Library today. That is exactly what Baldwin would stand up and demand six years later, and it was already happening inside his old junior high school.

Nine months after those boys finished their book, mothers in Harlem said they would go to jail and rot there before they let their own children walk into Junior High School 139.

There were nine of them, and their children were zoned into three Harlem junior highs. Junior High School 136, Junior High School 139, and Junior High School 120.

They knew those buildings from the inside. Overcrowded, dirtier, thinner curriculum, fewer resources, and more teachers standing in front of classrooms without a license to be there.

Brown v. Board of Education was four years old by then and nobody had ever pointed it at New York. That was the trick of it up North, no sign on the door and no governor blocking the entrance, just zoning maps, and the maps did the work quietly.

The Board of Education called it de facto, the result of housing patterns.

Nobody's fault.

One of those mothers was Mae Mallory, who had come up in Macon, Georgia, and had two children. In January 1957 she went down to a Board of Education hearing and said it out loud to the people who ran the schools.

Her daughter Patricia's school in Harlem, she told them, was just as "Jim Crow" as the Hazel Street School she herself had attended back in Macon. She used the Southern word on purpose, in a New York hearing room, to New Yorkers who were certain the word did not apply to them.

That September the parents went down to City Hall. Ella Baker was there with them, fifteen parents in all, sitting across from Mayor Robert Wagner and his school officials.

They got nothing.

In October 1958 they sued, asking a million dollars in damages and accusing the Board of a sinister and discriminatory purpose in keeping Harlem's schools segregated. The New York Times ran it as Harlem parents filing for a million.

Then the case sat there. Lawsuits are slow and children are not, and a seventh grader does not get that year back while lawyers file paper.

So at the start of the school year the mothers stopped sending their children in. Fifteen parents began it, and they were not willing to let their children go ignorant to make a point, so they built a school.

A Harlem minister named Eugene Callender opened his church for them. Volunteers came in to teach, and the parents' own lawyer and his wife took classes themselves.

Those children were taught English, math, social studies, world events, music, French, and art appreciation.

Art appreciation.

In a borrowed church room in Harlem in 1958, somebody stood in front of Black children and taught them how to look at a painting. And then the mothers shut it down.

Not because it failed. Because it worked, and working was the trap.

New York State law said a child had to be in school, and a parent who kept a child out could be fined or sent to prison. But their children were in school, learning more than they had been learning before.

Which meant the Board had no case to bring, and with no case there was no courtroom. And with no courtroom, no judge in the state of New York would ever be forced to look at what was inside 136, 139, and 120.

Their lawyer, Paul Zuber, understood the arithmetic.

The only way to be heard was to be prosecuted.

So the mothers ended the classes. They walked into that church, stopped the one good thing they had built, and sent their own children home to sit, so that the city would finally have a reason to come after them.

Some of the parents could not do it, and nobody should blame them. That is where fifteen became nine.

Understand what was being asked here.

Not a march, not a sign, not one hard afternoon.

They were being asked to keep their own children out of school on purpose, indefinitely, and to look like bad mothers in public the entire time. The city obliged them exactly.

On October 28, 1958, the Board of Education brought the parents in, in two separate cases. The charge was not truancy.

The charge was neglect.

The word the State of New York put on paper for those women was neglect. On December 4 the Times ran it plain, four mothers guilty in the school boycott, in front of family court judge Nathaniel Kaplan.

Four of them stood in a courtroom and were told they had neglected their children. Eleven days later, two of the others drew a different judge.

Her name was Justine Wise Polier, and the case in front of her carried a caption that ought to be carved into the side of the Board of Education building. In the matter of Charlene Skipwith and Sheldon Rector, children twelve years of age.

Two twelve year olds, entered in the record as neglected.

The parents did not come in with speeches. They came in with documented conditions inside those schools, and the pattern showing the same conditions turning up wherever the students were Black and Puerto Rican, and not turning up where the students were white.

On December 15, 1958, Polier dismissed the charges. She wrote that those children had been getting inferior educational opportunities in those schools by reason of racial discrimination.

If the city handed a child a discriminatory education, she ruled, the city could not then force that child to attend.

It was the first time a Northern court put it in writing.

Here is what it bought them. The Board agreed to transfer the nine mothers' own children into better schools, and for every other child in Harlem the schools stayed exactly as they were.

The million dollar damages suit went nowhere. And Mae Mallory, already watched by the FBI for years, went down to North Carolina afterward to support Freedom Riders, got accused of kidnapping, and spent years in a prison cell in Cleveland before leaving the country for good.

That is the receipt on a mother who wanted her daughter in a decent school.

All of that happened five years before Baldwin walked into that room and told those teachers to examine their own society. He was not asking them to imagine something.

And one hundred and ten days after he said it, the city answered him. Monday, February 3, 1964, roughly 460,000 New York City schoolchildren did not go to class, close to half the entire system.

Reverend Milton Galamison built it after the Board offered him integration spread across five more years and he refused to wait them out. Annie Stein organized alongside him, and Bayard Rustin ran the logistics five months after running the March on Washington.

There were picket lines outside hundreds of schools, and freedom schools opened in churches to teach Black history for the day. Then a march went on foot across the Brooklyn Bridge to the Board of Education on Livingston Street.

Bigger than the March on Washington, and by the numbers it still stands as the largest civil rights demonstration in American history.

You were probably never taught that it happened.

Read what those children were asking for and you are reading Baldwin's October talk back to him. They wanted children who looked like them in the pictures in the reading books, and Black contributions to history put into the textbooks properly.

They wanted Black principals, and a real number of Black teachers instead of a token. They wanted a child to be able to open a schoolbook and find himself inside it.

Baldwin had already put that in the title. The night he gave the talk it was called The Negro Child: His Self-Image, and the version the country kept is called A Talk to Teachers, named for the grown people in the chairs.

Sixty-some years on, New York State is still the most segregated state in the country for Black students.

In 2018 ninety percent of Black students in New York attended schools that were predominantly nonwhite, and the average Black student in the state sits in a building where roughly fifteen out of every hundred classmates are white.

Not Mississippi. New York.

He told them to examine the society that was educating them, and people have been quoting it ever since as though it were a thought. It was not a thought, because the society that educated him had a street address.

One hundred twenty West 140th Street, Junior High School 139, where Countee Cullen taught him French and told him he was going to be somebody. Twenty years after he walked out of that building, mothers in his own neighborhood stood in a family court rather than send their children into it.

One of them was Viola Waddy, and she had no podium, no publisher, and no magazine cover.

What she had was a reporter from the Amsterdam News named Sara Slack, a notebook, and a court date already on the calendar.

She told Slack they would go to jail and rot there if that was what it took, and their children still were not going into 136, 139, or 120. The Amsterdam News printed it on December 13, 1958, using her own words for the headline.

We'd rather go to jail.

Baldwin gave that idea its most beautiful words, and it deserves every screen it travels on. Nine women in Harlem had already paid its price, in a family court, in December, with their children's names typed onto the paperwork.

Charlene Skipwith. Sheldon Rector.

Twelve years old, filed as neglected.

Next time that sentence comes across your screen on a black square, put their names underneath it.

text:
I'm home after two weeks that felt like two months... and a few of the lessons surprised me.

I met with 3 billionaires, launched Own or Be Owned, walked 170,000 people through the 12 profit levers, met with YouTube execs, recorded podcasts with a guy who's done $2 billion in sales and a woman who's screened 2 million executives, and launched our new business tech product.

Here are 12 lessons from two weeks of too many meetings:

1. Stop improving broken systems. Question why they exist. Joe Liemandt's Alpha School has kids finishing core academics in 2 hours a day while reportedly learning twice as much. Most people would use AI to make the 6 hour school day 10% better. Joe asked why school needs 6 hours at all.

2. Take smarter risks. Jenny Just turned $1.5M into a multibillion-dollar company, PEAK6. Her edge is nearly 30 years of decisions where the feedback is immediate and the stakes are real. Confidence is the receipt you get after surviving risk over and over.

3. Build an ecosystem of assets, not just one business. David Adelman started with student housing (Campus Apartments, $2B+ in assets) and kept going: alternative assets, a family office, the Philadelphia 76ers. Instead of asking what business to build, think about assets you can own to make every other one more valuable.

4. Every billionaire I met was weirdly comfortable being misunderstood. They make fewer decisions, but bigger ones, and they go all in on them. From the outside, that looks crazy. But you can't build an abnormal life while trying to look normal.

5. An audience is not a business. We walked 170,000 people through 12 profit levers in three days. That attention is powerful… but it only matters if it turns into customers.

6. Nothing X-rays a company like a live launch. Three days live exposed every weak spot in our messaging, tech, team, offer and follow up. Too many people joined for Zoom to handle.
Our payments broke. Amazon pulled our listing because the demand looked fake. Scale finds every crack you've been ignoring.

7. Information is cheap. Most owners already know what's wrong. They just need to DO THE THING.

8. The best operators simplify aggressively. A lesson from Dean Graziosi, right hand to Tony Robbins: great operators don't leave a meeting with 30 priorities. They leave with one constraint.

9. Creators are quietly becoming holding companies. Meeting with YouTube execs made this obvious. One video can bring in a customer, a hire, an acquisition, an investor and product launch.

10. The best conversations rarely happen onstage. One of the most valuable ones of the trip was at 9 am in a café. The rest happened backstage, in cars, and in the ten minutes before my next meeting.

11. Growth is usually hiding behind one uncomfortable decision. Raise the price. Kill the offer. Replace the person. Narrow the customer.

Two weeks. Three cities. Three billionaires. One book launch. 170,000 owners.

My biggest takeaway of all?

The next level rarely requires more information... just moving faster.

text:
COREWEAVE $CRWV — WHY I'M BULLISH ON THE BUSINESS, BUT CAUTIOUS ON THE STOCK
I've been looking closely at CoreWeave as part of my AI infrastructure investment series.
After Nebius and IREN, CoreWeave presents a different investment challenge.
The demand is real. Revenue is growing rapidly. Customers are committing billions to AI computing.
But there's something I can't ignore.
CoreWeave is building an enormous AI cloud business using an equally enormous amount of capital.
And that raises a question:
Can CoreWeave turn its massive backlog into sustainable free cash flow without allowing debt and financing costs to overwhelm shareholder returns?
That's where my investment thesis begins.
🟢 1. THE REVENUE GROWTH IS IMPRESSIVE
Look at Q2 2026:
🔹 Revenue: $2.58B, up approximately 112% YoY
🔹 Adjusted EBITDA: $1.51B
🔹 Adjusted EBITDA margin: 59%
🔹 Revenue backlog: approximately $104.2B
🔹 Additional early-Q3 customer commitments: more than $25B, excluded from the June backlog
Those are substantial numbers for a company operating in a relatively young industry.
And they tell me something important.
CoreWeave isn't simply building infrastructure and hoping customers arrive. It already has substantial contracted demand.
But backlog is not recognised revenue, and adjusted EBITDA is not free cash flow.
The company still has to deploy capacity, satisfy contractual obligations and earn enough to cover its financing and infrastructure costs.
🟢 2. COREWEAVE HAS A CLEAR COMPETITIVE IDENTITY
CoreWeave is not trying to replicate every service offered by AWS, Azure or Google Cloud.
Its focus is specialised AI computing.
That includes GPU infrastructure, high-performance networking and software designed to support demanding AI workloads.
And the infrastructure behind that strategy is becoming substantial.
At the end of Q2 2026, CoreWeave reported:
🔹 1.5GW of active power
🔹 Approximately 3.7GW of contracted power
That gives the company considerable capacity to support customers as AI workloads expand.
Its competitive advantage could come from doing a narrower set of things exceptionally well.
For AI developers, speed, reliability and access to computing capacity matter.
But there's a catch.
Specialisation creates opportunity. It doesn't eliminate competition from hyperscalers or other AI cloud providers.
And contracted power is not the same as fully operational, revenue-generating capacity.
CoreWeave must continue proving that its infrastructure can be deployed efficiently and that its platform offers customers a compelling reason to stay.
🟢 3. PRICING POWER IS AN ENCOURAGING SIGNAL
One development caught my attention.
In September, CoreWeave disclosed that it had signed short-duration contracts at approximately $40M per megawatt in annualised revenue pricing.
These contracts generally covered three to six months.
That's encouraging because it suggests demand remains strong enough for CoreWeave to secure attractive pricing on certain new capacity commitments.
But I wouldn't extrapolate that pricing across its entire business.
That figure reflects specific short-duration agreements, not the average realised revenue across CoreWeave's infrastructure.
Shorter contracts introduce renewal risk, and today's favourable GPU pricing may not last indefinitely.
The real opportunity is turning strong demand into durable margins across multiple generations of hardware.
🟢 4. THE CUSTOMER BASE AND BACKLOG PROVIDE VISIBILITY
CoreWeave has built relationships across AI developers, hyperscalers and enterprise customers.
That matters because AI computing demand isn't coming from one industry or one application.
Training large models requires enormous computing resources.
Inference creates a different, potentially recurring demand profile.
Enterprise adoption could broaden the customer base further.
And CoreWeave's reported $104.2B backlog provides substantial visibility into future revenue opportunities.
But visibility isn't certainty.
A large backlog provides visibility, but customer concentration means that visibility can still carry substantial risk.
The timing of revenue recognition, deployment schedules, customer commitments and contract renewal economics all matter.
And I want to see CoreWeave become less dependent on a relatively small group of very large customers over time.
Backlog growth is encouraging. Backlog conversion into profitable, cash-generating revenue is what ultimately matters.
🟠 5. CAPITAL EXPENDITURE IS THE BIGGEST CHALLENGE
This is where I become considerably more cautious.
Management's FY2026 outlook included:
🔹 Revenue: $12.4B–$13.2B
🔹 Capital expenditure: $35B–$39B
That is an extraordinary level of investment relative to current revenue.
Of course, infrastructure is built upfront and generates revenue over time.
So comparing one year's capex with one year's revenue doesn't tell the whole story.
But CoreWeave's SEC filing shows just how capital-intensive this expansion has become.
For the first six months of 2026:
🔹 Operating cash flow: +$3.66B
🔻 Investing cash flow: −$14.87B
🔹 Financing cash flow: +$13.99B
Those figures deserve attention.
CoreWeave is generating positive operating cash flow. That's encouraging.
But its infrastructure investment is substantially larger than the cash being generated internally.
The gap between operating and investing cash flows was approximately $11.2B in just six months.
That isn't a formal free-cash-flow calculation, but it illustrates the scale of the company's funding requirements.
CoreWeave is investing heavily in GPUs, networking equipment, servers and data centre infrastructure.
And much of that investment must happen before the associated revenue and cash flow arrive.
The problem isn't a lack of demand. It's whether the future cash generated by that demand will justify the enormous upfront investment.
The more capital a business requires, the more important its returns on that capital become.
🟠 6. DEBT AND FINANCING COSTS CANNOT BE IGNORED
This is the biggest reason I'm cautious about the stock.
CoreWeave's Q2 2026 results show:
🔹 Adjusted EBITDA: $1.51B
🔹 Adjusted operating income: $128M
🔻 GAAP operating loss: approximately $49M
🔻 Net interest expense: approximately $640M
🔻 Net loss: approximately $626M
That gap matters.
CoreWeave is generating substantial adjusted EBITDA, but depreciation, other operating costs and financing expenses create a very different picture further down the income statement.
Strong adjusted EBITDA doesn't automatically translate into strong earnings or free cash flow.
And the balance sheet makes the challenge even clearer.
At June 30, 2026:
🔻 Total indebtedness: $35.6B
🔹 Cash and equivalents: $5.52B
🔹 Total reported liquidity: $15.55B
That liquidity figure includes approximately $10.01B of available credit facilities. It isn't all unrestricted cash.
CoreWeave reported approximately $13.99B in net cash provided by financing activities during the first half of 2026, highlighting its reliance on external funding to support expansion.
In August, CoreWeave announced a further $2.6B financing facility supported by AI infrastructure and customer commitments.
That provides additional funding flexibility, but the duration of customer contracts relative to financing obligations introduces potential refinancing and residual-value risks.
This isn't automatically a broken business model.
Infrastructure companies often carry significant debt during expansion.
And long-term customer commitments can help support financing.
But the economics still have to work.
CoreWeave must generate enough cash over the life of its infrastructure assets to cover financing costs, depreciation, reinvestment and ultimately deliver returns to shareholders.
Revenue growth can be exceptional while equity returns remain disappointing.
That's the distinction I don't want investors to overlook.
🔴 7. THE RISKS ARE REAL
I see several risks that investors shouldn't underestimate.
🔻 GPU depreciation and technological obsolescence
🔻 Debt servicing and refinancing requirements
🔻 Customer concentration
🔻 Potential shareholder dilution
🔻 Construction and deployment delays
🔻 GPU rental pricing pressure as competition expands
🔻 Contract renewals and infrastructure utilisation
There's also a growing question about how AI infrastructure financing behaves if customer demand, asset values or operating performance deteriorate.
That matters when expensive computing assets are financed against expected future cash flows.
And there's another consideration.
Even if AI demand continues growing, the economics of providing that computing capacity could become more competitive over time.
More infrastructure supply, more efficient chips and changing customer requirements could put pressure on pricing.
A large backlog can support financing. It cannot eliminate financial risk.
🎯 MY TAKEAWAY
I'm bullish on CoreWeave's business opportunity because the company has already demonstrated substantial demand, rapid revenue growth and a strong position in specialised AI computing.
Its infrastructure scale and backlog make it an important player in the AI buildout.
And the positive operating cash flow is encouraging.
But I'm more cautious about the stock.
The market has seen the contracts.
Now I want to see whether CoreWeave can convert:
BACKLOG → REVENUE → OPERATING CASH FLOW → FREE CASH FLOW → SHAREHOLDER RETURNS
That's the investment test.
My bullish case isn't simply that CoreWeave will become a much larger company.
It's that CoreWeave could eventually generate enough cash flow to justify the enormous capital required to build that business.
Until that becomes clearer, I see an attractive AI infrastructure opportunity accompanied by substantial financial risk.
Can CoreWeave grow into its capital structure and generate attractive returns for shareholders, or will financing costs and continued investment absorb too much of the value created?
Bullish on the business. Cautious on the stock. Watching cash flow, debt, utilisation and returns more closely than the backlog headlines.

text:
Why India can’t allow Starlink

99.9% of India has now 5G internet access at the cheapest cost in the world(0.17 dollars),

Starlink offers satellite internet that can reach places where traditional broadband is difficult to provide. And yes, most Indians probably won’t buy it because of its high upfront cost and expensive plans.

So this isn’t necessarily about Starlink replacing Jio or Airtel.

But if most Indians can’t afford it anyway, what exactly is India protecting by keeping it out?

Is there a bigger reason we’re missing?

To understand India, you first need to understand its social and geographical diversity.

Different cultures, religions, languages and communities coexist in incredibly dense spaces. When so many identities, beliefs and traditions share the same streets, public gatherings and celebrations can sometimes turn into flashpoints.

That’s why, around festivals, religious processions and other major gatherings, we often see reports of local clashes and unrest across different parts of the country.

And when political parties get involved, things can become even messier. What might have remained a local dispute can quickly turn into a much larger political confrontation.

Imagine a religious procession in an Indian city. A few people create a disturbance. A local political leader jumps in, fuels tensions, and suddenly, a minor incident starts turning into a riot.

Then someone spreads fake news online claiming that a boy from one community has been kidnapped by another. Panic spreads, people get provoked, and the situation spirals out of control.

In such situations, authorities sometimes suspend mobile internet to contain rumours and prevent further escalation. Is it ideal? No. Is it sometimes used as an emergency measure? Yes.

Now imagine a political leader or an organisation has access to Starlink during such a crisis. If satellite internet remains available while local networks are shut down, they could potentially use it to circulate misinformation and inflame tensions even reaching supporters in other parts of the country.

Now imagine a political leader or an organisation has access to Starlink during such a crisis, they will use this to spread information and spread lies. They can even  provoke their community living in other parts of the country,

The government knows this very well. We haven’t talked about places like Kashmir, where this tech can be used to what extent by militants or Pakistan to communicate with the terrorists.

This is the same reason the Bitchat app was blocked earlier by the govt (Bitchat is basically a Bluetooth-enabled chat app which doesn’t require internet to communicate with your friends). Now Jack Dorsey is not as influential, but Elon is. He knows how to use X, or himself, to pressure other governments or people, whether they support his tech or not.

For the past few days, Elon Musk has been making allegations against the Indian government and Ambani, including claims about funding the BJP.

But here's what I find interesting: Musk himself spent heavily to help Trump win the US election and publicly stood alongside him.

Political parties depend on funding to run election campaigns. People and businesses fund candidates because they believe in their promises, share their ideology, or expect their interests to align.

So why is political funding acceptable when it comes from people Musk supports, but suddenly suspicious when it involves people or parties he opposes?

You can't demand accountability from others while treating your own side as exempt from the same scrutiny.

Here’s a question for America:

If the US can restrict Chinese companies like BYD and Huawei over national security concerns, why should India be expected to welcome Starlink without raising similar questions?

Starlink is an American satellite internet service. There have been concerns about the security implications of foreign-controlled communications infrastructure, including its potential use by intelligence agencies. These concerns deserve serious scrutiny, not blind acceptance.

India has every right to assess who controls the infrastructure, who can access its data, and what risks it could pose to national security.

If national security is a legitimate reason for America to restrict foreign technology, why is it unreasonable for India to apply the same standard to American technology?

National security cannot be a principle that applies only when it benefits America.

I’ve been in Tamil Nadu for the last 4 days, and this morning, something interesting happened.

A family suddenly showed up outside my hotel, asking the reception to call me.

I went downstairs and met the family. He said that he has been following me on social media for the last 2-3 years.

I thanked him and we talked for around thirty minutes, but what was troubling me the most was how he knew I was staying in this hotel.

So I decided to ask. He replied that one of his relatives lives around this area and had spotted me entering the hotel earlier.

The relative felt too shy to come and meet me, so he told him instead, and he brought his  family to see me.

I was at a hospital yesterday, and one person recognised me and started shouting with joy when he saw me.

In my experience, everyone in Tamil Nadu is extremely cheerful and sweet. They will literally go out of their way to help you.

So far, I have met around 10 people who know me, and each of them has gone out of their way to help me.

When I was at the hospital, the guy who recognised me stayed with me for the entire 3 hours because I couldn't speak Tamil.

He spoke to everyone on my behalf in Tamil and then translated everything back to me in English.

I never thought that I’d be getting so much love in Tamil Nadu, or that a state 2,000 km away from my home would have so many people who love me.

If you are not from Tamil Nadu, trust me, everything negative you see about the place on social media is a lie.

Each and every person is sweet and helpful, except auto drivers as they scammed me once, but it’s fine.

Everyone should visit Tamil Nadu once in their life and experience the warmth and love the people here have to offer. It is a truly beautiful state. I've fallen in love.

text:
Islam is not compatible with the west. 

Ani O’Brien Jul 26, 2026
The long campaign to criminalise criticism of Islam continues to demand blasphemy laws.

The Law Commission Hara ngākau kino | Review of hate crime law has surprised me. In an area crowded with panic, symbolism, and bad drafting, it has refused to solve the wrong problem. In Hara ngākau kino, it concluded that New Zealand should keep the current sentencing model, under which hostile motivation aggravates an existing offence, rather than create standalone hate-crime offences. It recommended practical reforms instead, including a hate-crime flag at charging stage, formal recording in court records, express judicial statements when hostility is proved, broader coverage for associated victims and bystanders, the addition of sex to the statutory list, better guidance and training, and annual publication of police and court data.
Just as important, the Commission did not pretend that hate crime and hate speech are the same thing. Hate speech was explicitly outside the scope of the review, even though submitters repeatedly raised it. The report distinguishes between punishing violent or intimidating conduct and criminalising expression about ideas, beliefs, and doctrines. New Zealand should preserve that distinction like its constitutional life depends on it. Because it does.

The political pressure to bring in hate speech laws has not gone away. In fact, it has begun to show a more honest shape, one that is driven largely by demands from Islamic lobbyists for blasphemy laws. The Federation of Islamic Associations of New Zealand’s (FIANZ) own proposed definitions extend well beyond direct incitement of violence to speech that “denigrates”, “demeans”, “vilifies” or promotes hostility towards religious beliefs and practices. Its suggested warning signs include calling members of a group liars, cheats or criminals, alleging conspiracies, or associating the group with child abuse. Note that FIANZ want the belief and practices protected, not just the adherents of the beliefs.

No organisation has pursued the expansion of New Zealand’s hate speech laws with greater persistence than FIANZ. At this point, it is becoming difficult to identify a political controversy involving religion, extremism, or social cohesion that FIANZ does not use as another opportunity to demand restrictions on speech. It has become something approaching organisational singularity.

FIANZ was advocating for expanded hate speech and hate crime laws immediately after the Christchurch mosque attacks in 2019. In 2022, when the Labour Government proposed adding religious belief to the protected categories in the Human Rights Act, FIANZ did not celebrate the change as sufficient progress. It criticised the Government for failing to go further, complained that the proposal did not cover electronic communications adequately, and argued that the relevant provision should instead be placed in the Crimes Act.

In 2023, it demanded a firm timetable, dedicated funding, and additional resources to complete the legislation. FIANZ representatives argued that social cohesion initiatives would not work unless backed by law, dismissed objections as coming from only a small number of people, and suggested that the Ministry of Justice should simply get on with producing the legislation.

When the National-led Government halted the hate speech review in 2024, FIANZ returned to the media to demand an explanation. Its representative insisted that hate speech and hate crime were inseparable and that “you can’t have one without the other.”

In 2025, after Brian Tamaki’s supporters tore and burned religious and political flags at a protest, FIANZ again called for a legislative framework protecting faith communities. The display was ugly, provocative, and deliberately offensive. The correct response in a free country is condemnation, ridicule, counter-protest and, where genuine threats or disorder occur, enforcement of existing law. FIANZ’s instinct was once again to reach for new speech restrictions.

Then, in May 2026, FIANZ warned that New Zealand was experiencing its worst anti-Muslim environment in two decades and renewed calls for “legislative safeguards”. Its chairman described a “hate soup boiling over” and argued that inflammatory rhetoric was creating the conditions for violence. Violence enacted by who?

Yet the minister responsible for the intelligence agencies said the national threat level remained steady, the NZSIS had not identified one ideology as presenting a greater current threat than others, and the Prime Minister said he had seen no intelligence indicating an increased threat specifically to Muslim communities.

And now, following the Law Commission’s 2026 report, FIANZ is back again. Its response was not simply to disagree with the report’s conclusions. It is complaining that hate speech was excluded from the terms of reference and urging political parties to return to the Royal Commission’s proposals. Its spokesperson, Abdur Razzaq, dismissed thousands of free speech submissions as potentially little more than one person repeatedly clicking a button, while presenting FIANZ’s own preferred interpretation of public opinion as authoritative.

To FIANZ, every offensive protest is evidence that speech laws are inadequate, every delay is a betrayal, every review that does not deliver the desired result is too narrow, and every government that hesitates is accused of abandoning vulnerable communities. Most manipulatively, every objection is reframed as indifference to the victims of Christchurch.

The murder of 51 Muslims in Christchurch was an atrocity, and Muslim New Zealanders are entitled to the full protection of the criminal law. But that does not mean FIANZ is entitled to dictate the boundaries of lawful public discussion. Victimhood does not come with a veto over civil liberties, and the horror of one terrorist attack cannot become a permanent blank cheque for censorship.

We must all see FIANZ for what it is; a political organisation that lobbies for greater power for itself. This can be seen in the distinction FIANZ continually blurs between protecting Muslims and protecting Islam. Muslims are people and they possess rights. Islam is a religion and it must remain open to scrutiny, mockery, rejection, and fierce criticism, just as Christianity, Judaism, Hinduism, atheism, and every political ideology must be.

FIANZ participates vigorously in contested cultural debates. In 2023, it issued an “urgent advisory” encouraging Muslim parents to object to Pride Week activities in schools. It provided template letters and urged parents to make their opposition known to principals, boards, and teachers. That was entirely within its democratic rights. Religious communities are free to object to state-funded messages about sexuality and gender. But the principle must work both ways. FIANZ cannot demand the freedom to tell schools that Islamic parents reject aspects of Pride while also seeking laws broad enough to punish criticism that comes the other way.

FIANZ’s persistence is politically understandable. Advocacy groups exist to advocate, and an organisation representing Muslim associations will naturally focus on the fears and interests of Muslim communities. Its original calls for improved recording of hate-motivated crimes were also reasonable. In 2019, it joined calls for police to collect better information and for the law to distinguish hate-motivated offending from ordinary crime. But their campaign has moved far beyond better data and stronger protection from violence. It has become a sustained effort to obtain legal protection from certain forms of expression. And because the definition of “hate” remains elastic, the power being requested would ultimately be exercised not only against violent extremists, but against ordinary citizens.

FIANZ can keep demanding. The rest of us have every right, and every reason, to keep saying “no”.

I repeat: People have rights, religions do not. We understood that when we repealed the offence of blasphemous libel in 2019, with the Government stating that the provision was obsolete and inconsistent with modern protections for freedom of expression. That was the correct decision then, and it remains the correct principle now. The state may protect citizens from threats, discrimination, and violence, but it has no business shielding “sacred” claims from challenge, mockery, insult, or criticism.

International human rights law supports this although it is under similar pressure to capitulate to the Islamic lobby. The UN Human Rights Committee’s General Comment 34 states that prohibitions on displays of lack of respect for a religion, including blasphemy laws, are incompatible with the ICCPR except in narrow circumstances, and it specifically says such laws cannot be used to prevent criticism of religious leaders or commentary on doctrine and tenets of faith. The Rabat Plan of Action went further and called national blasphemy laws counter-productive because they stifle the healthy debate and criticism that free societies need.

New Zealand’s own public authorities already recognise the difference. Police explain that some hateful expression may be “awful but lawful” and that speech alone is not a basis for arrest unless it crosses a criminal threshold. A liberal democracy does not merely protect the devout. It protects the sceptic, the apostate, the dissenter, the atheist, the reformer, and the person who has left the faith community of their birth. The moment the law starts treating criticism of religion as legally suspect, those people are the first to lose.

New Zealand keeps batting back attempts at speech suppression. Aside from the almost-introduction of hate speech laws under Labour a few years ago, there was also the fortunately terminated Human Rights (Incitement on Ground of Religious Belief) Amendment Bill which would have extended sections 61 and 131 of the Human Rights Act to religious belief, using language about words that are “threatening, abusive, or insulting” and likely to excite hostility or bring groups into contempt or ridicule. Elastic definitions of “hostility” would have been used not to protect Muslims as citizens but to slide into protecting Islam as an ideology.

Blasphemy-style laws repeat old hierarchies and function as power grabs. They protect the beliefs of some people from criticism, make it easier for them to punish ex-believers, and tell women inside conservative faith communities that they may not complain of mistreatment because it denigrates the theology underwriting it. It is a process of enforced submission.

If you think this is all theoretical, you should look overseas. Pakistan’s blasphemy regime has roots in British colonial law, but its modern Islamic expansions have created some of the harshest religious-offence provisions in the world. Academic Junaid Hafeez was arrested after students accused him of anti-Islam blasphemy on social media, held in solitary confinement after attacks by other prisoners, and sentenced to death in 2019. His lawyer, Rashid Rehman, was murdered.

Indonesia offers the same lesson in another form. Human Rights Watch reported that restrictions on the Ahmadiyah community, sold by officials as necessary to reduce violence, in fact fuelled hatred and failed to stop attacks. Reuters has also reported that Indonesian courts jailed comedian Aulia Rakhman for joking about the name Muhammad.

Even Britain, which abolished blasphemy laws, shows how quickly the same instinct returns by another route. Section 29J of the Public Order Act expressly protects discussion, criticism, ridicule, insult and abuse of religions and their beliefs or practices. That safeguard exists because Parliament understood that protecting believers from hatred must not become a ban on criticising belief. Yet Hamit Coskun was still prosecuted and convicted in 2025 after burning a Qur’an outside the Turkish consulate, before his conviction was overturned on appeal. The original conviction, and the CPS’s earlier use of wording directed at the “religious institution of Islam”, showed how easily ordinary public-order tools can be steered towards de facto blasphemy when officials forget the difference between hostility to people and attack on ideas. If that can happen in a jurisdiction with an explicit free-expression clause, New Zealand should not flatter itself that vague “anti-hostility” definitions would stay narrow here.

The current terrorism landscape does not justify insulating ideology from criticism. The terrible Christchurch Terror Attack in 2019 is often used as a justification as to why free speech should be disregarded in favour of blasphemy laws. It is incredibly hard to argue against invocations of the massacre as we are somewhat collectively traumatised by the horrors of that day.

Nonetheless, if we are actually honest about the true nature of terrorism in the 21st century it must be acknowledged that there is something profoundly absurd about creating new protections around Islam. Across the Western world, security agencies are dealing with a continuous stream of Islamist plots, radicalisation cases, terrorist propaganda, attempted attacks, and completed atrocities. The threat is very real, immediate, organised, and ideological. It consumes enormous police and intelligence resources every day. Why should the ideology that is behind the overwhelming majority of terroristic violent attacks globaly be the one our governments protect?

The Global Terrorism Index 2026 reports that terrorism deaths in the West surged by 280%. The same body reports that youth radicalisation is rising and that lone-wolf attacks accounted for 93% of fatal attacks in the West over recent years. That is the profile of a threat that is decentralised, memetic, online, emotionally charged, and often wrapped in political or religious grievance. You do not defeat that threat by teaching the public that the ideology behind it may not be named, analysed or condemned without legal risk. You meet it by exposing ideas to light before they harden into permission for violence.

Caveat time. Of course that does not mean ordinary Muslims are terrorists, although moderates do not tend to speak out or condemn the extremists much. It does mean that Islamist terrorism is real, persistent, and disproportionately significant within the contemporary scope of terrorist threats.

There is also a moral obscenity in responding to Islamist violence by curtailing the freedoms of its intended victims. Jihadists have repeatedly murdered people for drawing cartoons, writing books, teaching history, leaving Islam, criticising clerics or simply refusing to obey religious taboos. To answer that violence by making the taboo more enforceable is to reward the threat. This is a thugs’ veto. It tells the fanatic that intimidation works.

Instead of confronting this reality, we are constantly told that the urgent problem is actually excessive scrutiny of Islam. Apparently, while police officers investigate bomb-making, knife plots, recruitment networks, and teenagers consuming jihadist propaganda, the rest of us must become more circumspect about discussing the belief system invoked by the perpetrators.

A religion that is overtly political and that makes claims about law, sex, family, dress, apostasy, blasphemy, warfare, and the organisation of the state is theocratic. And we must ensure it cannot enter the public square carrying a rulebook for everyone else and then demand immunity from reply.

Islam is not a race nor an immutable characteristic. It is a collection of theological claims, moral rules, historical traditions, legal doctrines, and political interpretations. And there is a legitimate and necessary right to criticise Islam for doctrines and practices that are fundamentally at odds with liberal democracy. That statement should not be controversial. Religions are systems of ideas and those ideas affect real people, especially when religious institutions seek political influence or when believers attempt to turn doctrine into law.

Islamic societies and institutions vary, but there are plainly significant numbers of Muslims whose interpretations of Islam subordinate women. These can include male guardianship of adult women, unequal inheritance, unequal evidential status, restrictions on dress and movement, tolerance of polygamy for men, pressure into arranged or forced marriages, acceptance of male violence, and systems in which divorce is substantially easier for husbands than wives. In some jurisdictions, women are punished for sexual conduct, pregnancy outside marriage, or alleged breaches of modesty while male violence against them is excused, minimised or concealed. Underage marriage for girls is also widely accepted by the faith.

It is not anti-Muslim to say that these practices are wrong. It would, in fact, be a betrayal of Muslim women not to say it.

Western feminists would never accept the argument that Christianity must be protected from criticism because some Christians might feel targeted. They readily criticise Catholic teachings on abortion, evangelical views on sexuality, and conservative Christian attitudes toward women. Yet that strident advocacy for women’s rights collapses when Islam is involved. Fear of appearing prejudiced overrides the basic feminist obligation to tell the truth on behalf of women.

The same double standard appears in relation to homosexuality. In Muslim-majority countries, homosexuality remains criminalised, and penalties can include imprisonment, corporal punishment, or death. Even where such laws are not enforced to their maximum extent, gay people face family rejection, forced marriage, intimidation, blackmail, and violence. A gay person has every right to criticise a religion whose authoritative texts, clerics or institutions describe his or her relationships as immoral, corrupting or worthy of punishment. It is frankly insane that when Islam advocates for our murder we are condemned for calling it out.

Tolerance cannot mean that liberal people must tolerate doctrines that deny their equality while being forbidden to describe those doctrines honestly. This is where Karl Popper’s tolerance fallacy is evident. A society committed to tolerance cannot survive if tolerance is interpreted as an obligation to submit indefinitely to movements that reject reciprocity, suppress dissent, and seek to deprive others of the very freedoms they themselves enjoy.

The Paradox of Tolerance: Should We Not Tolerate Some Views? – Builders

Popper’s argument was that danger arises when tolerance ceases to be a liberal virtue and becomes a tool by which illiberalism advances.

Liberal societies rightly allow Muslims to practise their religion. But liberalism cannot require women, gay people, apostates or secular critics to remain politely silent about doctrines that subordinate them. It cannot offer religious conservatives the freedom to condemn homosexuality while denying homosexuals the freedom to condemn religious homophobia. It cannot protect the right to teach that women must obey men while treating feminist criticism of that teaching as hatred. The bargain is not that one group may make sweeping moral claims about everybody else while its own beliefs are placed off limits.

The paradox of tolerance is not an excuse for suppressing Islam, nor for restricting the civil liberties of Muslims. It is a warning against allowing tolerance to be manipulated into surrender. Liberalism must be confident enough to defend freedom of religion without abandoning freedom from religion, and to protect minority communities without granting minority doctrines authority over what the rest of us may say.

When extremist violence is committed in the religion’s name, it is preceded by ideas including a theory of divine authority, a division between believer and infidel, a grievance rendered sacred, a justification for violence, and a promise of spiritual reward. Police may disrupt the final stages, but a free society also has to challenge the preceding arguments. That requires people to be free to discuss doctrine, expose preachers, compare interpretations, investigate institutions, satirise and critique, and say plainly when an idea is dangerous.

You cannot counter extremist ideology while forbidding accurate descriptions of it.

Censorship hands extremists a monopoly. Special definitions of “Islamophobia” or “anti-Muslim hostility” begin with conduct everyone agrees is wrong, such as threatening Muslims or denying them equal treatment, then expand until criticism of Islamic beliefs, political movements, or historical practices is treated as an attack on Muslim people. The protected category shifts from the believer to the belief.

That is how a blasphemy law is built in a secular country. Nobody announces that God must be protected from insult. They say a community must be protected from harm and redefine theological criticism as group hostility. The enforcement mechanism may be a criminal prosecution, an employment investigation, a regulatory complaint, or a professional sanction, but the message is the same: you cannot criticise Islam.

Christianity is criticised relentlessly in New Zealand, and that is fair game in a free society. Its scriptures are mocked and its teachings on sexuality, marriage, abortion, and sex/gender are challenged in the media, universities, and politics. Christians may object, protest, boycott, or attempt to persuade others that the criticism is unfair. What they cannot do is demand that the state silence their critics. That is how a liberal democracy should function. No religion has a right to legal protection from criticism simply because its adherents find it offensive.

The same principle must apply equally to every religion. Muslims are entitled to the full protection of the law against threats, discrimination, and violence, just as Jewish New Zealanders are entitled to protection from the disturbing rise in antisemitism seen since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023. But protecting people does not require protecting ideas. Islam may be criticised for its doctrines, history, institutions, or treatment of women, homosexuals, apostates, blasphemy, or political authority, just as Christianity and Judaism may be criticised for theirs. Religious ideas belong in the marketplace of ideas alongside every other worldview. They should succeed or fail through persuasion, not legal privilege.

So the choice in front of New Zealand is not between caring about vulnerable communities and defending free speech. That is a false framing, and it has done enough damage already. The real choice is between a legal order that protects citizens as equal rights-bearers, and a legal order that starts smuggling sacred immunity and blasphemy laws back into public life under therapeutic language. The Law Commission has shown the better path with stronger consequences for hate-motivated violent offending, clearer denunciation, better data, better enforcement, no new offence architecture built on a nebulous concept of hate, and no confusion between violence and disagreement.

New Zealand repealed blasphemous libel because it recognised that modern democracy cannot treat irreverence as a crime. It should not now recreate the same logic in updated vocabulary. We do not need anti-blasphemy law with a diversity label. We do not need a doctrine of “religious harm” so malleable that it chills journalists, apostates, ex-Muslims, feminists, satirists, scholars, and ordinary citizens who want to speak plainly about what religions teach and demand. We need a state confident enough to say that no mosque, church, temple, synagogue, prophet, scripture, imam, pastor or ideology is above criticism. Not one.

text:
🌊 Where History Meets the Horizon: The Yellow Sea from Penglai Pavilion, Yantai, Shandong, China 🇨🇳

Standing at the magnificent Penglai Pavilion, one is greeted by a breathtaking panorama of the vast Yellow Sea, where the endless blue waters merge seamlessly with the distant horizon. Located in the coastal city of Yantai, this iconic historical landmark offers a captivating blend of natural beauty, cultural heritage, and timeless Chinese charm.

Perched along the northern coast of the Shandong Peninsula, Penglai Pavilion is renowned for its rich history, traditional Chinese architecture, and legendary association with the mythical Eight Immortals, who are said to have crossed the sea. For centuries, this enchanting coastal setting has inspired poets, artists, scholars, and travelers with its mystical atmosphere and spectacular seascapes.

From the pavilion, the expansive Yellow Sea unfolds like a living canvas, its shimmering waters reflecting the changing hues of the sky. Gentle sea breezes, distant coastal landscapes, and the tranquil rhythm of the waves create a sense of serenity, inviting visitors to pause and appreciate the harmony between land, sea, and sky.

More than just a scenic viewpoint, Penglai Pavilion is a place where China’s ancient legends meet the beauty of the natural world. Every glance across the sea evokes a sense of wonder, reminding us of the enduring connection between history, mythology, and the vastness of nature.

text:
🏝️ Europe’s Most Beautiful Islands That Look Like Paradise on Earth! 🌊✨

Here are 10 of Europe’s most beautiful islands to add to your travel bucket list! 🌍

🌋 1. Santorini, Greece 💙
Whitewashed houses, blue-domed churches, volcanic cliffs, and legendary sunsets over the Aegean Sea. 🌅

🏖️ 2. Sardinia, Italy 💎
Discover emerald waters, powdery white beaches, and the spectacular coastline of the Costa Smeralda. 🐚

💙 3. Hvar, Croatia ⛵
A Mediterranean gem featuring lavender fields, historic stone streets, hidden coves, and crystal-clear waters. 🌿

🌿 4. Madeira, Portugal 🌺
A paradise of green mountains, dramatic sea cliffs, misty forests, and breathtaking coastal hiking trails. 🏞️

🏰 5. Skye, Scotland 🧚
Explore otherworldly landscapes, rugged coastlines, fairy-tale rock formations, and the magical Fairy Pools. 🌫️

🌊 6. Capri, Italy 🛥️
Famous for its Blue Grotto, towering Faraglioni sea stacks, and glamorous Mediterranean charm. ✨

🐚 7. Milos, Greece 🤍
Home to surreal white volcanic rock formations, colourful fishing villages, and the lunar-like beach of Sarakiniko. 🌊

🌺 8. Mallorca, Spain ☀️
From turquoise hidden coves to the dramatic Serra de Tramuntana mountains, Mallorca offers the perfect mix of adventure and relaxation. 🏖️

❄️ 9. Lofoten Islands, Norway 🌌
Imagine red fishing cabins beneath towering mountains, Arctic beaches, midnight sun in summer, and Northern Lights in winter. 🏔️

🌴 10. Corsica, France 🐬
A stunning blend of rugged mountains, turquoise bays, charming hilltop villages, and the dramatic cliffs of Bonifacio. 💙

✨ The best part? Every island has its own personality. Whether you dream of Mediterranean beach escapes, wild Arctic scenery, or peaceful mountain villages beside the sea, Europe has an island waiting for you.

💬 Your turn: Which island would you visit first — Santorini, Madeira, Milos, or Lofoten? Tell us in the comments!

📌 Save this post for your next European adventure and share it with someone who dreams of island hopping! 🌍✈️

Gavi Mutt Seer Inaugurates Mysuru Dasara 2026; CM D.K. Shivakumar Hails Festival as Symbol of Harmony

Mysuru, Karnataka

Sri Abhinava Gavisiddeshwara Swamiji, seer of the renowned Gavi Mutt in Koppal, inaugurated the #MysuruDasara 2026 festivities atop Chamundi Hills on Sunday by lighting the ceremonial lamp and offering floral tributes to Goddess Chamundeshwari.

The inauguration was held at 12:07 pm during the auspicious Dhanur lagna. The presiding deity, adorned in Hamsavaahini alankaara and draped in a purple saree, was placed in a specially erected silver mantapa beside the #ChamundeshwariTemple.
Chief Minister #DKShivakumar joined the seer for the inaugural ceremony. Earlier, the dignitaries offered special prayers at the temple before participating in the official programme.

Addressing the gathering, Abhinava Gavisiddeshwara Swamiji described Mysuru Dasara as a celebration that connects #Karnataka's rich heritage across generations.“Dasara narrates the glory of our past, energises the present and serves as a guiding force for the future. It is a Triveni Sangama of the past, present and future. This reflects the greatness of #Kannada land and the depth of Karnataka's cultural heritage,” he said.

The event witnessed the participation of more than 200 pontiffs from various mutts, along with spiritual leaders representing different faiths, including #Sikh and #Tibetan delegations, highlighting the festival's spirit of inclusivity and communal harmony.

Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar emphasized the administration's commitment to inclusive progress, invoking the symbolic meaning of lighting the ceremonial lamp.
​"The revered Swamiji noted that lighting the lamp signifies a confluence of four guiding lights of thought," Shivakumar said. "The power of Chamundi represents strength, the Swamiji represents wisdom, Dasara embodies our culture and our government stands as the flame of equality."

Invoking poet laureate Kuvempu's vision of Karnataka, the Chief Minister said the state government remains committed to fostering peace, harmony and inclusive development, "Through strength comes achievement, through wisdom comes development, through culture comes equality and through equality comes peace,” he said.

Elaborate security arrangements were made across Chamundi Hills and #Mysuru city for the high-profile event. The security measures were overseen by #MysuruPolice Commissioner Seema Latkar to ensure the smooth conduct of the #Dasara inauguration.

Mysuru Dasara, Karnataka's state festival, is celebrated as a showcase of the state's cultural heritage and traditions, drawing lakhs of devotees and visitors from across the country and abroad.

@GovTimWalz @keithellison You both are the handmaidens of Satan.  Truly Demonic.
From a Christian perspective grounded in Scripture, the central issue is the status and treatment of a living human being once born.

The Bible consistently treats human life—including the life of the unborn and the newly born—as bearing the image of God and therefore possessing intrinsic dignity and worth. Genesis 1:27 and 9:6 establish that human beings are made in God’s image, which is the foundation for the prohibition against taking innocent human life (Exodus 20:13; Genesis 9:5–6). Psalm 139:13–16 and Jeremiah 1:5 describe God’s intimate knowledge and forming of a person even in the womb. Luke 1:41–44 shows the unborn John the Baptist responding to the presence of the unborn Jesus, indicating personhood before birth. Once a child is born alive—breathing, with a beating heart, or other signs of life—Scripture offers no basis for treating that child as anything less than a full human person under God’s protection.

Proverbs 6:16–17 lists “hands that shed innocent blood” among the things the Lord hates. Jesus repeatedly elevated the vulnerable and the little ones (Matthew 18:1–6, 10; 19:14). He warned that it would be better for someone to have a millstone hung around their neck than to cause one of these little ones to stumble or perish. The biblical pattern is one of defending the weak, the orphan, and the infant, not creating legal space in which their survival is made less mandatory.

In the specific case of an infant born alive (including after an attempted abortion), Christian ethics rooted in these texts would require the same reasonable, life-preserving medical care that would be given to any other infant of comparable viability and condition. Distinguishing between comfort care for a child with a condition incompatible with life and the deliberate withholding of ordinary measures that could preserve the life of a viable infant is a medically and morally significant line. Changing a statute so that the explicit duty shifts from “preserve the life and health” to a more general “care,” while simultaneously ending reporting requirements, moves the legal standard in the direction of less protection for that born infant. From a biblical standpoint, that direction is difficult to reconcile with the duty to protect the innocent and the vulnerable.

The visible celebration at the signing does not change the legal text, but it does reveal priorities. Scripture repeatedly contrasts those who rejoice over the shedding of innocent blood or the oppression of the weak with those who mourn and act for justice (see, for example, the prophetic critiques in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel). A Christian response is not primarily one of rhetorical labels such as “demonic,” but of sober recognition that a society’s laws and public rejoicing over the reduced protection of the smallest and most dependent members reveal what that society values most.

Christian conviction on this point does not require denying medical realities, the rarity of the cases, or the difference between pre-viable infants and those who could survive with ordinary care. It does require insisting that once a child is born alive, that child is a neighbor whose life is not disposable and whose protection is not optional. The biblical call remains to “rescue those being led away to death” (Proverbs 24:11) and to treat the least of these in a manner consistent with the image of God they bear.

New system that generates power, charges drones, and offers launch space can transform warfare | Prabhat Ranjan Mishra, Interesting Engineering

A new system has been introduced and it integrates renewable energy, autonomous robotics and unmanned aircraft to support continuous drone operations without conventional fuel resupply.

Persistent Drone Operations Nanogrid, the first integrated solution that combines Sesame Solar’s self-generating mobile power, Target Arm’s robotic arm and drone magazines for autonomous drone launch and recovery, and AG3 Labs’ attritable, unmanned aircraft into a single system for training and forward expeditionary use.

Continuous drone operations with no fuel resupply

This solution will enable continuous drone operations with no fuel resupply. Operators can remotely monitor the Nanogrid’s energy performance and control the robotic arm and drones.

“Mobile electric power is a critical fifth supply requirement along with food, water, munitions, and fuel. If a forward expeditionary team can’t power its drones, or their batteries fail from heat or cold, warfighters lose one of their most valuable assets,” said Lauren Flanagan, CEO and co-founder of Sesame Solar.

“Together with Target Arm and AG3 Labs, we’ve built a comprehensive solution that eliminates the fuel supply chain while keeping drones in the air for extended durations.”

The launch comes as federal policy moves decisively toward domestic production. Executive Order 14307 directs agencies to expand U.S. UAS manufacturing and reduce reliance on foreign-made drones, and the Department of Defense has moved this year to arm units with small, U.S.-sourced drones at scale. As a domestically manufactured solution, the Persistent Drone Operations Nanogrid meets these requirements, while providing a comprehensive solution that improves operational readiness and supply chain security.

A drone is only as good as its next charge. The U.S. Army has documented this gap, citing that there is no standard procedure to get backup power out to a drone launch team. In remote, contested or austere environments, an autonomous solution that can transport, charge and safely store in a wide range of temperatures, launch, recover and recharge drones with minimal detection signatures can save lives while improving mission outcomes, according to a press release.

“Every system we build at Target Arm starts with the same question: does this bring someone home safe?” said Jeffrey A. McChesney, CEO & Founder of Target Arm.

“The launch and the recovery are two of the most exposed moments of a drone mission – someone standing in the open, waiting on an aircraft. Ralar takes a person out of that moment entirely. What makes our system even more unique is that drones can be launched from a moving vehicle or a boat, so warfighters never need to stop to complete their mission.”

The solution integrates Target Arm’s Ralar system, which is an autonomous robotic arm launch and recovery system that lets drones deploy, recover, recharge and relaunch with no pilot on-site and while moving. TargetArm’s drone magazines work with the Ralar system to autonomously cycle drones through deployment, for persistent 24/7/365 coverage.

ISR, communications relay and, for defense users, kinetic payloads. SPADE can be flown one-to one or controlled one-to-many as an autonomous swarm, supporting training, first responder, law enforcement, military and special operations missions.

The Persistent Drone Operations Nanogrid is available as a stand alone solution or in a series of two to twelve Nanogrids, creating a turnkey MIL-STD mobile microgrid, which can also charge man-portable batteries and other forward expeditionary equipment.

“Operators shouldn’t need a different drone for every mission — they need one airframe they can reconfigure in the field and put up in numbers,” said Nick Smock, Co-Founder/Head of Growth at AG3Labs.

“Put that on a system that launches, recovers and recharges itself, and you have persistent capability without adding a single person to the team.”

text:
Mobility Service Dogs, a Steady Partner for Every Day
Sunday, Oct 11, 2026

For many people with physical disabilities, independence comes down to small things: a phone dropped on the floor, a door that will not open, a light switch out of reach. Mobility service dogs are trained to handle those moments. The US Department of Justice ADA guidance lists pulling a wheelchair among the tasks that make a dog a service animal, and notes that the task must be directly related to the person's disability.

Canine Companions, which has paired service dogs with people with disabilities free of charge since 1975, trains its dogs to retrieve and deliver dropped items, tug open doors and drawers, push automatic door plates, turn lights on and off, help remove a sock or jacket, and pull a lightweight manual wheelchair over a short distance.

Some mobility dogs also do balance work such as counterbalance or bracing, where the handler leans on the dog to steady themselves or stand up. This is demanding work for a dog's body, and not every program offers it. Canine Companions says it does not place dogs to bear weight while walking or getting up after a fall.

The Mobility Dog Resource Group, working with veterinarians and service dog organizations, recommends that dogs doing load bearing work be physically mature, usually 18 to 24 months old or more, with X rays of the hips, low back, elbows and shoulders, and a custom fitted mobility harness. For bracing, it recommends a dog at least 24 inches tall at the withers and at least half the partner's weight, with only a few pounds of pressure, briefly and only while the dog stands square and still. Atlas Assistance Dogs notes that some organizations are moving away from bracing in favor of counterbalance and momentum pulling.

When you see a mobility team out in public, the kindest thing is to let the dog work. That steady, quiet partner is doing a job that keeps someone moving through their day.

Watch Dogs of Service from Iowa PBS on YouTube

Sources: US Department of Justice ADA guidance, Canine Companions, Mobility Dog Resource Group, Atlas Assistance Dogs, photos via Wikimedia Commons by Zipster969 of Pawsitivity Service Dogs and John Robert McPherson, CC BY SA 4.0.

**The main legal issues raised in the post (and its immediate thread) are these:**

- **Lanham Act § 43(a) reverse passing off for creative works**  
  The post’s core discussion is accurate: after *Dastar Corp. v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp.* (2003), reverse-passing-off claims under the Lanham Act are heavily restricted when the dispute involves writings, analyses, videos, frameworks, or other communicative/expressive content. The Supreme Court held that “origin of goods” means the producer of the tangible product offered for sale, not the author of the ideas or content embodied in it. Allowing reverse-passing-off claims merely to force authorship credit would create a perpetual quasi-copyright outside the Copyright Act’s limited term and formalities. Courts (including in Oregon) have applied this to reject pure attribution claims for copyrightable or copyrighted expressive material. Lack of credit alone is generally not enough when the defendant produces the copies being distributed.

- **Copyright as the primary available remedy**  
  The post correctly identifies copyright infringement (unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or derivative works of original expression fixed in a tangible medium) as the stronger and more direct route for the types of Blogspot writings, behavioral analyses, frameworks, and videos the author describes. It notes the practical advantages of U.S. Copyright Office registration (statutory damages, attorney’s fees, presumptions of validity, and the ability to sue in federal court) and the utility of DMCA notices. Ideas, facts, and concepts themselves are not protected—only the particular expression.

- **Narrower surviving Lanham Act theories**  
  False-advertising claims under § 43(a)(1)(B) can sometimes still be viable if a defendant makes affirmative, material commercial misrepresentations about the nature, characteristics, qualities, or source of the work (beyond simple non-attribution). Reverse passing off remains more available for tangible physical goods from which marks are removed. State unfair-competition claims are generally weak alternatives for pure creative works because they often track *Dastar* and face copyright preemption under 17 U.S.C. § 301 when they essentially allege unauthorized copying of expressive content.

- **Personal allegations of trademark theft and related harms**  
  The author claims she has a “stolen trademark,” has been deemed too disabled to own her own agency or work, and is on fixed income. In the surrounding thread she alleges long-running appropriation of her research/blog content (described as reverse passing off and related cybersquatting), identity issues, and inaction by Eugene Police on reports she says she mapped out. These remain unadjudicated public assertions; the post itself frames the legal discussion as general information, not legal advice for any specific situation, and notes that outcomes depend on facts, evidence, and jurisdiction.

- **Police / institutional response issues**  
  Hashtags and related posts in the thread allege that police have engaged in or enabled reverse passing off, treated crime victims as enemies, or failed to act on mapped reports involving IP and related claims. Police generally have broad discretion not to investigate civil intellectual-property disputes; such matters are ordinarily pursued through civil litigation, Copyright Office processes, or platform tools rather than criminal enforcement.

In short, the post’s doctrinal summary of *Dastar* and the limited role of reverse passing off for creative works is solid, while the personal trademark, disability, content-appropriation, and police-related claims are presented as the author’s own unresolved allegations. For any real dispute of this type, copyright registration and enforcement plus consultation with an IP attorney are the pathways the post itself emphasizes.
