text:
Florida prints the username and password to its business filings on a public web page.

Log in and you get the filings the state added that workday for free.

Most marketers who find it grab the brand-new LLCs and start pitching.

So does everyone else.

And registering a company tells you very little about what it can afford or needs help with.

The more interesting list is businesses that just changed something.

Colorado gives this data away too. 

Its September file had:

11,450 new LLCs.
622 name changes.
42 merger filings.
31 LLCs converted to corporations.

Most marketers stop at the first line.

A name change can point to a rebrand or acquisition. A merger can leave teams working across separate CRMs, books, and processes. Converting an LLC to a corporation can accompany plans to raise money.

None of those guarantees a buyer.

But each gives you something specific to investigate before you pitch.

Compare that with buying a database, filtering for recent funding, and emailing the same founders everyone else found.

By the time you spot the announcement, their inbox is already filling up.

A state filing gives you another place to look.

Here's how I'd use it.

Start with a state that makes the data available.

Florida publishes free daily files of new filings and events. Annual reports and address changes aren't included, so don't build a “they just moved” campaign around those downloads.

Colorado publishes its business register and transaction history on data,colorado,gov.

Then pick ONE event that connects to something you sell.

If you build websites, investigate name changes. Compare the old and new names, then check the website, Google results, and business listings for inconsistencies.

If you handle CRM migrations or bookkeeping, investigate mergers. Find out which companies are involved and whether they’re combining operations.

Treat conversions as a weaker signal. Check for hiring, expansion, or funding plans before deciding there's an opportunity.

The filing is your starting point. The research gives you the offer.

Next, find the actual decision maker.

The name on the filing may belong to a lawyer or filing service. Colorado doesn't require LLCs to list their owners.

Find the company website, identify who handles the problem you spotted, then use an email tool to find their contact details.

And give them something better than “we help businesses like yours.”

For a name change, I'd check for lingering references to the old name BEFORE sending:

“Hey [name], saw the name change filed this month. Are you updating the brand too? Found a couple of listings still using [old name]. Want me to send them over?”

Only say you found them if you actually did.

Now you've given them a reason to reply. And their answer tells you whether there's a bigger project behind it.

Do a small batch each week. Track which filing types lead to real conversations and paid work.

That's how you find out whether you've found a useful buying signal or just another list.

Include a real postal address and an opt-out in your emails, and honor it.

P.S. Which filing would you watch for what you sell?

text: When will it finally be enough? When will we stop, in effect, playing for Team Trump?  Putin's attacks on the Ukrainian civilian population are growing ever more brutal.  But Trump isn't calling for Putin to finally be put in his place. No: Ukraine needs a new president.  On Saturday, Russian glide bombs struck residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia. 20 dead, including three children. One of them was a six-year-old girl. Her birthday would have been at the end of the month, her grandfather said through tears.  Zelenskyy says this is how Russia thanked him for easing the diesel sanctions: with five glide bombs on residential buildings.  With the man responsible for this war, Trump is closing diesel deals, loosening sanctions, and spreading the lie that Zelenskyy is to blame for everything.  In September, Zelenskyy was still thanking him for the "hellish sanctions" law against Russia. In October, the same Trump loosens sanctions against Russia so the diesel can flow.  Zelenskyy could have ended the war many times by now, Trump piles on. That Ukraine has repeatedly offered ceasefires and Putin rejected them—he lies away in front of running cameras.  When will it be enough for us? When will someone in Europe finally demand economic sanctions against Trump?  But we'll keep wrinkling our noses and otherwise staying silent. At least as long as Europe can't replace the American intelligence data itself.  That's Trump's leverage. Because the biggest concern in Kyiv isn't even his remark about the "new president," but that he might halt intelligence cooperation with Ukraine. According to the Financial Times, the US has already threatened in talks in Miami to restrict cooperation if Ukraine continues its attacks on Russian refineries.  And yet the same Financial Times reported a year ago that US intelligence had spent months helping Kyiv hit exactly those kinds of refineries. When it comes to reconnaissance and especially early warning against missile attacks, there are still sensitive dependencies.  Less reconnaissance means less warning. And less warning can mean more dead. More children under rubble like now in Zaporizhzhia. Trump knows what power this dependency gives him. That's why he can afford such threats.  The rest is almost banal: Already in September, the diesel price in the US had hit a record high of six dollars per gallon, and on November 3rd, the election is held. That diesel is so expensive mainly because of the Iran war, which Trump himself started in February, he conveniently leaves out. The arsonist demands that Ukraine, which is already in flames, now help him put out the fire.  Trump wants Kyiv to spare Putin's refineries so people in Ohio can fill up cheaper. He hasn't made a comparable public demand in this context that Putin finally stop his attacks on Ukrainian cities.  The uncomfortable answer to the question "How much longer?" is therefore: until Europe can close this gap itself. With its own reconnaissance, air defense, and ammunition.  And that's when I wonder how our Europe—with its scientists, engineers, industries, and its enormous economic potential—still hasn't managed, in the fifth year of this war, to have solutions for TODAY.  Not just sometime, when there might not be much left of Ukraine.  And yes, Europe has economic leverage against Washington. The EU has a ready package of countermeasures in the drawer, affecting US imports worth 93 billion euros. At the end of July, the Commission suspended it again, this time without an end date.  In principle, it could be reactivated, though it was created for the trade conflict with the US, not for Trump's Ukraine policy.  But for that, we'd need the guts that the Easter bunny brings us. Europe could hurt the US economically where it hurts. But for that, it would have to be willing to pay a price itself.  And that doesn't sell well at the ballot box or in the balance sheets.  That's why we're faced today with a grotesque situation: Ukraine has been defending itself for more than four and a half years against a Russian war of annihilation.  And the president of its most important ally is doing business with the aggressor, demanding military restraint from the attacked country, and calling for the ouster of its president.  Europe protests. Europe worries. Europe looks to Washington.  Putin keeps bombing. And Trump remains our closest ally. And for lunch today, there are fish sticks.

text:
When I lived in Georgia, I told my American neighbor I was “away to get the messages.”

“Post office?” he asked.

“No, I need potatoes.”

He looked at me for a moment, giving Scotland every opportunity to explain itself.

Back home, “the messages” means groceries.

Once we’d settled that, he offered me a lift.

At the supermarket, I picked up a small chicken.

“How many are you feeding?”

“Just me.”

He considered this, then put a larger chicken in my basket.

“Come over tonight. We’ll stick it on the grill.”

By six, his wife had made a salad and another neighbour had brought corn. I offered to help and was given a beer and a chair, apparently both essential to the cooking process.

We sat outside until the porch lights came on.

I’d intended to buy enough for a quiet dinner alone. Instead, there were six of us passing bowls round a table.

As I left, he called after me.

“Next time you need messages, knock first.”

I’ve never had such a lovely arrangement with a postman.

text:
A county party boss struck 5,286 voters off Gary's rolls, most of them Black. It was the fall of 1967, and those voters were about to choose Richard Hatcher, a 34-year-old lawyer, as the first Black mayor of their Indiana steel town. The boss could do it because he sat on the board that ran the county's elections. So how did every one of those names get back on the list before Election Day?

Hatcher wired the U.S. attorney general, Ramsey Clark, and asked the Justice Department to step in. Then he went into federal court and charged that the county's party officials were breaking the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

That took nerve, because he was suing the party whose nomination he had just won, under a law barely two years old.

Within two days, every name that had been dropped was quietly put back. Clark sent 22 FBI agents to Gary to go through the records.

The agents set up at the Lake County courthouse in Crown Point and photographed the registration records. They checked the new voters in the white neighborhoods one name at a time, and they found people who did not exist.

On November 6, 1967, the day before the election, three federal judges heard Hatcher's case and the government's together. An FBI agent who lived in Gary testified that investigators had found 1,096 ghost voters in 33 precincts. A ghost voter is a name on the list with no real person behind it.

Then a precinct committeewoman from Glen Park, an all-white precinct where she had been a party official for twelve years, took the stand. She testified that party workers told her to register voters who were not real.

She had added 51 of them herself.

Out of court, she explained why she had come forward. "They told me that we would have to cheat because the other side was cheating," she said.

"They had me believing that Hatcher was a Communist. But what I was doing began to bother me. I just couldn't live with it."

A Communist. The man she meant had once worked as a deputy prosecutor for that same county.

Thirteen hours before the polls opened, the judges ordered more than 1,000 false names off the lists. Indiana's governor had 300 state troopers and 5,000 National Guardsmen ready to enter Gary on 30 minutes' notice.

All of that, so the Black half of one steel town could choose its own mayor.

Hatcher's story started on July 10, 1933, in Michigan City, Indiana, where he was born the youngest of 13 children. His father molded railroad car wheels, and his mother worked in a factory.

Hatcher went to Indiana University on an athletic scholarship and joined an NAACP picket of a segregated restaurant there. In law school at Valparaiso, he helped organize a sit-in at a Michigan City lunch counter.

Hatcher finished law school in 1959 and went to work as a lawyer and deputy prosecutor in Lake County. In 1963, Gary voters elected him to the city council, and the council made him its president in his first term.

On the council, Hatcher went after the covenants that kept most Black families in Gary's midtown section. A covenant was a clause in a property deed saying who could and could not live there. Hatcher wanted an open housing law to end them.

"Every time it came up for a vote the council chambers would be packed with screaming and yelling," Hatcher told Chicago public radio station WBEZ in 2012. "They were yelling and all kinds of racial slurs and they would intimidate."

"I introduced that bill at least six times," he said. "It was defeated five times."

The sixth time, it passed.

On May 2, 1967, Hatcher beat the sitting mayor in the Democratic primary by about two thousand votes. Police shut down six blocks of Broadway for four hours so the crowd could celebrate.

Gary had not elected a Republican mayor since 1938, so a Democratic nomination usually settled things. Hatcher's did not.

The county Democratic chairman came to collect. He wanted the party to pick Hatcher's police chief, his city attorney and other top posts.

Hatcher said no.

The party then went to work for the Republican in the race. Hatcher's campaign had spent most of its money winning the primary.

He had won the party's nomination and lost the party in the same season.

Hatcher scraped together $8,000 and bought full-page ads in The New York Times and Gary's Post-Tribune. The ad read, "Richard Hatcher is battling bigotry and ignorance. And he needs your help."

Those pages brought in more than $250,000, along with TV invitations and fundraisers from national figures like Senator Robert Kennedy. "It was unbelievable," Hatcher said in 2011. "We ended up having enough money to run a decent campaign."

He kept a framed copy on his office wall. Of everything a politician could hang up, he chose the page where he asked for help.

Gary voted on November 7, 1967, the day after the judges ruled, and Hatcher won.

The outgoing mayor called it "the most peaceful election in Gary's history." Time magazine put his margin at 1,389 votes that week, and later counts put it nearer 2,200. Time wrote that with a margin that thin, the scheme would have worked.

Hatcher was not alone that night, because Carl Stokes won in Cleveland the same day. The two of them became the first Black men elected mayor of American cities with more than 100,000 people.

At his inauguration in January 1968, Hatcher called Gary "a rising sun." "Together, we shall beat a way; together, we shall turn darkness into light, despair into hope and promise into progress," he said.

His friend the Rev. Jesse Jackson later recalled that big-name stars came to that inauguration. Hatcher insisted a youth group perform, and Jackson told WBEZ in 2019 that the group turned out to be the Jackson 5.

By Jackson's telling, nobody in that room had come to hear those kids.

The open housing law did what Hatcher meant it to do. Black families could move where they wanted, and Hatcher said later that it sped up white families leaving the city.

"People panicked and so that's when they began in serious numbers to move out," he said.

South of Gary lay open land that was not yet a town. State law kept a buffer zone around cities of Gary's class, so no new town could form right against their borders.

A couple of state legislators from the region pushed through a bill to take it away. One of them later told WBEZ that people called him the father of the town of Merrillville.

Merrillville became a town in 1971, pressed right up against Gary's edge. White families leaving Gary now had somewhere to go that was still right next door.

The shops and banks followed the families south. On Broadway, a lot of owners who left just boarded up their buildings. A woman who grew up in Gary told WBEZ they never even sold them.

In September 1971, Hatcher chaired a planning meeting for a national Black political convention. Organizers had struggled to find a city willing to host it, and Hatcher offered Gary.

"We should do it at a place where Black people from all over the country could feel comfortable," he said.

From March 10 to 12, 1972, about 3,000 delegates and 7,000 more visitors came to Gary's West Side High School. The city had one hotel, so the gathering ran out of a public school.

Hatcher gave one of the keynote speeches to the crowd in that school. "Will we walk in unity or disperse in a thousand different directions?" he asked.

"Will we act like free black men or like timid, shivering chattel?"

Chattel means property, the legal word once used for enslaved people. Hatcher told the crowd the answers were theirs to give, and that "history will be the judge."

He had already given his own answer, four years earlier, in federal court, against his own party.

The steel jobs went next. U.S. Steel, which founded Gary in 1906, cut its workforce there from 35,000 in the early 1970s to 25,000 by the early 1980s.

That is 10,000 paychecks gone from one town's kitchen tables.

By 1987, Gary had lost 50,000 residents, and crime had climbed. His obituaries would call his years in office marred by the city's decline.

His critics had real complaints, and in 1971 a Black physician backed by the old machine ran against him. The doctor said crime was rising, and that the city had torn down thousands of homes and built back only 300.

The record also holds what Hatcher built, including hundreds of millions in federal dollars and the city's first public housing in nearly two decades.

Many inner-city neighborhoods got regular garbage pickup for the first time. When he took office, two city department heads were Black, and ten years later 25 of the 40 were.

The police chief's job, the one he would not hand to the party, went to a Black officer.

In 1987, after twenty years as mayor, Hatcher lost the Democratic primary. Police closed Broadway again, this time so people could celebrate his loss.

It was the same street.

In 2011, Hatcher told the Associated Press he was proud of his years in office. "Maybe for some people in Gary it may not be better," he said. "But for others it may seem very much better."

In October 2019, a bronze statue of Hatcher was unveiled outside Gary's City Hall. He was 86, and he told WBEZ, "I feel wonderful, wonderful."

He died two months later, on December 13, 2019, in a Chicago hospital.

For years, a lot of people in Gary blamed Hatcher for what happened to their city. That bill came with one name on it, and it was his.

The legislators who took down Gary's buffer are not on it. Neither are the 10,000 steel jobs, or the stores that boarded up and headed south.

Hatcher asked the country for help once, in plain words, and people answered. The least he is owed back is the whole bill, with every name on it.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXcAK
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

text:
🚨WOW!!!

An 18-year-old saw an 80-year-old man with a walker crossing a busy Arizona road in shoes that were FALLING APART...

...so he pulled over, took the shoes OFF HIS OWN FEET, and gave them to him!!!

He found out the man had just lost his wife, bought him dinner, sat with him for hours, invited him to church, raised him $10,000 and now they talk on the phone EVERY SINGLE DAY!!!!

“I just felt like God told me to go over there.”

His name is Jordan Hope.

He’s a recent high school graduate from Maricopa, Arizona who runs his own computer-building business.

He was on his way to the bank to deposit some money when he drove past a Walgreens on John Wayne Parkway.

Then he saw the man’s feet.

“His shoes were like maybe a fourth on his foot.”

So Jordan pulled over, got out, and took off his own size 13 Nike slides and he handed them over and stood there in the road in his socks.

“I just felt like God told me to go over there.”

He had NO IDEA a woman named Yareli Madrid was filming the whole thing from the parking lot.

He drove off, but something told him to turn back.

He found the man inside the Walgreens, helped him pick up his prescription, and bought him his favorite candy.

Peanut M&Ms.

Jordan took time to speak to the man and that’s when Jordan learned the man’s wife had passed away just TWO WEEKS earlier.

“That honestly broke my heart.”

The older man's name is Roy, he’s 80 years old.

Jordan offered to take him to lunch at Culver’s, but a medical condition makes Roy’s legs swell so badly he couldn’t get into Jordan’s car.

So Jordan called him a rideshare and met him at the restaurant, they picked up the food, followed him ALL THE WAY HOME.

...and then he stayed, just to talk.

“So he didn’t feel that loneliness, you know?”

Someone posted the video trying to find out who this young man was, with a message for his parents:

“If this is your son, you did something right.”

Now Jordan calls Roy EVERY SINGLE DAY to check on him and a GoFundMe for Mr. Roy has already raised over $10,000+ for groceries and expenses.

The two of them are even talking about going to church together. ❤️

Jordan says this wasn’t his plan, he says God “interrupted my plans for that day to carry on his plans.”

He’s EIGHTEEN YEARS OLD.

GOD BLESS Jordan Hope, and GOD BLESS Mr. Roy.

THIS IS THE AMERICA I KNOW!!! 🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸

Read this fully before applying. It’s deliberately honest.

Who we are : 
https://t.co/z4z7KqgklP is an early-stage startup building for India’s Gen Z — deals, rewards and AI tools in one app (Android, iOS and web). We work with partners like HDFC Bank and Visa on campus programmes. We are not funded by a big VC, we are not a “cool” 9-to-6 workplace, and we are not hiring for a high CTC. We are hiring for one thing: fire in the belly.

Who we’re looking for : 
Freshers or people with basic experience. We genuinely cannot afford experienced professionals right now, and we’re not pretending otherwise. Attitude will matter far more than talent. If you’re hungry, fast, and want to learn by doing, keep reading.

The role : 
You’ll sit next to the founder — a CEO with 25+ years in AI and SaaS tech startups — and act as his shadow. Every meeting, every partner call, every campaign. 

You’ll own:
All campaigns, end to end — campus drives, partner offers, app launches

Our social media pages — content, posting, community, numbers. 
In-app push notifications and all user communication
Day-to-day coordination with partners like banks fintechs — follow-ups, MOMs, decks
Tracking decisions and action items from every founder meeting and chasing them to closure

Whatever else the week throws at you — tech, sales, marketing, ops. 

What it’s actually like : 
The work will be relentless, and so will the learning. The CEO may get an idea at 3am and want you to look into it right then. You need to be reachable, quick on WhatsApp, and sharp in communication at all hours. This is a front-row seat to how a startup is really built — partnerships, product, growth, fundraising — from close quarters, every single day. Social media exposure comes with the territory.

What you get
An experience of a lifetime — and that’s the honest pitch. Direct mentorship, real ownership from day one, and the kind of exposure that usually takes years to earn. You will be on the table with the who's who in tech fintech banking & the consumer internet. You will be at the center stage of events, award & cerimonies but you have to burn the midnight oil here, be ready to carry standees in public transport to the event site. It ain't easy - you will live the CEO's life dude! 

What you won’t get : 
A big salary, fixed hours, or a quiet job. If you’re joining for CTC alone, for a 9-to-6 routine, or for a comfortable title, this isn’t it. Please don’t apply.

Must-haves : 
Excellent written and spoken communication, and a warm, confident personality

Comfortable with tech — apps, analytics, basic tools, talking to developers
Good instincts for sales, marketing and coordination

Organised, proactive, owns things nobody handed them - Full-time from our office in Andheri East, Mumbai. 

If this fired you up instead of scaring you off, DM me or email [akshay@genzdealz.ai] with a short note on why you’re the one. No formal cover letter needed - Welcome to everything GenZ!

Two-month cinematic campaign will spotlight the strength, perseverance, and everyday craftsmanship of the contractors behind the work.

October 11, 2026 — Earth Care – Rent A Tech is partnering with a major New York photo studio for “Pros in the Wild,” a visual storytelling series documenting Earth Care professionals where their skills matter most: on the job.

Over the next two months, camera crews will visit select Earth Care jobs to photograph and film pros completing tasks on site. With cinematic imagery and an emphasis on the people behind each project, the series will capture the concentration, physical effort, problem-solving, and pride that turn a customer’s request into completed work.

From preparing a wall to making a repair or putting the finishing touches on an installation, the campaign will bring viewers closer to the craft—and to the individuals who practice it every day.

Real Work. Human Stories. Cinematic Vision.

“Pros in the Wild” is built around five themes: struggle, perseverance, strength, dedication, and loyalty.

These themes will shape stories about navigating challenges, staying focused through demanding tasks, honoring commitments, and taking pride in a job well done. The camera will explore the details customers may rarely notice: the careful preparation before a repair, the patience required to solve an unexpected problem, and the effort behind a finished result.

The campaign’s creative ambition is to give everyday craftsmanship the attention and visual impact it deserves. Each featured project offers an opportunity to show how skill, persistence, and care come together in the work of independent contractors.

Bringing Future Pros and Customers Closer to the Work

For people considering joining Earth Care – Rent A Tech, the series will offer a firsthand look at what working through the platform can involve. Viewers will see participating pros in actual job settings, gaining a clearer understanding of the tasks, environments, and commitment involved in serving customers.

For customers, the campaign will highlight the hard work contractors contribute every day—and the people whose knowledge and effort help keep homes and communities functioning.

By sharing these stories publicly, Earth Care aims to increase visibility for professionals in its network while encouraging broader appreciation for handypeople, gig workers, and tradespeople as a whole.

Continuing a Tradition of Supporting Tradespeople Through the Arts

“Pros in the Wild” continues Earth Care’s commitment to connecting the trades with creative expression.

Following its 2025 handyman music collection and 2026 digital games, Earth Care is expanding that tradition through cinematic photography and film. Together, these projects reflect an effort to create a culture around the work—one that recognizes contractors’ experiences, celebrates their contributions, and makes room for creativity alongside practical support.

Music gave that culture a soundtrack. Digital games added opportunities for play and connection. “Pros in the Wild” now brings the camera directly to the job site, placing working professionals at the center of the story.

The Houthis have now renewed their attacks on Saudi airports, once again targeting civilian infrastructure. And once again, we need to get our framing of the Houthis right.

They are not a state actor, not an armed resistance movement, and certainly not a legitimate government. They are a radical, extremist militia that hijacked the Yemeni state by force and has behaved accordingly ever since.

Once you understand who they are and how they operate, their actions should hardly come as a surprise. Kidnapping, torturing and killing civilians, besieging entire cities, planting millions of landmines, forcibly recruiting children, disappearing humanitarian workers, sinking commercial ships, and bombing civilian airports are not isolated excesses. They are part of a consistent pattern of coercion, intimidation, and violence.

The Houthis have never needed much of a pretext to commit atrocities. What changes is the justification they offer, the enemy they invoke, and the political circumstances they exploit. What remains constant is their willingness to make civilians pay the price.

And this is precisely why treating the Houthis as just another political actor with legitimate grievances fundamentally misreads the problem. It rewards their use of violence as a negotiating tool and encourages the belief that escalating attacks will eventually translate into political concessions.

There is also a dangerous tendency to view Houthi aggression exclusively through the Saudi-Iranian rivalry or the wider regional confrontation. That framing overlooks the most important fact: Yemenis were the Houthis' first victims, and they continue to bear the heaviest burden of their rule.

The latest attacks on Saudi airports are not some sudden departure from Houthi behavior. They are a continuation of it, only with a wider target list.

The international community needs to stop treating every new Houthi escalation as an isolated crisis and start confronting the underlying problem. Geography may change, targets may change, and political slogans certainly change. But the nature of the militia, and the threat it poses to Yemen and beyond, does not.

text:
“GOVERNOR UBA SANI FACES ANOTHER RESOUNDING INTER-FAITH ENDORSEMENT IN KADUNA”
  
BY Muhammed Ali Ahmed

For Kaduna, peace carries a meaning deeper than the absence of confrontation. It is the reassurance that a citizen’s faith will neither diminish belonging nor determine access to public opportunity. It is the freedom to cultivate land, educate children, practise religion and pursue a livelihood without the apprehension that difference may become a sentence. 

At a Special Interfaith Dialogue in Kaduna on 5 October 2026, religious leaders offered compelling testimony that Governor @ubasanius’s administration is steadily restoring these assurances to a state long troubled by communal distrust.

The event, held at the newly-inaugurated Abba Kyari Banquet Hall, Sir Kashim Ibrahim House, examined three years of peaceful coexistence and inclusivity. Organised by the Kaduna State Bureau of Interfaith, it brought Muslim and Christian leaders into a common conversation about governance, reconciliation and development. Their commendations, including calls for Uba Sani’s re-election, drew strength from specific experiences—roads requested had been delivered, religious communities felt recognised, and former sceptics acknowledged that performance had altered their judgement. The endorsement was therefore grounded in the relationship between government decisions and everyday life.

Governor Uba Sani distilled his approach with unusual clarity: “Our model is very simple. It does not need any study. It is about justice. It is about bringing everyone to the table.” Behind that formulation lies a consequential understanding of leadership. In a divided society, fairness must become visible in appointments, investments, access and language. Citizens must encounter a government whose conduct reassures them that their identities are respected and their needs count. His achievement has been to make that reassurance central to his administration’s public purpose.

Recalling the atmosphere he inherited, Sani said: “When we came into office, we inherited a state that was highly toxic and divided.” He described situations in which people declined to develop allocated land because they feared living among communities of another faith. “For me, it is unacceptable and we should not allow it to continue in Kaduna State,” he declared. His determination to confront such estrangement recognises that communal division impoverishes everyone, narrows residential choices, weakens commerce and teaches children to inherit suspicions they did not create.

His formal address supplied the governing principle: “No citizen should feel compelled to diminish an identity to enjoy belonging.” Equally, he insisted, “no identity should confer superior entitlement to public protection, opportunity or justice.” These are substantial commitments in Kaduna, where religion and ethnicity have too often been recruited into political competition. Sani recalled that his oath on 29 May 2023 bound him to fairness irrespective of affiliation. The dialogue demonstrated how seriously religious leaders now regard his efforts to honour that obligation.

The Chairman of the Christian Association of Nigeria in Kaduna State, Reverend Caleb Ma’aji, offered a particularly concrete assessment. At the Christmas Carol of 22 December 2024, he had requested three roads: Nasarawa–UNTL–First Bank, PAN Drive–Television Garage–Sabon Tasha, and Romi–Karatudu. Two, he told the gathering, had been completed; the third was nearing completion. Such testimony matters because public confidence grows when requests become projects and projects become usable infrastructure. For communities accustomed to questioning whether government would hear them, delivery provides an answer more persuasive than ceremonial assurances.

The Bloody Fate of Kostaq Kotta: From the Prime Minister's Bench to the Torture Chamber
During the 1920s and 1930s, Kostaq Kotta stood at the absolute zenith of his political power. He served as a two-time Prime Minister of Albania, Speaker of Parliament, and Minister of the Interior. During this phase of triumph, he confidently signed a state decree authorizing the construction of a new, maximum-security prison in the town of Burrel. At the time, he had no idea that he was laying the very foundation for his own brutal execution by installments.
When fascist Italian troops invaded Albania on April 7, 1939, Kotta abruptly lost his job as Prime Minister. However, instead of following King Zog into safe exile, he decided to go into hiding on his own in Thessaloniki, Greece—a fateful mistake. From that moment on, the Albanian, Greek, and Yugoslav communists declared him public enemy number one.
The year 1945 brought the most absurd welcoming committee in Albanian criminal history to his doorstep. Three secret agents knocked on his door: an Albanian communist, a Russian KGB agent, and a Greek spy. With artificial politeness, they offered Kotta his old job as Prime Minister back on behalf of the new Albanian dictator, Enver Hoxha. Kotta smelled a rat instantly and pulled his gun, but he was shot, wounded, and forcefully dragged into a car bound for Tirana.
Following a show trial by the communist regime, Kotta entered the very hell he had helped create. He was thrown into Cell No. 7 of the notorious Burrel Prison. There, guards and agents of the Albanian secret police (Sigurimi) unleashed unprecedented cruelty upon the former head of state.
Kotta was subjected to severe abuse and harsh conditions by the regime. Reports indicate he endured systemic mistreatment and a severe deprivation of basic necessities, including food and water, which rapidly deteriorated his health. During his imprisonment, he suffered severe physical trauma under custody, which the prison management officially recorded as an accident.
Between 1947 and 1949, Kotta succumbed to the harsh conditions and treatment within the facility. To prevent his grave from becoming a symbol for anti-communist resistance, his body was buried anonymously within the prison grounds. To this day, the exact location of his remains is unconfirmed. His death inside the very institution he had authorized remains a notable and tragic irony in modern Albanian history.

📋 Countries and ports offered to Ethiopia—and rejected:

1. 🇩🇯 Djibouti — Port of Tadjoura

• Djibouti offered Ethiopia a 60% stake in the Port of Tadjoura, along with a dedicated berth and maritime corridor.

• Ethiopia rejected the offer, demanding a full maritime corridor under its own sovereignty rather than merely a commercial stake.

2. 🇸🇴 Federal Somalia

• Somalia offered access to the ports of Bosaso, Kismayo, Merca, Hobyo, and Garacad.

• Ethiopia was not satisfied with these offers and preferred negotiating with the breakaway region of Somaliland regarding the Port of Berbera, sparking a diplomatic crisis with Mogadishu.

3. 🇰🇪 Kenya — Port of Lamu

• Kenya offered the Lamu Port-South Sudan-Ethiopia-Transport (LAPSSET) corridor project, which includes the Port of Lamu.

• Ethiopia views this as a strategic alternative but has not adopted it as a final choice; it has demanded what it describes as a "sovereign maritime outlet" rather than simply using the ports of other nations.

⚠️ Important Note:

• Sudan: An offer to use Port Sudan is actually available and ongoing—and Ethiopia currently uses it. However, there has been no new offer that was rejected; rather, border tensions and disputes have led to reduced reliance on it.

• Eritrea: It did not offer its ports (Assab and Massawa) to Ethiopia; instead, it was Ethiopia that demanded access to them and threatened to seize control of them—a move Eritrea flatly rejected.

✅ Why did Ethiopia reject all these? The proposals?

• Abiy Ahmed insists on a "sovereign maritime outlet"—meaning a coastal strip owned by Ethiopia, rather than merely using other countries' ports or holding a commercial stake in them.

• Consequently, he turned to negotiations with Somaliland to secure a 20-kilometer coastal strip at the port of Berbera for a 50-year period, in exchange for potential recognition of Somaliland's independence.

The shining pearl of the #Persian #Gulf!  Experiencing the magical and peaceful nights of Kish Island is a memory that stays in your heart forever. 

History and Culture of Kish Island
Kish Island's history is as rich and colorful as its landscapes. Archaeological findings suggest that the island has been inhabited for over 3,000 years. Historically, Kish was a bustling trading center, famed for its pearls and silk. Its strategic location in the Persian Gulf made it a key maritime crossroads linking the ancient civilizations of Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley, and beyond.

The island's historical significance is further underlined by mentions in classic texts like the ‘Achaemenid Inscriptions’ during the reign of Darius the Great, indicating its prominence in the Persian Empire. Over the centuries, Kish witnessed the rise and fall of empires, with each era leaving its mark on the island's culture and architecture.

Kish's Ayani House
One of the most beautiful tourist attractions on Kish Island, Kish's Ayani House is one of the most beautiful and oldest attractions. 
Kish Island, renowned for its unique attractions, features the historic Ayani House, a testament to the island's rich heritage dating back to the Ilkhanid era. Nestled within Kish's ancient Harire city, this site, with its distinctive star-shaped tiles, reflects the opulence of its original inhabitants and the architectural styles of Iran's storied past.
Situated on the northern coast, the Ayani House complex includes remnants of a bathhouse, mosques, and ancient qanats, revealing insights into a once-thriving city's daily life and strategic importance. Despite time's toll, the site's strategic coastal location and its network of canals suggest multifaceted historical roles, from fishing activities to defense mechanisms.
The bathhouse, part of the complex, stands out as one of Iran's oldest, showcasing unique architectural features that hint at its communal use despite its seemingly private design. For those visiting Kish Island, Ayani House offers a deep dive into Iran's cultural and architectural heritage, making it a must-visit destination for history enthusiasts and travelers alike.
Cultural Significance and Local Customs
Kish Island today is a melting pot of cultures and traditions, reflective of its storied past. While modern development has brought contemporary influences, traditional Persian customs remain deeply ingrained in the local way of life. Hospitality is a cornerstone of Kish culture, with visitors often welcomed with open arms and warm smiles.
Local customs are also evident in the island's celebrations and festivals, which often blend Islamic traditions with ancient Persian rituals. These events provide a glimpse into the soul of Kish, showcasing music, dance, and culinary practices passed down through generations.

Influence of Persian and Maritime Heritage
The influence of Kish's Persian and maritime heritage is omnipresent. This is seen in the island's architectural gems, such as the ancient city of Harireh, which dates back to the 8th century, and the grandeur of traditional bazaars where artisans sell crafts that have been part of Kish's culture for centuries.

The sea has played a crucial role in shaping the island's identity. This is reflected in the local cuisine, which heavily features seafood, and in the enduring practices of fishing and maritime trade. The island's relationship with the sea is also celebrated through various sea-related festivals and activities, ensuring that the maritime heritage continues to be an integral part of Kish's cultural tapestry.

In sum, Kish Island is not just a place of scenic beauty but also a living museum of Persian and maritime history, offering a rich cultural experience to its visitors.

text:
Before We Fix the SGR, Fix the Purpose.

Before we fix the standard gauge railway, we must settle what economy we want it to serve. A railway should connect production, industry and markets according to a development strategy we have chosen for ourselves.

The African Great Lakes Corridor offers an opportunity to give that strategy practical form. Imagine connecting lakes Malawi, Tanganyika, Kivu, Edward and Albert through shipping services and connecting railways and roads. The preliminary concept sketches approximately 640 km of new railway within a wider lake, river and rail route of about 4,500 km from Mangochi to Khartoum. These are indicative planning estimates to be tested through feasibility studies.

Around this network, we could develop industries and trading centres whose prosperity grows through exchange with their neighbours. Farmers could reach regional buyers, with storage and processing facilities reducing losses. Fisheries could support food industries, minerals could supply manufacturing, and shipping could sustain businesses in vessel construction and maintenance.

This opportunity deserves priority in our infrastructure planning and early study. We must establish what each region can produce, what its neighbours need and which missing connections prevent that trade. These decisions should guide the routes, capacity and sequencing of the SGR. We should develop the productive economy and its transport connections together.

Much of Africa’s inherited transport infrastructure was organised to carry raw materials from the interior to coastal ports for export. That geography served colonial economic priorities. Modernising the tracks while preserving the same narrow purpose risks modernising our dependence.

Decolonising infrastructure means giving African production, consumption and ownership a decisive place in its design. A sack of beans from Kasese should reach a buyer in Goma without transport costs and border delays swallowing the farmer’s profit. Our minerals should sustain industries here, while our engineers and manufacturers acquire capabilities and businesses through the investment itself.

We need a regional programme that brings the countries sharing these lakes around one development agenda. It would require agreements on cross-border trade, navigation and security, with clear responsibility for maintenance. Communities and businesses along the corridor must help shape the programme and share its benefits.

The immediate task is a jointly funded feasibility programme. It should examine demand, engineering requirements and the full cost of moving goods, including transfers between ships and trains. Proposed dams, locks and railway alignments must be assessed against alternatives. Protecting the lakes and surrounding livelihoods must be a condition of success.

Implementation should proceed in useful phases, beginning where studies identify viable shipping services, priority port improvements and feeder connections. Reliable electricity and simpler border procedures must accompany these investments. Each phase should deliver benefits while strengthening the next.

Financing and procurement must also build African economic power. Transparent contracts should create meaningful opportunities for capable local firms, with technical training and maintenance funded from the beginning. Success should be measured through growing enterprises, better incomes and more value retained within the region.

The first infrastructure we must fix is the connection between our resources and our own prosperity. Let that purpose determine where we lay the rails, build the ports and invest our public money.

text:
Black parents walked their own children to the front of the line, three weeks after a massacre. That was Fifth Avenue on July 28, 1917, when several hundred children dressed head to foot in white stepped off behind muffled drums with thousands of grown folks falling in behind them. Twenty thousand people packed both sidewalks and watched them go by without hearing one word for thirty-four blocks.

The sign was a drawing, blown up large and mounted on a pole so a person could hold it above their head. It showed a Black woman down on her knees in front of the President of the United States.

She was asking him to bring democracy home to America before he shipped it across the ocean to Europe. A police officer looked at that picture on Fifth Avenue on the morning of Saturday, July 28, 1917, and ruled it out of the parade.

The organizers pulled it from the line. Thousands of Black New Yorkers were about to walk thirty-four blocks down the richest street in America without saying one word out loud.

And a drawing was still too much.

To understand why anybody would draw a woman on her knees, you have to go west, to a river town in Illinois where the packing plants had been hiring.

Mabel Randall was twenty-four years old and had been living in East St. Louis about a year and a half. On the evening of July 2, 1917, the windows and the door of her house came in.

She got down under the bed with her child and stayed there until dark. When it was dark enough to move, she went next door and asked the white woman who lived there if they could hide underneath her house.

The woman said no. She said she had chickens in the yard.

So Mabel Randall found a coal house instead, and she and her people piled stoves on top of themselves and lay there until four in the morning. Then she walked to the railroad yards, waited an hour and a half, and made the ferry across the river to St. Louis with what she had on her back.

That is the East St. Louis massacre in one household.

Now multiply it by six thousand people put out of their homes in roughly a day.

The reason was money, and nobody bothered hiding it. White workers at the packing houses and the aluminum plant had walked out on strike, and the companies filled the empty jobs with Black workers coming up from the South.

In late May, six hundred union men marched on City Hall to demand the city stop the new arrivals. The secretary of the Central Trades and Labor Union put the grievance in writing, complaining that ten thousand undesirable Negroes had poured in and suggesting something be done to get rid of a portion of the ones already there.

Five weeks later the town came apart.

Mineola McGee was a chambermaid. She earned three dollars and fifty cents a week and had been in East St. Louis since the eighth of February.

On Tuesday morning, sometime between seven and eight o'clock, she walked to her job at Mrs. Gray's house and reached for the door. The bullet caught her in the arm.

She said afterward that the only two people she could see anywhere on that street were a soldier and a policeman, and that she believed it was one of those two who shot her. She fainted, and came to in the back of a patrol wagon.

At the hospital they took the rest of the arm off. When she gave her statement to the investigators, she added two more things at the end of it.

She had not been able to find one relative since it happened, not the cousins, not the aunt, not the uncle.

And no insurance.

Narcis Gurley was seventy-one years old. She had lived in that city for thirty years, keeping roomers and taking in laundry, which is thirty years of somebody else's shirts.

She watched the house near hers catch, and she heard men out in the street, so she stayed inside, because the street was worse than the room. Then her own roof started coming down on her.

She came out badly burned. A white man in the crowd said to leave the old women alone, and that one sentence from a stranger is the only reason she lived.

She lost everything she had.

Rena Cook had been out fishing that day. She was riding home on the Alton streetcar with her husband and her son when a crowd stopped the car at Collinsville and Broadway and ordered the white passengers off.

Then they came in and took her husband and her boy. Both of them were killed in the street, and two policemen stood there and watched it happen.

She was beaten until she lost consciousness, and woke up two days later in St. Mary's Hospital.

Lulu Robinson was thirty-three and eight months into her new life in that city. Between five and six on Monday evening the shots started coming through her walls, and she and her twelve-year-old son backed up against the plaster trying to get out of the way of them.

She was hit three times, in a finger, in the shoulder, in the face. Her son was hit twice and died.

She never saw her husband again.

The official count of Black dead in East St. Louis was thirty-nine. The NAACP sent W. E. B. Du Bois and the writer Martha Gruening out there to take statements and photographs in person, and what they published in The Crisis that September put the real number somewhere between one and two hundred.

Around four hundred thousand dollars in property burned, Black-owned and white-owned both. Nine white residents also died.

A reporter for the St. Louis Star watched an elderly woman walk past the police station that night carrying everything she had left in the world. It came to a worn pair of shoes, which she was not wearing because she was barefoot, one extra calico dress, an old shawl, and two puppies.

She was crying, and she went by the lit windows of City Hall without seeing anybody, because there was nowhere in particular for her to go.

Days later, Martha Gruening found another woman poking through the ashes of her own house. She was sixty-five, her family had gotten out, and almost nothing else had.

She asked Gruening a question this country has still not answered properly.

We can't live South and they don't want us North. Where are we to go?

Then came the part that turned the grief into something harder.

Near Cahokia Creek, Gruening fell into conversation with two young Illinois militiamen from a town called Olney. They boasted to her about what had been done to people in that water.

She asked them how many they had killed themselves. They were vague about the count, but they were perfectly clear that they had been shooting to kill.

She took it to the Military Board of Inquiry and offered to travel anywhere, Olney included, to point the two of them out. The board asked her whether she supposed the boys had only been showing off for a lady.

They said such jesting was in bad taste, but boys will be boys. They told her identification was impossible now, because those troops had already been sent home, and that it was rather late in the proceedings to be raising it at all.

Then seven officers in a room gave a woman a lecture about her heavy responsibility as a writer, and warned her not to leave the world with the wrong impression of the Illinois militia. They said they had gone through the evidence exhaustively and found not one instance of misconduct.

Gruening asked them one question back. If there had been that much heroism, how did so many Black people end up dead and only eight white men?

There was no answer to that.

That was what New York was reading in July of 1917. Not rumor, and not a number.

Names, ages, weekly wages, street addresses, and a file already being closed.

James Weldon Johnson called a meeting at St. Philip's Church in Harlem. He had been the NAACP's field secretary for barely a year.

The room floated the sensible plan, which was to rent Carnegie Hall and hold a protest meeting indoors, the way respectable organizations expressed themselves. Johnson wanted Fifth Avenue.

He remembered a suggestion made at an NAACP conference the year before, by Oswald Garrison Villard, about what a crowd could do by marching and making no sound at all. Villard's own mother had led a silent peace parade in 1914, and Johnson took the whole shape of it, the mourning clothes and the covered drums, and turned it on lynching.

They had ten days to build it.

Pastors were asked to empty their pews into the street. A leaflet went out dated July 24 with a section printed on it under the heading "Why We March."

It said they marched to make another Waco, another Memphis, another East St. Louis impossible, and to see the people responsible answer for it. It said they marched because they considered it a crime to stay quiet in the face of such acts.

It said they marched because they wanted their children to live in a better land than the one that had fallen to them. At the bottom it asked people to be in line on Saturday and show they had not gone numb to the sorrows of their own race.

The Reverend Charles Martin, a West Indian minister who founded the Fourth Moravian Church, put his name to it. He signed off yours in righteous indignation.

Saturday arrived in the middle of a record heat wave. They gathered on Fifth Avenue between 55th and 59th in the kind of July air that glues a collar to a neck, and the men were dressed in wool.

The children went to the front. Several hundred of them, dressed head to foot in white.

Sit with what that decision actually was. Three weeks after a mob had gone through a neighborhood in Illinois and not spared the children in it, several hundred Black parents in New York walked their own children to the head of a line and sent them out ahead of everybody.

Behind the children came the women, thousands of them, also in white. The men were last, in dark suits, and some of them wore United States Army uniforms, because Black soldiers had already landed in France that spring.

At the very front walked the drummers. The drums were muffled, wrapped so the sound came out low, and they kept a slow cadence, the beat you hear at a funeral instead of a parade.

Then the first drumbeat landed and the whole street started moving. Nobody chanted, and nobody sang.

Crossing 50th they went by St. Patrick's Cathedral, and at 42nd they went by the library. Through the thirties they passed department stores where they were welcome to spend money and not welcome to stand behind the counter.

Mounted police rode the flanks the entire way. Around twenty thousand people packed both sidewalks to watch, Black and white together, and plenty of the white ones had no idea what they were looking at.

So Black Boy Scouts moved through the crowd handing out the leaflet, because the marchers had agreed not to explain themselves out loud. The explaining was left to the banners, and they came down the avenue one behind another like sentences in a letter.

One counted 2,867 Black Americans lynched in thirty-one years and pointed out that not one murderer had suffered for any of it. One said race prejudice is the offspring of ignorance and the mother of lynching.

One asked mothers whether lynchers go to heaven. One said, with no decoration at all, that their hands were full of blood.

One reminded Fifth Avenue that the first blood spilled for American independence belonged to a Black man named Crispus Attucks. One did plain arithmetic, that they had fought for the liberty of white Americans in six wars, and their reward was East St. Louis.

And one, up near the head of the line, put the question to the President that the country was working very hard not to hear. Mr. President, why not make America safe for democracy?

Somewhere in that procession was a gap where a drawing should have been.

James Weldon Johnson wrote later that the streets of New York had witnessed a great many strange sights, and he judged they had never witnessed one stranger than this. He also noticed that some of the people standing on the curb were crying.

The line held the whole way. Past the hotels, past the churches, past the shops, thirty-four blocks of people refusing to make a sound while a city stared at them and their children walked out front.

At 23rd Street, at Madison Square, they finally broke ranks. And a few cheers got loose.

That was the first noise out of them since 57th Street.

Four days later, on the first of August, eleven of them were standing inside the White House with a scheduled appointment. They had brought a petition with them.

The names on it included James Weldon Johnson, the Harlem realtor John E. Nail, the Reverend Frederick A. Cullen, and the clubwoman Maria C. Lawton. Madam C. J. Walker was there too, a woman who had come up out of the Louisiana cotton fields and built a fortune selling hair products to Black women.

Their paper reminded the President that Black men were wearing his country's uniform in France at that exact hour. It asked him to make lynching a federal crime.

Joseph Tumulty, the President's secretary, came out and told them Wilson was too busy to receive them. They had traveled down from New York for an appointment arranged in advance, and now they stood in a corridor while a man explained the President's schedule to them.

They left the petition on a desk and went home.

Two weeks later Wilson sat with a smaller group and heard them out. Eleven months after that, in July of 1918, he issued a written statement discouraging mob violence.

It went out to the press, he never spoke it aloud, and it never asked Congress for a law.

The killing did not slow down.

The number of lynchings in America rose after the parade and did not fall back below the 1917 level until 1923. The Dyer Anti-Lynching Bill was introduced the next year and died.

Something close to two hundred anti-lynching bills were put before Congress between the end of the Civil War and the civil rights movement, and every last one of them was killed, most in the Senate. Lynching became a federal crime on March 29, 2022.

One hundred and five years after those people walked down Fifth Avenue without saying a word to ask for exactly that.

Two sets of photographers worked the route that Saturday, the Underwood and Underwood studio and a man named Cyril T. Adams. Their prints sit at Yale today, inside the papers James Weldon Johnson and his wife Grace kept for the rest of their lives.

You can look at the children in white any time you want. What you cannot look at is the sign that got pulled.

No photograph of it exists in the parade record, because it never entered the parade. All that survives of it is a sentence in the next morning's New York Times, describing what it had shown.

So the only place left in this country where that woman is still on her knees in front of that President is inside a description, in an old newspaper, in a paragraph almost nobody reads.

A description weighs nothing at all. It costs about ten seconds to hand to somebody else.

Picture it one time before you go. A drawing on a pole, walked back down the sidewalk at 57th Street and out of the line, past thousands of people who had already agreed not to say a word.

text:
DAILY SCRIPTURE — OCTOBER 11, 2026

YOU ARE NOT JUST ANOTHER FACE IN THE CROWD

1 Corinthians 12:27 (NLT)
“All of you together are Christ’s body, and each of you is a part of it.”

Imagine a community devastated by a powerful storm. Homes are damaged, trees are down, and families are struggling.

One person brings a chainsaw. Another brings food. Someone offers shelter. Another kneels beside a hurting neighbour and prays.

Not everyone is standing in the spotlight. Not everyone has a title or a microphone.

They’re simply using what God has placed in their hands.

And together, something beautiful begins to happen. A broken community starts coming back to life.

That’s how the body of Christ is meant to function!

Some preach. Some teach. Some encourage. Some give. Some pray. Others quietly serve where nobody sees.

But every member matters!

Never confuse being unnoticed by people with being unimportant to God.

The hand cannot do the work of the foot. The eye cannot replace the ear. God has placed each member in the body for a purpose.

We don’t need to compete for recognition. We need to come together in unity, each doing what God has called us to do.

And remember, no man, ministry, or organization is the head of the body.

WE ALREADY HAVE A HEAD. HIS NAME IS JESUS CHRIST!

TODAY’S MISSION: Stop comparing your calling to someone else’s. Ask God how you can strengthen His body with what He’s already placed in your hands.

PRAYER: Lord Jesus, help us recognize the value of every member of Your body. Remove pride, jealousy, and division. Teach us to work together in love, remembering that all glory belongs to You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

#FaithFamilyFreedom #DailyScripture #BodyOfChrist #JesusChrist #ChristianUnity

text:
Conclusion: Did Arnold Save the Northern Army?

The historiographical debate surrounding Valcour Island reveals an important distinction between the strategic value of Arnold’s naval construction campaign and the consequences of his decision to engage the British fleet. While Kelly emphasizes the delaying effect of Arnold’s resistance, Schnitzer attributes Carleton’s withdrawal primarily to the formidable defenses at Ticonderoga and Mount Independence. Laramie places the battle within the broader logistical difficulties confronting the British, while Brumwell identifies the naval arms race of the preceding summer as the more consequential contribution to American strategic success.

Weddle offers perhaps the most pointed challenge to the traditional narrative by examining Arnold’s departure from Gates’s original defensive strategy. The American fleet was intended to contest British passage through the Crown Point narrows while remaining intact to support the defense of Ticonderoga. Arnold’s decision to move north and force an engagement at Valcour Island resulted in the destruction of nearly his entire squadron, depriving the American army of a naval screen while imposing only a limited delay on the British advance.

The central question, therefore, is whether Arnold’s celebrated stand at Valcour actually preserved the northern army or whether the decisive strategic advantage had already been secured through months of naval construction, fortification, and reinforcement. By October, Carleton confronted an increasingly unfavorable combination of logistical constraints, deteriorating weather, and formidable American defenses. His decision to withdraw reflected these broader operational realities rather than the outcome of the naval battle alone.

The construction of Arnold’s fleet unquestionably contributed to the American defensive effort by forcing the British to expend precious campaigning time establishing naval superiority. Whether its destruction at Valcour Island advanced that objective remains considerably more debatable. The American strategic success of 1776 should not be confused with a vindication of every tactical decision that preceded it. Arnold’s contribution to delaying the British invasion was substantial, but the evidence presented by these historians suggests that the fleet’s greatest strategic value may have been realized before the battle began.

text:
A Historiographical 250th Thread: Reconsidering the Battle of Valcour Island, October 11, 1776

As we commemorate the 250th anniversary of the Battle of Valcour Island, it is worth revisiting a longstanding historiographical debate: Did Benedict Arnold’s naval engagement actually save the American northern army in 1776, or has the battle’s strategic significance been exaggerated at the expense of the larger defensive campaign?

Historians Jack Kelly, Eric Schnitzer, Michael Laramie, Stephen Brumwell, and Kevin Weddle offer differing interpretations of Arnold’s actions, the destruction of the American fleet, and the factors that ultimately persuaded Sir Guy Carleton to abandon his advance southward along Lake Champlain.

Kevin Weddle: The Strategic Cost of Arnold’s Decision

Let’s begin with Kevin Weddle, whose analysis places considerable emphasis on the American debate over the defense of Crown Point.

General Horatio Gates favored withdrawing the Continental Army to Fort Ticonderoga, where a stronger defensive position could be established. The deteriorating fortifications at Crown Point would be abandoned as a principal defensive post, with the site instead serving as a smallpox hospital.

This proposed withdrawal alarmed New England’s revolutionary governments, which feared that abandoning Crown Point would expose an important invasion corridor into their territories. To address these concerns, Gates assured them that Arnold’s newly constructed Lake Champlain fleet would protect the northern approaches.

Weddle emphasizes the explicitly defensive nature of Gates’s instructions to Arnold. The fleet was intended to prevent the British from passing through the narrows near Crown Point while preserving its own strength. If the British proved too powerful, Arnold was expected to conduct a fighting withdrawal rather than sacrifice the fleet in a decisive engagement.

This distinction becomes central to Weddle’s interpretation.

The American defensive strategy rested on two complementary objectives: strengthening the fortifications at Ticonderoga and maintaining a naval force capable of contesting British movement along Lake Champlain. The fleet was not simply an instrument for delaying the enemy; its continued existence was itself a strategic asset.

Yet Arnold moved his squadron approximately fifty miles north of its intended defensive position, ultimately establishing an ambush at Valcour Island. Weddle attributes this decision, at least in part, to Arnold’s inadequate intelligence concerning British naval capabilities and movements.

Although Arnold’s position initially offered tactical advantages, the engagement resulted in the near-total destruction of his fleet. The surviving American vessels escaped under cover of darkness, only to be pursued southward. Arnold eventually burned several remaining vessels near what became known as Arnold’s Bay.

Weddle also draws attention to criticism of Arnold’s decisions from within the American officer corps. The destruction of the fleet deprived Ticonderoga of the naval screen that Gates had originally intended to preserve.

In this interpretation, the battle itself accomplished remarkably little. Arnold’s ambush delayed the British advance by only a matter of days, while the loss of his squadron eliminated an important component of the American defensive system.

Carleton’s subsequent decision not to assault Ticonderoga owed considerably more to the extensive American fortifications, the strength of the defending army, the lateness of the campaigning season, and his own cautious assessment of the situation.

text:
Jack Kelly: Valcour as a Strategic American Success

Historian Jack Kelly places substantially greater emphasis on the importance of Valcour Island and Arnold’s determination to delay the British invasion.

Although the Americans suffered a devastating tactical defeat, Kelly’s interpretation situates the engagement within the broader struggle to prevent Carleton from advancing southward before winter.

From this perspective, Arnold’s willingness to confront a superior British fleet helped frustrate the invasion timetable. The battle’s significance lies less in the number of vessels destroyed than in its contribution to the cumulative delays that prevented the British from exploiting their naval superiority in 1776.

The destruction of Arnold’s fleet, therefore, does not necessarily invalidate the strategic value of his resistance.

Eric Schnitzer: The Fortifications, Not the Fleet

Saratoga National Historical Park historian Eric Schnitzer offers a considerably more skeptical assessment.

Schnitzer challenges the familiar narrative that Arnold’s sacrifice at Valcour Island saved the American cause by delaying the British invasion. In his interpretation, the engagement itself accomplished relatively little, setting the British advance back perhaps only a day or two.

Instead, Schnitzer directs attention to the formidable defensive preparations undertaken at Fort Ticonderoga and Mount Independence.

The expansion of the fortifications, combined with the substantial American garrison, presented Carleton with the prospect of a difficult and potentially prolonged siege at precisely the moment when the campaigning season was drawing to a close.

The British commander had achieved naval supremacy on Lake Champlain, but naval supremacy alone could not guarantee the capture of a heavily defended fortress.

Schnitzer’s interpretation consequently shifts the credit away from Arnold’s dramatic naval engagement and toward the less celebrated labor of fortification, reinforcement, and defensive preparation.

Michael Laramie: Logistics, Timing, and Carleton’s Calculations

Michael Laramie acknowledges the catastrophic losses suffered by Arnold’s fleet but places greater emphasis on the logistical and psychological consequences confronting Carleton after the engagement.

Having secured Crown Point, the British commander still faced the formidable task of advancing against Ticonderoga, maintaining an extended supply chain from Canada, conducting a siege, and potentially garrisoning the captured position through the winter.

These were not minor considerations. Every additional mile southward increased the logistical demands on an army operating at the end of an already shortened northern campaigning season.

Laramie’s interpretation suggests that even a relatively brief delay could acquire significance when combined with deteriorating weather, the requirements of siege warfare, and the immense difficulties of sustaining British operations so far from their Canadian bases.

The destruction of Arnold’s fleet did not resolve these problems. Instead, Carleton was left to calculate whether the potential rewards of continuing the invasion justified the operational risks.

Here, Valcour’s importance emerges less from its immediate tactical consequences than from its place within a deteriorating strategic situation.

🙏 Ishtakameshwari Temple, Srisailam, is a hidden spiritual gem nestled deep within the dense Nallamala Forest, about 20–21 km from the main Srisailam Temple. This ancient cave shrine, believed to date back to the 8th–10th centuries, is dedicated to Ishtakameshwari Devi, whose name means the Goddess who fulfills the heartfelt wishes of her devotees. The temple is known for its unique four-armed stone idol with a serene smile, which differs from the traditional eight-armed form of the Goddess. Devotees also speak of the idol’s forehead having an unusually soft, skin-like texture, adding to the mystery and spiritual significance of the shrine. Located inside a tiny natural cave that accommodates only a few devotees at a time, the temple offers an intimate and deeply spiritual experience. It is traditionally associated with the local Chenchu tribal community, whose close connection with the Nallamala forests forms an important part of its heritage. The Andhra Pradesh Government and Forest Department support the protection of the temple and its surrounding forest area by regulating visitor access, maintaining approach routes, safeguarding the natural environment, and preserving this sacred heritage site. In the Markapuram region and nearby Nallamala forest areas, their cooperation is essential for balancing pilgrimage, tribal traditions, wildlife protection, and forest conservation. More than a place of worship, Ishtakameshwari Devi Temple represents a remarkable blend of faith, mystery, ancient history, tribal heritage, and nature, making it a sacred destination hidden in the heart of the Nallamala wilderness. 🌿🕉️
