text:
A monkey slapped a man's fish into the river. Then she took his hat.

Not for fun. Not for food. For a reason you won't believe until you see the last ten seconds.

I've watched this clip nine times. The first time I laughed. The second time I stopped laughing. By the fifth, I was pausing it frame by frame, because I realized I wasn't watching a prank.

I was watching a negotiation.

Let me explain why this clip is breaking my brain, and why, if you scroll past it, you're going to miss one of the strangest things an animal has ever done on camera.

THE FIRST THING YOU'LL THINK

You'll think: classic thief monkey. Grabs stuff, runs away, humans scream. We've all seen it a thousand times.

That's exactly what the monkey wants you to think, and it's exactly why you'll be wrong.

Because a thief takes the valuable thing and runs. A thief doesn't knock the dinner into the river first. A thief doesn't pick the one item that has no food value at all. A thief certainly doesn't make sure the man is following.

Something else is happening here. Something with a plan. Something with a destination.

And the destination is the part that got me.

WHY A HAT?

Ask yourself one question before you watch: out of everything a monkey could grab from a person, why would she choose a hat?

You can't eat it. You can't drink it. It doesn't taste like anything, and it's too big to hide.

But a hat has three properties that make it the perfect tool, if you're a primate who understands more than you're supposed to:

It belongs to him. It's his. It smells like him. It's part of him.

He will want it back. Badly. Instantly.

It's light enough to carry while moving fast, and obvious enough that he can't lose sight of it.
Read that again. That isn't the profile of loot. That's the profile of a leash.
She didn't steal the hat to keep it. She stole it to be followed.

THE FISH WAS NOT AN ACCIDENT EITHER

I know what you're thinking. "It was an accident, the monkey just knocked the fish over."

Maybe. I'm not claiming she planned the fish. I'm saying that the sequence matters, and the sequence is wild:

First, the man loses something he cared about. Then he's angry, distracted, vulnerable. Then the hat disappears. Then the chase starts.

By the time he realizes where he's going, he has already walked a long way behind a small animal who keeps looking back to check that he's still there.

Yes. She keeps looking back.

Hold on to that detail. Because in animal cognition research, looking back to check that someone is following you is not a small thing. It is one of the biggest things.

WHAT SCIENTISTS WOULD CALL THIS

In behavioral science there's a concept called joint attention. It means: I know you can pay attention to things. I know you can be directed. I'm going to get you to look at what I want you to look at.

Human babies develop it around nine to twelve months. It's one of the foundations of language, teaching, cooperation, and basically everything that makes us civilization-builders.

For a long time, the textbooks said monkeys didn't do this. Apes in captivity might point and gesture. Monkeys? Not really. They react, they grab, they scatter. They don't guide.

Then videos like this one start showing up, and a lot of people in white coats start quietly rewriting their notes.

I'm not going to tell you what the monkey in this clip is "really" thinking. Nobody can. But I will tell you that when you watch her check over her shoulder, wait for him, and move on again, you'll feel the hair on your neck move.

THE ONE EXPERIMENT YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT

Years ago, a researcher named Laurie Santos ran a series of experiments with rhesus macaques. The setup was almost comically simple: two humans, each holding a grape. One human faces the monkey. The other has turned away.

Which human does the monkey steal from?

The one who isn't looking. Every time. Reliably.

Think about what that requires. The monkey has to understand that a human has a point of view. That "seeing" is something that can be on or off. That a person who can't see you can't stop you.

That's not instinct. That's a model of someone else's mind.

Now apply that to the clip. If a monkey can work out what a human can and can't see, can she work out what a human will do if his hat disappears? Can she predict that he will follow?

Watch the video and decide for yourself. I have my answer. I'm not going to spoil it.

THE MONKEYS WHO RUN A PROTECTION RACKET

If you think "monkey uses hat as leverage" sounds like a stretch, I have bad news.

At a famous temple in Bali, a population of long-tailed macaques has developed something researchers describe as a robbing-and-bartering system. Translation: they snatch things from tourists, sunglasses, phones, hats, and hold them until someone hands over food.

It's not random. Researchers who studied it found that the monkeys tend to wait. They hold the object. They watch the human's reaction. When the human offers a snack, they hand the item back.

Some of them appear to figure out that certain objects get a better return than others. A phone gets a better deal than a flip-flop.

Let that sink in. A monkey, in the real world, has worked out that human objects have value, that humans will pay to retrieve them, and that the value varies. And the knowledge spreads through the group like a business model.

Now imagine one of them with a different goal. Not a snack. Something else entirely.

Imagine one who isn't asking for payment at all.

Imagine one who just needs a human to follow her.

WHAT DO YOU THINK SHE WANTED?

I'm going to ask you not to scroll to the end of the clip. I'm going to ask you to guess first.

A monkey knocks the dinner into the river, steals the hat, and leads a man down a path, glancing back the whole time.

Where is she taking him?

Option A: She's luring him away so her group can raid his stuff. Option B: She's just playing, and the "following" is a coincidence. Option C: She wants something from him that only a human can give.

Pick one. Then watch the video.

If you picked C, you're going to want to sit down for the ending.

WHY THIS CLIP IS GETTING UNDER MY SKIN

I've been looking at animal videos for years. Most of them follow the same rhythm. Cute thing happens. Funny thing happens. Done.

This one has a different rhythm. It builds. Every few seconds the situation changes, and every change makes the previous interpretation look a little more naive.

At the start you're laughing at a man who lost his fish. In the middle you're wondering why a monkey would want a hat. By the end you're not laughing at all. You're holding your breath.

That progression is rare. Most content gives you the punchline at the beginning and spends the rest of the time diluting it. This clip does the opposite. It hides the real story until it's ready.
And when the real story arrives, it reframes everything that came before it. You'll want to rewatch from the start, and every earlier moment will look different.
That's the mark of a story, not a stunt.

THE TWO KINDS OF ANIMAL VIDEOS

There are two kinds of viral animal clips.

The first kind shows you an animal doing something cute. You watch it, you smile, you share it, and you forget it by dinner.

The second kind shows you an animal doing something that doesn't fit. Something that sits in the gap between what we think animals are and what they appear to be. You watch it, you get a strange feeling in your chest, and three days later you're still thinking about it in the shower.

This is the second kind.

I don't say that lightly. I've seen cats open doors, crows solve puzzles, octopuses escape tanks. Those are impressive. This is something else, because it isn't a trick. It's a situation. It has stakes, a cause, and a direction. And it involves another living being who isn't in the frame yet.

THE MEMORY THING
Here's something people forget about monkeys: they remember.
Not just where the food is. They remember faces, favors, insults, and who owes whom. A macaque can hold a grudge. A vervet can recall who groomed her last week. Primate social life runs on a ledger, and the ledger is detailed.

That matters for this clip, because the monkey isn't dealing with a stranger in a vacuum. She's dealing with a human she may have seen before. A place she knows. A route she's taken. A pattern of how people behave around her.

When she makes her move, she isn't improvising from zero. She's drawing on a lifetime of watching humans react to things.

She knows that when a man's hat goes, he runs. She knows that when something he owns is taken, he doesn't let it go. She knows how people work.

And she is using that knowledge for something that has nothing to do with the hat.

THE ALARM CALL PROBLEM

Another fact I love: vervet monkeys have different alarm calls for different predators. One call for a leopard. A different one for an eagle. A different one for a snake. And the rest of the troop responds accordingly: climb the tree, look up, scan the ground.

That's not a single scream that means "danger." That's a vocabulary. It's information with a specific meaning that other monkeys decode in a fraction of a second.

When people hear "monkeys can communicate," they imagine something simple. Hunger, fear, anger. But the reality is that primates move meaning around constantly, with sounds, glances, postures, and touch. They have an entire social language that we barely understand.

Now ask: what does a monkey do when she needs to communicate with an animal that doesn't speak her language?

She improvises. She uses what she has. She finds the thing that will make the human pay attention and keep paying attention.

A hat. A chase. A glance back over the shoulder.

It's not a word. But it's a sentence.

THE FAIRNESS EXPERIMENT THAT WENT VIRAL FOR A REASON

You may have seen the famous capuchin clip: two monkeys, side by side, doing the same task. One gets a cucumber. The other gets a grape. The monkey with the cucumber looks at the grape, looks at the cucumber, and then throws the cucumber back at the researcher.

Frans de Waal and Sarah Brosnan ran that experiment, and it blew open a debate about whether animals have a sense of fairness.

I bring it up because it illustrates something important about how primates see the world. They don't just react to what happens to them. They compare. They evaluate. They judge whether a situation is right.

A monkey who can feel that a situation is unfair is a monkey who can also feel that a situation is wrong. That something is missing. That something needs to be fixed.

And a monkey who feels that something needs to be fixed might do something drastic to fix it.

Like pushing a man's dinner into a river. Like taking his hat. Like walking him, step by step, to the one place he needs to be.

SO WHO IS THE REAL CHARACTER HERE?

Let's talk about the man for a second.

He's not the hero of this story. He didn't plan anything. He was sitting there with a fish, minding his business, and suddenly his evening fell apart. He's confused. He's annoyed. He's chasing a monkey for a hat.

That's what makes this so compelling. He's us.

He represents every person who has ever assumed they were in control of an encounter with an animal. Every person who looked at a monkey and thought, "I'm the smart one here."

And then the monkey turned around, checked that he was still following, and kept walking.

I'm not saying the man was foolish. I'm saying that for a few minutes of this video, the roles are reversed. The human is the one being led. The animal is the one who knows where the story is going.

That inversion is the whole reason the clip works.

THE FOUR SECONDS THAT CHANGE EVERYTHING

There's a moment in the video, I won't tell you when, where the energy shifts.

Up to that point, everything can be explained away. Mischief. Opportunism. A lucky grab.

Then something happens, and you realize that none of the earlier explanations hold up anymore. The monkey's behavior stops being funny and starts being deliberate. Every earlier detail snaps into focus. The fish. The hat. The glances back. The pace.

I've watched people react to it. They go quiet. Then someone says, "Wait, go back." And they watch it again, and this time they're not laughing at all.

That's the moment I want you to experience. Not because it's shocking in a graphic way, there's nothing like that here, but because it quietly rearranges your assumptions.

You think you know what kind of video this is. You don't.

HOW MONKEYS LEARN TO READ US

One thing that gets lost in these conversations is how much monkeys study humans.

In places where monkeys live near people, temples, towns, riversides, they spend their lives watching us. They learn our schedules. They learn what makes us react. They learn which of us carry food, which of us scare easily, which of us will chase and which will give up.

They read us the way we'd read a crowd in a foreign country. Gestures. Tone. Speed. Posture.

Some populations have been doing it for generations. The knowledge gets passed from mother to infant to cousin to troop. A young monkey doesn't have to figure out from scratch that humans want their hats back. She just watches an older monkey do it, and she learns.

So when you watch a monkey take a hat and lead a man away, you may be watching something that took many monkey generations to develop.

You may be watching culture.

THE PART WHERE I TELL YOU WHAT I THINK

I'll be honest. I went into this clip expecting to write a funny post. A joke about a monkey stealing a hat, a pun about fishing, a quick laugh.

I came out of it unable to write anything funny at all.

Because somewhere around the fourth watch, I stopped seeing a monkey and started seeing a mother.

I'm not going to explain that. I'm not going to say why. If I do, I'll take away the thing that made it hit me.

But I'll tell you this: I've spent a long time studying why some content makes people stop scrolling, and the common thread is always the same. It's not shock. It's not novelty. It's the sudden realization that the thing in front of you is more than it looked.

This clip does that. And it does it with no music, no narration, no setup. Just an animal, a hat, a man, and a decision.

WHY YOU CAN'T FAKE THIS

People ask me whether clips like this are staged. It's a fair question. The internet is full of trained animals, scripted skits, and clever edits.

Here's how I look at it.

Staged animal content has a signature. The animal repeats a clean action. The camera is positioned perfectly. The human reacts on cue. Everything lands exactly when it should, because someone rehearsed it.

Real moments look messier. The framing is a little off. People talk over each other. Nobody knows what's coming, so nobody is ready. The most important thing happens while the camera is pointed slightly in the wrong direction.

That messiness is the proof. You can't script hesitation. You can't direct an animal to stop, look back, and decide the human is worth waiting for. If you've ever tried to get a wild monkey to do anything on command, you know how absurd the idea is.

What you're seeing is a real animal, making a real choice, in real time. And the people holding the camera had no idea what they were filming until it was almost over.

THE CROWS, THE OCTOPUS, AND THE MONKEY

We love to rank animal intelligence. Crows are the clever ones. Octopuses are the weird ones. Dolphins are the friendly ones. Monkeys are the mischievous ones.

But those labels are cartoons. They flatten what's actually going on.

A crow can solve a multi-step puzzle, but a crow isn't going to hold your hat hostage. An octopus can unscrew a jar from the inside, but an octopus isn't going to walk you across a field. A dolphin can cooperate with fishermen, but a dolphin can't pick up your belongings and run.

Monkeys occupy a unique position. They have hands like ours, faces like ours, and social lives that mirror ours in unsettling ways. They live close to us. They watch us. And when they decide to engage, they have the tools to do it on our terms.

Hands that can grab. A brain that can plan. A history of living alongside us. It's a dangerous combination, and I mean that in the best possible way.

WHAT THE ALGORITHM WON'T TELL YOU

Let me say something about why you probably haven't seen this clip yet.

Platforms reward fast reactions. A video that makes you laugh in two seconds beats a video that makes you think for two minutes. A clip that starts with a punchline beats a clip that builds to one.

This clip is the opposite of that. It starts quiet. It asks for patience. It makes you wait. And the reward for waiting is one of the more memorable moments I've seen this year.

Most people will scroll past. They'll see a monkey and a man and assume they already know the story. They'll keep moving.

You don't have to be one of them.

You can give it ninety seconds. You can watch the whole thing, with the sound on, and let it do what it does. And when it's over, you can come back here and tell me whether you felt it too.

THE QUESTIONS THAT WILL STAY WITH YOU

I'll leave you with a few questions. You won't be able to answer them until you've watched.

When did she decide? Was it before the hat, or after the fish, or somewhere in between?

How did she know he would follow her? Was it a guess, or was it knowledge?

What was she afraid of? Because there's a moment where you can see it, and it changes everything.

And the biggest one: when you realize what she was doing, what does that tell you about the animals we share the world with? What else are they trying to tell us that we keep reading as noise?

A SMALL TEST

Here's a test I use on every piece of content I share.

If I could only describe it in one sentence, would that sentence make someone stop and say, "Wait, what?"

For this clip, the sentence is: a monkey tricked a man into following her by stealing his hat, and the reason she did it will stay with you.

That's it. That's the whole pitch. No exaggeration needed. No clickbait. The reality is strange enough.

WHY I'M PUTTING THIS ON MY TIMELINE

I don't post everything I find. I see hundreds of clips a week. Most of them are fine. A few are good. Almost none of them are worth a long post.

I'm writing this one because it did something to me that content rarely does. It made me feel like I'd been underestimating something. Not just monkeys, but the whole idea of how much is happening behind the eyes of the animals around us.

We spend a lot of time asking whether animals can think like us. We spend much less time asking whether they can care like us.

This clip doesn't answer that question. But it makes it very hard to keep treating it as a joke.

THE THEORY NOBODY WANTS TO SAY OUT LOUD

Here's the uncomfortable version of this story.

If you strip away the humor, the hat, and the river, what's left is an animal that identified a problem, found a person who could help, and figured out how to make that person pay attention.

That's not mischief. That's asking for help.

And it raises a question scientists have been circling for decades: do wild animals ever seek out humans on purpose, because they understand that humans can do things they can't?

There are stories. Dolphins bringing injured companions to divers. Dogs leading rescuers to trapped owners. Wild birds guiding people to honey, a partnership between humans and honeyguides that appears to go back a very long time. Researchers have documented that the birds respond to specific human calls and lead people toward bees' nests.

Those are cases where an animal has learned that a human is useful. This clip suggests a monkey may have reached a similar conclusion, and found her own way to act on it.

I'm not asking you to believe it. I'm asking you to watch carefully, and then see if you can still believe the opposite.

THE DISTANCE BETWEEN US IS SMALLER THAN WE THINK

Humans and macaques share a common ancestor from something like twenty-five million years ago. That's a long time. It's also not nearly as long as it sounds when you consider how much we still have in common.

The same basic emotions. The same attachment systems. The same stress responses when a baby is in danger. The same urge to do something, anything, when someone you love needs you.

When a human parent hears a child cry, the body reacts before the mind does. Heart rate. Adrenaline. A single narrowed focus.

There is no reason to think a monkey mother feels any less. And there's no reason to think she wouldn't do something unusual, even something risky, if she believed it would work.

That's the line this clip walks. It's funny on the surface. It's deeply serious underneath.

WHY THE ENDING HITS HARDER THAN IT SHOULD

I've thought about why this video lands the way it does, and I think it comes down to contrast.

For most of the runtime you're being told one story: silly monkey, unlucky man, comedy of errors. Your brain settles into that frame and relaxes.

Then the frame breaks.

The best storytellers know that the strongest emotion doesn't come from sadness or joy on their own. It comes from the shift between the two. From the moment you realize you were laughing at something that deserved your respect.

That shift is the engine of this clip. And the person who filmed it didn't engineer it. They just kept recording, and reality did the rest.

BEFORE YOU WATCH

A few things to know.

Watch the whole thing. The first half is setup. The second half is the story.

Watch the monkey's face, not the man's. The man is reacting. The monkey is deciding.

Watch what she does every time he falls behind. That's the detail that gives it away.

And watch the ending twice. The first time you'll be caught off guard. The second time you'll see everything you missed.

THE PART THAT MAKES ME THINK ABOUT US

Watch how the man reacts once he understands.

There's no speech. No dramatic music. He doesn't need either. His posture changes, his pace changes, and the whole tone of the encounter shifts from irritation to something much quieter.

That's the human half of this story, and it matters just as much. Because understanding is a two-way street. The monkey had to read him. He had to read her. And for a few minutes, across a gap of twenty-five million years, two very different minds managed to meet in the middle.

How often does that happen? How often do we stop, look at an animal, and ask what it's actually trying to say?

Most days, we don't. We're busy. We assume. We shoo them away, laugh, film, scroll.

This time, somebody paid attention. And look what happened.

ONE MORE THING BEFORE YOU PRESS PLAY

Don't watch this on mute. Don't watch it while you're typing. Don't watch it as background noise while you eat.

Give it the same attention the monkey gave that man.

She waited for him. She checked on him. She trusted that if she kept going, he would keep coming.

The least we can do is return the favor and stay until the end.

AFTER YOU WATCH

Come back and tell me three things:

Where did you realize what was happening?

Did you laugh, or did you go quiet?

Do you think she planned it from the start?

I read every reply. And I've been surprised, again and again, by how differently people read this clip. Some see a trick. Some see a plea. Some see something they can't put into words.

There's no wrong answer. But there is a right way to find out, and it starts with pressing play.

THE LAST THING

We live in a world that is very good at making us feel like we've seen everything. The same jokes. The same formats. The same reactions.

Every once in a while, something breaks through. Something small, unscripted, and strange. Something that reminds you that the world still has surprises in it, and that some of them are happening in places you'll never visit, to animals you'll never meet, in moments nobody planned to record.

This is one of those moments.

A monkey. A fish. A hat. A river. A man who had no idea he was about to become part of someone else's story.

Watch it.

Then tell me you didn't feel it too.

If this made you curious, repost it. Not for me. For the next person who's about to scroll past something they'd remember for the rest of their life.

text:
I stand with America and I stand with God’s Holy Land.
Until the day the Good Lord decides to take me home, I will always carry Israel close to my heart.

It is the place where God called Moses up the mountain and gave him the Ten Commandments with His own hand (Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 5). The law was not given in some distant, nameless land. 

It was given in the region of the people He had redeemed and brought out of Egypt, the same people He promised Abraham He would make a great nation and give a land forever (Genesis 12:1-3; 15:18; 17:7-8).

It is the place where King David reigned, wrote the Psalms, and received the covenant promise that his throne would be established forever. The Lord said, “I will raise up your offspring after you… and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:12-13). 

From David’s line the Savior would come. The Psalms themselves cry out from that land songs of the King, songs of the Temple, songs of the Messiah who would suffer and reign.

It is the place where Jesus was born in Bethlehem, just as Micah prophesied: “But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah… from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel” (Micah 5:2). 

It is the place where He walked, taught, healed, and fulfilled the Law and the Prophets. And it is the place of the greatest sacrifice in history. 

Outside the walls of Jerusalem, the Lamb of God was offered once for all. “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities… and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:5-6). There the blood was shed that purchased the church, and there the empty tomb declared that death is defeated.

This is not a political slogan for me. It is the geography of redemption. God chose that land, that people, and those places to bring the Messiah into the world and to keep His covenants. 

I will not be ashamed of that. I will not trade it for the approval of the moment.

Until He calls me home, Israel stays close to my heart because the Word of God is still true, the covenants still stand, and the Savior who walked those hills is still Lord of all.👑🇺🇸🇮🇱

🤯An incredible report with some rare deets. 
If true , is an account where the Aliens go to some length is explaining their position. Unlike an abduction, this seems to be a chance encouter. 

Picture a young Soviet officer,  Gali Galiev , in winter 1948, heading home to see  family . He gets caught in a blizzard, loses the road, and falls into a hole. Lying there, he sees a light in the clouds that gets closer, then goes out. Then a huge dark shape hangs overhead, a round hatch opens, and something lifts him inside.

Inside is a bright, round room with strange devices and four small beings, about 1.5 meters tall, with large dark eyes and reddish-violet skin. He says they talked to him without any speech (but their lips were moving as reported always) , he could hear, as if they were reading his thoughts. They offered him warm air to dry his clothes and something to eat. Then they started asking about Soviet weapons, ammunition, and anti-aircraft defenses. He was surprised they weren't interested in big guns or the German V2 rockets, which they said they'd already intercepted and studied !!!! They studied German rockets !!

The details that stand out most come from the conversation that followed. The aliens said they could create fields around their craft that push back shells and bullets, and that light and radio waves bend around them, which is why they're invisible to our eyes and radar!!!! First mechanistic explanation and acknowledgment of invisibility ! . In humid air, they said, the craft can look like a blurry glowing ball.(plasma orbs!? ) . They also claimed they can project strong fields over long distances to cut or burn things (can they and do they cut stone this way ) , control electron movement so wires become insulators or superconductors, make artificial diamonds of any size, and use gold and copper for conductors. They said all of this is only for defense and that they study Earth without threatening anyone.

Then they showed him a film about a star system called Tau, about 12 light-years away, which is a bit smaller and cooler than our sun. Two planets there matter most: Tagir, roughly Earth-sized and mostly ocean, and Zukra, smaller, drier, and colder. Both have 12-hour days. Tagir was once a thriving world with floating cities, fish-harvesting ships that lure fish with signals, underwater harvesters, and light-powered "Tau batteries" in building tiles. Its people used wind and starlight for energy and refused nuclear power. But the story goes that nuclear weapons, once controlled by supposedly super-intelligent computers, were triggered during a planetquake. The air reached 200 degrees, the water boiled, and radioactive rain killed everything. The survivors on Zukra later found the planet contaminated.

The aliens also said they collect seeds from Earth to send home, and that contact with humans happens regularly, usually one person at a time. They explained why they don't show themselves openly: people would want to understand their technology, get in the way, and force them to use weapons that could kill people. As for the witnesses, they said nobody would believe the witness, and the witness would start doubting their own memory. That's why Galiev stayed quiet for long.

Before releasing him, they showed him a three-dimensional map of Kazan, the Volga, the railway, Arsk station, and the Ashit River near his village. Then they showed him his parents sleeping, and they woke up alarmed. text:
Even modest improvements in vehicle lifetime and inspection time would compound enormously across hundreds of thousands of annual launches.

But there is a distinction between improving a rocket’s material properties and eliminating the need for physical refurbishment. Extreme thermal cycling, vibration, erosion, and fatigue remain formidable.

What makes this entire technological convergence intriguing is that it offers several independent routes to lower costs: energy, fabrication, materials performance, and automation.

We don’t need molecular assemblers that can build entire rockets for nanotechnology to become economically transformative. We need sufficiently good control over materials at small scales that building and maintaining large machines becomes dramatically easier.

And that is considerably closer to the current research frontier than the old science-fiction vision of unrestricted nanobots.

text:
Any real gamer who grew up with an NES in the living room, the power light glowing red while the rest of the house pretended not to hear the endless crashes and thuds, played Paperboy. Not the tourists who drift through modern open worlds collecting checkmarks and calling it engagement, not the ones who need a map, a waypoint, and a tutorial that lasts longer than the entire original cartridge. This was the game you rented for the weekend or saved up paper route money to buy outright because the idea of pedaling a bike down a suburban street while the neighborhood tried to murder you felt like the purest distillation of 1980s American childhood. It stands out from every other title in its field because its field barely existed. Arcade cabinets and home consoles of the mid to late eighties were drowning in space shooters, platformers, and mazes where the fantasy was becoming someone else entirely. Paperboy refused the fantasy. It made the job itself the fantasy, then weaponized every ordinary detail of that job until the ordinary became an obstacle course of pure chaos. That refusal is what makes it unique, what makes it a masterpiece, and what keeps it a cultural icon decades later when most games from that era have faded into pixelated footnotes.

You are a kid on a bike delivering The Daily Sun through a neighborhood that looks like a Norman Rockwell painting only if Rockwell had been on a sugar high and decided every lawn ornament was a landmine. The street scrolls toward you in that odd isometric angle that never quite felt natural on a controller yet somehow became second nature after a few dozen crashes. Your bike never stops. Up on the d pad speeds you, down brakes, left and right weave, and the A or B button flings a tightly rolled newspaper that arcs leftward depending on how hard you lean. Land it in the mailbox of a white, blue, or yellow house and the points rain down hard. Drop it on the porch and you still succeed but the score feels thinner. Miss entirely or, worse, smash a subscriber window by accident and that house turns red the next morning. Red houses are open season. Windows shatter for points, garbage cans topple, tombstones tip, bushes explode. The game never lectures you about this choice. It simply lets the newspaper itself become the instrument of both duty and petty vandalism, and the player discovers the lesson in the score. Precision under pressure is the real currency. You cannot stop to line up a shot. The skateboarder is already rolling at you, the dog is already lunging, the breakdancer is already spinning in the middle of the sidewalk for no reason except that 1988 thought breakdancing was still peak suburban menace. Every throw is a calculation made while the world refuses to pause. That calculation is the entire point. Modern games give you aim assist and bullet time and then wonder why the moment feels hollow. Paperboy trusts you to learn the arc of the paper the way you once learned the weight of a real rolled newspaper on a real porch.

The week structure turns the whole thing into a quiet sermon on consequences. Monday starts with a map of the street. Ten houses want the paper. Deliver to all of them without damage and the next day a new subscriber appears, the route slowly filling with more targets that must be hit or lost forever. Fail and the route shrinks until the headline screams that the paperboy has been fired and the digitized voice that somehow survived the port declares the end. There is no narrative cutscene explaining this. The game simply advances the day, changes the color of the houses, and lets you feel the weight of the previous choices every time you roll out again. Sunday papers are heavier, the throws slower, the margin thinner. The training course at the end of each street, the ramps and targets and the timer, is not a bonus stage so much as the final exam of the shift. Crash there and you lose nothing but the points you could have earned. Survive the week and the headline changes to something almost proud. The lesson is not subtle once you feel it: the work is the same every morning, the neighborhood does not care about your excuses, and the only progress is the accumulation of perfect days. You either keep the customers or you watch them vanish one by one. That is the takeaway buried inside the color coded houses. Responsibility is a score multiplier, not a moral. Chaos is also a score multiplier. The game refuses to pick a side for you.

What makes the experience fun, even when it is frustrating enough to make you slam the controller and swear you are done, is the pure kinetic satisfaction of the throw itself. The paper leaves the hand, arcs, and either thuds into the mailbox with that perfect sound or shatters glass. The bike leans. The obstacles approach at speeds that force split second decisions. Dogs, cars, runaway tires, tornadoes, the occasional Grim Reaper who has no business being on a residential street yet somehow fits the tone better than any alien invasion ever could. The era it came from is written into every sprite. This is 1988 America filtered through arcade exaggeration: kids still had paper routes, BMX bikes were status symbols, breakdancers and skateboarders were the local hazards, and the suburban dream was still close enough that satirizing it felt fresh rather than nostalgic. The NES port, developed by Eastridge Technology and published by Mindscape in December of that year, stripped the custom handlebars of the arcade cabinet and the higher resolution display, yet somehow kept the soul. The controls are stiff, the graphics are chunky, the music is thin compared to the arcade original, and British magazines of the time called the conversion offensive and derisive. Players did not care. It sold in the millions. Real gamers who grew up with it remember the feeling more than the frame rate. You rented it, you played until your eyes crossed trying to track both the mailbox and the hydrant, you died three times and started over, and you came back the next afternoon because the street still felt alive in a way no other cartridge on the shelf managed.

The uniqueness lives in that refusal to be anything else. Other games of the period asked you to save the world or rescue the princess or clear the screen of invaders. Paperboy asked you to finish the route. The obstacles are not enemies so much as the ordinary world weaponized. A manhole, a fire hydrant, a kid on a tricycle, an old woman, a swarm of bees if you slow down too long in the arcade version. The isometric view, inspired by earlier experiments like Zaxxon, forces you to read depth and timing in a way side scrollers never required. You are always moving forward. There is no reverse. There is no pause that lasts more than a blink if you mash the start button too casually, a quirk of the NES version that somehow feels appropriate. The game is a single continuous decision. Throw or weave. Deliver or destroy. Survive the day or watch the subscribers leave. That continuous decision is what modern open world tourist games cannot replicate no matter how many side activities they stuff into the map. You are not exploring. You are working. The work is the game.

Behind the scenes the whole thing began in a brainstorming session at Atari in February 1983. Designer Dave Ralston, who had actually been a paperboy as a kid in a family of paperboys, sketched the idea on a transparency for an overhead projector: a kid on a bike, an isometric street, green arrows showing the path. Programmer John Salwitz was initially unconvinced. He expected spaceships. The early prototypes leaned into pure surrealism with giant snails, ducks in suits, rolling pianos, and scientists at pianos. Focus groups rejected most of it. The team stripped the weirdness back to the everyday and left just enough of the strange, the Grim Reaper included, to keep the tone from becoming pure simulation. The arcade cabinet used modified handlebars from the Star Wars yoke so the act of steering felt physical. The hardware pushed medium resolution at 512 by 384 when most games were stuck at 320 by 240. The NES version arrived as a last minute replacement for another project at Summer CES 1988 and became one of the first games developed in the United States for the system. It outsold the arcade cabinets in raw numbers. Salwitz later admitted the home version crushed the original in the only metric that eventually mattered: people actually played it in their living rooms. The sequel added a papergirl and more routes and never quite recaptured the same magic. The original remains the one that stuck because it never tried to be more than the route.

Every real gamer who grew up with it still feels the lean of the bike when a dog appears. That feeling is the cultural icon. It is the masterpiece because it turned the most ordinary job a kid could have into the purest expression of timing, consequence, and controlled chaos the NES ever offered. You play it to learn that the throw matters more than the story, that the day is the same until you make it different, and that the neighborhood will always try to run you down no matter how carefully you aim. The modern games that pretend to offer freedom never force you to keep pedaling. Paperboy never lets you stop. That is why it endures.

text:
High taxes (especially the Corporate Activity Tax), regulatory burdens with slow permitting/land-use restrictions, and high costs of living/housing plus a weak business climate (including talent and urban issues) are the top recurring reasons.
These emerge consistently from a 2025 University of Oregon study commissioned by Business Oregon (surveying nearly 400 traded-sector businesses), Oregon Business & Industry data, Tax Foundation rankings, CNBC Top States for Business, and business leader accounts. Oregon has seen more expansion of operations out-of-state (rather than a pure mass headquarters exodus), with 68% of surveyed firms contacted by out-of-state recruiters (from places like Texas, Arizona, Idaho, and the Carolinas) ultimately expanding or moving some activity elsewhere. Closures have also outpaced new openings in recent data.
1. High taxes and rising tax burden
Oregon relies heavily on income taxes and added the Corporate Activity Tax (CAT) in 2019 (effective 2020). The CAT is a gross-receipts tax: $250 plus 0.57% on taxable Oregon commercial activity above $1 million (with a 35% subtraction for certain costs). It applies across entity types, hits low-margin firms hard even in loss years, and has generated substantial revenue while raising the effective business tax burden.
Statewide effective business taxes rose roughly a third from 2019–2023 (more steeply in the Portland metro area, reported around 80%+ in some analyses). Oregon ranks poorly on Tax Foundation measures for corporate taxes (often near the bottom) and has fallen sharply on overall tax competitiveness. Businesses cite this alongside high individual income tax rates as a key reason they expand elsewhere (e.g., to lower-tax states). Examples include Dutch Bros shifting significant headquarters functions to the Phoenix area.
2. Regulatory burdens, permitting delays, and land-use rules
Oregon is frequently ranked among the most regulated states (around 7th in some counts). Businesses report frequent regulatory changes that are hard to track, duplicative rules, and lengthy, expensive permitting. Strict urban growth boundaries and related land-use processes make it time-consuming and costly to expand industrial land or sites—delays of years are common. This limits growth opportunities and makes the state less competitive when other places offer faster timelines and incentives.
The UO study lists the regulatory climate among the main “push factors” driving investment away, alongside tax policy. Manufacturing has been particularly affected amid broader sector challenges.
3. High costs (housing, land, wages) and unfavorable business climate
Housing shortages and high costs of living raise labor expenses and make it harder to attract and retain talent. Surveys show 57% of responding businesses rated Oregon as only “fair” or “poor” for doing business, citing cost of living, taxes, economic conditions, and issues such as crime and homelessness (especially noted in the Portland area post-2020). High relative wages and limited industrial land compound this. The overall business climate has deteriorated in rankings: CNBC’s America’s Top States for Business placed Oregon around 42nd in 2026 (down sharply from 17th in 2017), with especially weak scores for cost of doing business and business friendliness.
Other states pull firms with incentives, lower operating costs, and pro-growth messaging. Oregon retains some “anchor” advantages (quality of life for some, existing workforce/assets, no general sales tax), but the push factors have outweighed them for many expansion decisions since 2020. State officials and business groups have acknowledged the retention challenge, with efforts like Gov. Kotek’s Prosperity Roadmap aimed at improving the climate, though rankings and survey data have continued to reflect concerns.

Alignment Healthcare was founded in 2013, and the 10-K opens not with a market-size chart but with a mission statement: "Improve Healthcare, One Senior at a Time." Four core values follow as a bulleted list — always put the senior first; support the doctor; use data and technology to revolutionize care; and act with a serving heart. It is rare for an SEC filing to describe a serving heart. The heart is not a reportable segment.

The founding story, as the company tells it, is personal: "We created Alignment after our own families faced frustrating experiences within the fragmented healthcare system." The filing describes loved ones "left to navigate a care delivery and insurance landscape fraught with confusion and complexity," and says seniors are "disadvantaged by misaligned incentives that dominate today's healthcare system." Naming your company after the thing you say the industry lacks is a commitment. Every quarterly report becomes a small grammatical test.

The stated ambition is to "bring this senior-first healthcare experience to millions in the United States, become the most trusted senior healthcare brand in the country, and ultimately 'do well by doing good.'" That last phrase arrives in the filing already wearing its own quotation marks, the punctuation equivalent of a small apologetic cough.

The scale that mission has reached is 236,300 Health Plan members at the end of fiscal 2025 — members enrolled in the HMO and PPO contracts the company calls the Alignment Health Plan — from around 13,000 at inception. For the 2025 plan year the company offered Medicare Advantage plans in 45 markets: 22 in California, 16 in North Carolina, three in Arizona, two in Nevada and two in Texas. The company states those markets collectively include approximately 8.4 million Medicare-eligible seniors. California alone accounts for nearly half the market count, which tells you where the model was built before it went travelling.

Revenue over those same years moved from $1.17bn in fiscal 2021 to $3.95bn in fiscal 2025. Net income over the same span moved from -$195.3m to -$978,000.

text:
A California man says his father may have been the Zodiac Killer and unlike many theories surrounding one of America’s most infamous unsolved murder cases, parts of this claim can actually be tested.

Jacob Lehman alleges that his biological father, scientist Peter A. Lehman, was the unidentified killer who murdered five people and wounded two others across Northern California in 1968 and 1969 before taunting newspapers with ciphers, threats and the now-famous crossed-circle symbol.

So BPI News went through the claim piece by piece.

Peter Lehman really was a physical chemist who went on to conduct postdoctoral research at UC Berkeley. If he was already living there when the murders began, he would have been within realistic travelling distance of every confirmed Zodiac crime scene.

But there is a problem: the exact date he moved to Berkeley remains unclear. His University of Chicago doctoral thesis was published in December 1969 after the confirmed Zodiac killings had already taken place. 

That does not prove he was still in Chicago, but it makes his whereabouts in 1968 and 1969 one of the most important unanswered questions.

Then there are the Wing Walker boots.

The Zodiac left distinctive boot impressions at Lake Berryessa. Lehman’s son says his father wore size 10 shoes and was training as a pilot.

The FBI record, however, describes the boots as size 10½.

Close but not the exact match sometimes presented.

The scientific connection is also intriguing. Lehman was a highly trained physical chemist. The Zodiac later sent detailed bomb diagrams involving ammonium nitrate, fuel and electrical triggering mechanisms.

Interesting? Yes.

Proof? No.

Then there is Eureka.

A disputed Zodiac communication was mailed from Eureka, California, in 1990 close to Arcata, where Lehman later built his career.

But that card has never been conclusively authenticated as Zodiac correspondence.

And then we get to the part of the story that could actually change everything: DNA.

A hair was reportedly preserved beneath a stamp on authenticated Zodiac correspondence connected to murdered taxi driver Paul Stine.

For decades, a rootless hair offered limited forensic possibilities.

That is no longer necessarily true.

New forensic techniques can recover nuclear DNA from rootless hair, potentially allowing investigators to make powerful family comparisons that were impossible when the evidence was first examined.

If that hair survives, if its chain of custody is intact and if investigators believe it belonged to the person who mailed the letter, modern DNA technology could potentially test this theory rather than argue about photographs, personalities and coincidences.

BPI News found no evidence that Peter Lehman has ever been publicly named by police as a Zodiac suspect.

There is currently no known DNA, fingerprint, handwriting or physical-evidence match connecting him to the crimes.

We also found that some of the wider allegations made about his later life do not stand up cleanly against the public record.

So does the theory collapse?

Not quite.

Does the evidence currently point to Peter Lehman as the Zodiac Killer?

No.

But there are enough verifiable details particularly his Berkeley connection and the existence of potentially testable forensic evidence to ask a much more useful question:

Where exactly was Peter Lehman on 20 December 1968, 4 July 1969, 27 September 1969 and 11 October 1969?

BPI News has examined the timeline, the boots, the police descriptions, the bomb letters, the Eureka card and the DNA evidence in detail.

•  Depression and bipolar/mood disorders
•  Anxiety disorders and OCD
•  Eating disorders
•  Addictive disorders and co-occurring (dual-diagnosis) conditions
•  Schizophrenia and related disorders
•  ADHD and other attention/behavioral issues

Services span the continuum of care: inpatient hospitalization, residential programs (such as diagnostic assessment and short-term residential treatment at Sibcy House), partial hospitalization (PHP), intensive outpatient (IOP), outpatient therapy and medication management, and specialized multi-day diagnostic assessments for complex or treatment-resistant cases. It also offers advanced treatments like TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation), ECT, DBT, and others.

text:
Trump says Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire", but neither Moscow nor Kyiv has confirmed it.

In a Truth Social post on Sunday, he said both sides would halt attacks on energy infrastructure: "Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" The FT reports Ukraine had not been informed.

The announcement follows Trump's demand that Kyiv stop striking Russian refineries, and talks in Miami where US, E3, European Commission, NATO and Ukrainian officials discussed winter preparedness, including energy resilience.

The Ukrainian and European delegations left Miami earlier than planned. Zelensky still said Kyiv needs the Americans "to try to stop this war".

On Moscow's side, Putin told Trump in their October 9 call that Russia's war aims remain unchanged. War monitors note that Russia has offered no concessions and has rejected the compromise proposals put forward by the US and Ukraine.

Whether the truce holds rests on confirmation from both capitals. Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are preparing a new unified proposal ahead of the next US engagement with Russia.

text:
The D2C wholesale market that $ASTS is defending isn’t really the main focus for $SPCX bigger ambitions.

From a pure telecom gap-filling standpoint, the market for Direct-to-Cell service is still relatively limited. Most estimates put global D2C revenue around the tens of billions of dollars by 2030, which is a lot smaller than the consumer and enterprise broadband business SpaceX/Starlink already has running at scale, covering aviation, maritime, government, and fixed locations. For SpaceX, D2C is more like an extra capability layer on top of its connectivity platform rather than the core of its revenue or strategy.

What matters more strategically is that D2C can serve as one way to connect edge devices. As agent workloads and physical AI grow, things like vehicles, robots, industrial sensors, and remote assets still need connectivity in places with no ground coverage. SpaceX can lower orbits, combine that with orbital data centers, and use its existing satellite scale to offer lower-latency direct links, tying compute closer to the endpoints.  That approach is fundamentally different from ASTS, which relies heavily on telecom wholesale partnerships and focuses on unmodified phones.

ASTS does have advantages from its large antennas, which help with link budgets, and from its relationships with carriers. But constellation size, launch cadence, and capital intensity remain clear weak points. Carriers also don’t strictly need ASTS, since alternatives like SpaceX exist. SpaceX, by contrast, benefits from vertical integration across its own launches, satellite numbers, spectrum, and products, plus a wider set of use cases. For them, D2C is mainly a tool to expand edge connectivity coverage, not a make-or-break bet.

In short, ASTS is putting most of its resources into a relatively small niche that’s still largely controlled by telecom operators, while SpaceX is aiming at a much larger connectivity and compute platform. That difference in focus is a big reason their risk profiles and long-term valuation logic look so different.

You can’t help but marvel at the talent Chuck Norris so consistently managed to avoid. With that ridiculous haircut and enough body hair to furnish a studio apartment, he resembles an Ewok who’s been thrown out of a karaoke bar.

Yet this extraordinary little creature forged a long and successful career out of looking as though someone had explained acting to him over a bad telephone connection.

In Walker, Texas Ranger, Chuck demonstrated a remarkable emotional range: suspicious of a criminal, disappointed in a criminal, and about to kick a criminal. Sometimes, in the more demanding episodes, he narrowed his eyes.

Always an optimist, Chuck landed on his feet—usually because the scene required nothing more complicated. His natural gift for stealing scenes lay in entering them and making off with every trace of dramatic tension.

Then came Steven Seagull, a man who spent decades being unconvincing as people who were already written unconvincingly. Occasionally they made him the star, presumably after the remaining cast checked the emergency exits. He brought to action cinema the brooding menace of a nightclub bouncer trying to remember where he’d parked.

Alongside Jean-Claude Van Damme, they formed the holy trinity of inspirational inadequacy. They offered hope to anyone who lacked talent or charisma: you, too, could achieve fame without either ever becoming an issue. Van Damme at least did the splits, giving audiences two directions in which to look away.

Just when the dream seemed complete, Dolph Lundgren appeared: a wardrobe with cheekbones, sent to settle an argument between other wardrobes.

Together, these immortals of wooden performance proved that a blockbuster could be low-budget in every respect except explosions—and that a script could apparently be written by someone who’d heard about human conversation but never actually attended one.

They didn’t merely lower the bar. They kicked it, shot it, and walked away from it in slow motion.

text:
Last night at least 12 people were killed and 309 wounded in a Houthi attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. Saudi Arabia’s response is unlikely to prioritize the “protection of civilians, and self-control” as it encouraged Israel to do in the wake of October 7. But nor, to its great detriment, will it take the Israeli route: the one that leads to lasting security.

The strike comes a week into Operation Dawn of Yemen, a Saudi-backed offensive by Yemeni government forces against the Iranian-backed Houthis. With the help of some 100 Saudi jets, government-aligned forces have already retaken key stretches of coast along Bab el-Mandeb. But even as the Houthis are hard-pressed, and Yemeni officials talk optimistically of driving all the way to Houthi-held Sanaa, the Saudis are keeping one eye on the rearview mirror.

After joining the Iran war late and hesitantly, firing their first missiles at Israel only a month in, the Houthis largely held their fire against the Jewish state and found a much softer target in the Gulf monarchy. In July they declared a naval blockade on the kingdom. Riyadh’s response has typically been tepid: limited airstrikes and quiet diplomacy.

That has long been the Saudi playbook. Even at the height of its war on the Houthis, the kingdom kept one hand extended. In 2019, after Houthi-claimed drone strikes on its oil facilities, it said it viewed a Houthi truce offer “positively.” In 2020 it told the Houthis, through back channels, that it would sign a UN-brokered nationwide ceasefire in exchange for a buffer zone on its border. In 2021 it publicly offered a ceasefire and the reopening of Sanaa airport, with its foreign minister declaring “it is up to the Houthis now.” Since the 2022 truce, the kingdom has largely halted offensive operations even in the face of sporadic provocations. Even when the United States and Britain began addressing the Houthi problem in January 2024, Riyadh called for “self-restraint” from the sidelines. As recently as mid-September, with the Houthis fresh from seizing Mocha, the kingdom reportedly offered them a two-week ceasefire and direct talks through Omani mediators.

Rather than a new dawn for Riyadh’s Yemen policy, this war is simply a means to negotiate. After the Houthis’ advance last month, Riyadh concluded that it could not enter new talks while the Houthis held Bab el-Mandeb. Without U.S. support, it will likely declare victory if it simply pushes the Houthis off the Red Sea coast and restores quiet.

If this mowing-the-grass strategy sounds familiar, it is because the kinship between the Houthis and Hamas runs deeper than shared enemies and sponsors. Both terror groups have been the object of a far more technologically advanced neighbor’s conceptzia: the belief that an enemy sworn to your destruction can be bought off or contained.

In place of suitcases of Qatari cash, Riyadh reportedly paid Houthi civil servants out of its own pocket. And when the Houthi flood came, it dwarfed October 7. Instead of several thousand gunmen, some 100,000 fighters reportedly massed without Saudi intelligence noticing, then swept down the Red Sea coast in September and seized Bab el-Mandeb.

This is where the two countries diverge.

Surveying the destruction of its territory, Israel understood that such a threat could not be allowed to rebuild on its border, and, despite American misgivings, went about uprooting Hamas. The Saudis, looking at their burning tankers and smoldering oil facilities, also resolved that the situation had to be dealt with. So they called Washington for help, were rebuffed, and settled for a particularly aggressive round of mowing.

The gap is starker still on what should have been a shared revelation for Riyadh and Jerusalem: Iran. Israel’s strategy has been criticized at home for fighting the tentacles rather than striking the head of the octopus. Saudi strategy deserves harsher criticism: it fights a tentacle while negotiating appeasement with the head. Despite Iran’s fingerprints being all over the Houthi escalation, the Saudis are still seeking an accommodation with the creature.

Perhaps Israelis should thank Moses for bringing us to the only area in the region not overflowing with oil. Lacking vast natural resources, and with them an indispensable place on the world stage, Israel has never comfortably settled into the role of a status quo power. In the rare moments it slipped into such complacency, it was brutally reminded that the status quo is one in which it is surrounded by enemies eager to overturn its status as existing. Constant struggle for survival is practically a core tenet of Zionism.

That Israel has never had the luxury of the status quo lies at the root of what separates it from many of America’s allies, and from America itself. It is why the Houthis will happily strike King Khalid International Airport but now think twice about Ben Gurion. It is why the Saudis will not try anything without Washington holding their hand, while Washington grips Israel’s for dear life to keep it from upending the status quo.

That fear of a new Middle East is the great achievement of Iran and its proxies: without a nuclear weapon, they have built a Cold War-style balance of terror that much of the West fears to provoke.

The Houthis in the mountains of northern Yemen present a different challenge from Hamas in its tunnels under Gaza, but the lesson of appeasing terror is the same. If the Saudis want to find themselves safer five years from now, they should start reading up on Zionism.

text:
*CHILDISH TRUMP*

The United States is engaged in a confrontation with Iran, while Russia has been reported as providing various forms of support to Tehran. Against that backdrop, the decision to allow increased Russian diesel exports, reportedly aimed at lowering fuel costs, raises important strategic questions.

In a recent announcement, President Trump outlined an arrangement that would permit Russia to supply diesel to U.S. and international markets, along with temporary sanctions relief. At the same time, reports have indicated that Russia has offered assistance to Iran during the ongoing conflict.

Critics argue that this creates an apparent policy inconsistency. On one hand, Washington is taking a hard line against Iran; on the other, it is easing economic restrictions on a country accused of backing Tehran.

There is no direct evidence that revenues from the proposed fuel arrangement have funded actions against U.S. forces. Nevertheless, the public is entitled to understand how policymakers evaluated the potential geopolitical risks against the anticipated economic benefits.

Reducing energy costs is a legitimate objective. However, any effort to lower fuel prices should be examined carefully to ensure it does not unintentionally strengthen governments whose interests may conflict with those of the United States.

Several questions remain unanswered. What conditions and protections are built into the agreement? What commitments, if any, were secured from Moscow? And to what extent will consumers actually benefit from lower fuel prices?

Rather than accepting the deal at face value, lawmakers and the public should closely scrutinize its long-term economic and strategic implications.

The central issue is whether this represents a carefully calculated diplomatic move or an expensive policy choice that could generate unintended consequences in the future.

‼️BREAKING || TIME TO LEAVE SLOVYANSK -- RESIDENT FILMS SHATTERED FLATS AS TRUMP ANNOUNCES UKRAINE ENERGY CEASEFIRE

Slovyansk -- A resident filming the wreckage of a block of flats says in Russian that it is now time to leave the city. His warning accompanies scenes far removed from Trump's ceasefire announcements.

The camera sweeps across a courtyard strewn with debris, shattered windows and damaged balconies before returning to a collapsed section of the building. Concrete floors have fallen into a heap. Rooms stand open to the air, with a broken slab hanging above the wreckage.

Ukrainian authorities said Russian airstrikes partially destroyed two blocks of flats and injured seven people. Seven other residential blocks and a shop suffered damage.

Meanwhile, Trump announced an immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. "Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote. Ukrainian officials initially told CNN that the announcement had taken them by surprise.

Zelensky subsequently expressed support but said Ukraine was awaiting details from Washington, stopping short of confirming that a settled agreement was already operating. 

Moscow did not immediately comment.

Earlier, responding to Trump's call for Ukraine to choose a new president, Zelensky told ABC: "With all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader."

He offered Trump to persuade Putin to accept a full 60-day ceasefire, and Ukraine would organise a vote.

That demands considerably more than a pause in attacks on energy infrastructure. With even the narrower arrangement awaiting clarification, a comprehensive two-month truce looks a remote basis for promising elections.

Zelensky invokes the people's right to choose while leaving the vote dependent on a ceasefire nobody has secured.

text:
FAULTLINE | WORLD THIS WEEK
11 OCTOBER 2026

THE NEXT CRISIS MAY BEGIN WHERE THE LAST ONE LEFT AN EXIT

Imagine running a shipping company. The oil is ready, the buyer is waiting, and the ship is available. But the route is dangerous, insurance costs are rising, and nobody can tell you whether the journey will be safe next week.

You don't need to run out of oil to have a crisis. You only need to lose confidence that you can deliver it.

That is the bigger story emerging from Yemen this week.

01 | YEMEN - A LOCAL WAR IS REACHING FAR BEYOND ITS BORDERS

Fighting between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces has intensified around Bab al-Mandab, the narrow passage connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. On 10 October, a Houthi attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300, according to Saudi authorities. Donald Trump said the US might join Saudi strikes against the Houthis, but no decision to intervene had been announced. 
The timing matters. Hormuz is already disrupting energy flows, and Bab al-Mandab is another important route for trade between Asia and Europe. If both remain dangerous, shipping companies face fewer reliable options, higher insurance costs and longer journeys.

The danger is not necessarily that both routes close completely. It is that businesses can no longer count on either one being safe and predictable.

02 | THE PEOPLE WHO PAY MAY BE THOUSANDS OF MILES AWAY

When shipping becomes less predictable, the cost travels. Fuel distributors pay more to move supplies, manufacturers face delays, and governments importing energy have less room to protect households from higher prices.

Meanwhile, the humanitarian cost inside Yemen is mounting. The International Organization for Migration reported that more than 184,000 people were displaced between 1 August and 4 October, with thousands more forced from their homes in a single week.
The people closest to the fighting suffer the most direct damage. But the economic consequences can reach families and businesses far beyond the battlefield.

03 | INDIA'S CRITICAL-MINERALS PROBLEM SHOWS THE SAME WEAKNESS

India wants to reduce its dependence on China's dominant position in rare-earth processing. Northern Myanmar has valuable deposits, and the historic Stilwell Road could offer a route towards Indian processing facilities. But armed conflict, contested territorial control and weak infrastructure make that a difficult prospect. China already has the processing capacity and supply-chain links that India is trying to build.
This is a different problem from Yemen, but the underlying lesson is similar. Finding a resource is not the same as securing a dependable supply. The minerals must be extracted, transported, processed and turned into products that factories can use.

Strategic independence is built across an entire supply chain, not simply by finding another source.

WHAT COULD HAPPEN NEXT?

My forecast is that the reliability of trade routes could become as important as the availability of the goods moving through them. Watch whether fighting around Bab al-Mandab continues, whether Washington commits directly to the Yemen campaign, and whether shipping and energy costs begin rising together again.

This is a risk scenario, not a certainty. A ceasefire or a lasting improvement in shipping security could change the picture quickly.

THE FAULTLINE VIEW

A crisis rarely sends its bill to only one address. Yemen faces the war. Shipping companies face the risk. Importing countries face the cost. Households may eventually face higher prices.
India's search for critical minerals points to the same wider challenge: having access to something valuable is not enough if you cannot move it, process it or depend on it when conditions change.

The question for the coming weeks is simple.... if one route becomes dangerous, how many reliable alternatives does the world actually have?

 FAULTLINE

text:
US Sanctions on ICC Meet Wide Global Opposition; Israel Lone Public Backer
NEW YORK: The US decision on Friday to impose sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) has drawn wide opposition worldwide, including from close allies. The move has exposed a diplomatic divide over international justice as the court pursues Israeli leaders accused of war crimes in Gaza.
Six European countries, Canada and Japan jointly rejected the sanctions, while the European Union and UN Secretary-General António Guterres separately condemned them. Announcing the measures, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "Either the ICC ends its threats, or we will end the ICC." The development follows the November 2024 arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza, and long-standing US opposition to the court's jurisdiction over Americans. Neither the US nor Israel is a member of the ICC, which has 125 member states.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, together with their Canadian and Japanese counterparts, expressed strong disagreement with the sanctions and reaffirmed "unwavering" support for the court's independence, impartiality and integrity. The eight countries warned the measures could significantly affect the court's work, staff and their families, and pledged to work together to uphold international accountability. Switzerland separately opposed measures undermining the court's independence. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said: "We will do whatever it takes to defend the ICC." Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot strongly condemned the sanctions and called for activating the EU's blocking statute to protect the court and those supporting it.
The European Commission called Washington's announcement deeply regrettable and said the EU is ready to take any necessary steps to let the court continue its investigations and prosecutions and to protect EU operators in the single market. It said the six-month period before the sanctions take effect offers room for dialogue with Washington. European Council President António Costa said the EU would adopt appropriate measures to protect the court, its members and staff.
Guterres, through his spokesperson, said the decision is a serious blow to the collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar, and urged states to uphold their obligations under international law.
The ICC rejected the US measures as an attack on the rule of law and an attempt to obstruct justice. ICC President Tomoko Akane, who was personally sanctioned by Washington in August, said the court will continue to carry out its duties independently and impartially, based solely on law and evidence. The court urged its 125 member states to take concrete steps to protect its role.
Israel was the only government to welcome the sanctions as of Friday. Netanyahu praised Trump and Rubio, writing on X: "The ICC is not a court. It is a political body."
