text:
THE POLITICS OF PERPETUAL GRIEVANCE

What happens when a political movement needs the problem to survive in order to preserve its own power?

A grievance begins with a problem.

Sometimes the problem is real. Sometimes it is exaggerated. Sometimes it is inherited from a previous administration. Sometimes it is created by the very policy introduced to solve it.

The first question is not whether people are suffering.

It is who understands the problem, who benefits from the explanation, and whether the proposed solution actually works.

Because there is a difference between solving a problem and building a political identity around it.

And that difference matters.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

I. THE GRIEVANCE

Every political movement needs a reason to exist.

Some organize around liberty. Others around national identity, religion, economic interests, or a vision of social justice.

But a movement organized around grievance faces a particular temptation.

If the grievance disappears, what holds the movement together?

The problem becomes more than a problem.

It becomes an identity.

The identity creates a constituency. 
The constituency creates political power. 
And political power creates institutions, careers, budgets, and incentives.

None of this proves that a grievance was invented or that its advocates are dishonest.

It does, however, raise a question that every citizen should ask:

Does the movement measure its success by the problem it solves—or by the support it maintains?

Those are two very different measurements.

A doctor wants the patient to recover.

A political movement that depends on permanent illness has a different incentive.

The analogy is not proof of misconduct. 
It is a test of incentives.

And incentives deserve examination.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

II. THE ENEMY

A grievance becomes politically powerful when it acquires an enemy.

Someone caused your suffering.

Someone took what belonged to you.

Someone stands between you and the life you deserve.

Sometimes there is evidence of wrongdoing, and identifying responsibility is necessary.

But the political temptation is to turn a complicated problem into a simple moral drama.

You are the victim.

They are the cause.

We are your defenders.

Give us the power to defeat them.

The explanation provides something emotionally satisfying: a recognizable source of blame.

It also offers relief from uncertainty.

You no longer have to examine competing explanations, conflicting evidence, unintended consequences, or your own assumptions.

You know who is responsible.

Or, at least, you have been told who is responsible.

This is where grievance can become a political instrument.

The enemy must remain visible. The threat must remain urgent. The public must remain convinced that the next election, the next program, the next expansion of authority will finally resolve the problem.

And if the promised solution fails?

The explanation can change.

The previous administration sabotaged it.

The opposition obstructed it.

The institutions resisted it.

The public did not give it enough time.

There wasn’t enough funding.

There is always another explanation.

And sometimes that explanation is correct.

The question is whether it can be tested against evidence—or whether every possible outcome is used to justify the same conclusion.

If success proves the movement right and failure also proves the movement right, what evidence could ever prove it wrong?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

III. THE PROMISE

Enter the politician.

He understands your frustration.

He knows your enemies.

He has a plan.

He promises affordable housing, secure employment, lower prices, better healthcare, economic justice, national renewal, or an end to corruption.

Some of these goals are legitimate. 
Some policies genuinely help people. 
Government can perform necessary functions, and collective action can address problems that individuals cannot solve alone.

The question is not whether government should ever act.

The question is whether the proposed action can deliver what is promised—and at what cost.

A promise is not a result.

A speech is not a policy evaluation.

An intention is not evidence.

Yet political communication often encourages us to confuse them.

The politician tells you what you will receive.

He spends less time explaining what you will pay, what authority the government will acquire, what unintended consequences may follow, or what happens if the program fails.

The benefits are immediate in the imagination.

The costs are distant, dispersed, or hidden.

That imbalance is politically useful.

You vote for the promise today.

You may not discover the full price until years later.

And by then, the politician may be gone, the program may have expanded, and another politician may be promising to repair the consequences.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

IV. THE ARSONIST AND THE FIREFIGHTER

Imagine a building on fire.

People are frightened. 
Smoke fills the corridors. Nobody knows where the flames began.

A man appears wearing a firefighter’s helmet.

He points toward the burning building.

He identifies the guilty party.

He promises to put out the fire.

The crowd listens because the danger is real and the need for help is urgent.

But suppose the man is also holding the match.

The image captures a political danger: the possibility that someone may help create, intensify, or prolong a problem and then use the resulting emergency to demand greater authority.

That possibility must be demonstrated in each case. The metaphor itself does not establish guilt.

But it tells us what to investigate.

Did the policy create incentives that made the problem worse?

Were warnings ignored?

Were alternatives suppressed?

Did officials acknowledge failure and change course?

Or did they use the failure to argue that they needed still more power to complete the original plan?

The fire is the emergency.

The helmet is the performance of competence.

The match is the responsibility that must not be examined.

And the crowd?

The crowd is too busy watching the flames to ask who struck the match.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

V. FATHER CHRISTMAS AND THE HIDDEN BILL

The firefighter promises safety.

Father Christmas promises gifts.

More benefits. 
More subsidies. 
More programs. 
More protection. 
More money directed toward worthy causes.

The political appeal is understandable.

People want security. 
They want their families to prosper. 
They want a fair opportunity to build a decent life.

A government program is not automatically a trick, and a public benefit is not automatically dependency.

The important questions concern its design, financing, incentives, results, and effects on individual independence.

Who pays for the benefit?

Who receives it?

What behavior does it encourage?

Does it address the underlying problem, or merely compensate for its consequences?

Can the program survive without continuously expanding?

What happens when the money runs out?

And what happens when the program fails to achieve its stated objective?

The gift is visible.

The bill may be distributed across taxpayers, borrowers, consumers, future generations, or people who never had a meaningful voice in the decision.

A subsidy can help one person while imposing costs on another.

A regulation can protect one interest while restricting another.

A benefit can provide immediate relief while creating incentives that deserve scrutiny.

These are not arguments against every public program.

They are arguments for examining the complete transaction.

What did the government promise? 
What did it deliver? 
What did it cost?

And what would have happened if the same resources had been used differently?

A citizen who asks these questions is not heartless.

He is taking responsibility for the decision.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

VI. WHEN THE SOLUTION BECOMES THE SYSTEM

Here is where the problem becomes more serious.

A program is introduced to solve a problem.

The program develops a bureaucracy.

The bureaucracy develops procedures, budgets, and institutional interests.

People build careers around its administration. 
Organizations become dependent on its funding. Constituencies come to rely on its benefits.

Over time, the institution may acquire reasons to preserve itself that are distinct from the original purpose.

This does not mean every institution deliberately perpetuates the problem it was created to solve.

It means institutions have incentives, and those incentives can diverge from their stated missions.

A program intended to reduce poverty may be judged by how much money it distributes rather than whether fewer people need assistance.

An agency intended to address a problem may be rewarded for expanding its jurisdiction rather than demonstrating that the problem is diminishing.

A political movement may promise to dismantle a failed system, only to discover that the system offers useful constituencies, dependable funding, and a permanent reason to campaign.

The original promise survives.

The measurement of success changes.

Instead of asking, “Has the problem been solved?” the system begins asking, “Are we doing enough?”

And doing enough can become an endless proposition.

There is always another appropriation.

Another initiative.

Another task force.

Another emergency.

Another promise.

The machinery can continue operating long after its original justification has weakened.

That is not proof of a conspiracy. 
It is a reason to demand measurable objectives, independent audits, transparent costs, and a willingness to terminate programs that fail.

A government capable of acting must also be capable of admitting error.

Otherwise, failure becomes an argument for expansion.

__________________________________

THE EMULSIFIER: THE FAILURE BECOMES THE EXCUSE

The promise fails. 
The Emulsifier goes to work.

The failure is not evidence that the doctrine may be wrong. 
It becomes evidence that the doctrine has not been implemented completely enough.

The predecessor failed. 
The successor knows why.

The opposition obstructed it. The institutions resisted it. 
The people were not ready. 
The revolution was betrayed.

There is always another explanation.

The contradiction disappears beneath the explanation, and the original promise emerges intact.

The Emulsifier converts failure into justification.

The socialist does not have to abandon the destination. 
He only has to convince the public that the next road will finally get them there.

And when that road fails?

The Emulsifier is ready.

The grievance remains. 
The label changes. 
The promise begins again.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

VII. ANGER IS NOT JUDGMENT

Anger has a legitimate place in human life.

It can alert us to injustice, betrayal, and danger.

But anger is not a substitute for judgment.

When people are angry, they may become more receptive to explanations that identify a villain and promise immediate relief.

The political temptation is to keep the emotion alive.

Repeat the grievance.

Repeat the accusation.

Repeat the promise.

Make the threat feel urgent.

Make the proposed solution feel inevitable.

Eventually, the question can change.

Instead of asking, “Does this policy work?” people ask, “Does this politician understand my anger?”

Instead of asking, “What does the evidence show?” they ask, “Whose side are you on?”

Instead of evaluating a decision by its consequences, they evaluate it by the satisfaction of seeing an enemy defeated.

At that point, political judgment risks becoming tribal loyalty.

And once loyalty becomes the test, failure becomes difficult to acknowledge.

To admit that a policy failed may feel like betraying the movement.

To question the leader may feel like helping the enemy.

To reconsider the evidence may feel like surrender.

The individual becomes trapped by a decision he once made freely.

This is why citizens must be willing to question their own side.

Especially their own side.

A political movement deserves no exemption from scrutiny merely because its promises appeal to our values or its enemies offend us.

If your principles disappear when your preferred politician takes power, they were not principles. 
They were permissions.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

VIII. THE INDIVIDUAL AND THE TRANSACTION

The answer is not to become cynical about every political promise.

Cynicism can be another form of surrender. 
If nothing can be trusted, there is no reason to investigate anything.

The answer is disciplined skepticism.

Examine the grievance.

Establish the facts.

Identify the proposed solution.

Calculate the costs.

Look for unintended consequences.

Ask who gains authority.

Ask who bears the burden.

Establish what measurable outcome would count as success.

Then ask what evidence would demonstrate failure.

A serious proposal should survive serious questions.

A serious politician should be willing to explain the trade-offs.

And a serious citizen should be willing to change his mind when the evidence demands it.

This is not a demand for perfect government. 
No political system can eliminate every hardship, prevent every mistake, or satisfy every competing interest.

It is a demand for accountability.

The citizen is not merely a recipient of benefits.

He is not merely a member of a grievance.

He is not merely a vote to be mobilized.

He is an individual with the responsibility to think, judge, and decide.

That responsibility cannot be outsourced to a politician, a party, an institution, or an intellectual who claims to understand your interests better than you do.

You may accept a policy.

You may reject it.

You may support collective action when the evidence justifies it.

But you should understand the transaction before you consent.

Because consent without examination is an invitation to manipulation.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

IX. THE PERFORMANCE REVIEW

Every political movement should face the same questions, regardless of its label.

What problem did you promise to solve?

What evidence established the nature and scale of the problem?

What did your policy accomplish?

What did it cost?

What unintended consequences followed?

Did the policy increase individual freedom and opportunity, or restrict them?

Did it reduce the need for intervention, or create a permanent justification for more?

What would convince you to change course?

These questions do not presume that every grievance is fabricated, every public benefit is harmful, or every politician is dishonest.

They establish a standard by which political claims can be judged.

A movement that genuinely wants to solve a problem should welcome evidence of progress.

A government that values the public interest should welcome independent scrutiny.

A citizen who values freedom should welcome the opportunity to question those who exercise power in his name.

The test is not whether the politician sounds compassionate.

The test is whether the policy produces the promised result without imposing unjustified costs or sacrificing principles that matter.

Do not measure political success by the intensity of the promise. 
Measure it by the consequences of the policy.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

X. THE QUESTION THAT REMAINS

Return to the burning building.

The crowd is still there.

The politician is still wearing the helmet.

The gift box is still open.

The promises are still being made.

Perhaps he really can help.

Perhaps his critics are wrong.

Perhaps the fire has causes that nobody fully understands.

Then investigate.

But do not let urgency eliminate judgment.

Do not let anger determine what counts as evidence.

Do not mistake the promise of protection for proof of competence.

And do not assume that a person who offers to solve your problems has an unlimited claim to your trust.

Ask who started the fire.

Ask who benefits from its continuation.

Ask whether the proposed solution works.

Ask what it costs.

Ask what happens if it fails.

Most importantly, ask yourself whether you are judging the policy by its results—or defending it because you have already invested your identity in the promise.

Because the most consequential political transaction may not be the money exchanged.

It may be the judgment surrendered.

You give the politician your vote.

He gives you a promise.

The promise may succeed. 
It may fail. 
It may even produce consequences nobody anticipated.

But your responsibility does not disappear when the ballot is cast.

You remain responsible for examining what happens next.

What did you give away in exchange for what you were promised?

And if the promise has failed:

What evidence would convince you that the next promise is different?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE SOCIALIST ARSONIST: ON GRIEVANCE, PROMISE, AND THE MACHINERY THAT NEVER SHUTS DOWN

And here is where the SOCIALIST enters the picture.

The socialist promises to eliminate exploitation. 
When the promised transformation fails, he does not necessarily abandon the doctrine. 
He identifies the failure of the socialist before him, explains why the previous attempt was insufficient, and promises a more complete version.

Lenin condemned the failures of the old order. 
Stalin condemned the failures of his predecessors. 
Hitler condemned the failures of the Weimar Republic — and the treaty the Allies imposed before it.

Each successor found reasons why the revolution had not yet delivered its promised destination.

The label changes. 
The explanation changes. 
The machinery expands.

The grievance remains.

And every new failure becomes an argument for another intervention, another sacrifice, another transfer of authority to those who claim to know how society must be reorganized.

This is the succession problem at the heart of the argument: when the promised destination never arrives, the movement can turn its failure into a reason to continue.

But what happens when people stop believing the promise?

What happens when grievance no longer produces consent?

That is when we must examine the machinery behind the promise—and what happens when persuasion gives way to coercion.

NEXT: THE SECRET POLICE
______________________________________
ETHOS

The promise was to eliminate exploitation.

That was always the promise, on every version of the label.

But a promise does not establish a result.

A grievance does not establish a cause.

An enemy does not establish a solution.

And anger does not establish the truth.

This is not cynicism.

It is a performance review.

Envy is the frequency evil broadcasts on.

It offers the listener a convenient explanation, a recognizable enemy, and the intoxicating possibility that someone else can be made responsible for everything that went wrong.

The politician supplies the signal.

The movement amplifies it.

The institution preserves it.

And the individual must decide whether to think for himself or simply receive it.

Freedom requires more than the right to vote.

It requires the willingness to question the person for whom you voted.

It requires the courage to examine a promise after you have believed it.

It requires the discipline to acknowledge failure, even when admitting it means your opponents were right about something.

The machinery depends on the citizen who stops asking questions.

It becomes more difficult to operate when the citizen demands evidence.

Do not ask only who promises to put out the fire.

Ask who struck the match.

Ask who profits while the building burns.

And never surrender your judgment merely because someone promises to make your anger feel like justice.

He gave his intellect to an idea.

Evil collected the dividend.

NEXT: THE SECRET POLICE

text:
When prices rise, the pattern is ancient and predictable. 

Those who control the levers of money and power rarely accept responsibility for the resulting hardship. Instead, they point to convenient villains.

Rome debased its currency and blamed Christians. Medieval authorities faced economic distress and hunted witches. 

In our era, the preferred scapegoat is the billionaire—or the “greedy” corporation, the speculator, the person who simply built something people wanted.

Steve Forbes puts it plainly in this conversation with Stossel: politicians play on the resentment they caused with their own policies. 

When governments expand entitlements they cannot afford, when central banks create money to paper over deficits, and when regulations and taxes distort incentives, the result is inflation and slower real progress. 

The people who notice that their paycheck buys less are then invited to direct their anger at those who succeeded in the market rather than at the policies that eroded their purchasing power.

This is not a defense of every wealthy person or every business practice. 

Markets contain fraud, mistakes, and inequality of outcomes. 

But the core claim is narrower and more important: sustained inflation is primarily a monetary phenomenon, and the political incentive is almost always to redirect blame rather than constrain spending or stabilize the currency. 

History supplies the examples; the current political rhetoric supplies the continuity.

Forbes’s broader argument, threaded throughout the interview, is that free markets and entrepreneurship solve problems of knowledge, coordination, and innovation that centralized direction systematically cannot. 

Wealth is not a fixed pie that the successful are merely hoarding; under conditions of liberty it expands. 

When that process is undermined by easy money and political redistribution, the resulting frustration becomes a political resource for the same people whose policies helped generate it.

The video is worth watching not because it offers a simple partisan score-settling, but because it treats a recurring historical failure mode with clarity: the temptation, when money loses value, to punish the productive rather than discipline the institutions that debased it. 

That pattern is older than any current billionaire, and understanding it remains relevant regardless of which party currently holds the printing press.

text:
Will Nvidia buy Reflection outright or just hire the team?👇
⠀
Reuters, citing the Financial Times, reported that Nvidia ($NVDA) is in talks to deepen its investment in Reflection or acquire the company.
⠀
The report quoted people with direct knowledge saying the talks are still in early stages and a deal could still fall apart.
⠀
Multiple people familiar with the matter told the Financial Times a deal could be reached in the coming weeks.
⠀
A Bloomberg report published by The Straits Times on October 11, 2026, quoted a person familiar with the matter as saying Nvidia is in early talks to raise its stake in Reflection or give the startup compute.
⠀
The person asked not to be named because the matter is private.
⠀
The person said this would strengthen Nvidia's ties with a key open weights model developer, but the two sides haven't agreed on any deal terms.
⠀
Bloomberg reported that Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment and Reflection declined to comment.
⠀
For the Financial Times report, Reflection declined to comment and Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
⠀
Seeking Alpha, citing the FT, said neither Nvidia nor Reflection responded to the FT's request for comment.
⠀
Reuters, which cited the Financial Times story, said it couldn't immediately verify the report.
⠀
-----
⠀
🔴 Follow me on X: @rich_compass
⠀
U.S. stock, crypto, and technical analysis
⠀
-----

▋ Talks are early and deal terms remain open
⠀
The Financial Times said the deal could take several forms, including an acqui-hire where Nvidia hires the team and licenses the tech instead of buying the whole company, which could avoid a lengthy regulatory review.
⠀
Seeking Alpha, citing the Financial Times, said that besides an acquisition, Nvidia could also make an additional equity investment in Reflection or reach a deal to supply more chips or compute.
⠀
Bloomberg also cited an earlier Financial Times report, saying the talks could lead to an acquisition offer.
⠀
The deal size and equity stake were still uncertain at the time.
⠀
The Seeking Alpha piece, citing the Financial Times, said it had not obtained the deal terms under discussion.
⠀
Bloomberg, citing an earlier Wall Street Journal report, said Reflection had talked about raising $2.5B at a $25B valuation.
⠀
With no deal terms agreed, an acquisition by Nvidia or a deeper investment isn't the only possible outcome.
⠀
Raising money on its own is another path that already exists.
⠀
That's a limited read based on the reports, not a done deal.

▋ An $800M backing and a $25B valuation tag
⠀
The Financial Times reported Nvidia is already a major financial backer and strategic investor in Reflection, having previously invested $800M in the startup.
⠀
Reflection was founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou.
⠀
It builds tools that can automate software development, a fast-growing AI use case.
⠀
The Financial Times said Reflection CEO Laskin told CNBC in April that the Nvidia-backed startup was raising new money at a $25B pre-money valuation, meaning the valuation before the funding.
⠀
Reflection's official Newsroom lists an April 23, 2026, article where the CEO confirmed the latest funding round closed at a $25B pre-money valuation.
⠀
Earlier, Reflection's official Newsroom also listed a March 2, 2026, article about the Nvidia-backed 'open' AI startup raising money from investors at a valuation of more than $20B.
⠀
TechCrunch reported on July 14, 2026, that Reflection was valued at $25B pre-money at the time, with investors including Nvidia, Sequoia Capital, and Lightspeed Venture Partners.
⠀
However, the report's figure of nearly $2.6B in total funding conflicts with other data: private market database Forge shows Reflection had raised about $4.63B as of April 2026.
⠀
In its July 14, 2026, report, TechCrunch added a correction noting an earlier version had the wrong last known valuation for Reflection, showing that reporting on the company's valuation has been inconsistent.
⠀
Reflection's official site divides its business into four parts.
⠀
Open weights models let customers inspect, fine-tune, and deploy them on their own terms.
⠀
Open-source software helps customers build AI systems they can control and audit.
⠀
Infrastructure offers open models through an API platform and supports customer deployments in self-built environments, including private clouds, on-premises systems, air-gapped setups cut off from outside networks, and edge devices.
⠀
Solutions services come from a team that works directly with customers, helping them go from idea to app design, development, and deployment.

▋ Low compute claims but no multimodal support
⠀
The Financial Times reported that Reflection launched its first open weights model, Beam, on the Monday before the report, aiming to compete on coding and agentic tasks with cheaper Chinese models like DeepSeek and Kimi.
⠀
Beam launched in early October 2026 and targets enterprise customers and developers, Bloomberg reported.
⠀
Reflection said on October 5 that the model is designed to perform well on coding and AI agent tasks at a lower cost than many competing products.
⠀
The company also said Beam scores about the same as GLM-5.2, Chinese company https://t.co/1dC6VWIdZu's flagship open model, on advanced reasoning benchmarks.
⠀
Reflection's official blog says Beam is its first open weights model and uses a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture.
⠀
It has 501B total parameters and activates 23B of them for each token, or piece of text, it processes.
⠀
The model is built for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads.
⠀
It was pretrained on 23.8T filtered high-quality tokens from sources including the web and proprietary licensed datasets.
⠀
On training, the company said Beam's high-compute reinforcement learning (RL) used 10,500 Nvidia GB300 GPUs over four weeks, generating more than 100M model interaction attempts, or rollouts.
⠀
Pretraining was done on a cluster of 6,144 Nvidia GB300 NVL72 GPUs in under four weeks.
⠀
Inference efficiency is the advantage the company stresses.
⠀
Reflection says Beam can match GLM-5.2's scores on advanced reasoning benchmarks, and its generation-phase compute, estimated from active parameters and generated tokens, is about one-third to one-fourth of GLM-5.2's.
⠀
That estimate doesn't include preprocessing of input text, context-dependent attention compute, or extra serving system overhead.
⠀
It's not a measured inference cost.
⠀
On coding and agentic tasks, the company says Beam can compete with the larger open model GLM 5.2 and comes close to Qwen 3.8-Max.
⠀
Frontier open models like Kimi K3 still lead on raw capability.
⠀
The model was still going through final red-team testing, which looks for safety issues, and other evaluations at the time.
⠀
The company gave early versions to select users and opened a waitlist.
⠀
The company planned to release the model weights under an Apache 2.0 license within that month, along with documentation and a full set of tools to run, evaluate, and fine-tune the model.
⠀
It called Beam the first model in the series.
⠀
Still, the benchmark table in Reflection's official blog shows Beam trails some competing models on several agentic coding benchmarks.
⠀
For example, it scored 44.4 on DeepSWE v1.1, below GLM 5.3's 61.0, Kimi K3's 68.0, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash's 74.2.
⠀
It scored 80.1 on Terminal Bench v2.1, below Kimi K3's 88.3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash's 90.6.
⠀
In the table, multiple scores for several comparison models are marked as not reported (NR).
⠀
Reflection's official blog also says Beam is a text-only model and can't directly handle multimodal input.
⠀
It can only use information from other modalities when that information is represented as text.

▋ Locking down chip access with a deal up to $6.3B
⠀
Reflection told TechCrunch it would pay $150M a month from July 1, 2026, through 2029 for immediate access to Nvidia's latest GB300 chips and supporting hardware at SpaceX's Colossus 2 data center near Memphis, Tennessee.
⠀
The deal is worth up to $6.3B, and after the first three months either side can choose to end it with 90 days' notice.
⠀
TechCrunch noted that Reflection's compute deal with SpaceX is smaller than SpaceX's deals with Anthropic at $1.25B a month and Google at $920M a month, both of which also run through 2029.
⠀
It's Reflection's first compute deal.
⠀
Reflection also signed a compute deal valued at over $1B with European AI infrastructure company Nebius, TechCrunch reported on July 14, 2026.
⠀
Nebius was spun off from Russian tech company Yandex and will give Reflection access to Nvidia's latest chips.
⠀
The same report said Nebius, shortly after getting a $2B investment from Nvidia, signed a five-year infrastructure deal with Meta worth up to $27B.
⠀
The year before, Nebius signed a multi-year deal with Microsoft worth up to $19.4B.
⠀
A Reflection spokesperson told TechCrunch in a written statement that recent events show how important open source is to the AI ecosystem, as more countries and companies see the risks and costs of relying entirely on closed models.
⠀
The spokesperson said the SpaceX deal shows Reflection's strategic importance in the frontier AI ecosystem, and more compute means more room to scale and build the world's best open models.

▋ Jensen Huang backs open weights against Chinese models
⠀
Seeking Alpha, citing the Financial Times, said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed for an 'ecosystem' of open weights for AI, which lines up with the company's direction of investing in open weights model companies.
⠀

text:
Daytona Beach, Florida, 1904 — A Glimpse Into a Forgotten Summer. People gathered along Daytona Beach in Florida, enjoying the ocean air and the simple pleasures of a day by the sea. Their clothing reflected another era, when long dresses, formal outfits, and carefully styled hats were part of everyday life.

The beach looked different from the busy tourist destination we know today. There were no modern smartphones, no social media, and far fewer cars on the roads. For many visitors, a trip to the beach was a special opportunity to escape daily routines, spend time with loved ones, and enjoy the beauty of the Atlantic Ocean.

As people walked along the shore, they could hear the waves rolling onto the sand and feel the ocean breeze against their faces. Some may have been visiting with family, while others might have been meeting friends or exploring the growing seaside community.

None of them could have imagined how much the world would change over the next century. Buildings would rise, roads would expand, and Daytona Beach would become famous for tourism and motorsports.

Today, this old photograph offers us a precious glimpse into ordinary life more than 120 years ago. The people in the picture may be long gone, but their moment beside the ocean remains. **Time moves forward, generations disappear, and places transform—but an old photograph can bring a forgotten day back to life.**

The @135SportsData Dynasty Players to Watch. Early slate. Giants vs. Commanders and Browns vs. Jets.

New York: Malik Nabers sixth overall pick in RD 1 of the 2024 Draft, former LSU WR listed at 6 foot, 200 pounds. Nabers immediately established himself as an elite NFL target earner with 109 catches for 1,204 yards and 7 TDs as a rookie, but a major knee injury interrupted that trajectory last season. He has worked his way back into form this year and enters Week 5 with 18 catches for 208 yards and a TD through four games, including his best performance of the season last week with 6 catches for 112 yards and a score against Arizona. Nabers returned to full practice Friday and carries no game designation despite dealing with knee soreness earlier in the week. Want to see whether last week was the beginning of the real breakout after a difficult recovery, whether Jameis Winston continues feeding him high value targets and whether Nabers can reestablish himself as one of the safest elite young WRs in dynasty. 

Washington: Treylon Burks 18th overall pick in RD 1 of the 2022 Draft, former Arkansas WR listed at 6 foot 2, 225 pounds. Burks entered the league after producing 146 catches for 2,399 yards and 18 TDs at Arkansas, but injuries and inconsistency prevented his Tennessee career from ever matching the draft investment. Washington has given him another opportunity, and the early results have been strange but interesting: only 3 catches through three games, but 60 yards and 2 TDs, including a 47 yard touchdown last week against Indianapolis. Jayden Daniels returns tomorrow, Stefon Diggs is out and Terry McLaurin is questionable, potentially creating the biggest opportunity Burks has seen in some time. Want to see whether Washington gives the former first round pick real target volume rather than isolated big play opportunities, whether Daniels can unlock the size and downfield ability that once made Burks such an intriguing prospect and whether this becomes the beginning of a legitimate second act for a dynasty asset that had nearly fallen off the map. 

135Sports⁠.com

Cleveland: Quinshon Judkins 36th overall pick in RD 2 of the 2025 Draft, former Ohio State and Ole Miss RB who entered the league after three consecutive 1,000 yard college seasons. Judkins produced 827 rushing yards and 7 TDs as a rookie while adding 26 catches for 171 yards, then opened Year 2 as Cleveland’s clear lead back. Through four games he has 59 carries for 177 yards and a TD plus 15 catches for 96 yards. The rushing efficiency has been disappointing at only 3 yards per carry, but last week offered an encouraging all around performance with 17 carries for 53 yards and a TD plus 6 catches for 43 yards. The Jets are allowing 123.5 rushing yards per game. Want to see whether Judkins can finally turn strong volume into an efficient rushing performance, whether the increased receiving role sticks and whether a young back with second round capital and a secure workload can start converting opportunity into the kind of production that pushes him into a higher dynasty tier. 

New York: Braelon Allen 134th overall pick in RD 4 of the 2024 Draft, former Wisconsin RB listed at 6 foot 1, 235 pounds. Allen finished three college seasons with 3,494 rushing yards and 35 TDs before entering the NFL as one of the youngest players in the league. Through four games this season he has 33 carries for 120 yards and a TD, but the real dynasty opportunity has arrived because Breece Hall has been ruled out again with a quad injury. Allen handled 14 carries for 59 yards plus 2 catches for 8 yards last week against Chicago and now gets another chance to show what the Jets offense looks like with him operating near the top of the backfield. Want to see whether Allen gets true lead back volume, whether the 235 pound power profile translates into goal line opportunities and whether he can establish a startable weekly floor instead of remaining valuable primarily as Hall’s backup.

🚨COORDINATE WITH EXISTING NY STATE AGENCIES TO PARTNER —  As a parent of a disabled person, in the assessment there MUST be focus to SEPARATE & DISTINGUISH people who are suffering from mental illness (ie: schizophrenia, bipolar, etc) and those who are intellectually & developmentally disabled [id/dd] (ie: autism, down syndrome, cerebral palsy, etc) who may be unable to communicate and going through a traumatic event that may appear to be mental health related but is not directly & you do NOT necessarily want to “institutionalize”… that would get some serious negative scrutiny! 

I WOULD REACH OUT TO:

(1) COUNCIL ON DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES (NY-CDD): NY-CDD is the federally mandated state Developmental Disabilities Council under the DD Act. It is not a direct service provider. Instead, it advances self-advocacy, systems change, inclusion, and public policy through grants, pilot projects, the five-year State Plan, and training. It currently supports related efforts such as the Annual Advocacy Institute (with The Arc New York & the New York Alliance for Inclusion & Innovation), and grants for advocacy training and statewide networks (e.g., with Syracuse University). At least 60% of Council members are people with developmental disabilities or family members. (website: https://t.co/L0sVWHBKY7) 

(2) PARTNERS IN POLICYMAKING (a nationwide program within CDD): Partners in Policymaking (PIP) is a national leadership training model for adults with developmental disabilities and parents/family members of young children with developmental disabilities. 

It builds knowledge of disability policy, best practices, & advocacy skills so participants can partner with policymakers and influence systems change. IT WOULD BE ADVISABLE TO HAVE PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES, & PARENTS INVOLVED or on some type of a CIVIL COMMITMENT BOARD or integrate into some type of role within the office — to address issues directly related to id/dd disabled individuals. 

(3) DISABILITY RIGHTS NEW YORK (DRNY): Disability Rights is federally designated Protection and Advocacy (P&A) system (and Client Assistance Program). Every state and territory has one of these independent, federally funded organizations under laws such as the Developmental Disabilities Assistance and Bill of Rights Act. 

Disability Rights provide FREE legal advocacy, investigate abuse and neglect, monitor facilities, enforce rights, and pursue systemic change for people with disabilities. 

In New York, that role is filled by Disability Rights New York (DRNY). It was designated as the state’s P&A/CAP system in 2013 (previously was held by a state commission). DRNY is a nonprofit that offers free legal and advocacy services to children and adults with disabilities. 

Its work includes individual representation, investigations of abuse/neglect or rights violations, facility monitoring, training, and systemic advocacy across areas such as education, community living, employment, healthcare, voting, and more. It administers the standard suite of P&A programs:
• PADD for developmental disabilities, 
• PAIMI for mental illness, 
• PAIR for individual rights, 
• CAP, and others

•  Phone: (518) 432-7861 or 
• Toll-free (800) 993-8982

text:
There's a magical island off the Irish coast that inspired the myth of Atlantis, but it only appears on certain days of the year. Well, according to ancient folklore anyway. It's called "Hy-Brasil" and it's said to lie far out in the Atlantic off the wild west coast. For centuries it even appearing on maps. 

The unusual name Hy-Brasil comes from Uí Bhreasail, meaning “descendants of Bresal,” an ancient Irish clan name. Some scholars connect it to the Old Irish word bres, meaning “noble” or “fortunate” which fits its reputation as the Island of the Blessed. There's obviously some crossover with that other mythic realm Tír na nÓg, the “Land of Eternal Youth”. 

It's a place where mortals might cross into the Otherworld. The fact  it was on sea charts and maps made this paradise all the more tantalising. But there was a catch. Hy-Brasil was said to be shrouded in mist, visible only once every seven years. 

Even then, it could slip away, sometimes even sinking or floating into the air (!) just as sailors thought they had reached it. When described, it was often a place of extraordinary beauty with an abundance of pleasure and wealth on offer. Sometimes home to a wise old man who imparted secret knowledge to those lucky enough to land there.

That last particular promise of secret wisdom would prove profitable for conmen and false profits peddling information to the guililble and the desperate that they'd either heard second hand or actually gained in person from a visit there. 

So where exactly was this heavenly holiday resort? Well, unlike many purely mythical lands, Hy-Brasil enjoyed a strange legitimacy because cartographers occasionally recorded a location. The 1325 Dulcert map shows it as a perfect circle, divided by a central channel. Circlular island bisected are also associated with the myths of Atlantis. 

The 1373 Pizzigano map and others of the 14th–17th centuries placed it west of Ireland, sometimes moving it further into the Atlantic as cartographers updated their charts.More than one expedition even set out in search of it during the Age of Exploration.

Sightings of Hy-Brasil persisted for centuries. The most famous came in 1674, when Captain John Nisbet claimed to have landed on the island, met a mysterious wise man, and returned with gold and silver. Even into the 19th century, mariners reported glimpses of strange landmasses west of Galway Bay. 

Some modern historians suspect these might have been sightings of Porcupine Bank, a now submerged shoal roughly 200 km west of Ireland, which would sometimes appear just above water in the right conditions. Others suggest mirages or Fata Morgana illusions tricked sailors into seeing phantom lands.

Basically Hy-Brasil, like most human heavens, speaks more about the desires and fears of the dreamer than it does about what actual Paradise should be. As such, it was a mirror to the Irish folk psyche. And as important as the promise of that place was how illusive the destination was. Emerging only after ages and only epheremally, likely to disapear over the horizon faster than you can desperately swim to its shores.

Irish Guide Dogs for the Blind, 50 years

@irishguidedogs is Irish Guide Dogs for the Blind, the national charity helping people with sight loss and families of children with autism achieve mobility and independence. It began in 1976 in a small farmhouse in County Cork, founded by Mary Dunlop and Jim Dennehy, who had lost his sight eight years earlier.

In 2005 it introduced an assistance dog programme for families of children with autism, the first organisation in Europe to do so. All of its programmes are offered free of charge, with support and aftercare, and this year the charity is celebrating its 50th anniversary.

#OnThisDay October 11, 1863: Letters From Vermilionville.

On October 11, 1863, Union Lieutenant Thomas L. Evans of the 96th Ohio Volunteer Infantry wrote a letter to his sister from Vermilionville, Louisiana, present-day Lafayette in Lafayette Parish. His correspondence provides a valuable firsthand account of military operations in southwestern Louisiana during the American Civil War. Evans described the difficulties of marching from Franklin to Vermilionville, the sugar plantations encountered along the route, and his thoughts about Ohio elections occurring hundreds of miles from home. Although his letter documented ordinary experiences rather than a major battlefield engagement, it offers important evidence of Union military activity, Louisiana's plantation economy, and the relationship between soldiers and political life during the war.

Vermilionville occupied an important geographical position within Louisiana's Bayou Teche region. Founded during the early nineteenth century, the community developed around land associated with Jean Mouton and the establishment of St. John the Evangelist Catholic Church. Lafayette Parish was created from St. Martin Parish in 1823, with Vermilionville becoming its parish seat. By 1863, the surrounding countryside contained agricultural properties connected to the region's sugar-producing economy. The community retained the name Vermilionville until 1884, when it was renamed Lafayette in honor of the Marquis de Lafayette.

Evans's presence resulted from Union operations directed by Major General Nathaniel P. Banks, commander of the Department of the Gulf. Following the Union victory at Vicksburg in July 1863, federal military authorities continued operations throughout Louisiana and sought opportunities to extend their control westward. Banks also pursued plans involving Texas, whose connection to the Confederacy remained strategically important. A failed Union expedition against Sabine Pass in September 1863 preceded a renewed overland advance through southwestern Louisiana.

In October, Union forces under Major General William B. Franklin advanced through the Bayou Teche country. Federal troops moved through Franklin and New Iberia toward Vermilionville, encountering Confederate resistance along their route. Official military correspondence dated October 9 recorded that the XIX Corps had reached Bayou Vermilion, where Union cavalry engaged Confederate forces. Bridges were under construction, and additional troops prepared to cross the waterway. Banks simultaneously directed elements of the XIII Corps to advance from New Iberia, demonstrating the coordinated movements required to sustain the campaign.

Against this military background, Evans composed his October 11 letter. His account of the difficult march from Franklin to Vermilionville documents the physical demands imposed on soldiers operating across southern Louisiana. Long-distance movement remained central to Civil War campaigning, particularly where roads, waterways, and transportation facilities determined the accessibility of military positions. Evans's observations supplement official reports by recording experiences that command correspondence did not always emphasize.

His references to sugar plantations are particularly significant. Sugar cultivation formed a major component of Louisiana's antebellum economy, supported substantially by enslaved African American labor. The plantations encountered by Union troops represented an agricultural system profoundly affected by secession, emancipation, military occupation, and wartime disruption. Evans's observations place the Union army directly within this landscape. His letter therefore contributes to understanding the relationship between military operations and the economic institutions that shaped nineteenth-century Lafayette Parish.

The correspondence also reveals the continuing importance of national politics among Union soldiers. Evans discussed the unusual circumstances of Ohio elections while serving far from his home state. Political developments remained important to soldiers whose military service separated them from ordinary civic participation. Ohio's wartime political contests concerned questions of Union preservation, military policy, and political leadership. Evans's remarks demonstrate that military service did not eliminate soldiers' interest in elections or their connections to northern communities.

The broader correspondence preserved by Eastern Washington University provides additional context for Evans's wartime experiences. His letters document service near Vicksburg, subsequent operations in Louisiana, and later captivity following his capture in western Louisiana in April 1864. His October 1863 account forms part of this extensive personal record.

The historical significance of Evans's Vermilionville letter rests in its combination of military, economic, political, and local evidence. Official reports establish the strategic circumstances surrounding the Union advance, while Evans supplies a participant's perspective on marching, plantation landscapes, and political concerns. Together, these sources illuminate southwestern Louisiana's place within the wider Civil War and preserve an individual soldier's observations of a community undergoing profound historical change.

The idea comes from the ancient belief that sacred objects could not be deceived.  Crosses and the Ruins of Ani  Since you've often asked about Ani, several local legends developed after the city's abandonment.  One legend claims that:  The crosses remained guarding the churches long after the people left.  Another says:  Angels continued to pray in the ruined sanctuaries where crosses still stood.  Some travelers in later centuries reported hearing stories that lights appeared among ruined churches at night. Historians treat these as local folklore, not documented supernatural events.  The Cemetery Crosses  Perhaps the darkest Armenian cross folklore concerns graveyard crosses.  In folk belief:  A neglected grave might produce restless dreams. A fallen cross should be restored. Stealing stone from a grave marker invited misfortune. Spirits remained peaceful when their cross was maintained.  Many such beliefs survived in rural communities well into modern times.  Crosses Against the Al  One particularly ancient Armenian tradition involved the Al, a feared supernatural being from Armenian folklore.  The Al was blamed for:  Night attacks Illness around childbirth Unexplained weakness  People sometimes placed crosses, prayers, or blessed objects near mothers and infants as protection.  This reflects the blending of older Armenian supernatural beliefs with Christian symbols.  The Dark Winter Crosses  In old mountain regions there were tales of lonely crosses standing in snowfields.  The stories often say:  Wolves would not pass the shadow of a blessed cross. Travelers trapped in blizzards found shelter after praying before one. Spirits of the wilderness could not cross ground marked by it.  These legends are especially atmospheric around places like the highlands near Ani, where medieval churches and khachkars stand against harsh winter landscapes.  A Gothic Armenian Folklore Image  Imagine a moonlit winter night outside the walls of Ani. Snow covers the ruined streets. A solitary khachkar leans beside a forgotten path. Wind moves through the empty churches. Villagers once whispered that no spirit could pass that stone, because although the city had died, the ancient cross remained awake, keeping watch over the lost capital until dawn.  That image is not a historical fact, but it captures the mood of many Armenian folk stories in which ancient crosses are less symbols of death than silent guardians standing between the living world and the unknown.    Ani Sun Magazine X Protection Against Evil  Yes. There are a few real Armenian monastery legends that were actually recorded and passed down around specific monasteries. They are legends, not verified historical events, but they are genuine traditions attached to real places.  Geghard Monastery and the Invisible Army  One of the darker legends surrounds Geghard Monastery, the famous cave monastery that once housed the relic known as the Holy Lance, the spear believed in Armenian tradition to have pierced Christ's side. The monastery's very name, "Geghard," means "spear."  A later Armenian legend says that when the conqueror Tamerlane sought to seize the relic, his soldiers entered the monastery and encountered an invisible heavenly army. Some were said to be struck blind, others paralyzed with fear, forcing the invaders to retreat.  The story reflects a common Armenian theme: sacred monasteries protected not by earthly soldiers, but by unseen divine guardians.  The Holy Spring Beneath the Mountain  Before Christianity, the site of Geghard Monastery was associated with a sacred cave spring. When Christianity arrived, the monastery was founded around that ancient holy place. Traditions grew up around the spring, whose waters were believed to possess healing powers.  Some local stories claimed the spring never truly slept and that the mountain itself remembered the prayers spoken there.  The Whispering Stone Chambers  A particularly eerie tradition attached to Geghard concerns its acoustics.  The monastery contains chambers carved directly into solid rock. According to local legend, the stone walls remember every prayer ever spoken within them. The tale arose because chants echo for an unusually long time in the carved halls.  A visitor standing alone in the darkened chambers can easily understand how such a legend developed.  Tatev's Shaking Pillar  At Tatev Monastery stands the famous Gavazan, or "staff," a stone column constructed in the 10th century.  Historically, it functioned as an architectural and warning feature. Over time, legends developed that the pillar moved when danger approached or when hostile forces neared the monastery. The monastery itself became associated with miraculous protection during periods of invasion.  For medieval villagers, a moving stone column overlooking a deep gorge must have felt deeply uncanny.  The Lost Monasteries of Ani  Among the ruins of Ani, many churches and monastic buildings stand abandoned today.  Travelers in later centuries recorded local stories that lights appeared among the ruins at night, while some guides spoke of hearing distant bells from churches where no monks remained. These are folk traditions rather than documented medieval accounts, but they became part of the atmosphere surrounding the "City of 1,001 Churches."    Many vampire legends developed in territories affected by these border conflicts.  Long Turkish War (1593-1606)  Particularly associated with:  Siege warfare Devastated villages Plague outbreaks  Exactly the sort of historical background that later produced dark folklore.  Spain Reconquista  A centuries-long struggle between Christian and Muslim kingdoms.  Gothic remains:  Desert monasteries Border castles Mountain fortresses  Many Spanish ghost stories occur in former frontier zones.  Peninsular War (1808-1814)  Napoleonic invasion.  Famous for:  Ruined abbeys Devastated villages Guerrilla warfare  Many Spanish haunting legends emerged after this period.  Africa Ethiopian-Adal Wars  One of the most dramatic religious wars in African history.  Gothic imagery:  Rock-hewn churches Burned monasteries Mountain sanctuaries  The Ethiopian Highlands have an atmosphere surprisingly similar to some Armenian mountain regions.  Mahdist War (Sudan)  Known for:  Desert battlefields Isolated forts Religious visions and prophecies  Creates a very different but equally haunting landscape.  Which Region Feels Most Like Gothic Armenia?  For someone interested in Ani, khachkars, ruined monasteries, winter folklore, and cross legends, the closest comparisons are:  Eastern Anatolia and Armenia (Ani, Kars, Van) Georgia (Tao-Klarjeti ruins, mountain monasteries) Medieval Hungary and Transylvania Carpathian Ukraine Ethiopian Highlands  All share:  Frontier warfare Monasteries on cliffs Ancient crosses Sacred mountains Lost settlements Folklore of protection against evil Ruins that inspired legends long after the wars ended  The most haunting Armenian example remains Ani itself: a medieval capital emptied by war, invasions, earthquakes, and shifting trade routes, leaving churches, monasteries, caves, and khachkars standing in silence on the frontier. That combination of real history and later folklore is what gives Ani its uniquely gothic character.  Provide your feedback on BizChat If we focus specifically on Ani and its immediate frontier region, the city's history is essentially a succession of wars, sieges, invasions, and shifting empires. This is one reason Ani feels so "gothic" today. The ruins are not the remains of a city destroyed in one event. They are the result of centuries of conflict.  1. The Bagratid-Arab Frontier  Before Ani became Armenia's capital, it stood in a borderland contested between Armenian rulers and Arab emirates.  Historical reality The Bagratid Armenian kings gradually expanded their power. Frontier fortresses guarded river crossings and trade routes. Noble houses competed for influence. Gothic atmosphere  Imagine:  Beacon fires on distant hills Armed horsemen crossing snowy plains Monasteries acting as frontier refuges Khachkars standing beside military roads  This is the world from which Ani emerged.  2. Byzantine Takeover of Ani (1045)  One of the most important events in Ani's history.  Historical fact  The Byzantine Empire absorbed the Armenian kingdom, and Ani passed under Byzantine control.  Gothic consequence  Many Armenians later viewed this as the end of an independent golden age.  In folklore and national memory this event can feel almost like:  A kingless city awaiting disaster.  Because only decades later a much greater threat arrived.  3. The Seljuk Capture of Ani (1064)  This is perhaps the most famous war linked to Ani.  Historical fact  The forces of Alp Arslan captured Ani in 1064 after a siege.  Why it matters  Contemporary sources describe extensive destruction during the capture.  For many Armenians this became one of the defining tragedies of medieval Armenian history.  Gothic imagery  This is the source of many later images associated with Ani:  Breached walls Burning churches Fallen banners Empty streets Refugees fleeing into winter  Many of the later legends about cursed ruins and lost grandeur draw emotional power from this event.  4. Georgian-Armenian Reconquest  Ani did not simply vanish after 1064.  Historical fact  Control of the city changed multiple times.  Armenian and Georgian forces later regained influence in the region.  The city experienced periods of recovery and rebuilding.  Gothic element  Ani becomes a city repeatedly rescued and repeatedly endangered.  It survives.  Then falls.  Then revives.  Then falls again.  This cycle gives Ani an almost legendary character.  5. Mongol Invasions (13th Century) Historical fact  The Mongols entered the Caucasus and transformed the political landscape.  Ani came under Mongol domination.  Gothic consequence  The city survived physically but was increasingly weakened.  Trade shifted.  Political centers changed.  The sense of a great city fading began.  Imagine:  Half-empty districts Winds moving through unused buildings Wealth disappearing from former marketplaces 6. Timur's Era  Although Ani was already in decline, the period associated with Timur added to regional instability.  Historical reality  The Caucasus experienced repeated campaigns and devastation.  Folklore  Many local stories later condensed centuries of warfare into tales of a single great catastrophe.  In reality the decline was gradual, but legends often imagine one final night when everything ended.  7. Ottoman-Persian Frontier Wars  For centuries the region containing Ani became a border zone between competing empires.  Historical consequences Military movement through the region Depopulation in some areas Shifting loyalties Economic decline  Many settlements around Ani shrank or disappeared.  Gothic atmosphere  A ruined medieval capital standing in a contested frontier becomes an ideal setting for folklore.  8. Russian-Ottoman Wars  By the nineteenth century the wider Kars region around Ani became strategically important again.  Russian and Ottoman forces repeatedly fought across eastern Anatolia and the Caucasus.  What visitors often forget  When Russian archaeologists first seriously studied Ani, the landscape around the ruins was itself shaped by recent military history.  Ani was not simply a medieval ruin.  It also stood within a modern frontier zone.  Folklore vs History Around Ani History  What actually destroyed Ani?  Not one curse. Not one invasion.  Instead:  Sieges Political changes Shifting trade routes Earthquakes Population decline Frontier warfare  over centuries.  Folklore  People later imagined:  Angels guarding empty churches Bells ringing from ruined monasteries Saints protecting khachkars Lights among the ruins Sacred crosses watching over the abandoned city The Most "Gothic" Moment in Ani's History  If you're seeking the darkest historically grounded scene, it is probably this:  Winter after the Seljuk capture of 1064.  The walls still stand.  The Cathedral still rises above the plateau.  Snow falls through damaged districts.  Merchants are gone.  Refugees have fled.  Monks continue praying in churches surrounded by devastation.  The khachkars remain standing.  And far beyond the walls, wolves cross the frozen steppe.  That image is not legend. It is the kind of landscape that centuries of real warfare around Ani made possible. Ani was not destroyed by a single siege. What makes Ani so fascinating is that it endured waves of sieges, conquests, and recaptures over nearly two centuries.  Why Ani Was So Hard to Capture  Before discussing the sieges, it helps to understand the city's defenses.  Ani sat on a naturally fortified plateau. Deep river gorges protected much of the city, while massive walls defended the more accessible approaches. Medieval writers described it as extraordinarily difficult to conquer.  Imagine:  Cliffs dropping into the Akhurian River. Multiple defensive walls. Narrow approaches. Towers overlooking ravines.  This is one reason so many attackers needed lengthy sieges rather than direct assaults.  First Great Crisis: Byzantine Pressure (1041-1045) Battle of Ani (1042)  After the death of Armenian king Hovhannes-Smbat, the Byzantine Empire attempted to absorb the kingdom.  Armenian forces under Vahram Pahlavouni defeated a Byzantine army attacking Ani. This victory allowed the crowning of Gagik II as king inside Ani's cathedral.  Gothic image  This was one of the last moments of independent royal Ani:  knights riding beneath cathedral towers, banners over the walls, church bells celebrating victory.  But the triumph was temporary.  Fall to Byzantium (1045)  Ani's final loss to Byzantium came more through political maneuvering than through a dramatic storming of the walls.  According to historical accounts, King Gagik II was summoned to Constantinople, and after political pressure and internal divisions, Ani was surrendered to Byzantine control.  History No famous last stand. No burning breach. The kingdom ended through diplomacy and pressure. Why it mattered  The city lost its Armenian royal government just before the Seljuk advance.  The Most Famous Siege: Alp Arslan (1064) Background  By 1064, Ani was under Byzantine control.  Alp Arslan, ruler of the Seljuks, marched into Armenia with an army equipped with siege specialists and siege engines.  Defenders  The city was commanded by Byzantine governors Duke Bagrat and Gregory.  The Siege Begins  The siege lasted about 25 days.  Medieval accounts describe the Seljuks employing sophisticated siege methods:  wooden towers, mangonels and stone-throwers, archers, sapping and undermining operations, artificial earthworks built against the walls.  One account describes a huge wooden tower carrying troops and siege engines close to the walls. Another describes engineered mounds built from earth and straw to raise attackers above defensive positions.  The Breach  Several medieval sources agree that the walls eventually failed.  Accounts differ on the details:  some emphasize mining beneath the walls, others describe parts of the wall collapsing, others mention heavy bombardment by siege engines.  Once the defenses were breached, Seljuk forces entered the city.  The Sack  This became the most traumatic event in Ani's history.  Contemporary and later sources describe:  large-scale killing, mass captivity, looting of the city.  This siege is one of the principal reasons later Armenian memory viewed 1064 as a catastrophe.  The Georgian–Shaddadid Struggle  Many people imagine Ani's history ended in 1064.  It didn't.  Afterward, Ani passed into the hands of the Shaddadids, and over the following century the city became the object of repeated wars involving Georgia and regional Muslim rulers.  Siege of 1124  The Georgian king David IV attacked Ani and captured it from the Shaddadids.  This marks the beginning of a period in which Ani repeatedly changed hands.  Siege of 1161  King George III of Georgia captured Ani. According to historical summaries, a coalition of neighboring Muslim powers then attempted to recover it.  This created a cycle:  capture, reconquest, siege, recovery.  Ani effectively became a frontier city between rival powers.  Siege of 1174  Another major Georgian offensive under George III.  Siege of 1199  Queen Tamar's forces captured Ani again. Under Georgian and Zakarid influence, the city experienced an important revival.  For a time, Ani regained much of its prosperity.  The Mongol Catastrophe Siege and Capture  The Mongols attacked Ani in the 13th century.  Sources agree that the city was captured and devastated in 1236.  The History Museum of Armenia specifically notes that the Mongols captured and destroyed Ani, causing large-scale flight of its population.  Why This Was Different  After earlier conquests, Ani usually recovered.  After the Mongol conquest, recovery became increasingly difficult.  Trade patterns changed, populations moved, and the city's role diminished.  The Final Enemy: Not an Army  The most successful attacker of Ani was not a kingdom.  It was time.  After centuries of warfare:  trade routes shifted, populations declined, earthquakes struck, especially the devastating earthquake of 1319, the city gradually emptied.  By the 17th century, Ani had been abandoned.  History vs. Gothic Memory History  Ani was conquered many times:  Byzantines (1045) Seljuks (1064) Shaddadids Georgians Zakarids Mongols (1236) Gothic Memory  What remains today are:  breached walls, ruined cathedrals, silent monasteries, empty caravan roads, khachkars facing the wind.  The siege most deeply remembered in Armenian historical memory is still the 25-day siege of 1064, when Alp Arslan's army finally broke through what many considered one of the strongest cities in the Caucasus.  Ani was one of the strongest fortified cities in the medieval Caucasus. Its defenses combined natural geography, massive walls, towers, and the weapons of a wealthy royal capital.  Natural Defenses  Ani stood on a plateau almost surrounded by deep river gorges. Medieval writers emphasized that ravines and steep drops protected much of the city, making large-scale assaults difficult except from certain approaches. Attackers could not simply surround the city evenly on all sides.  A defender standing on the walls could look directly down into the ravines below.  The City Walls  Ani's most famous defenses were its enormous walls.  Historical descriptions emphasize:  Multiple defensive lines. Massive stone fortifications. Strong towers. Narrow approaches. Gates protected by defensive works.  The city was considered so formidable that medieval sources described it as extremely difficult to conquer.  A  These weapons helped push enemies back from the walls.  Swords  Used in close fighting.  If enemies entered the city, street fighting would have relied heavily on swords and shields.  Stones and Gravity  One often-forgotten weapon was simply height.  Defenders could drop:  Stones Rubble Heavy objects  onto attackers below.  A city built on cliffs already possessed a major advantage.  Weapons Used Against Ani  The siege of 1064 gives us much clearer information about the attackers' weapons.  The army of Alp Arslan brought specialized siege equipment and engineers.  Mangonels  Large stone-throwing machines were used during the siege.  Simplified:  Plain Text O <- stone   | / \ / \   ====== Frame ======  They hurled rocks at walls and defenders.  Wooden Siege Towers  One source describes a large wooden tower containing soldiers and a mangonel.  Purpose:  Bring archers up to wall height. Shield attackers. Create a platform for assault. Mining and Sapping  Perhaps the most dangerous technique.  Attackers attempted to weaken the walls from below. Sources describe efforts to destroy wall supports and undermine fortifications.  Basic idea:  Plain Text WALL ██████   || ||   Tunnel ========  If enough support was removed, part of the wall could collapse.  Naphtha Weapons  One medieval account mentions naphtha throwers being used during the siege operations.  Naphtha was a flammable substance that could be used in siege warfare.  The Most Impressive Defensive Feature  If I had to choose one thing that made Ani so formidable, it was not a weapon.  It was the combination of:  Deep river gorges. Massive walls. Narrow approaches. Wealth sufficient to maintain strong fortifications.  Medieval observers treated Ani almost like a giant stone fortress-city rather than a typical town. That is why the 25-day siege of 1064 became so famous: many contemporaries regarded the city as nearly impregnable, yet the Seljuk engineers eventually breached its defenses and captured it.  Viewed today from the ruined walls above the Akhurian Gorge, you can still see why generations of Armenians believed Ani could withstand any army. The landscape itself was a weapon. Medieval sieges were usually not dramatic one-day assaults. Most commanders preferred to make a city surrender, because storming fortified walls was expensive, slow, and deadly. NEWTON COUNTY, GEORGIA — A horrifying Georgia murder case involving 19-year-old Morgan Bauer has resurfaced following the sentencing of #KatelynGoble to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Bauer moved from South Dakota to Georgia shortly before her disappearance in February 2016. Prosecutors said Goble, who also worked as an exotic dancer, befriended the young woman and offered her a temporary place to stay.

Bauer then vanished. Her family would spend approximately seven years wondering what happened to her.

Investigators eventually determined that Bauer had been murdered. According to prosecutors and evidence presented in court, Goble and her then-boyfriend, Jonathan “Alexander” Warren, were responsible for her death.

Authorities said Bauer was strangled, dismembered and burned. Goble later led investigators to Bauer’s charred and dismembered remains at a property in Porterdale.

Even more disturbing allegations emerged as investigators uncovered what happened after Bauer was killed.

Court testimony and reporting on the case said portions of Bauer’s remains were consumed, while Warren was accused of having sex with Bauer’s corpse.

Warren previously pleaded guilty to charges including malice murder, tampering with evidence, concealing a death and necrophilia. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Goble was later convicted and sentenced in September 2026 to life without parole for malice murder, along with additional sentences related to concealing Bauer’s death and tampering with evidence.

FAMILY SAYS MORGAN WAS MUCH MORE THAN A “STRIPPER”

Although headlines surrounding the case have described Bauer as a stripper, her family wants people to remember that her occupation did not define her.

Bauer’s stepmother pointed out that Morgan had reportedly worked as a stripper for only about two weeks, but she had been their child for 19 years.

That distinction is important as the horrifying circumstances surrounding her death continue to attract national attention.

#MorganBauer was a 19-year-old daughter whose family spent years searching for answers, and nearly a decade after she disappeared, those responsible for her death have now been sentenced to spend their lives behind bars.

text:
The Seventh-day Adventist Church significantly shaped early American nutrition science and the professionalization of dietetics through its 19th-century health reform movement. Shortly after the church’s 1863 organization, cofounder Ellen G. White promoted temperance and a plant-centered diet of grains, fruits, nuts, and vegetables, drawing on biblical references such as Genesis 1:29. In 1866 Adventists established the Western Health Reform Institute in Battle Creek, Michigan (later the Battle Creek Sanitarium). Under the direction of John Harvey Kellogg (trained with Adventist support), the institution became a major health center emphasizing vegetarian meals, hydrotherapy, and lifestyle changes. Kellogg and colleagues developed practical foods including flaked cereals (precursors to corn flakes), peanut butter, granola, and early meat analogs, helping shift American breakfast patterns away from heavy meat and toward grain-based options. These innovations commercialized vegetarian foods on a large scale. 
Lenna Frances Cooper, chief dietitian at the Battle Creek Sanitarium and trained under Kellogg, co-founded the American Dietetic Association (now the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics) in 1917 and helped establish formal dietetics education grounded in vegetarian principles. Adventists later founded Loma Linda University, which has offered nutrition programs since the early 20th century and conducted the large Adventist Health Studies. These prospective cohort studies of tens of thousands of Adventists provided key epidemiological evidence linking vegetarian diets to lower rates of heart disease, certain cancers, diabetes, and longer lifespan. 
The church continues to favor vegetarianism as part of its broader “health message,” viewing the body as a temple and encouraging plant-based eating for physical and spiritual reasons. While not a mandatory doctrine for membership, it is strongly promoted through institutions, food companies, education, and research, contributing both historical food innovations and ongoing scientific data on plant-based diets.

text:
I like researching what is going on in the world when it comes to EVs, solar, batteries, and renewables in general and how they can help families around the world live better lives. Today that brings me to Britain. 🇬🇧

Britain's heating dilemma has me thinking about solar, batteries, and energy independence.

It's October 11, and people across the UK are debating whether they can afford to turn on their central heating. With electricity costing roughly 26 pence per kWh ($0.348/kWh) and energy bills climbing again, I understand their concerns.

Here in Colorado, I installed solar. My 24 panels can produce over 50 kWh on a good summer day, and I pay around 10 cents per kWh for electricity from the grid. We have two people working from home, an EV, and a house full of electrical equipment. I'm now looking at adding battery storage to make better use of the electricity we produce.

That got me thinking about British families.
What if more homes had rooftop solar, battery storage, and high-efficiency heat pumps? Solar could generate electricity during the day, batteries could store excess production or cheaper off-peak electricity, and heat pumps could provide heating without burning natural gas.

Britain already offers grants of up to £7,500 ($9,931) toward qualifying heat pump installations. There are also programs helping eligible lower-income households install insulation, solar panels, and efficient heating systems.

And here's something worth considering. Research from the UK's Energy Saving Trust found that combining solar, batteries, heat pumps, and the right electricity tariff could reduce household energy bills by around £800 ($1,059) annually, with some combinations saving £1,000 ($1,324) or more.

Of course, Britain doesn't get Colorado's sunshine, particularly during winter. Solar production drops when heating demand rises. And these systems require significant upfront investment. That's why insulation, affordable financing, and sensible energy policies matter just as much as the technology.

I didn't install solar because I wanted another gadget. I wanted more control over my family's energy costs. Shouldn't British families have that same opportunity?

YAHOO TURNED DOWN $44.6 BILLION. IT LATER SOLD ITS CORE BUSINESS FOR $4.5 BILLION.

In February 2008, $MSFT  offered $31 a share for Yahoo. About $44.6 billion, roughly 62% above the market price.

In the video below, the Associated Press reports the bid the day it landed.

Yahoo's board said the offer undervalued the company. It pointed to its own three-year plan and its new advertising platform.

Microsoft raised the offer to $33 a share. Yahoo wanted $37.

Steve Ballmer wrote that Microsoft wouldn't go that high. In May 2008, Microsoft walked away.

The years that followed were rough. In 2016 Yahoo agreed to sell its core internet business to Verizon.

Two data breaches delayed the closing, and the price was cut. In June 2017, Verizon closed the deal at $4.48 billion.

That is about one tenth of what Microsoft had offered nine years earlier.

Was this the most expensive "no" in tech history?

Interviewed by Fox News on immigration and integration in Europe:

Swedish Political scientist Daniel Schatz says, "The real divide is increasingly not between left and right, but between those who believe a state may set firm conditions for membership in a national community, and those who fear those conditions can become discriminatory or exclusionary. It is about whether integration is a voluntary offer or a civic obligation. That question cuts across traditional party lines."

Schatz said that the politics of migration are driven less by numbers than by visibility. "A country can have falling asylum numbers and still experience an intensifying migration debate if voters believe integration has failed," he said. "Essentially, the issue is not whether Europe should have immigration. It is whether Europe still has the confidence to expect newcomers to join the society they entered."

Schatz said that any successful integration model in Europe "will not be one that is simply ‘tough’ or simply ‘welcoming.'… A state that cannot enforce its borders or its basic civic rules eventually loses the public confidence needed for a generous and sustainable integration policy."
