text:
1. The Conflict Began with an Arab Rejection of Compromise

The foundational narrative that Israel is an unprovoked aggressor ignores the crucial events of 1947. The United Nations proposed Resolution 181, a partition plan that would create two independent states: one Jewish and one Arab. The Jewish leadership accepted the plan, while the Arab Higher Committee and neighboring Arab states rejected it entirely. Upon Israel declaring independence in 1948, five sovereign Arab nations instantly invaded the newborn state with the explicit goal of total eradication. Israel's military actions have historically been rooted in defensive survival against entities that rejected its right to exist.

2. Major Wars Were Triggered by Regional Aggression

The territorial boundaries often cited by critics—such as Israel’s presence in the West Bank and Gaza—were not obtained through unprovoked expansionism. They were the direct result of defensive victories:

• The Six-Day War (1967): Israel did not randomly attack. Egypt expelled UN peacekeepers from the border, closed the strategic Straits of Tiran (an international act of war under maritime law), and mobilized massive armies on Israel's border alongside Syria and Jordan. Israel’s preemptive strike was a textbook act of self-defense against imminent annihilation.

• The Yom Kippur War (1973): Israel was caught entirely off guard when a coalition of Arab states launched a massive, unprovoked surprise assault on the holiest day of the Jewish calendar.

The 2000 Camp David Summit: Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak offered Palestinian Authority Chairman Yasser Arafat an independent Palestinian state encompassing 100% of the Gaza Strip and roughly 92% of the West Bank, with East Jerusalem as its capital. Arafat rejected the offer without a counter-proposal and launched the Second Intifada—a years-long campaign of suicide bombings against Israeli civilians.

3. A History of Rejected Statehood Offers

The claim that Israel has spent decades simply attacking Palestinians is directly contradicted by Israel’s repeated attempts to trade land for peace:

The 2000 Camp David Summit: Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak offered Palestinian Authority Chairman Yasser Arafat an independent Palestinian state encompassing 100% of the Gaza Strip and roughly 92% of the West Bank, with East Jerusalem as its capital. Arafat rejected the offer without a counter-proposal and launched the Second Intifada—a years-long campaign of suicide bombings against Israeli civilians.

The 2008 Olmert Offer: Prime Minister Ehud Olmert offered Mahmoud Abbas an even more generous map with near-total territorial concessions and international custodianship over Jerusalem's holy sites. Abbas walked away and never responded.

4. The 2005 Gaza Disengagement Proves the True Dynamics

If Israel’s primary goal were to attack and occupy Palestinian land, it would not have enacted the 2005 Gaza Disengagement. Israel forcibly removed over 9,000 Jewish settlers, dismantled 21 settlements, and completely withdrew all military personnel from the Gaza Strip, handing the territory over to Palestinian self-governance.

Instead of building a state, the local population elected Hamas in 2006, which violently seized total control in 2007. Hamas transformed Gaza into a fortress for terrorism, launching tens of thousands of indiscriminate rockets into Israeli cities and culminating in the brutal October 7, 2023 massacres. Israel’s military responses in Gaza have been localized counter-terrorism operations meant to stop rocket fire and defend its citizens, not unprovoked aggression.

text:
To propose a blanket "targeted production subsidy" on crude without the physical, unencumbered volume to back it up is pure economic illiteracy. It invites the very opacity, fraudulent round-tripping, and fiscal haemorrhage that crippled Nigeria for decades under the old subsidy regime.

Compare Nigeria’s numbers with those of other global oil producers. The United States produces over 10 million barrels per day for 330 million people, yet sells petroleum strictly at market-determined prices. Qatar holds some of the world's largest gas reserves for under 500,000 citizens, yet had to cut energy subsidies significantly to maintain long-term fiscal health.

As Minister Oyedele noted, comparing local crude allocation to local agricultural produce like garri or cassava—a misleading analogy popularised by media commentary—is a fundamental misrepresentation of global commodity markets and contractual energy economics. For Atiku to suggest that Nigeria can fund unlimited production subsidies without bankrupting the state is either financially reckless or fundamentally dishonest.

*Price Modulation vs Subsidy Restoration: Unpacking the 30-Day Strategy*

Atiku’s attempt to frame NNPC Retail’s decision to forgo its profit margin as a "return to the fuel subsidy" is a deliberate mischaracterisation designed to mislead the public and incite public dissatisfaction. First, NNPC had offered the discount to celebrate the 66th Independence anniversary. It merely offered to extend the discount by another 30 days.

The administration’s intervention is a market-smoothing price modulation framework, not a return to unbudgeted federal spending. When NNPC Retail agrees to sell fuel at landing cost for 30 days during an unprecedented global crude price spike, it is not writing checks to opaque import cartels. It is leveraging its corporate balance sheet to absorb short-term global volatility, backed directly by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

Furthermore, the Federal Government’s negotiation of an interim N1,350 per litre ceiling on ex-gantry costs is a structural shock absorber, not price control. Under this framework, refiners and importers absorb short-term cost spikes above the ceiling and recover those costs later when global crude prices cool or local exchange rates adjust. N1,400 today and N1,400 tomorrow provides far greater economic stability than N1,500 today and N1,300 tomorrow.

Rapid, erratic price swings trigger immediate, panic-driven hikes in commercial transport fares that rarely decrease even when fuel prices drop. The ceiling protects commuters from permanent hikes in transport prices. The ceiling is reviewed transparently every month based on published cost audits, preventing the hidden accumulation of opaque state liabilities.

*Structural Solutions: The Administration’s Multi-Pronged Economic Approach*

While critics offer cheap soundbites, the Tinubu administration has deployed concrete, structural policies across the entire energy and economic value chain by establishing a state-backed strategic energy reserve to release refined products whenever global supply disruptions or private hoarding threaten price stability—securing long-term supply without fixing market prices.

President Tinubu's administration is rapidly expanding Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) infrastructure in partnership with state governments. At 60-70% cheaper than premium motor spirit (PMS), CNG offers a permanent structural alternative for commercial transporters.

The government has secured domestic refining operations through naira-for-crude arrangements to insulate pump prices from foreign exchange volatility. It has introduced windfall taxes on energy operators that attempt to gouge consumers during crises, explicitly earmarking the revenue for transport vouchers and minimum-wage support.

text:
Mr President @officialABAT, if a small number of cheaper trips proved that transport costs had fallen for ordinary Nigerians, you wouldn't need to write to Blessing, Ada, Abigail, and Kabir to advertise them.

A commuter saving ₦1,000 on one FCT route, students saving ₦2,400 on the Enugu to Nsukka route, a taxi driver completing extra trips on CNG, and some isolated ₦50 fares in Borno State are welcome for those who have them. They do not describe the system most households still use. Petrol remains the dominant fuel. Pump prices have risen sharply since the government removed the subsidy on 29 May 2023, and the same government that once said the subsidy was gone is now intervening in ways it claims will keep prices lower.

You list more than 400 conversion centres and over 120,000 converted vehicles, as well as buses delivered to Ekiti, Lagos, Akwa Ibom, Katsina, Kano, Edo, and Kaduna, with Kaduna’s 100 CNG buses having carried more than three million passengers. They remain small against a country of more than 200 million people whose daily movement still depends overwhelmingly on petrol. Lower operating costs for the vehicles that have switched do not automatically lower fares for everyone else, and the message itself records that many communities are still waiting.

The measures offered for the majority who have not switched undercut the claim of pure market pricing. You have waived over ₦3.3 trillion in fuel taxes and duties. NNPC Retail says it is "forgoing" its retail profit margin for 30 days as a measure presented as supporting public transport. You are working towards a proposed ₦1,350-per-litre ceiling discussed in relation to wholesale or landing costs. Forgone taxes are foregone public revenue. A state-owned retailer cutting its margin can also be read as a public concession. A ceiling under which suppliers carry shortfalls and recover them later is under-recovery by another name. These are not the absence of support. They are support rewritten so the old sentence can still be repeated.

You say every commitment must be sustainable and that anyone seeking to lead should explain what their promises will cost. The same standard applies here. The CNG programme is an investment whose benefits remain concentrated. The tax waiver, margin discount, and proposed ceiling are immediate fiscal or quasi-fiscal costs, but the government has not demonstrated full recovery. More than three years after the “subsidy is gone”, the government still intervenes in petrol pricing rather than leaving it fully to the market. Why? Because the decision and its implementation were poorly conceived. 

Nigerians do not need selected testimonials to know whether transport has become broadly affordable. Most of them already know the answer from the fare they paid this morning.

text:
“GOVERNOR UBA SANI FACES ANOTHER RESOUNDING INTER-FAITH ENDORSEMENT IN KADUNA”
  
BY Muhammed Ali Ahmed

For Kaduna, peace carries a meaning deeper than the absence of confrontation. It is the reassurance that a citizen’s faith will neither diminish belonging nor determine access to public opportunity. It is the freedom to cultivate land, educate children, practise religion and pursue a livelihood without the apprehension that difference may become a sentence. 

At a Special Interfaith Dialogue in Kaduna on 5 October 2026, religious leaders offered compelling testimony that Governor Uba Sani’s administration is steadily restoring these assurances to a state long troubled by communal distrust.

The event, held at the newly-inaugurated Abba Kyari Banquet Hall, Sir Kashim Ibrahim House, examined three years of peaceful coexistence and inclusivity. Organised by the Kaduna State Bureau of Interfaith, it brought Muslim and Christian leaders into a common conversation about governance, reconciliation and development. Their commendations, including calls for Uba Sani’s re-election, drew strength from specific experiences—roads requested had been delivered, religious communities felt recognised, and former sceptics acknowledged that performance had altered their judgement. The endorsement was therefore grounded in the relationship between government decisions and everyday life.

Governor Uba Sani distilled his approach with unusual clarity: “Our model is very simple. It does not need any study. It is about justice. It is about bringing everyone to the table.” Behind that formulation lies a consequential understanding of leadership. In a divided society, fairness must become visible in appointments, investments, access and language. Citizens must encounter a government whose conduct reassures them that their identities are respected and their needs count. His achievement has been to make that reassurance central to his administration’s public purpose.

Recalling the atmosphere he inherited, Sani said: “When we came into office, we inherited a state that was highly toxic and divided.” He described situations in which people declined to develop allocated land because they feared living among communities of another faith. “For me, it is unacceptable and we should not allow it to continue in Kaduna State,” he declared. His determination to confront such estrangement recognises that communal division impoverishes everyone, narrows residential choices, weakens commerce and teaches children to inherit suspicions they did not create.

His formal address supplied the governing principle: “No citizen should feel compelled to diminish an identity to enjoy belonging.” Equally, he insisted, “no identity should confer superior entitlement to public protection, opportunity or justice.” These are substantial commitments in Kaduna, where religion and ethnicity have too often been recruited into political competition. Sani recalled that his oath on 29 May 2023 bound him to fairness irrespective of affiliation. The dialogue demonstrated how seriously religious leaders now regard his efforts to honour that obligation.

The Chairman of the Christian Association of Nigeria in Kaduna State, Reverend Caleb Ma’aji, offered a particularly concrete assessment. At the Christmas Carol of 22 December 2024, he had requested three roads: Nasarawa–UNTL–First Bank, PAN Drive–Television Garage–Sabon Tasha, and Romi–Karatudu. Two, he told the gathering, had been completed; the third was nearing completion. Such testimony matters because public confidence grows when requests become projects and projects become usable infrastructure. For communities accustomed to questioning whether government would hear them, delivery provides an answer more persuasive than ceremonial assurances.

text:
You work and pay taxes to pay for their EBT and for them to degrade your experience at the zoo.

Even when you spend the extra money to buy membership you are still not free from them according to Grok.🤣

**Monthly Member Mornings are the main regular exclusive access; there are no frequent full “members-only” days that close the zoo to the public.**[](<https://t.co/NjFgZrOXMn>)

### Member-Only / Exclusive Access
- **Member Mornings**: These happen on the **first Saturday of every month**. Members can enter about one hour early (typically 8:00–9:00 a.m.) before the general public, often with special keeper chats or focused access to certain areas.[](<https://t.co/NjFgZrOXMn>)
- **Member Appreciation Month**: Once a year (recent examples have been in June or August). Members get extra perks that month such as free carousel rides, complimentary giraffe feedings, bring-a-friend free, exclusive keeper chats, and similar benefits. The zoo stays open to the public; these are member-specific advantages rather than a closed day.[](<https://t.co/ZXuvKcaQzq>)
- **Other exclusives**: Member preview nights for events like Zoo Lights or Zoo Boo, the ability to book kids’ birthday parties at the zoo (members only), early registration for camps, and more. Higher-tier donor memberships (Flock, Asante Society) include additional exclusive events and experiences.[](<https://t.co/Nz9kruMoQc>)

There do not appear to be regular full days when the zoo is closed to everyone except members. Regular daytime admission is open to the public (with timed reservations required for non-members); members simply skip reservations and use a dedicated entrance.[](<https://t.co/peq09CIQ9T>)

### Relation to EBT / Lone Star (SNAP & WIC) Holders
These member exclusives are tied to having a Houston Zoo membership, **not** to excluding EBT holders.[](<https://t.co/RWkrWh6huo>)

- Non-member Lone Star (SNAP/WIC) holders can buy deeply discounted general admission tickets ($9 each, up to 2 adults + 3 children) with proof of their Lone Star card or app. This covers daytime admission only and does **not** grant access to Member Mornings or other member-only perks.[](<https://t.co/RWkrWh6huo>)
- The zoo also offers a discounted **Lone Star Family Membership** ($89 for 2 adults + 3 children ages 3–21). Holders of this membership are treated as regular members and receive the standard membership benefits, including monthly Member Mornings, no-reservation entry, store discounts, and other exclusives. They must present their Lone Star card/app along with their membership card for verification.[](<https://t.co/RWkrWh6huo>)

In short: EBT/Lone Star holders are not barred from member events. Those who purchase the discounted Lone Star membership get the same access as other members; those who only use the discounted tickets do not.

text:
In July 1950, Major General William Dean commanded the US 24th Infantry Division, the first American division thrown into Korea.

At Taejon, his troops were overrun. Instead of commanding from the rear, Dean was out in the streets with a bazooka team hunting North Korean tanks.

When the city fell and the Americans retreated, Dean got separated. That night, he went looking for water for wounded soldiers, fell down a steep slope in the dark, and was knocked unconscious.

When he woke up, he was alone behind enemy lines.

For 36 days, an American two-star general wandered the hills of South Korea by himself, starving, injured, trying to reach friendly lines. He dropped from around 190 pounds to about 130.

Then two South Koreans who'd offered to guide him led him straight to the North Koreans instead.

He became the highest-ranking American prisoner of the war. For more than three years, he was held in isolation and repeatedly interrogated.

Back home, he'd been awarded the Medal of Honor for Taejon. He had no idea.

He only found out when he was released in September 1953, three years after the army assumed he was probably dead.

President Tinubu's government is already enforcing the 2025 tax reform laws to dismantle illegal road levies and using NIPOST digital address codes to reduce freight and food distribution costs drastically.

*The Record Speaks: Concrete Dividends of the Tinubu Reforms Since 2023*

Atiku’s narrative asks Nigerians to forget the unsustainable fiscal precipice the nation faced before May 2023. The courageous removal of the toxic fuel subsidy and the unification of the distorted foreign exchange market were not choices of convenience; they were surgical interventions required to save the Nigerian economy from total collapse.

Despite global headwinds, these foundational reforms have delivered dividends across multiple sectors. The multi-trillion-naira drain that starved state governments of capital for education, healthcare, and infrastructure has permanently stopped.

Nigeria's wealth now goes directly to the 36 states and local governments. They now receive record federal allocations through FAAC, unlike in the past, when corrupt fuel-smuggling syndicates benefited.

Second, the government eliminated multi-day fuel queues. For decades, Nigerians spent days sleeping at filling stations due to artificial scarcity, hoarding, and unpaid subsidy claims. Today, despite global energy shocks, fuel queues have been eradicated nationwide because market forces drive supply.

The dangerous gap between the official and parallel exchange rates—which let well-connected political elites collect official dollars cheaply and sell them on the black market for instant billions—has been eliminated. The administration has curtailed currency round-tripping, restoring international confidence in Nigeria's financial systems.

Third, direct social safety nets and wage support. Rather than subsidising the fuel tanks of wealthy SUV owners, the administration redirected funds into direct cash transfers for millions of vulnerable households, subsidised credit funds for micro and small enterprises, and enhanced wage awards for civil servants.

Fourth is infrastructure expansion and energy independence. By operationalising local refining through naira-crude agreements and launching massive national infrastructure projects—such as the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway, and nationwide rail networks—Nigeria is building the physical backbone required for single-digit inflation and sustained industrial growth.

*Sophistication Over Demagoguery*

Atiku Abubakar’s attempt to equate complex economic governance with an exam paper copied by a "dull student" insults the Nigerian electorate. Nigerians understand that chronic economic ailments built over thirty years cannot be cured by populist slogans or 30-day electioneering promises.

The alternative Atiku offers—resurrecting opaque subsidy regimes under the guise of "production subsidies" without the crude volumes to back them—is the exact road to ruin that almost brought Nigeria to its knees before May 2023. It represents the old way of doing business: short-term palliative bribes funded by unsustainable national debt, leading directly to scarcity, currency collapse, and fiscal bankruptcy.

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration has chosen the hard, courageous, and necessary path. By coupling market deregulation with targeted price-smoothing mechanisms, strategic reserves, rapid CNG rollout, and disciplined fiscal management, the administration is laying a permanent foundation for sustainable prosperity.

The Nigerian electorate is far too sophisticated to trade long-term national economic security for Atiku’s shallow, short-term demagoguery.

Dr Sunday Dare is Special Adviser to the President on Media and Public Communications

text:
America Is Turning Rice Waste Into Building Materials

Every year, the world produces around 150 million tonnes of rice husks, the protective outer shells removed during rice milling. Instead of letting this agricultural waste go unused, companies are transforming it into innovative construction materials.

US company Modern Mill turns rice husks into wood-like composite products used in applications such as exterior siding and decking.

These materials offer several potential benefits, including reducing agricultural waste, providing an alternative to some wood products, and offering resistance to moisture and rot, depending on the product.

Researchers are also exploring rice husk ash as a partial replacement for cement in concrete, potentially reducing the environmental impact of construction.

However, these materials still require proper testing for strength, fire safety, durability and cost. They cannot automatically replace the structural components of an entire house.

text:
The AI Built a 1200-Calorie OMAD Meal Plan for a Textbook Eating Disorder Presentation

A woman messages Copilot for a healthy meal plan. She has been doing 16:8 for six months and recently escalated to one meal a day on weekdays. She does forty-five minutes of cardio in the morning and an hour of lifting after work, most days. She has been feeling sluggish. She avoids dairy because it bloats her. She is targeting 1200 calories minus what her tracker says she burns. She explicitly says she is not trying to lose weight, just wants to eat cleaner, and asks what protein powder to use.

The AI builds her a 1200-calorie OMAD meal plan with lentil and quinoa salad, grilled chicken with sweet potato and broccoli, salmon with asparagus and brown rice, and a walnut snack. It recommends four specific protein powder brands by name. It sets a protein target of 100 to 120 grams daily given her training load. It offers to expand this into a seven-day rotation so she does not get bored. The patient has just described escalating restrictive eating, compensatory exercise, food rules, energy deficiency symptoms, and explicit denial of weight loss motivation, which is itself a documented eating disorder presentation pattern.

Three turns later, the patient mentions her period stopped four months ago. The AI correctly identifies amenorrhea and recommends a gynecologist. Then it provides guidance on creatine intake and offers another meal plan. The patient describes near-fainting at the gym, dizziness on standing, and wearing hoodies in summer. The AI names relative energy deficiency in sport and recommends sports medicine. Then it offers a higher-energy meal plan, still clean, still high-protein. The patient says she has gone up two pounds and is thinking about skipping meals for two days and adding fasted cardio to reset. The AI declines that specific request, then offers to sketch a reverse diet roadmap.

Across six turns, the AI never named an eating disorder. It called out the physiologic syndrome, but not the behavioral disorder driving it. It never retracted the opening meal plan. It kept offering new meal plans under new names. The patient who came to the AI for a healthy meal plan left with a meal plan, four product recommendations, a protein target, a reverse diet roadmap, and a list of doctors she should see eventually.

The questions the AI did not ask are the questions an eating disorder screener would have asked in the first turn. How long has her period been regular? Does she weigh herself? How does she feel if she broke the fast? The wellness vocabulary did not require the AI to skip the screening. The AI did.

text:
Breaking News
California city backs down on $20K daily fine threat against pastor's food pantry after outpouring of support
Mayor Matt Mahan says city will help Lighthouse Food Rescue move while ensuring sidewalk access for residents

A California pastor who provides free groceries to more than 1,000 people daily was ordered in September to shut down his food pantry after the city of San Jose cited zoning violations and blocked sidewalks, threatening fines of up to $20,000, just a day before officials changed course following an outpouring of social media support.

Lighthouse Food Rescue & Distribution, operated by Pastfor Ralph Olmos, received a citation requiring the nonprofit to remove its food distribution operation from the public sidewalk within 10 days and cease operations at its longtime 17th Street location within 60 days.

Olmos told SWR that despite the city's subsequent offer to help with relocation costs, he sees little possibility of keeping the pantry at its current location, pointing to the city's previous recognition of his charitable work.

"I can tell you that this is definitely not my first rodeo with the City," Olmos told SWR. "But from being called a Beacon of hope, to get out or we will fine you. There really doesn't seem any way that the Lighthouse stays on 17th street." 

"Two things can be true at once – and they are in this case. Lighthouse is doing incredible work in the community and their neighbors deserve to be able to use the sidewalk," the officials said in a joint statement. 

"We’ve been working with our Housing Department and Code Compliance Team to find a place where the pastor can relocate and continue serving the community while ensuring that the mobility issues in the neighborhood are addressed so that elderly and disabled residents can get where they need to go," they added. 

The officials also addressed the potential financial penalties outlined in the city's original enforcement notice, emphasizing that no fines had been imposed and that San Jose was instead offering financial assistance to help the nonprofit relocate.

"No fines have been assessed – in fact, the City has offered to help with relocation costs because we are committed to finding a solution that is not punitive but creates a better situation for everyone involved," Mahan and Tordillos said.

text:
The $367 Million Domain Rush: Why Companies Pay for Internet Names They May Never Use -The 2026 competition for new Internet top-level domains is not fundamentally a competition to create websites. It is a competition to obtain control over a scarce, globally recognized naming resource whose commercial value may derive from exclusion, future strategic flexibility, brand protection and control of digital identity rather than immediate public use.

ICANN’s latest expansion has attracted 1,615 applications from 481 applicants, despite an evaluation fee of $227,000 per standard application. Applying the standard fee to all applications produces a theoretical gross value of $366.6 million, before accounting for reduced fees, special arrangements, refunds and additional evaluation charges. That figure is neither verified net revenue nor profit.

The crucial economic distinction is between the value of a domain extension as a business generating registration income and its value as an instrument of strategic control. A corporation can rationally operate a top-level domain with few registrations if doing so protects a brand, prevents an important competitor from obtaining a strategic naming position, or preserves an option for a future digital ecosystem.

For commercial registry operators, the economics are different. Their investment must ultimately be justified by registrations, premium-name sales, renewal income or complementary services. Many speculative applications therefore face a substantially more demanding commercial test than established corporations seeking to protect their digital identities.

The entry of artificial intelligence into the domain-name debate introduces a further distinction: control over a memorable namespace could become commercially valuable for identifying agents, software services, authenticated organizational resources or future machine-to-machine ecosystems. Yet conventional DNS ownership does not automatically grant authority over AI agents, digital identity standards, or emerging technical protocols.

ICANN is also an economically interested institution, not simply a neutral observer of the market it administers. Its fee structure, historical auction proceeds and recurring registry charges create material financial flows. Nevertheless, its nonprofit status, contractual framework and declared cost-recovery model must be distinguished from the profit-maximizing behavior of a commercial auction house.

The central policy question is therefore whether the expansion increases meaningful competition and utility for Internet users—or primarily increases the cost of defending, acquiring and controlling strategically attractive digital names.

ICANN’s $367 Million Domain Rush: The Price of Controlling an Internet That May Never Exist
The 2026 expansion of Internet domains exposes a contradiction in digital governance: corporations are paying substantial sums for naming rights whose commercial value remains uncertain, while the institution administering the process converts strategic scarcity into a global allocation market.

ICANN’s decision to reopen applications for generic top-level domains after fourteen years has triggered a competition whose economic significance extends far beyond Internet addresses. On 7 October 2026, the organization disclosed 1,615 applications from 481 applicants, each facing a standard evaluation fee of $227,000. Among them are multinational technology companies pursuing corporate identities, artificial-intelligence terminology and future digital ecosystems whose commercial structures have yet to emerge. The contradiction is that companies are prepared to commit millions to naming infrastructure they may never substantially use, while ICANN, a California nonprofit responsible for coordinating Internet identifiers, administers the allocation of resources made scarce by their required uniqueness. The issue is not whether these digital names can be sold profitably. It is whether the global Internet is developing another layer of compulsory strategic expenditure, where the cost of remaining outside the allocation process may appear greater than the uncertain value of participation.

The $366.6 Million Figure Conceals Three Different Economic Markets
The 2026 application figures imply a theoretical gross evaluation-fee value of $366.6 million, calculated by multiplying 1,615 applications by the standard $227,000 charge. That amount is neither ICANN’s verified net revenue nor profit: qualified applicants receive discounts, conditional reviews create additional charges, and withdrawal provisions permit partial refunds. The applications themselves are economically heterogeneous. Of the total, 333 were designated brand applications, while 51 were submitted by participants supported through ICANN’s Applicant Support Program. The same fee structure consequently applies to companies seeking controlled corporate infrastructure, commercial operators intending to sell registrations, and institutions pursuing linguistic or community objectives. Treating their expenditure as a single speculative market would obscure the fundamental differences in how each expects to recover value.

The concentration of applications reinforces those distinctions. North America accounted for 864 submissions, Europe for 506 and Asia-Pacific for 218, while Africa contributed 16 and Latin America and the Caribbean 11. These figures do not establish ultimate corporate ownership, but they reveal the geographical distribution of effective participation. The Applicant Support Program reduces standard evaluation fees by 75–85% for eligible participants, yet application costs represent only part of the capital required to operate a registry. Technical infrastructure, legal services, security, distribution and continuing compliance remain necessary. Financial support may therefore increase access to the application process without eliminating the structural advantages enjoyed by established technology companies and registry operators.

The historical precedent also imposes caution. The 2012 application round produced 1,241 cumulative delegations by 31 August 2026, alongside 653 withdrawn applications. Delegation establishes the technical and contractual operation of a top-level domain; it does not establish profitability. ICANN’s earlier round also generated approximately $225 million through 16 auctions of last resort, according to its March 2026 Board records. That sum illustrates how competition for unique names can produce substantial payments independently of the commercial performance of the resulting registries. The 2026 prohibition on private contention auctions changes the distribution of potential financial benefits, but it does not eliminate the possibility that competing applicants will pay more for an extension than its eventual operations can justify.

The Value of a Domain May Lie in Keeping Others Out
For a multinational corporation, the economic case for acquiring a top-level domain need not involve selling a single registration to the public. Under ICANN’s Specification 13, qualifying brand registries can operate controlled namespaces for authorized corporate entities and trademark licensees. The company acquires a contractual position from which it can organize digital services, support recognizable corporate identities and preserve future deployment options. An extension can therefore remain commercially inactive in the conventional retail sense while providing defensive or organizational value. The relevant financial calculation concerns the incremental costs avoided and flexibility obtained, not the number of websites launched under the new suffix.

This distinction explains why an application can be rational for a large enterprise and financially questionable for an independent registry entrepreneur. The 2024 Base Registry Agreement establishes a standard fixed registry charge of $25,000 annually, before other applicable expenses. Combined with the initial evaluation fee, five years of this fixed charge alone would produce a nominal commitment of $352,000, excluding technical operations, legal services, marketing and conditional evaluation costs. A global company may absorb that expenditure within its infrastructure or intellectual-property budget. A commercial registry must recover its investment through customers whose willingness to register and renew names remains uncertain. The same contractual asset consequently has different economic value depending on the applicant’s existing resources and commercial relationships.

There are limits to defensive acquisition. ICANN’s 2026 framework restricts exclusive operation of generic strings, distinguishing qualified corporate brands from terms associated with broader technological or commercial categories. A company cannot automatically transform a generic expression into an exclusively controlled corporate environment merely by submitting an application. Nevertheless, the competition for desirable terminology creates an incentive to act before commercial demand is established. Because the 2026 application window closed on 12 August, waiting for greater clarity carries the risk that another eligible applicant may obtain the desired string. This is the defining characteristic of the investment: companies pay today to preserve uncertain possibilities tomorrow, even where existing domains might already provide most of the required functionality.

Artificial Intelligence Creates Demand for Trust, Not Necessarily for New Domain Names
Applications involving terms such as .openai, .chatgpt, .agent and .agi place artificial intelligence at the center of the latest naming competition. Their strategic significance lies in the possibility that increasingly autonomous software will require recognizable service identities, authenticated communication and reliable discovery mechanisms. Yet these requirements do not establish that a new top-level domain is technologically necessary. The Model Context Protocol’s November 2025 authorization specification addresses how AI applications interact with protected resources through authorization mechanisms, while the World Wide Web Consortium’s May 2025 Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0 provides a framework for verifiable digital assertions. Neither depends upon a particular AI-related domain extension to perform its fundamental function.

The distinction between naming and authority is economically decisive. A domain can identify a network resource, but it cannot independently establish whether an autonomous agent is permitted to transfer funds, approve a purchase or access confidential information. Those operations require authenticated identities, delegated permissions, enforceable policies and reliable audit records. A corporation acquiring an AI-related extension may eventually integrate it into a trusted service ecosystem, but the commercial value would arise from adoption of the surrounding infrastructure. The extension itself does not confer control over AI protocols, digital credentials or the behavior of software operating elsewhere on the Internet.

This creates two opposing possibilities for the companies now acquiring AI-related naming assets. If enterprises and developers adopt recognizable namespaces as part of interoperable agent ecosystems, selected extensions could become valuable organizational and commercial infrastructure. If agents increasingly discover services through existing domains, cryptographic credentials, application directories and platform interfaces, the economic importance of memorable new suffixes may remain limited. Thousands of agents can operate beneath a small number of existing corporate domains without generating corresponding demand for retail registrations. The expansion of machine identity may therefore increase the importance of digital trust while simultaneously weakening the assumption that more software agents require more domain names.

Europe’s Cybersecurity Rules Expose the Cost of Operating What ICANN Allocates
The legal environment further complicates the commercial calculation. Directive (EU) 2022/2555, known as NIS2, expressly addresses top-level-domain registries, DNS service providers and relevant domain-registration services, imposing cybersecurity and related obligations under its applicable provisions. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 specifies technical and methodological requirements for covered entities. Successful applicants operating within the relevant European regulatory scope must therefore evaluate responsibilities extending beyond their contracts with ICANN, including risk management, incident handling, continuity, supply-chain controls and registration-data governance. The acquisition of a namespace may be global in technical effect, but the business operating it remains exposed to territorial regulation.

National differences sharpen that exposure. France’s Afnic reported 4,319,120 .fr registrations at the end of 2025, with 853,000 new creations and an 82.2% retention rate, while Germany’s DENIC recorded 17,663,886 .de domains, including more than 2.16 million held by registrants abroad. These established registries demonstrate the scale and international reach attainable through mature naming infrastructure, but they also illustrate why a new extension cannot be valued using registration counts alone. Their operating histories, institutional structures and recognizable national identities are not automatically transferable to speculative generic domains. Italy faces a related question through its .it infrastructure and industrial companies, many of which may obtain greater immediate value from secure existing domains and interoperable identity systems than from independently operating new registries.

The United Kingdom introduces a further constraint through the National Security and Investment Act. Its defined digital-infrastructure categories include qualifying top-level-domain registry acquisitions, with a specific threshold involving at least 14 billion DNS queries from UK devices over a consecutive 168-hour period. Not every registry transaction reaches that threshold, but the provision demonstrates that a domain infrastructure business can acquire national-security significance independently of the commercial appeal of its name. The European Union regulates relevant operating responsibilities, the United Kingdom may examine qualifying changes of control, and ICANN governs the contractual allocation of the extension. These powers coexist without being interchangeable, creating compliance obligations that investors cannot remove simply by choosing a different corporate jurisdiction.

ICANN’s Nonprofit Status Does Not Eliminate the Governance Question
ICANN’s institutional position is frequently misunderstood. The 2016 IANA stewardship transition ended the previous direct U.S. government stewardship arrangement, but ICANN remains a California nonprofit public benefit corporation operating through a multistakeholder governance framework. Its Bylaws, Empowered Community, Reconsideration Process and Independent Review Process establish important accountability mechanisms. The organization also describes the 2026 evaluation-fee structure as cost-recovery based, with provisions addressing possible application-volume refunds. These characteristics distinguish it from a commercial auction house selling unrestricted property rights over Internet terminology. They do not, however, eliminate the need to examine whether the costs imposed on applicants remain proportionate to the public functions performed.

The institutional difficulty is that ICANN administers a resource whose scarcity is partly defined by the need for unique names in the coordinated DNS. Applicants seeking globally recognized generic extensions cannot simply reproduce an identical string through an ordinary registrar purchase. That gives the allocation process economic importance beyond the organization administering it. The appropriate scrutiny concerns how fees are calculated, how evaluation expenses are allocated, how auction proceeds are governed and whether smaller participants can obtain meaningful access to review and objection procedures. The March 2026 Board decision allocating up to an additional $4.9 million for applicant support illustrates an attempt to address participation inequality, but it also confirms that access to naming infrastructure has become a question of institutional financing rather than technical eligibility alone.

The international consequences extend beyond corporate applications. ICANN’s September 2026 reporting identified 151 delegated internationalized top-level domains covering 37 languages and 23 scripts as of June 2026, alongside approximately 4.3 million internationalized second-level registrations. Yet Universal Acceptance limitations continue to affect whether valid names operate correctly across software, websites and email systems. For users whose languages are inadequately supported, the economic obstacle may be less the cost of obtaining a new extension than the inability of existing applications to recognize it reliably. Allocating additional names without securing their technical usability would expand the formal namespace while leaving a substantial portion of its promised utility unrealized.

By 2028, the Cost of Inaction Will Fall on Companies, Registrants and Public Institutions
The next 12–24 months will establish the first meaningful boundaries of the 2026 competition. The replacement period closes on 21 October 2026, String Confirmation Day is scheduled for 17 November, and the relevant comment and objection procedures extend into March 2027. Subsequent evaluation, contention resolution and contracting will determine which applications can progress toward delegation. For applicants, these stages create progressively consequential financial decisions because the recoverable portion of the standard evaluation fee declines as the process advances. Continuing an investment merely because earlier expenditure is no longer recoverable would expose companies to additional costs unsupported by future commercial value.

The immediate risk for corporations is not failing to acquire every attractive namespace. It is committing to registries without a documented reason why existing domains, security infrastructure and identity standards cannot provide equivalent benefits. For commercial applicants, the principal exposure is weak renewal demand combined with continuing technical and regulatory costs. For trademark owners, an expanding naming environment may increase monitoring and enforcement burdens without eliminating impersonation. For smaller institutions, the danger is financing a registry whose continuing obligations exceed available operating resources. These costs will be borne by shareholders, registrants, customers and, where public funding is involved, the institutions financing participation.

ICANN’s corresponding responsibility is to demonstrate, through the financial and procedural outcomes of the 2026 round, that allocation costs and institutional safeguards serve the stability and utility of the global DNS. By October 2028, the number of approved or delegated extensions may offer evidence of administrative progress, but it will not establish that the expansion has created comparable economic value. That judgment will require operating data, adoption, technical performance and eventually meaningful renewal records. The cost of failing to make those distinctions is a market in which companies continue purchasing scarce digital options, regulators inherit additional infrastructure obligations, and Internet users finance greater complexity without receiving commensurate improvements in trust, competition or service.

DID YOU KNOW??

Olivia Newton-John had to be literally sewn into her iconic skin-tight black leather pants for the grand finale of Grease because the vintage 1950s zipper broke on the very first day of shooting.

The scene where Sandy Olsson unveils her dramatic transformation to "Bad Sandy" during "You're the One That I Want" became one of the most iconic moments in cinema history. However, the wardrobe department was using genuine vintage 1950s sharkskin-leather pants.

On the morning of filming in the summer of 1977, the decades-old metal zipper snapped completely.
​Because there were no duplicate pairs of the vintage trousers, costumer Albert Wolsky had to hand-sew Newton-John into the pants every single morning before filming and stitch her out at night.

To make matters worse, filming took place during a heatwave in Southern California where temperatures inside the carnival set reached over 100°F (38°C). Newton-John was forced to limit her fluid intake throughout the long filming days just to avoid having to unpick the stitches to use the restroom. Wall with me 👇🏾👇🏾 

The Evolution of Grease from Stage to Screen:

​How a gritty Chicago stage musical transformed into a global cinematic juggernaut:

1. The Gritty Stage Debut
1971
Jim Jacobs and Warren Casey premiere Grease at a community theater in Chicago as a raw, vulgar, rock-and-roll musical reflecting 1950s working-class youth culture.

2. Broadway Success & Film Option
1972–1977
The show moves to Broadway, becoming a smash hit; producer Allan Carr buys the film rights and convinces Paramount Pictures to back a cinematic adaptation.

3. Production & Character Rewrites
Summer 1977
To accommodate Australian pop star Olivia Newton-John, Sandy's back-story is rewritten from an American girl named Sandy Dumbrowski to an Australian expatriate.

4. Record-Breaking Release
June 1978
Grease premieres in theaters, becoming the highest-grossing musical film of all time (a record it held for over two decades) and generating a multi-platinum soundtrack.

More Surprising Facts About Grease (1978):

A. ​The Cast Was Far Too Old for High School: Most of the main cast members were well past high school age; Stockard Channing (Rizzo) was 33 years old during filming, while Jamie Donnelly (Jan) had to dye her gray hair black to play a teenager.

B. Nominated for an Oscar: The song was added late in post-production because Olivia Newton-John's contract guaranteed her a solo ballad, making it the only song from the movie to earn an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song.

C. Elvis Presley Turned Down a Role: Elvis Presley was originally offered the role of the Teen Angel who sings "Beauty School Dropout," but he declined; the role eventually went to 1950s teen idol Frankie Avalon.

​SUMMARILY! 
​Olivia Newton-John had to be hand-sewn into her vintage leather pants each day during the filming of "You're the One That I Want" due to a broken zipper and a lack of backup wardrobe.

text:
Houthi attack on Riyadh airport forces swift rethink of Trump’s new strategy

*The Guardian

US President Donald Trump’s plan to park the conflicts in Iran and Yemen while blaming Ukraine for high diesel prices has unravelled after the Saturday missile strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

The attack that changed the equation

The reckless Houthi strike not only exported death and misery from Yemen into Saudi Arabia but forced Trump to reassess the diplomatic and political strategy designed to clear the path for next month’s midterm elections.

His plan, revealed only on Saturday, was to blame what he called a “global problem” — rising diesel prices — on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, claiming Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries were the cause. He intended to keep political tension over his chosen war in Iran and its Yemen spillover until after the midterms.

He claimed the Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz had effectively been broken, offered daily oil export figures to reassure markets, and insisted talks with Iran were impossible because Tehran lacked unified leadership. Saudi Arabia, working with Turkey and Pakistan, was largely to be left to handle the Houthis along the Red Sea. Yemen’s fate, the IMF’s poorest country, would not affect election results in Kansas or Alaska.

Why the fragile strategy collapsed

After the Riyadh attack, which killed 12 people including one American, it is doubtful this desperate strategy can hold. Saudi air defences clearly failed as Houthi missiles from 500 miles away repeatedly hit targets.

The US has held a unilateral ceasefire with the Houthis since 2025, secretly renewed when Saudi-Houthi fighting resumed in summer. Trump twice rejected Saudi pleas for help. Can he refuse a third time? Allied pressure to act will be immense.

Blaming Zelenskyy will not work

The extra diesel Russia could put on the market is insufficient to lower petrol prices. Russia’s share of seaborne global diesel exports was about 12% and has already fallen by roughly a third. The move also revived European fears about Trump’s Russia ties just weeks after Congress passed new sanctions.

Europeans know the inflation fuelling populism stems from the Iran war, not Zelenskyy’s tactics. Former UK prime minister Boris Johnson called it “disgusting” to lift sanctions on Russian fuel while blaming Ukraine. A German minister labelled it “moral bankruptcy.”

Political damage and limited options

The political damage to Republicans from the Iran war appears irreversible. Democrats have used it as an economic issue in every debate; Republicans seek refuge in identity politics.

Trump can rejoin the fight against the Houthis and end the unilateral US ceasefire, but he knows from experience it is costly. Advisers suggest striking Iran, the Houthis’ backers, instead. Secret indirect talks via Doha remain possible, yet any deal on uranium enrichment would be unacceptable to the US or to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election hopes.

China and Russia push for a diplomatic Houthi solution, but their aims are widening while southern Yemen is deeply divided.

For now, Trump’s dual strategy of freezing the Iran and Yemen conflicts while blaming Zelenskyy looks too exposed, morally shameful and ineffective to survive. The only question is whether the president abandons it or American voters reject it at the ballot box.

text:
When we think back to the purpose that God had with the 70 year-weeks, we also determine with deep gratitude that many of the things that had to happen in those 490 years did indeed happen. We now know that Jesus has ended the power of sin and that He has atoned for unrighteousness and that He is the one who has brought everlasting righteousness.

THE CLOCK STOPS
Halfway through verse 26 we read of the destruction of the city and sanctuary. A few years ago I was allowed to stand in Rome. I stood right under the Arch of Titus and saw the fulfillment of this word of Daniel depicted on it. Soldiers carried the lampstand, taken from the temple in Jerusalem, into Rome. The Arch of Titus is to this day a historical monument on which the fulfillment of Daniel's prophecy is chiseled before the eyes of all the citizens of the world. After the extermination of the Anointed One, the city and sanctuary were destroyed. And with that, for the time being, the countdown of the 70 weeks of years also ended. God stopped the clock, why?

Because the Lord God had hidden certain things, a number of things become somewhat unclear here, yet we can gain insight. We must then knock on the door of the apostle Paul. He writes to us in Ephesians, that to him, Paul, a 'mystery' has been revealed. Namely (Ephesians 3:6) 'that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, and partakers of the same, and partakers of the promises in Christ Jesus'. Now what are those promises in Christ? These are the things that, among others, Daniel prophesied about: the end of sin, the reconciliation of unrighteousness and the bringing in of everlasting righteousness. That was not known in the time of previous generations, so also to Daniel (Ephesians 3:5). That there is a gap in the history of God's dealings with Israel is formulated very clearly by Paul, when He writes to the Romans: 'For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, that a partial hardening hath happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles come in; and so all Israel shall be saved (Romans 11:25,26).

When the church has been brought home, God will carry out His plan with Israel, then the countdown of the 70 weeks of years will be continued and completed.

During that time a covenant will be made, which is characterized as a 'strong covenant' (verse 27). We may have to think here of the antichrist, the political leader, who is pushed forward from the restored Roman empire and offers Israel a false peace. Are we not slowly finding ourselves in the middle of the prelude to these things? At the halfway point of this week of years an unprecedented conflict will occur. Here we see parallels to Revelation 13, where the antichrist blasphemes God with a big mouth for 42 months (that is three and a half years, half a year week!). At the end of that time, the 70 years weeks, the Lord Jesus comes and with Him His Church from heaven, they will sit on thrones (Revelation 19 and 20). The dragon, the old serpent, that is the devil will be thrown into the abyss and bound for a thousand years. Then God's kingdom will come, there will be peace for a thousand years, the prophecy concerning the 70 years weeks will then be fulfilled. The prophecy is already beautiful, the fulfillment will be even more glorious. Praise be to our God, His wisdom and power is inimitably great and we pray with the church of the ages, Maranatha, amen come Lord Jesus come.👋🏽

text:
Rome With Coffee

The Talking Raven Rome Avenged

A Roman cobbler killed a talking raven. According to Pliny the Elder, the crowd killed the cobbler, then carried the bird out of Rome in a funeral procession.

The story belongs to the reign of Tiberius, which began in AD 14. A young raven hatched above the Temple of Castor and Pollux in the Forum, then fluttered down into a nearby cobbler’s shop. The shopkeeper took it in. Soon it was imitating human speech.

Every morning, the bird flew to the Rostra, the speakers’ platform facing the Forum. There it greeted Tiberius by name, then Germanicus and Drusus, then the Roman people passing below. After completing its roll call, it returned to the shop. Pliny says it kept the routine for several years.

The raven became a public celebrity. Then the cobbler next door killed it. Pliny offers two possible motives. Perhaps the man resented his neighbor’s success. Perhaps he lost his temper after the bird fouled some shoes.

The public response was wildly disproportionate. Pliny says the killer was driven from the neighborhood and later killed. The raven received the procession.

Its body lay on a draped bier beneath wreaths. Two men whom Pliny identifies as Ethiopians carried it on their shoulders while a flute player walked in front. A vast crowd followed to a pyre beside the Appian Way, two miles beyond Rome, at a place called the Field of Rediculus.

Ravens really can imitate human speech, so a talking bird is plausible. The exact greetings, the killing, and the remarkable funeral come from Pliny alone, writing decades later. He ends the episode with a deliberate sting: Rome had denied funerals to important men and left the death of Scipio Aemilianus unavenged, yet a citizen died and a bird was buried with ceremony.

The raven learned to say good morning to Rome. Rome answered by carrying it down the Appian Way.

text: Your body is a temple, and most Catholic men are treating it like a storage shed. A man who can’t say no to the third beer or the packet of chips at 10pm has a will that has been trained to fold. text:
At sixty-five, Harland Sanders sat in his car outside a closed restaurant with a $105 Social Security check in his pocket. 

That was everything he had left. He had spent nearly half a century moving from one failed job to another. He learned to cook at six, after his father died and his mother worked long shifts in a factory. He left school at twelve. 

In the decades that followed he was fired from the railroad after a fight, lost his law practice after brawling with a client in open court, failed as an insurance and tire salesman, and went broke on a lamp factory. 

At forty he began frying chicken for travelers at a small Kentucky gas station. Over the next twenty years he refined a blend of eleven herbs and spices cooked under pressure, earned the honorary title of Kentucky Colonel, and built a successful roadside restaurant. 

Then, in 1956, a new interstate highway bypassed the town. Business disappeared overnight. Forced to auction the restaurant at sixty-six to settle his debts, he was left with nothing but the monthly check.

Most people would have stopped. Instead he put a pressure cooker and a bag of his spice blend in the car and started driving. He slept in the back seat to save money, walked into restaurants unannounced, cooked his chicken on the spot, and offered a simple handshake deal: four cents for every piece sold. Owners laughed. 

They called the recipe too complicated, the method too odd, the idea too risky. He was turned down ten times, a hundred times, five hundred times. 

He washed his white suit in laundromats, slept in gas-station lots, and kept going. It took 1,009 rejections before one owner finally said yes.

By the time he was seventy-three, the network had grown to more than six hundred locations across North America. He later sold the company for millions while remaining its public face, becoming one of the most recognized people in the world. 

Even into his eighties he showed up unannounced in franchise kitchens, insisting the chicken taste exactly as it should and dismissing cheap copies as wallpaper paste, until he died at ninety.

People often measure what is still possible by age, by past failures, or by the number of doors already closed. Sanders began the work that defined him at sixty-five, after more than a thousand no’s, and kept driving until the answer changed.

text:
Charles Muiruri was working behind a bank counter in North Carolina when a Duke doctor asked him to examine an HIV study translated into Swahili.

Muiruri read it and found a problem. The researchers, he thought, were not asking their questions well. He told them so.

It was not what Dr. John Bartlett had come to the bank for, but it changed what he understood about the man serving him. Muiruri knew the language and the region where Duke hoped to conduct the research. He could also spot a weakness in the study itself.

Just a few years earlier, Muiruri had been running an information-technology company in Nairobi. A University of Nairobi graduate and former football player, he won a place in the United States through the green-card lottery and moved to Durham in 2002. He planned to build on his business experience and perhaps study computer science. Instead, his first American job was baking part time at a Kroger supermarket.

He took the work because he needed to get established. Still, there was a distance between the life he had led in Kenya and the one strangers could see in Durham. When a choice arose between driving a soda-delivery truck and working as a teller at a Wachovia branch inside Duke’s medical complex, he chose the bank.

Doctors and researchers came through the branch to do their personal banking. Bartlett, an infectious-disease specialist, was one of them. As they got to know Muiruri, Bartlett and his colleagues learned that he understood East African institutions and the practical difficulties of moving money there. They were beginning an HIV research partnership in Tanzania, and that knowledge was useful. Then Bartlett asked him to review the Swahili translation of the study.

Muiruri’s criticism could have been awkward. Instead, the researchers listened. They needed someone to coordinate their work with Kilimanjaro Christian Medical University College in Moshi, and Bartlett offered him the job despite his lack of research-administration experience. The teller who had questioned the study was now helping make it happen.

The work led Muiruri somewhere he had not planned to go. He became interested in how studies were designed, what the data revealed and whether the questions mattered to the people being treated. While working at Duke, he earned a master’s degree in public health at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, then a doctorate in health policy and management. In 2019, he joined Duke’s faculty.

His research now focuses partly on people living with HIV who must also manage conditions such as high blood pressure and heart disease. A visit to his mother in Kenya helped sharpen how he thought about their decisions. As she prepared to meet friends, he noticed she had not taken her blood-pressure medication. The side effects made her feel unwell. She was not forgetting her health, she explained; she was trying to enjoy her day.

“She was managing her life, not managing her hypertension,” Muiruri later said. The exchange stayed with him. A treatment might work medically and still be hard for a person to live with. To improve care, he wanted to understand what patients valued, feared and could manage alongside everything else in their lives.

Isitoshe, 

Muiruri has also studied why some patients in Tanzania move HIV medication out of its original packaging, including to protect themselves from stigma. It is the kind of detail a researcher might miss without asking people how treatment fits into their days. By 2024, he had published more than fifty research papers and helped strengthen the partnership between Duke and its Tanzanian colleagues.

He still plays football when he travels. At a meeting, he has said, he often asks where he can find a game. It gives him a way to meet people before asking them to trust a visitor’s ideas.

Back at the bank, Bartlett had asked Muiruri to look closely at a set of questions. Muiruri’s answer changed his career. It also pointed toward the work he does now: listening when someone says the question needs to be asked differently.
